intro.t: The Gospel of the King and his kingdom, written to show that Jesus fulfils everything God promised Israel.
b: Matthew opens with a family tree reaching back to Abraham and David, and closes with the risen Jesus sending his disciples to ‘all nations’ (28:19). In between he shows again and again that Jesus fulfils the Old Testament: his birth, his home towns, his healing, his teaching in parables and his death were all foretold. He is the promised King, Immanuel, ‘God with us’ (1:23), who will be with his people ‘always, even to the end of the age’ (28:20).

Matthew gathers Jesus’ teaching into five great blocks, including the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), the parables of the kingdom (13) and the teaching on the end (24–25). It is the Gospel that mentions the church by name (16:18; 18:17), and it was the one most read and quoted in the early church.

The early church. The Gospel is anonymous, but ‘Matthew’ is the only name ever attached to it, and every manuscript title says ‘According to Matthew’. Papias (early 2nd century, quoted by Eusebius) wrote: ‘So then Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able.’ Irenaeus (about AD 180) says Matthew issued a Gospel among the Hebrews in their own language while Peter and Paul were preaching in Rome. Matthew was the tax collector Jesus called (9:9; Mark 2:14 calls him Levi); only this Gospel calls him ‘Matthew the tax collector’ in the list of the Twelve (10:3).

Where scholars stand. Most modern scholars doubt that the apostle wrote it as we have it. The main reason is that it uses about 90 percent of Mark, sometimes word for word, and it seems unlikely that an eyewitness apostle would depend so heavily on someone who was not. Its Greek also reads like original Greek, not a translation from Hebrew, so it may not be the Hebrew work Papias mentions.

The case for Matthew. The tradition is early and unanimous, and no rival name was ever proposed for such an important book. A tax collector would have been literate, used to keeping records, and able to work in Greek. If Mark preserves Peter’s preaching, an apostle could well choose to follow Peter’s outline and add his own material. Papias’s ‘oracles’ may refer to an earlier collection of Jesus’ sayings by Matthew, later incorporated into the Greek Gospel. Many conservative scholars therefore hold that Matthew was the author, or the source behind it.

b: Matthew is the most Jewish of the Gospels. It begins with a genealogy from Abraham, quotes the Old Testament constantly (often with ‘This took place to fulfil what was spoken’), takes Jewish customs for granted, and wrestles with the place of the Law. It was written for a church with a strong Jewish heritage, probably outside Palestine; Antioch in Syria is the most common suggestion, since Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, knew it early in the 2nd century, as did the Didache.

Most scholars date it AD 70–90, after Mark. Others argue for a date before AD 70, because several passages assume the temple is still standing (5:23–24; 17:24–27; 23:16–22). It was known and used by about AD 110, and became the most widely read Gospel in the early church.

hist.t: Matthew, Mark and Luke: who used whom? (the ‘Synoptic problem’)
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell many of the same stories, often in the same order and with the same wording; they are called the ‘Synoptic’ Gospels (Greek: ‘seen together’). Of Mark’s 661 verses, about 606 have a parallel in Matthew and about 380 in Luke; only some 31 verses of Mark have no parallel in either.

Mark first (Widely accepted). Since the 19th century most scholars have concluded that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used it, smoothing its rough Greek and adding their own material. The material Matthew and Luke share but Mark lacks (about 200–250 verses, mostly sayings of Jesus) is usually explained by a lost collection of sayings called ‘Q’ (from German Quelle, ‘source’). Some suggest Papias’s remark that Matthew compiled ‘the oracles’ refers to something like it.

Other views (Debated). Augustine thought Mark had abridged Matthew, and many Catholic scholars long defended Matthew’s priority; a minority still argue that Matthew came first, or that Luke used Matthew directly with no need for Q. No copy of Q has ever been found.

None of these theories requires that the Gospel writers were careless or untrustworthy. Luke openly says he used earlier accounts and eyewitness testimony (Luke 1:1–4). Using written sources was normal and responsible history-writing.

b: The question. Matthew and Luke, in two clearly independent accounts, both say that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father. Every major Christian church confesses it in the creeds: ‘incarnate by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin Mary’. Many modern scholars, however, doubt or deny its historicity. They read the birth stories as symbolic or theological writing rather than history, and note that Mark, John and Paul do not mention it.

The case for it. The New Bible Dictionary sets out the response. The two accounts are independent of each other but agree on the central fact. Other New Testament writers may show awareness of it: Mark alone calls Jesus ‘the son of Mary’ (Mark 6:3), unusual for a Jewish man; John records opponents hinting at illegitimacy (John 8:41); and Paul says God’s Son was ‘born of a woman’ (Galatians 4:4). There is no evidence that Jews expected a virgin-born Messiah, so the story was not invented to fit expectations; and pagan stories of gods fathering children on women are quite different from a conception without any male involvement. The deepest objection is usually to miracles in general; but if God really became man, a unique beginning is fitting. To accept the incarnation and reject the virgin birth, the article says, is ‘rather like straining out a gnat while swallowing a camel’.

read: The Gospels are ancient biographies: true accounts of a real person, written to show who he is and why he matters. Matthew does not always tell events in strict time order; he often groups material by theme. Five times a block of Jesus’ teaching ends with almost the same words, ‘When Jesus had finished saying these things’ (7:28; 19:1; 26:1; compare 11:1; 13:53). Those five blocks, set between stretches of story, are the backbone of the book (see the map above).

Read Matthew with the Old Testament close at hand. About ten times he writes that something happened ‘to fulfil’ what a prophet said, and he quotes or echoes the Old Testament far more often than that. ‘Fulfil’ in Matthew is wider than ‘predict’: sometimes a prophecy comes true; sometimes a pattern in Israel’s story (the exodus, the exile, the wilderness) reaches its full meaning in Jesus. Follow the links in the notes back to the passages Matthew quotes, and read their context.

Matthew, Mark and Luke tell many of the same events, often in similar words. Where a passage appears in more than one Gospel, the notes give the parallels so you can compare them; small differences usually show what each writer wanted to stress. Matthew writes as a Jew, for readers steeped in the Scriptures, and says ‘kingdom of heaven’ where the others say ‘kingdom of God’; the meaning is the same.

1.t: Three sets of fourteen, tying Jesus to Abraham and David. Four women appear in it — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — each with an irregular story, and each a reminder that this line runs through grace rather than respectability.
Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins; Immanuel, God with us. Matthew opens and closes his Gospel on that second idea — compare 28:20.

2.t: Gentile astrologers find him while the chief priests, who correctly quote the prophecy, stay home. Matthew's irony is deliberate.
Matthew reads Israel's history as being recapitulated in Jesus: down to Egypt, out again, through water, into the wilderness.

3.t: John's objection is reasonable. Jesus answers that it is to fulfil all righteousness — identifying himself with the people he came to save. The Father speaks and the Spirit descends.

4.t: Every reply Jesus gives is from Deuteronomy, from the very chapters about Israel's wilderness failures. He succeeds at the points where they fell.

5.t: Not entry requirements but a description of the people God blesses — and the list is comprehensively the opposite of what any culture rewards.
Jesus claims to fulfil the law rather than replace it, and then sets a standard exceeding that of the Pharisees, which would have sounded impossible.

5.h: Which Old Testament laws still apply
5.t: Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it. The historic Reformed way of reading this distinguishes three kinds of law: the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still binds; the ceremonial law of sacrifices, food and cleanness, which is fulfilled in Christ and no longer practised (Hebrews and Acts 15); and the civil law of Israel as a nation, whose principles of justice remain instructive but which is not a code for modern states. Not every Christian tradition uses these categories, but the conclusion is widely shared. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

5.h: You have heard… but I say
5.t: Six times. He is not correcting Moses but going behind the external rule to the heart, and claiming the authority to do it.

6.t: Six petitions in two halves: three about God's name, kingdom and will, then three about our bread, forgiveness and protection. The order is the lesson.
Three arguments — the birds, the lilies, and the futility of the anxiety itself. The instruction ends with seeking the kingdom first, which is the actual remedy.

7.t: Almost always quoted without verse 5, which assumes you will eventually help with the speck — after dealing with the plank.
The chapter closes with people who prophesied and cast out demons being told he never knew them. Matthew puts the most frightening verses in the Sermon at the end of it.

8.t: A Gentile soldier understands authority better than Israel does, and Jesus says so plainly.

9.t: He records his own story in a single verse and moves on. The quotation from Hosea — I desire mercy, not sacrifice — is used twice in this Gospel.

10.t: The hardest saying in the chapter. It is a statement about the effect of allegiance to Christ on families, not an endorsement of conflict.

11.t: The man who identified him at the Jordan sends from prison to ask whether he is the one. Jesus does not rebuke the question, and then calls John the greatest born of women.
The gentlest invitation in the Gospels, and it sits immediately after some of the sternest warnings.

13.t: The kingdom described as hidden, small, mixed, and immensely valuable. Note that several of them assume growth alongside opposition rather than instead of it.

16.t: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi. Interpreters divide over whether the rock is Peter, his confession, or Christ; what is not in doubt is that the church is Christ's and that he builds it.
An instrument of execution, to people who had seen them used. The metaphor has been softened by familiarity.

18.t: A process in three stages, aimed throughout at winning the brother rather than removing him. Verse 20 is about this context, not about prayer meeting attendance.
The parable that follows makes the arithmetic irrelevant: the debt forgiven is unpayable and the one refused is trivial.

22.t: Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19, joined. Jesus says everything else hangs on these two.

23.t: Seven denunciations of religious leaders, and then a lament over Jerusalem that shows the anger was grief. Read the last three verses before judging the tone of the first thirty.

24.t: As in Mark, the passage moves between the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the final return. Verse 36 states that the day is unknown even to the Son, which should end all date-setting. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

25.t: The criterion is treatment of the least of these. Whether that means all the poor or Christ's persecuted messengers is debated; either way, professed faith that ignores need is being judged.

Jesus speaks about judgement more often than anyone else in the New Testament, and this verse sets eternal punishment directly beside eternal life, using the same word. The historic Christian view, held across Catholic, Orthodox and nearly all Protestant traditions, is that hell is real and final. A minority of evangelicals, including John Stott, who held the view tentatively, have argued that the lost are ultimately destroyed rather than punished for ever. Both views take judgement seriously. What Scripture is clear on is that judgement is just, that no one will be condemned unfairly, and that Jesus himself came so that no one has to face it. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

26.t: Covenant language from Exodus 24, and the promise not to drink again until the kingdom. Matthew alone adds 'for the forgiveness of sins'.
Jesus stays silent until placed under oath, then answers with Daniel 7 and Psalm 110. The high priest's charge of blasphemy shows what was understood.

27.t: Darkness, the torn curtain, the earthquake, and a Roman officer's confession. Matthew adds tombs opening — a detail unique to him and much discussed.

28.t: All authority, therefore go. The trinitarian formula uses one name for three, and the promise that closes the Gospel answers the name Immanuel that opened it.

12.t: Two Sabbath confrontations. Jesus argues from David eating the consecrated bread and from the priests working on the Sabbath, then claims to be greater than the temple. The claim, not the healing, is what starts the plot in verse 14.

Attributing the Spirit's work to Satan, deliberately and settledly. It describes a hardened position rather than a stray thought, which is why anyone anxious about having committed it has shown by that anxiety that they have not. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.
Asked for a sign, Jesus offers only his own death and resurrection. Note that he treats Jonah and the Queen of Sheba as real.

14.t: Matthew alone records Peter getting out of the boat. The rebuke is for doubting rather than for trying, and the chapter ends with the disciples worshipping and calling him the Son of God.

15.t: The Corban abuse again: property dedicated to the temple so that it cannot support ageing parents. Jesus says the heart is what defiles, not the hands.
Her persistence is commended in the strongest terms Matthew gives to anyone's faith, and she is a Gentile.

17.t: Moses and Elijah appear and then vanish, leaving Jesus alone while the Father says to listen to him. Peter's offer to build shelters tries to make permanent what was never meant to be.
A small, strange episode. Jesus argues that sons are exempt, then pays anyway so as not to cause offence — a principle worth more than the coin.

19.t: Jesus goes behind the Mosaic permission to Genesis, treating the creation account as the standard. He grants one exception; the disciples' reaction shows how strict this sounded. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

Jesus permits divorce for sexual immorality, and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7. Beyond those two, Christians differ over whether remarriage is permitted, and churches take genuinely different positions. This is a place to seek counsel from your own church rather than settle it from a note. What is not in doubt is that Jesus treats marriage as a lifelong covenant instituted at creation, and that he says so to people looking for a loophole. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

He asks what good thing he must do, which is already the wrong question. Jesus' answer exposes the idol rather than setting a universal price, and the conclusion — impossible with men, possible with God — is grace stated plainly.

20.t: Those hired last are paid the same. The complaint is fair by every human standard, which is the point: grace is not wages and cannot be audited as though it were.
The mother of James and John asks for the best seats. Jesus answers with the ransom saying — he came to serve and to give his life for many.

21.t: Zechariah 9:9 deliberately enacted, then the temple cleared and the quotation from Isaiah about a house of prayer. Matthew adds that the blind and lame came to him there.
The chief priests understood the parable was about them, which Matthew records. The rejected stone becoming the cornerstone is from Psalm 118.

1.ctx: Family records mattered in Israel. They proved who you were, what land you could inherit, and whether you could hold an office such as priest or king. Matthew’s first words, ‘the record of the genealogy’ (literally ‘the book of the genesis’), echo the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. Compare Luke’s list in Luke 3:23–38.
1.mean: A list of names can look like the dullest possible way to begin a book, but for Matthew’s first readers it was thrilling. It answers the question every Jew was asking: has God kept his promises? Matthew’s opening line gives Jesus three titles. He is ‘Christ’, the Greek form of ‘Messiah’, the anointed King God had promised. He is ‘the son of David’, heir to God’s promise that David’s family would reign for ever (2 Samuel 7:16). And he is ‘the son of Abraham’, heir to God’s promise that through Abraham’s family all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). The list then walks through Israel’s whole history in three stages of fourteen generations: from Abraham to King David, the rise; from David to the exile in Babylon, the fall; and from the exile to the Christ, the long wait. Matthew is saying that the whole story has been heading here. Four women besides Mary are mentioned, which was unusual: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and ‘Uriah’s wife’ Bathsheba. Each has a surprising or scandalous story, and several were, or were linked with, foreigners. God worked through outsiders and sinners to bring his King. The list ends carefully. It does not say Joseph was Jesus’ father, but ‘the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus’: Joseph is his legal father, which makes Jesus David’s heir, but not his natural father, as the next passage explains.
1.big: Jesus is the goal of Israel’s whole history: the King promised to David and the blessing promised to Abraham, and God brought him through outsiders and sinners as well as kings.

vv.h: the genealogy of Jesus Christ
b: The phrase ‘book of the genesis’ is used in the Greek Old Testament for the creation of the world (Genesis 2:4) and of Adam (Genesis 5:1), and by Matthew’s time ‘Genesis’ was already the Greek name of the Bible’s first book. Most translations take Matthew’s phrase as the heading of the family list. Some scholars, such as Charles Quarles, argue that it is the title of the whole Gospel: a new ‘Genesis’, the story of a new creation beginning with Jesus (compare 19:28, ‘the renewal of all things’). Either way, many readers hear an echo of creation.

vv.h: Tamar … Rahab … Ruth
b: Tamar was probably a Canaanite (Genesis does not say; later Jewish tradition made her an Aramean), a widow who tricked her father-in-law Judah into fathering her children (Genesis 38). Rahab was a Canaanite prostitute in Jericho who hid Israel’s spies (Joshua 2). Ruth was a Moabite, from a nation barred from Israel’s assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), who came to trust Israel’s God. All three are in the King’s family tree. The Gospel that ends with ‘make disciples of all nations’ (28:19) begins by showing Gentiles already inside the story.

vv.h: by Uriah’s wife
b: Matthew does not name Bathsheba; he names her husband, Uriah the Hittite, whom David had killed to cover his adultery (2 Samuel 11). Even the greatest king in the line was a sinner. The list is honest: the Messiah’s family needed a Saviour too.

vv.h: the exile to Babylon
b: The second turning point is a disaster. King Jeconiah was taken to Babylon in 597 BC, and in 586 BC Jerusalem fell and David’s line lost its throne. God said through Jeremiah that none of Jeconiah’s descendants would prosper on David’s throne, and that even if he were a signet ring on God’s hand, God would pull him off (Jeremiah 22:24, 30). Yet the line continued through Zerubbabel, who led exiles home (Ezra 2:2), and to him God said, ‘I will make you like My signet ring’ (Haggai 2:23), reversing the sentence on his grandfather. God’s promise to David survived even the exile.

vv.h: Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus
b: Throughout the list the pattern is ‘A was the father of B’. Here it breaks. The Greek word ‘of whom’ is feminine: Jesus was born of Mary. Matthew is preparing for the virgin birth. Jesus receives David’s royal rights through his legal father Joseph, but his life comes from God.

vv.h: fourteen generations
b: Matthew has shaped the list into three fourteens, leaving out some kings (for example three between Joram and Uzziah, verse 8), which was a normal practice: genealogies traced descent, not every generation. Many have noticed that the Hebrew letters of David’s name (D-V-D) add up to fourteen. Counting the names is not straightforward: the third group reaches fourteen only if one name at a turning point is counted twice. Wesley thought David ends the first group and begins the second; Calvin put the difficulty down to copyists. Whatever the reason, the pattern says that history is not random. It moves to God’s timetable towards the Christ.

1.diff: Matthew’s and Luke’s lists. From David to Joseph, Matthew’s list (through Solomon and the kings) differs almost completely from Luke’s (through David’s son Nathan, Luke 3:23–38). Several explanations are offered. Many think Matthew gives the legal, royal line of succession and Luke the actual descent, perhaps through Mary; Calvin rejected the Mary view and held that both lists trace Joseph. J. G. Machen suggested that if Joseph’s father in Matthew (Jacob) died childless, his nephew Joseph, son of Heli (Luke), became his heir. Julius Africanus (about AD 230) explained it by a levirate marriage, a tradition he said came from Jesus’ relatives. Many critical scholars think the two lists were drawn up independently and cannot be harmonised. Both lists agree on the main point: Jesus was the legal heir of David through Joseph.

b: The two titles in verse 1 run through the whole Gospel. ‘Son of David’ is used by blind men, a Canaanite mother and the Jerusalem crowds (9:27; 15:22; 21:9); ‘son of Abraham’ points to the promise that all nations would be blessed, fulfilled when the risen Jesus sends his disciples to all nations (28:19). Matthew’s first and last chapters frame the book: from Abraham’s blessing for the nations to the commission to reach them.

Luke traces Jesus’ line back to Adam (Luke 3:38), stressing his connection with all humanity; Matthew begins with Abraham, stressing his connection with Israel’s promises. Both are true, and both serve the Gospel writers’ purposes.

l.t: God’s promise that through Abraham’s offspring all nations will be blessed.
God’s covenant with David: his throne will be established for ever.
A shoot from the stump of Jesse (David’s father) who will rule in righteousness, and to whom the nations will rally.
Paul: the promise was made ‘to your seed, meaning One, who is Christ’.
Jesus is ‘a descendant of David according to the flesh’, and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection.
Ruth the Moabite becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
The risen Jesus: ‘I am the Root and the Offspring of David’, David’s source as well as his descendant.

qs: What three titles does verse 1 give Jesus, and what promise lies behind each one?
Why do you think Matthew includes Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba?
The list shows God keeping his promises across two thousand years. Which of God’s promises do you find hardest to wait for?

1.ctx: Jewish marriage had two stages. First came a binding betrothal (‘pledged in marriage’), which could be ended only by divorce. Months later the bride moved into her husband’s home and the marriage was completed. Unfaithfulness during betrothal was treated as adultery (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). Luke tells the same events from Mary’s side (Luke 1:26–38; 2:1–7).
1.mean: Matthew tells the story from Joseph’s side. Mary is betrothed to him, legally bound but not yet living with him, when she is found to be pregnant. Matthew tells us at once what Joseph does not yet know: the child is ‘through the Holy Spirit’. Joseph is ‘a righteous man’. The law allowed him to accuse her publicly, which would have shamed her and could, in theory, have cost her life. Instead he decides on a quiet divorce. He will keep God’s law, but in the gentlest way it allows. Then God steps in. An angel tells Joseph in a dream not to be afraid to take Mary home, because the baby has been conceived by the Holy Spirit. Joseph is to name him Jesus, the Greek form of Joshua, which means ‘the LORD saves’, because he will save his people from their sins. Notice what kind of rescue this is: not first from Rome or from poverty, but from sin. Matthew then explains that all this fulfils Isaiah 7:14: the virgin will bear a son called Immanuel, ‘God with us’. Jesus is not just a messenger from God; in him God himself has come to be with his people. Joseph wakes and obeys at once. He takes Mary as his wife, does not sleep with her until the baby is born, and names the child Jesus. By naming him, Joseph adopts him as his legal son and so makes him heir to David’s throne.
1.big: Jesus is God with us, conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father, and he came to save his people from their sins.

vv.h: found to be with child through the Holy Spirit
b: Matthew states the miracle plainly and soberly. There is no suggestion, as in pagan myths, of a god taking a woman. The Holy Spirit, who hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), now brings about a new beginning in Mary’s womb. Luke says the same in his own independent account (Luke 1:35).

vv.h: a righteous man … unwilling to disgrace her publicly
b: Joseph believed the law and kept it, yet chose the gentlest course it allowed. Commentators note that he is a picture of the ‘greater righteousness’ Jesus will teach (5:20): righteousness that is full of mercy.

vv.h: He will save His people from their sins
b: ‘Jesus’ was a common name, but here its meaning is the point (BSB footnote: ‘Jesus means The LORD saves’). ‘His people’ is striking: in the Old Testament Israel is the LORD’s people. The promise echoes God’s new-covenant words in Ezekiel, that he would cleanse his people from their sins and save them (Ezekiel 36:25–29; 37:23). The rest of Matthew shows that ‘his people’ are all who follow him, Jew and Gentile, and that he saves them by giving his life (20:28; 26:28).

vv.h: Behold, the virgin will be with child
b: This is the first of about ten places where Matthew says ‘this took place to fulfil’ Scripture. In Isaiah 7 the prophet offered King Ahaz a sign from God when enemy kings threatened Jerusalem. Christians read the verse in different ways: as a direct prophecy of the Messiah only, or as a sign that had a first meaning in Isaiah’s day and its full meaning in Jesus (see Where readings differ). Either way, Isaiah soon speaks of a royal child called ‘Mighty God’ (Isaiah 9:6), and Matthew sees the promise of ‘God with us’ come true in Jesus.

vv.h: Immanuel (which means, ‘God with us’)
b: This name frames the whole Gospel. It is promised here at the start, and the last words of the book are Jesus’ promise, ‘surely I am with you always’ (28:20); in between he says that where two or three gather in his name, he is with them (18:20). Matthew’s whole story is about God with us in Jesus.

vv.h: he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him
b: Joseph never speaks a word in Matthew, but every time God tells him something, he obeys at once (compare 2:14, 21). He is a model disciple: quiet, immediate obedience. By naming the child, he publicly accepts him as his own son.

1.diff: ‘Virgin’ in Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek Old Testament that Matthew quotes uses parthenos, ‘virgin’. Christians read Isaiah in two main ways. Many conservative evangelicals take it as a direct prophecy of the Messiah: the sign is addressed to the whole ‘house of David’ (7:13), almah is never used in the Old Testament of a married woman, the Greek translators chose ‘virgin’, and the child is soon linked with the divine King of 9:6–7. Many other scholars, including many evangelicals, think the sign had a first fulfilment in Isaiah’s own day (7:16) and its full meaning in Jesus. Both agree that Matthew narrates a conception by the Holy Spirit without a human father. ‘Until’ (verse 25). Joseph ‘had no union with her until she gave birth’. Most Protestants take this to imply normal married life afterwards: ‘until’ usually implies a change, and the Gospels speak of Jesus’ brothers and sisters (12:46; 13:55–56). Catholic teaching confesses Mary’s ‘real and perpetual virginity’ (Catechism 499) and understands the ‘brothers’ as close relatives (500); the Orthodox also call her Ever-Virgin. The New Bible Dictionary notes that ‘The Reformers were virtually unanimous’ in holding it too. Calvin said this verse settles nothing either way: ‘no just and well-grounded inference can be drawn from these words of the Evangelist, as to what took place after the birth of Christ’; Wesley wrote, ‘It cannot be inferred from hence, that he knew her afterward’. See the note on Mark 6:1. ‘A righteous man’ (verse 19). Some read Joseph’s righteousness as mercy; Calvin and Wesley read it as faithfulness to the law, which meant he could not simply marry her, with his mercy shown in choosing to do it quietly. Wesley: ‘a strict observer of the law: therefore not thinking it right to keep her’.

b: The Holy Spirit’s work in Jesus’ conception is the beginning of a theme that runs through the Gospels: the Spirit comes on Jesus at his baptism (3:16), leads him into the wilderness (4:1), empowers his ministry (12:28), and is given by him to his people (3:11). The new creation begins in Mary’s womb.

The church has always confessed the virgin birth as part of the shared faith of all Christians: the Apostles’ Creed says ‘conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary’. It guards two truths together: Jesus is truly human, born of a woman, and truly God, whose life comes from above. See the History & setting drop-down in the introduction for the question of its history.

l.t: Isaiah’s sign to the house of David, quoted in verse 23. Read on to Isaiah 8:8, 10, where ‘Immanuel’ appears again (BSB footnote).
The child born to rule on David’s throne, called ‘Mighty God’.
God’s promise to save his people from their uncleanness and sins.
The LORD ‘will redeem Israel from all iniquity’: the closest Old Testament wording to verse 21.
The angel’s announcement to Mary: Luke’s independent account of the same miracle.
‘The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us’: John’s way of saying ‘God with us’.
God sent his Son, ‘born of a woman, born under the law’.
‘I am with you always’: the promise of Immanuel kept to the end of the age.

qs: How does Joseph show what it means to be ‘righteous’?
What do the names Jesus and Immanuel each tell us about who he is and what he came to do?
Joseph obeyed God, possibly at a cost to his reputation. Where might obeying God cost you something?

2.ctx: ‘Magi’ were a priestly and learned class from Persia or Babylon, known for interpreting dreams and the stars; the word is also used of sorcerers (Acts 13:6–8). Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome from 37 to 4 BC. He was an Idumean, not of David’s line, and was notoriously jealous of any rival. Only Matthew records this visit.
2.mean: Some time after Jesus’ birth, Magi arrive in Jerusalem, Herod’s capital, asking where the newborn ‘King of the Jews’ is. They have seen his star and have come to worship him. That question was dangerous. Herod held the title ‘king of the Jews’ and had killed members of his own family to keep it. No wonder he is disturbed, ‘and all Jerusalem with him’: everyone knew what Herod could do. Herod calls the chief priests and the experts in the Scriptures and asks where the Messiah is to be born. They answer at once from Micah 5:2: in Bethlehem, David’s home town, from which a ruler will come to shepherd God’s people. Then the irony unfolds. The religious leaders know exactly where the Messiah is, but Matthew records no one going the short distance to Bethlehem. Pagan foreigners, who have travelled hundreds of miles, are the ones who go. Herod secretly finds out when the star appeared, and sends the Magi on with a lie: tell me where he is, so I can worship him too. The star leads them to the house, and they are overjoyed. They kneel and worship the child and give him costly gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh. Warned in a dream, they go home by another road. Matthew is showing, right at the start, that Gentiles will come to worship Israel’s King, while many in Israel, especially its leaders, will not.
2.big: Gentile seekers come a long way to worship the King of the Jews, while Israel’s king plots to kill him and its scholars know where he is, but Matthew records none of them going.

vv.h: Magi from the east
b: Magi were associated with astrology and occult arts, which the Old Testament forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10–12) and mocks (Isaiah 47:13–14). That makes their coming all the more remarkable. God met them where they were, through a sign in the sky they were watching, and led them to his Son. Grace reaches people far from God.

vv.h: the One who has been born King of the Jews
b: Herod had been given the title ‘king’ by Rome; Jesus was born king. The same title will be written over Jesus on the cross (27:37). Matthew’s story of the King begins and ends with Gentiles calling him ‘King of the Jews’, the Magi in worship and the Roman soldiers in mockery.

vv.h: But you, Bethlehem
b: The quotation joins Micah 5:2 with words from 2 Samuel 5:2, where God told David, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel’ (BSB footnote). The Messiah is a shepherd-king like David. Micah goes on to say that this ruler’s greatness ‘will extend to the ends of the earth’ (Micah 5:4), which the Magi’s visit already begins to show.

vv.h: they fell down and worshiped Him
b: Matthew mentions worship three times in this story (verses 2, 8, 11). The same words, ‘fall down and worship’, are used when Satan demands worship and Jesus replies that worship belongs to God alone (4:9–10). Yet Jesus accepts worship throughout Matthew (14:33; 28:9, 17). The first people in the Gospel to worship him are Gentile foreigners.

vv.h: gold and frankincense and myrrh
b: These were royal gifts, the kind brought to kings (compare Isaiah 60:6, ‘bearing gold and frankincense’; Psalm 72:10–11). Christians have long seen meaning in them: gold for a king, incense for God, and myrrh, used in burial, pointing to his death (John 19:39). Matthew does not explain them, and the meanings are a later reflection, but they fit the story he tells.

2.diff: Later tradition called the Magi three kings (from the three gifts and Psalm 72:10) and gave them names; Matthew says neither. They found Jesus in ‘the house’, not the stable, possibly some months later (compare 2:16, ‘two years old and under’). Christians differ on whether the star was a natural event that God used or a miraculous light; see the history drop-down.

b: Isaiah 60 pictures the nations coming to Israel’s light, bringing ‘gold and frankincense’ and proclaiming the LORD’s praises (Isaiah 60:3, 6). Psalm 72 pictures kings of distant lands bringing gifts to the royal son. Matthew’s story of the Magi is the first taste of that ingathering of the nations, which the Gospel completes in 28:19.

The contrast between the Magi and the leaders in Jerusalem runs right through Matthew. Those who have the Scriptures but will not come to Jesus, and outsiders who come in faith, appear again in the Gentile centurion (8:10–12) and the Canaanite woman (15:28).

l.t: The ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd God’s people, whose greatness will reach the ends of the earth.
God’s words to David, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel’, joined to Micah in verse 6 (BSB footnote).
Nations and kings coming with gold and frankincense to worship.
Balaam, a foreign seer from the east, foretold ‘A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel’. Many early Christians connected this with the Magi’s star.
Jesus: many will come from east and west to feast with Abraham in the kingdom.
He came to his own, and his own did not receive him; but all who received him became children of God.

qs: Compare how Herod, the religious leaders and the Magi each respond to the news of Jesus’ birth.
Why is it significant that Gentile foreigners are the first to worship Jesus in Matthew?
The leaders knew the right answer but did not act on it. Is there anything you know about Jesus that you have not yet acted on?

hist.t: The star and the date of Jesus’ birth
b: When? Herod the Great died in 4 BC (a minority of scholars argue for 1 BC), and Jesus was born before that, probably about 6–4 BC. Our ‘AD’ numbering, worked out centuries later, placed his birth a few years too late. (See also the notes on Luke 2.)

What was the star? Suggestions include a conjunction of the planets Jupiter and Saturn in 7 BC and a short-lived new star recorded by Chinese astronomers around 5 BC. The New Bible Dictionary notes these possible confirmations but says they must be applied with caution. A star that ‘stood over the place’ suggests to many something beyond a natural event. Matthew’s interest is not astronomy but that God drew Gentiles to his Son.

Is the story history? Some scholars doubt it, because no other source mentions the Magi or the killing of the children. Others reply that the account is entirely in keeping with Herod’s character and with the expectation of a royal Messiah, and that its symbolic meaning does not count against its historicity.

2.ctx: Egypt had a large Jewish population, especially in Alexandria, and had long been a refuge for people fleeing danger in Israel (1 Kings 11:40; Jeremiah 43:1–7). Only Matthew records this journey.
2.mean: As soon as the Magi have gone, God acts to protect his Son. An angel warns Joseph in a dream that Herod is going to search for the child to kill him, and tells him to flee to Egypt. Joseph gets up that very night and goes. The family become refugees, and they stay in Egypt until Herod dies. Matthew sees this as fulfilling Hosea 11:1, ‘Out of Egypt I called My Son.’ In Hosea those words look back to the exodus, when God brought Israel, whom he called his ‘son’ (Exodus 4:22), out of slavery. Hosea was looking back to the exodus, though he also looked forward to a new rescue (Hosea 11:10–11). So what does Matthew mean by ‘fulfilled’? He means that Israel’s story is coming to its full meaning in Jesus. Israel was God’s son, but a disobedient one; Hosea goes straight on to say how Israel turned away to idols. Jesus is the true and faithful Son who will relive Israel’s story and get it right. Like Israel he goes down into Egypt and comes back; like Israel he will pass through water (his baptism) and be tested in the wilderness (chapter 4). But where Israel failed, he will obey.
2.big: Jesus relives Israel’s story as the true and faithful Son; even as a refugee child he is under his Father’s care.

vv.h: Take the Child and His mother
b: Notice the wording, repeated in verses 14, 20 and 21: not ‘your son and your wife’, but ‘the Child and His mother’. Matthew keeps the focus on Jesus, and quietly reminds us that Joseph is not his natural father.

vv.h: So he got up … by night
b: Again Joseph obeys immediately, without a word. The journey to Egypt was long and hard, and the family probably relied on the large Jewish communities there. God’s protection did not mean an easy road.

vv.h: Out of Egypt I called My Son
b: Hosea 11 goes on to promise that, after judgment, God would bring his people back from exile ‘from Egypt’ and Assyria (Hosea 11:10–11). So Hosea already joins the first exodus to a future, greater rescue. Matthew sees that greater exodus beginning with Jesus, the Son who leads God’s people out of slavery to sin.

2.diff: How does Matthew ‘fulfil’ Hosea 11:1? Hosea speaks of the exodus: ‘Out of Egypt I called My son’, meaning Israel. Most interpreters see typology: a pattern in Israel’s history reaching its fullest meaning in Jesus, the true Son. Some evangelical scholars go further. G. K. Beale argues that Hosea himself already saw the exodus as a pattern for a future rescue (Hosea 11:10–11), so Matthew develops Hosea’s own thought; John Sailhamer argued that the verse is messianic in its Old Testament setting. Many critical scholars think Matthew reads in a meaning Hosea did not have in mind.

b: Matthew’s infancy story deliberately echoes the story of Moses. A wicked king kills Hebrew baby boys, and one child escapes (Exodus 1–2); the king dies, and God tells the deliverer it is safe to return (Exodus 4:19, echoed in Matthew 2:20). Jesus is the new and greater Moses, who will lead a new exodus.

Jesus as the true Israel is a key to reading Matthew. He is God’s Son (3:17), tested forty days in the wilderness as Israel was tested forty years (4:1–11), and gives God’s law on a mountain (5:1). Where Israel failed, he obeys.

l.t: God’s love for his son Israel, Israel’s unfaithfulness, and the promise of a future return.
God calls Israel ‘My firstborn son’ and demands that Pharaoh let him go.
Pharaoh orders the killing of Hebrew boys; Moses is saved.
God tells Jacob not to fear going down to Egypt, and promises to bring him up again.
Christ was made like his brothers in every way, and because he suffered when tempted he can help those who are tempted.

qs: How does Matthew use Hosea 11:1, and why is it more than a simple prediction?
What parallels can you see between Jesus’ early life and Moses’ or Israel’s?
Jesus began life as a refugee. How might that shape the way Christians think about people who are displaced or in danger today?

2.ctx: Bethlehem was a small village, so the number of boys killed may have been small, perhaps a dozen or two. Rachel, Jacob’s beloved wife and mother of Joseph and Benjamin, died near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:16–20). Ramah, north of Jerusalem, was where the Babylonians gathered Jewish captives before taking them into exile (Jeremiah 40:1).
2.mean: When Herod realises the Magi have not come back, he is furious. To be sure of killing the child, he orders the death of every boy in and around Bethlehem aged two and under, a margin based on what the Magi told him about the star. It is a horrifying act, and Matthew does not soften it. He quotes Jeremiah 31:15. In Jeremiah, Rachel, the ancestral mother of Israel, is pictured weeping from her grave as her descendants are led away to exile in Babylon. She refuses to be comforted, because her children are gone. Now the same grief is heard in Bethlehem. But anyone who knew Jeremiah would remember what comes next. God tells Rachel to stop weeping, because her children will come back, and there is hope for the future (Jeremiah 31:16–17). A few verses later Jeremiah announces the new covenant, in which God will forgive his people’s sins (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Matthew is not saying that Herod’s crime was good. He is saying that God’s people are still living in the darkness of exile, and that the long-promised rescue has now begun in the very child Herod is trying to kill. Herod is fully responsible for his evil, yet it cannot defeat God’s purpose.
2.big: The coming of the King provokes violence against the innocent; God does not hide the grief, but sets it inside the story of his promised rescue.

vv.h: two years old and under
b: Herod’s cruelty matches what Josephus tells of his last years: he had his wife Mariamme and several of his own sons executed, and ordered that leading men be killed when he died so that there would be mourning in the land. The killing of a few village children would hardly have been noticed by historians recording such atrocities.

vv.h: Rachel weeping for her children
b: In the Greek, Matthew’s other fulfilment quotations usually say things happened ‘in order to’ fulfil Scripture (the difference does not show in most English translations). Here, and again with Judas’s death (27:9), he says only ‘then … was fulfilled’. Many commentators see this as deliberate: Matthew does not attribute human evil to God’s purpose in the same way.

Scripture does not give tidy answers to innocent suffering. It names it, grieves it, and promises that God will one day wipe away every tear. Rachel’s weeping is answered by the promise of return and the new covenant; Bethlehem’s grief is answered by the child who will give his own life and rise again.
The echo of Pharaoh is deliberate. Herod, the ruler of God’s people, acts like the pagan king who enslaved them. The real threat to God’s people now comes from within.

l.t: Rachel’s weeping, and God’s promise: ‘your children will return’.
The new covenant promised in the same chapter, sealed by Jesus’ blood (Matthew 26:28).
Pharaoh orders every Hebrew boy to be thrown into the Nile.
Rachel dies on the way to Bethlehem.
God will wipe away every tear; there will be no more death or mourning.

qs: Why does Matthew include such a painful event in the story of Jesus’ birth?
What hope follows Rachel’s weeping in Jeremiah 31, and how does it relate to Jesus?
How can this passage help someone who is grieving or angry at injustice?

hist.t: Herod and the killing of the children
b: No source outside Matthew records the massacre, and some scholars doubt it for that reason. But it fits what Josephus tells us of Herod in his last years: paranoid about rivals, he had his wife Mariamme and several of his sons killed, and as he was dying ordered leading men to be executed so that there would be mourning at his death. The killing of perhaps a few infants in a village would hardly have been noticed by historians recording such atrocities.

2.ctx: When Herod died in 4 BC, the emperor Augustus divided his kingdom between three sons: Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea; Herod Antipas received Galilee and Perea; Philip received lands to the north-east. Nazareth was a small village in Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament.
2.mean: After Herod dies, the angel appears to Joseph again. ‘Those seeking the Child’s life are now dead’, he says, so Joseph takes the family back to the land of Israel. Those words are almost exactly what God said to Moses in Midian, telling him it was safe to return to Egypt because the men who wanted to kill him were dead (Exodus 4:19). Once again Matthew is quietly showing Jesus as the new Moses. But danger is not over. Herod’s son Archelaus now rules Judea, and he is as brutal as his father. Joseph is afraid to settle there, and after another warning in a dream he goes north to Galilee and makes his home in Nazareth. Matthew says this fulfils what was said ‘through the prophets’: ‘He will be called a Nazarene.’ No single Old Testament verse says this, and Matthew says ‘prophets’, plural, so he is summing up a theme rather than quoting one text (see Verse by verse). Even Jesus’ obscure home town carries meaning. Step by step, through dreams, dangers and ordinary decisions, God has brought his Son to the place where he will grow up.
2.big: God guides his Son’s family step by step, and even Jesus’ humble home town carries meaning.

vv.h: those seeking the Child’s life are now dead
b: Matthew’s wording is very close to the Greek Old Testament of Exodus 4:19, where God tells Moses to return to Egypt because the men who sought his life are dead (BSB: ‘all the men who sought to kill you are dead’). Herod is cast as Pharaoh; Jesus as Moses.

vv.h: Archelaus was reigning in Judea
b: Archelaus began his rule by having about three thousand people killed at the temple during a festival uprising, according to Josephus. He was so hated that in AD 6 Augustus removed him and banished him to Gaul (see the drop-down). Joseph’s fear was well founded.

vv.h: He will be called a Nazarene
b: Two main explanations are offered. Many think Matthew is playing on Isaiah 11:1, where the Messiah is a ‘Branch’ (Hebrew netser) from Jesse’s roots; ‘Nazareth’ sounds like ‘branch-town’, and other prophets also call the Messiah the Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8), though with a different Hebrew word. Others think Matthew sums up prophecies that the Messiah would be despised (Isaiah 53:3), since Nazareth was an insignificant place (John 1:46). The two ideas fit together: the royal Branch grows from a humble, overlooked place.

l.t: God tells Moses that those who sought his life are dead: the words echoed in verse 20.
The ‘Branch’ from the stump of Jesse, a likely background to ‘Nazarene’.
The Messiah as the righteous Branch of David.
The Servant grows up like a tender shoot, despised and rejected.
‘Can anything good come from Nazareth?’
Luke’s account of the family settling in Nazareth, where Jesus grew in wisdom and stature.

qs: How does Matthew show God guiding the family through every stage of these events?
What might it mean that the Messiah came from an obscure and looked-down-on town?
Joseph made decisions with partial information and real fear. What does that say about how God guides us?

b: Archelaus ruled Judea from 4 BC with a brutality that matched his father’s worst. Josephus records that in the tenth year of his rule the leading Jews and Samaritans, ‘not being able to bear his barbarous and tyrannical usage of them’, accused him before Augustus, who banished him to Vienne in Gaul (AD 6). Judea then came under direct Roman governors, including later Pontius Pilate. Joseph’s fear was well founded.

3.h: The Mission of John the Baptist
3.ctx: Nearly thirty years have passed since chapter 2 (compare Luke 3:23). The Judean wilderness is the dry, rocky country between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. The Pharisees and Sadducees were the two leading religious parties. Parallels: Mark 1:1–8; Luke 3:1–18; John 1:19–28.
3.mean: John the Baptist bursts onto the scene with a short, urgent message: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.’ To repent is more than feeling sorry. It means a complete change of mind and direction: turning away from sin and back to God. The reason is that God’s kingdom, his promised rule through his King, is about to arrive. Matthew says John is the ‘voice’ Isaiah spoke of, calling people to prepare the way for the Lord. In Isaiah 40 that voice announced that God himself was coming to rescue his people from exile. John’s rough camel-hair clothes and leather belt are those of Elijah (2 Kings 1:8), and Malachi had said God would send Elijah before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). Huge crowds come out, confess their sins, and are baptised in the Jordan. But when Pharisees and Sadducees arrive, John does not flatter them. He calls them a ‘brood of vipers’, like snakes fleeing a fire. Being descended from Abraham will not save them; God could make children of Abraham out of the stones. What God wants is fruit: a changed life that shows the repentance is real. Judgment is close, like an axe already resting against a tree’s root. Then John points away from himself. Someone far greater is coming. John is not worthy even to carry his sandals, a slave’s job. John baptises with water; the coming one will baptise with the Holy Spirit and with fire, gathering his people like wheat and burning the useless chaff.
3.big: No religious background can replace a changed life; the King is coming, bringing the Spirit to those who repent and judgment to those who refuse.

vv.h: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near
b: Jesus will begin his own preaching with exactly the same words (4:17). ‘Kingdom of heaven’ is Matthew’s usual way of saying ‘kingdom of God’; Jews often spoke of ‘heaven’ out of reverence for God’s name. It means God’s reign, not a place: the time when God puts the world right through his anointed King (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14).

vv.h: Prepare the way for the Lord
b: In Isaiah 40:3 ‘the Lord’ is the LORD, God himself, coming to lead his people home in a new exodus. By applying the verse to John as forerunner of Jesus, Matthew quietly identifies Jesus with the LORD.

vv.h: camel’s hair, with a leather belt
b: Elijah was described as ‘a hairy man’ ‘with a leather belt around his waist’ (2 Kings 1:8). Jesus later says plainly that John is the Elijah who was to come (11:14; 17:12–13).

vv.h: Confessing their sins, they were baptized
b: Jews used ritual washings for cleansing, and many scholars think Gentile converts to Judaism were already being immersed (the clear evidence is a little later). John’s baptism was different: a once-for-all act of repentance in preparation for the coming King. For Jews to be baptised like converts implied that being born Jewish was not enough. Josephus also describes John’s baptism (see the drop-down).

vv.h: We have Abraham as our father
b: Many believed that all Israel had a share in the world to come simply by belonging to Abraham’s family. John denies that physical descent guarantees anything. Isaiah 51:1–2 calls Abraham ‘the rock from which you were cut’: God made a people from one man, and he can do it again. God’s true family is made of those who repent and believe (compare 8:11–12; Galatians 3:7).

vv.h: He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire
b: The prophets promised that God would pour out his Spirit and give his people new hearts (Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28). The coming one will do what only God can do: give the Spirit. ‘Fire’ is understood in two ways (see Where readings differ).

vv.h: His winnowing fork is in His hand
b: After threshing, farmers tossed grain into the wind with a fork. The heavy grain fell back to the floor; the light chaff blew aside and was burned. The Old Testament often uses chaff for the wicked (Psalm 1:4). John says the coming King will make the final separation, and the fire for the chaff is ‘unquenchable’.

3.diff: ‘With the Holy Spirit and with fire’. Some read Spirit and fire as one baptism: the Spirit’s purifying fire in believers, perhaps fulfilled at Pentecost, when tongues of fire appeared (Acts 2:3). Others, noting that ‘fire’ in verses 10 and 12 means judgment, read two baptisms for two groups in John’s mixed audience: the Spirit for the repentant and the fire of judgment for the unrepentant. Commentators are divided; both readings agree that the coming one brings the Spirit and that judgment is real.

b: John stands at the hinge between the Old Testament and the New. Jesus calls him more than a prophet, and yet the least in the kingdom is greater than he (11:9–11): he announced the kingdom, but did not live to see its full arrival at the cross, resurrection and Pentecost.

John’s call to ‘Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance’ runs through Matthew. Jesus will say that a tree is known by its fruit (7:16–20; 12:33). Christians differ on how faith and works relate, but agree that genuine repentance shows itself in a changed life (compare James 2:17).

l.t: Comfort for exiled Jerusalem, and the voice preparing the way for the LORD.
God promises to send his messenger, Elijah, before the day of the LORD.
God will sprinkle clean water and put his Spirit within his people: the promise behind John’s water and Jesus’ Spirit.
God will pour out his Spirit on all people.
The wicked are like chaff that the wind blows away.
At Pentecost the Spirit comes with tongues of fire, and Peter calls the crowd to repent and be baptised.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom without being born of water and the Spirit.

qs: What does John say real repentance looks like, and what does he say it is not?
Why does John refuse to accept ‘We have Abraham as our father’? What might people rely on in the same way today?
What fruit ‘in keeping with repentance’ might God be looking for in your life right now?

b: Josephus calls him ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who urged the Jews to practise righteousness and piety and to come to baptism, and records that Herod Antipas had him executed at the fortress of Machaerus (see 14:1–12). He differs from the Gospels in two ways: he says John’s baptism was not for the putting away of sins but ‘for the purification of the body’, and he gives Herod’s motive as fear that John would stir up a revolt, where Matthew gives John’s rebuke over Herodias.

3.ctx: Jesus travels from Nazareth in Galilee to the Jordan, a journey of several days. Parallels: Mark 1:9–11; Luke 3:21–22; John 1:29–34. Only Matthew records John’s protest.
3.mean: Jesus comes to John to be baptised. John is shocked and tries to stop him: ‘I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?’ John’s baptism was for sinners turning back to God, and John knows that Jesus is the greater one who will baptise with the Spirit. Jesus does not need to repent, so why is he here? Jesus answers that it is right for them to do this ‘to fulfill all righteousness’. He is not confessing his own sin. He is doing everything God requires, and he is standing alongside the sinners he came to save, taking his place with them. This is the first step on a road that leads to the cross, where he will carry their sins. As Jesus comes up out of the water, the heavens open. He sees the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and resting on him, and a voice from heaven says, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!’ Here the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are all present together: the Father speaks, the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends. The Father’s words combine two Old Testament passages. Psalm 2 speaks of God’s anointed King as his Son; Isaiah 42 speaks of God’s chosen Servant, in whom he delights and on whom he puts his Spirit. Jesus is both: the royal Son who will reign, and the Servant who will suffer for his people.
3.big: Jesus takes his place with sinners in obedience to the Father, and the Father and the Spirit publicly declare him the beloved Son and chosen Servant.

vv.h: I need to be baptized by You
b: John recognises Jesus’ greatness, as he said in verse 11. His protest is about Jesus’ greatness (3:11). The New Testament teaches that Jesus had no sin to confess (Hebrews 4:15), so his baptism was not a confession of his own sin.

vv.h: to fulfill all righteousness
b: ‘Righteousness’ in Matthew means doing God’s will (compare 5:6, 20; 6:33). Jesus submits to what God was doing through John, the prophet God had sent. By being baptised he identifies with his people, as the Servant of Isaiah 53 was ‘numbered with the transgressors’ and bore their sin (Isaiah 53:12).

vv.h: the heavens were opened
b: Ezekiel’s visions began when ‘the heavens opened’ (Ezekiel 1:1), and Isaiah prayed, ‘If only You would rend the heavens and come down’ (Isaiah 64:1). Now heaven opens over Jesus: God is acting to save.

vv.h: the Spirit of God descending like a dove
b: Many see an echo of creation, when the Spirit hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:2); some Jewish writers compared that hovering to a bird. Others recall the dove that brought Noah news of a new world after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12). Either way, the Spirit marks a new beginning. Isaiah had promised that God would put his Spirit on his Servant (Isaiah 42:1) and on the Branch from Jesse (Isaiah 11:2).

vv.h: This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!
b: ‘My Son’ echoes Psalm 2:7, where God says to his anointed King, ‘You are My Son’. ‘In whom I am well pleased’ echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God says of his Servant, ‘in whom My soul delights’. Some also hear ‘beloved son’ from Genesis 22:2, where Abraham is told to offer his only son Isaac. The same words are spoken again at the transfiguration (17:5).

3.diff: Why ‘to fulfill all righteousness’? Several readings are offered, and many commentators combine them: Jesus obeys God’s will by accepting John’s God-given baptism (Calvin: ‘that he might render full obedience to the Father’); he identifies with the sinful people he came to save; he points ahead to his death, which he later calls a baptism (Mark 10:38; Luke 12:50); he takes up the role of the Servant ‘numbered with the transgressors’ (Isaiah 53:12). Calvin added a further reason: ‘that he might consecrate baptism in his own body, that we might have it in common with him’. See also the note on Mark 1:1.

b: The baptism is one of the clearest scenes of the Trinity in the Gospels: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each distinct and all present together. Matthew ends with Jesus sending his disciples to baptise ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’ (28:19), one name for three persons.

Jesus’ baptism is the start of his saving work. He later calls his coming death a ‘baptism’ (Mark 10:38; Luke 12:50). Paul teaches that believers are baptised into Christ’s death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4). He stood with sinners in the water so that they might be united with him.

l.t: God says to his anointed King, ‘You are My Son’.
God’s chosen Servant, in whom he delights, on whom he puts his Spirit. Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1–4 in 12:18–21.
The righteous Servant who bore the sin of many and was numbered with the transgressors.
The Spirit over the waters at creation; the dove that announced a renewed world after the flood.
The same words from heaven at the transfiguration, with ‘Listen to Him!’
Baptism ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’.
God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us.

qs: Why did John try to stop Jesus, and how does Jesus answer him?
What do the Father’s words, drawn from Psalm 2 and Isaiah 42, tell us about who Jesus is?
Jesus heard his Father’s approval before he had done any public ministry. What difference does it make to know you are loved by God before you achieve anything?

4.ctx: Moses fasted forty days and forty nights on Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:28), and Israel was tested forty years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2). All three of Jesus’ replies come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses’ words to Israel about their wilderness years. Parallels: Mark 1:12–13; Luke 4:1–13.
4.mean: Straight after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. God does not tempt anyone to sin (James 1:13), but here he allows the devil to test his Son. After forty days without food Jesus is starving, and the devil strikes. All three temptations attack what the Father has just said: ‘This is My beloved Son.’ First: ‘If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.’ Use your power for yourself. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 8:3: people do not live by bread alone, but by every word God speaks. Obeying his Father matters more to him than food. Second, the devil takes him to the highest point of the temple and quotes Scripture himself, Psalm 91: throw yourself down, and God’s angels will catch you. Force God to prove his care. Jesus replies from Deuteronomy 6:16: do not put the Lord your God to the test. Trusting God does not mean demanding miracles on our terms. Third, from a very high mountain, the devil shows him all the kingdoms of the world and offers them all, if Jesus will bow down and worship him. It is a short cut: a crown without a cross. Jesus refuses: ‘Away from Me, Satan!’ Worship belongs to God alone (Deuteronomy 6:13). The devil leaves, and angels come and care for him. Where Israel failed in the wilderness, grumbling for food, testing God and turning to idols, Jesus, the true Son, stands firm.
4.big: Jesus, the faithful Son, defeats the devil by trusting and obeying his Father where Israel failed; his victory is the hope of all who are tempted.

vv.h: led by the Spirit … to be tempted by the devil
b: ‘Devil’ means ‘accuser’ or ‘slanderer’; in verse 10 Jesus calls him Satan, ‘adversary’. The Greek word for ‘tempt’ also means ‘test’. What the devil meant as temptation to sin, God meant as a test that his Son would pass.

vv.h: Man shall not live on bread alone
b: In Deuteronomy 8:3, Moses explains that God let Israel go hungry and then fed them with manna, to teach them that life depends on God’s word. Israel grumbled; Jesus trusts. He will feed thousands later (14:13–21), but he will not use his power to escape the path his Father has set him.

vv.h: He will command His angels concerning You
b: The devil quotes Psalm 91:11–12 and twists a promise of protection into a dare. Jesus answers Scripture with Scripture. Deuteronomy 6:16 refers to Massah, where Israel demanded water and asked, ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’ (Exodus 17:7). Jesus will not test whether God is with him.

vv.h: All this I will give You
b: After his resurrection Jesus will say, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me’ (28:18), on a mountain in Galilee. The devil offered the same kingdoms on a mountain, at the price of worshipping him. Jesus received them from his Father, at the price of the cross.

vv.h: Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only
b: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:13, which follows the great command to love God with all your heart (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Israel turned to idols again and again; Jesus gives undivided worship to God. Yet in Matthew Jesus himself receives worship (2:11; 14:33; 28:9, 17). Matthew sees no contradiction: later the disciples worship Jesus (14:33; 28:9, 17), and he accepts it.

vv.h: angels came and ministered to Him
b: The word ‘ministered’ often means serving food. The Father provides for his Son in his time, after the test, just as he fed Israel in the wilderness.

4.diff: Model or one-off victory? Christians have long read the temptations as a model for resisting temptation with Scripture, and the New Testament does say that Jesus, having been tempted, can help us (Hebrews 2:18; 4:15). Many commentators add that the story is first about who Jesus is: the obedient Son succeeding where Israel failed, a victory that was his alone and on which our hope depends. The two readings fit together.

b: Paul calls Jesus the ‘last Adam’ (1 Corinthians 15:45). Adam, in a garden full of food, listened to the tempter who questioned God’s word, and fell; Jesus, starving in a wilderness, held to God’s word and stood. Israel, God’s son, failed its forty years of testing; Jesus, the true Son, passed his forty days. His obedience reverses theirs.

The temptation is the beginning of a battle that runs through the Gospel. Jesus casts out demons as a sign that he has bound the ‘strong man’ (12:29). At Caesarea Philippi, when Peter urges him to avoid the cross, Jesus again rebukes Satan: ‘Get behind Me, Satan!’ (16:23). The same short cut, a kingdom without suffering, is offered once more.

l.t: God tested Israel forty years in the wilderness and fed them with manna, to teach them that people live by his word.
Fear and serve the LORD only; do not test him as at Massah.
The psalm the devil quotes, and the line he leaves out.
Massah and Meribah: Israel tests God by demanding water.
The serpent questions God’s word; Adam and Eve fall.
Jesus was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin.
Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

qs: What does each temptation try to get Jesus to do, and how does each of his answers respond?
How does this story show Jesus succeeding where Israel (and Adam) failed?
Which of these three temptations do you recognise most in your own life, and how could Jesus’ answer help you?

4.ctx: John was arrested by Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee (see 14:3–12). Capernaum was a busy fishing town on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee. In Old Testament times this area belonged to the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali, the first part of Israel to fall to the Assyrians (2 Kings 15:29). Parallels: Mark 1:14–15; Luke 4:14–15.
4.mean: When Jesus hears that John has been put in prison, he goes back to Galilee. He moves from Nazareth to Capernaum, a busy lakeside town, and makes it his base. Matthew sees in this move a fulfilment of Isaiah 9:1–2. That prophecy was about the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali. Isaiah called it ‘Galilee of the Gentiles’ because the Assyrians had settled many foreigners there. By Jesus’ day its towns were mainly Jewish again, but the name stuck. More than seven hundred years earlier, it was the first part of Israel to be crushed by Assyria and taken into exile. Isaiah promised that one day the people living in that darkness, in ‘the land of the shadow of death’, would see a great light. Now the light has come. Jesus does not begin his public work in Jerusalem, the holy city. He begins in the region that had suffered first and had long been looked down on. Matthew’s readers would also remember how Isaiah’s prophecy continues: a child is born to rule on David’s throne, called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6–7). From that time on, Jesus preaches the same message as John: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.’
4.big: Jesus brings God’s light first to the dark, despised, mixed-up places, and calls everyone to turn to God because his kingdom has come near.

vv.h: He withdrew to Galilee
b: Galilee was also ruled by Herod Antipas, who had arrested John. Matthew often uses ‘withdrew’ for moving away from danger (2:22; 12:15; 14:13), but here the move also fulfils Scripture. With John silenced, Jesus takes up the work in the north.

vv.h: Galilee of the Gentiles
b: The quotation is from Isaiah 9:1–2. Matthew often notices Gentiles: the women in the genealogy, the Magi, the Gentile centurion (8:5–13), the Canaanite mother (15:21–28). The light that dawns in Galilee will finally shine on all nations (28:19).

vv.h: From that time on Jesus began to preach
b: Matthew uses the phrase ‘from that time on Jesus began’ twice to mark the two great turning points of his story: here, the start of Jesus’ public ministry, and in 16:21, when Jesus begins to tell his disciples that he must suffer, die and rise.

l.t: Light for Galilee of the nations, and the promised child: ‘Mighty God … Prince of Peace’.
Assyria conquers Galilee and Naphtali and deports their people.
‘I am the light of the world’.
Simeon: Jesus is ‘a light for revelation to the Gentiles’.
The Servant given as a light for the nations.
The God who said ‘let light shine out of darkness’ has shone in our hearts in the face of Christ.

qs: Why is it significant that Jesus begins his ministry in Galilee rather than Jerusalem?
Read Isaiah 9:1–7. What else does that prophecy promise about the one who brings the light?
Who are the people in ‘darkness’ around you, and how might Jesus’ light reach them?

b: Capernaum, on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, was a small fishing town on the road to Damascus, with a tax post (compare Mark 2:14). A Roman milestone was found near the synagogue. The white limestone synagogue visitors see today dates from the 4th or 5th century AD (about 10,000 coins were found beneath its floor), but it stands on the foundations of an earlier one, probably the synagogue of Jesus’ day (compare Luke 7:5).

Just south of it is an octagonal church built over the walls of an earlier house. The excavators believe this was Peter’s house (Mark 1:29), venerated by Christians from early times; Italian archaeologists report the name Peter among graffiti scratched on its walls. The identification is reasonable but cannot be proved.

4.ctx: Fishing was a major industry on the Sea of Galilee. Fishermen were not the poorest of the poor; some owned boats and hired workers (Mark 1:20). John’s Gospel shows that Andrew and Peter had already met Jesus through John the Baptist (John 1:35–42), and Luke records a miraculous catch of fish (Luke 5:1–11). Parallel: Mark 1:16–20.
4.mean: Walking along the shore, Jesus sees two brothers, Simon (also called Peter) and Andrew, casting a net into the lake. He says to them, ‘Come, follow Me,’ ‘and I will make you fishers of men.’ At once they leave their nets and follow him. A little further on he sees two more brothers, James and John, in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets. Jesus calls them, and immediately they leave the boat and their father and follow him. Matthew tells this very simply, and the simplicity is the point. Jewish students usually seem to have chosen their own teacher; here Jesus chooses his disciples. He gives a command, ‘follow Me’, and a promise, ‘I will make you’. Following meant much more than walking behind him. A disciple lived with his master, listened to his teaching, learned it by heart, and copied his way of life. These men leave their business, their income and, in the case of James and John, their father. Jesus’ authority, which drove away the devil, now draws people to himself. And he gives them a new purpose: they spent their lives catching fish; now he will turn them into people who gather others into God’s kingdom.
4.big: Jesus calls ordinary people to leave everything and follow him, and promises to make them into people who bring others to God.

vv.h: Come, follow Me
b: The prophets called Israel to follow God. The nearest parallel is Elijah calling Elisha, who left his oxen to follow him (1 Kings 19:19–21), but Jesus calls people to himself with an authority no prophet claimed. Jesus calls people to follow him personally. Peter later writes that Christ left us an example, ‘that you should follow in His footsteps’ (1 Peter 2:21).

vv.h: I will make you fishers of men
b: It is a promise of transformation: Jesus will make them into something they are not yet. Later he tells a parable of a net gathering fish of every kind, an image of the kingdom (13:47–50). The fishermen will gather people for God.

vv.h: at once … immediately
b: Matthew stresses the speed and the cost. James and John leave not only the boat but their father, a hint of what Jesus will later say: following him comes before even family (10:37; 19:29).

Jesus calls them first to himself (‘follow Me’) and only then to a task (‘fishers of men’). Christian service grows out of knowing and following Christ, not the other way round. The Gospel ends with the same men sent to make disciples of all nations (28:19–20): those who were called to follow are sent to call others to follow.

l.t: Andrew meets Jesus through John the Baptist and brings his brother Simon.
The miraculous catch of fish and Jesus’ words, ‘from now on you will catch men’.
Elijah calls Elisha from his ploughing; Elisha leaves his oxen and follows him.
Jesus calls Matthew the tax collector with the same words: ‘Follow Me’.
The disciples are sent to make disciples of all nations.
Christ left an example, so that you should follow in his footsteps.

qs: What did these four men leave behind to follow Jesus?
What is the difference between Jesus’ command (‘follow Me’) and his promise (‘I will make you’)?
What would it mean for you to follow Jesus more closely this week, and who might you help to follow him?

4.ctx: Josephus says Galilee had over two hundred towns and villages. Syria lay to the north; the Decapolis (‘Ten Cities’, BSB footnote) was a group of largely Gentile cities mostly east of the Jordan. This summary is repeated almost word for word in 9:35, framing the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7) and the miracles (chapters 8–9).
4.mean: Matthew sums up Jesus’ early ministry in three words: teaching, preaching and healing. He teaches in the synagogues, explaining the Scriptures. He preaches ‘the gospel of the kingdom’, the good news that God’s promised reign has arrived in him. And he heals ‘every disease and sickness’ among the people. News spreads far beyond Galilee, into Syria, and people bring all kinds of suffering to him: illness, severe pain, demon possession, seizures, paralysis. He heals them all. Huge crowds follow him from every direction: Galilee in the north, Jerusalem and Judea in the south, the Decapolis and the land beyond the Jordan in the east, including many Gentile areas. Why does this matter? The prophets had said that when God came to save his people, the blind would see, the lame would walk and the sick would be healed (Isaiah 35:5–6). Jesus’ healings are signs that the kingdom has come and that he is the promised King (compare 11:2–5). They are not tricks to impress people; they are previews of the world God will one day make new, where there will be no more sickness or death.
4.big: Jesus’ teaching, preaching and healing show that God’s kingdom has arrived and give a preview of the world he will make new.

vv.h: the gospel of the kingdom
b: ‘Gospel’ means good news. In Isaiah 52:7 the messenger brings good news, saying to Zion, ‘Your God reigns!’ That is the gospel of the kingdom: God is now reigning through his King.

vv.h: healing every disease and sickness
b: Old Testament texts speak of the LORD as the one who heals all diseases (Psalm 103:3; compare Exodus 15:26). Matthew may be quietly showing Jesus doing what God does.

vv.h: Syria … the Decapolis … beyond the Jordan
b: The crowds come from Jewish and Gentile regions alike. The light promised to ‘Galilee of the Gentiles’ (4:15) is already drawing the nations.

Matthew frames the Sermon on the Mount and the ten miracles of chapters 8–9 with almost identical summaries (4:23 and 9:35). Jesus is the Messiah of word (chapters 5–7) and of deed (chapters 8–9). The two belong together throughout his ministry, and in the church’s mission too.

Will every believer be healed now? Jesus’ healings were signs that the kingdom had come, and Christians pray for healing with confidence; but the New Testament does not promise that every illness will be healed in this life. Paul left his co-worker Trophimus sick (2 Timothy 4:20) and lived with his own ‘thorn in my flesh’ (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Full healing belongs to the resurrection (Revelation 21:4). See also the note on Matthew 8:14 on healing and the atonement.

l.t: When God comes to save, the blind will see and the lame leap like deer.
The messenger who brings good news: ‘Your God reigns!’
The same summary repeated after the miracles of chapters 8–9.
Jesus points John to his miracles as proof that he is the Coming One.
The LORD forgives all your sins and heals all your diseases.
God will dwell with his people; there will be no more death, mourning or pain.

qs: What three activities sum up Jesus’ ministry here, and how do they belong together?
What do Jesus’ healings show about the kingdom of God?
How can Christians today hold together praying confidently for healing and trusting God when healing does not come?
