5.ctx: Matthew 4:23–25 ended with huge crowds following Jesus from every direction. Now he climbs a hillside in Galilee and teaches. This is the first of the five great blocks of teaching in Matthew (see the book map), and one of the longest stretches of Jesus’ teaching in the Gospels. Luke gives a shorter, similar sermon on ‘a level place’ (Luke 6:17–49). Jewish teachers usually sat to teach (compare 13:2; 23:2; Luke 4:20).
5.mean: Chapters 5–7 are the best-known words Jesus ever spoke, so it helps to see the whole before the parts. Jesus sees the crowds, goes up the mountain and sits down, and his disciples come to him. He teaches them, but the crowds are listening too (7:28). The Sermon is first of all for disciples: people who have already begun to follow him. That is why it opens with blessing, not with rules. It describes what life looks like when God is King. The Sermon moves in clear stages. First come the Beatitudes: who the blessed people of the kingdom are (5:3–12). Then their role in the world: salt and light (5:13–16). Then Jesus’ relationship to the Old Testament Law, and six examples of a righteousness deeper than the religious leaders taught (5:17–48). Then true worship: giving, prayer and fasting done for God, not for show (6:1–18). Then trust: treasure in heaven, and freedom from worry (6:19–34). Then how to treat others (7:1–12). Finally, a choice between two gates, two trees and two houses (7:13–27). Notice also the picture Matthew paints. Moses went up a mountain to receive God’s law. Now Jesus goes up a mountain and gives God’s teaching himself, with the words ‘But I tell you’. A greater one than Moses is here.
5.big: Jesus, the promised prophet greater than Moses, teaches those who follow him what life under God’s reign looks like, from the inside out.

vv.h: He went up on the mountain
b: Matthew does not name the hill; tradition places it above the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. He is more interested in what the mountain means. Charles Quarles points out that in the Greek Old Testament the exact phrase ‘went up on the mountain’ is used only of Moses going up Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:3; 24:18; 34:4). Matthew’s readers, who knew their Scriptures, would hear the echo at once.

The echo fits Matthew’s whole story so far. Like Moses, Jesus escaped a king who killed baby boys (2:16), came out of Egypt (2:15), passed through water (3:16) and spent forty days in the wilderness (4:2). Moses promised that God would raise up ‘a prophet like me’ and told Israel, ‘You must listen to him’ (Deuteronomy 18:15). On another mountain God will say of Jesus, ‘Listen to Him!’ (17:5).

vv.h: and sat down
b: Sitting was the normal posture of a teacher with authority, as in a synagogue (Luke 4:20) or ‘Moses’ seat’ (23:2). Jesus is not giving a casual talk; he is taking the teacher’s chair. The crowds notice: he teaches ‘as one who had authority’ (7:29).

vv.h: His disciples came to Him, and He began to teach them
b: ‘Disciple’ means learner or apprentice. So far Matthew has named only four (4:18–22), but the word here probably covers a wider group who have begun to follow him. The crowds stand around the edge. That picture matters: the Sermon describes the life of people who belong to Jesus, and it invites everyone listening to join them. It is not a set of rules to make yourself good enough for God; it is the way of life of people whom God has already welcomed (5:3).

5.diff: How should the Sermon be read? Christians have read it in several ways. Some, especially in the Lutheran tradition, have stressed it as a standard no one can meet, which shows us our sin and drives us to Christ. Older dispensational teaching saw it chiefly as the law of the coming kingdom: the Scofield Reference Bible (1917) said that in its primary application it ‘gives neither the privilege nor the duty of the Church’, though it has ‘a beautiful moral application to the Christian’. Most commentators, including Stott and Quarles, read it as Jesus’ teaching for his disciples: Stott calls it the pattern of a ‘Christian counter-culture’, and the New Bible Dictionary describes it as ‘a character sketch of those who have already entered the kingdom’, while warning against ‘crude literalism’ with its deliberately extreme sayings. The Anabaptist tradition (Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites) takes commands such as non-resistance and refusing oaths as direct rules for the church (Schleitheim Confession, 1527). Catholic teaching sees in the Sermon the expression of the ‘New Law’, which is ‘the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ’ (Catechism 1965–1966). Augustine said that anyone who studies it ‘will find in it, so far as regards the highest morals, a perfect standard of the Christian life’. Most agree that it shows what God’s people are meant to be.

b: The question. Matthew’s Sermon is much longer than Luke’s (Luke 6:20–49), and some of its teaching appears in Luke on other occasions: the Lord’s Prayer (Luke 11:2–4), worry (Luke 12:22–31) and the two masters (Luke 16:13).

The views. Calvin held that Matthew and Luke describe the same sermon and that ‘the design of both Evangelists was, to collect into one place the leading points of the doctrine of Christ, which related to a devout and holy life’. Most modern scholars likewise think Matthew has gathered teaching Jesus gave at different times into one great discourse, as he seems to do in his other four teaching blocks. Others point out that a travelling teacher would repeat his main themes many times, so similar sayings in different settings are no surprise, and that Matthew presents this as one occasion on one hill.

What is agreed. Either way, the words are presented as Jesus’ own teaching, and Matthew has arranged them with great care. The name ‘Sermon on the Mount’ is usually traced to the title of Augustine’s commentary on it.

b: The Moses pattern runs through the whole of Matthew, and it comes to a head on two more mountains. On the mountain of transfiguration Jesus shines with God’s glory, Moses and Elijah appear, and the Father says, ‘Listen to Him!’ (17:1–8). On the last page the risen Jesus meets his disciples on a mountain in Galilee and sends them to teach the nations ‘to obey all that I have commanded you’ (28:16–20). The Sermon on the Mount is the first and largest part of what he commanded.

The prophets looked forward to a day when God would write his law on his people’s hearts (Jeremiah 31:33) and put his Spirit within them so that they would walk in his ways (Ezekiel 36:26–27). The Sermon describes that kind of obedience: not outward rule-keeping, but a life that flows from a changed heart (5:8, 28; 6:21; 7:17).

God will raise up a prophet like Moses: ‘You must listen to him.’
Luke’s shorter Sermon on the Plain, with blessings and woes.
On another mountain the Father says of Jesus, ‘Listen to Him!’
On a final mountain Jesus sends his disciples to teach all nations to obey his commands.
The new covenant: God’s law written on the heart.
A new heart and God’s Spirit within, so that his people walk in his ways.
The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

What difference does it make that the Sermon begins with blessings rather than commands?
Which part of the Sermon (see the stages in the Meaning) do you find most attractive, and which most challenging?

5.ctx: ‘Blessed’ statements were familiar from the Old Testament (Psalm 1:1; 32:1), and Moses ended his life by blessing Israel: ‘Blessed are you, O Israel! … a people saved by the LORD’ (Deuteronomy 33:29). Jesus’ words also echo Isaiah 61, where God’s anointed one brings ‘good news to the poor’ and comforts ‘all who mourn’, the chapter Jesus read from in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–21). Luke has four blessings and four woes (Luke 6:20–26).
5.mean: The Sermon opens with eight short sayings called the Beatitudes, from the Latin for ‘blessed’. Each is an announcement, not a command. Jesus does not say ‘Try to be poor in spirit’; he says that such people are blessed, because God is on their side. ‘Blessed’ means more than happy. It describes someone God approves of and is pleased with, someone truly well off in his eyes, whatever they feel at the moment. The shock is in who Jesus calls blessed. Not the confident, the cheerful, the tough or the successful, but the poor in spirit, the grieving, the gentle, the hungry for what is right, the merciful, the pure, the peacemakers and the persecuted. The world would call most of these people losers. Jesus turns the world’s values upside down. These are not eight different kinds of people, each with a different reward. They are eight sides of one character: the person who lives under God’s rule. And each blessing comes with a promise of what God will do. Notice that the first and eighth end the same way: ‘theirs is the kingdom of heaven’, in the present tense. The promises in between are mostly future: they will be comforted, filled, shown mercy, will see God. The kingdom has already arrived with Jesus, and its people belong to it now, but its full joys are still to come. In verses 11–12 Jesus turns from ‘they’ to ‘you’ and speaks straight to his disciples: if you suffer because of me, rejoice. Finally, the Beatitudes describe Jesus himself. He is the gentle and humble one (11:29), the merciful one, the pure one, the peacemaker and the persecuted one. To follow him is to grow into his likeness.
5.big: God’s blessing rests not on the proud and successful but on those who know their need of him; their character is a picture of Jesus, and the kingdom of heaven is theirs now and fully in the age to come.

vv.h: Blessed
b: The Greek word is makarios. It translates the Hebrew ashre, which opens the book of Psalms: ‘Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked’ (Psalm 1:1). The English translation of Calvin’s commentary has ‘Happy’, and some modern versions have ‘Happy’ or ‘Fortunate’. But this is not a passing feeling. It is God’s verdict on a person’s situation. Calvin put it like this: ‘the disciples of Christ must learn the philosophy of placing their happiness beyond the world’.

In Greek the key words of the first four Beatitudes all begin with the same sound (p: poor, mourning, meek, hungry), and the eight are framed by the repeated promise ‘theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (verses 3 and 10). The careful shape suggests they were meant to be memorised, and they still are.

vv.h: the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven
b: In the Old Testament ‘the poor’ often means more than people without money. It means the humble and helpless who look to God because they have no one else, those he promises to rescue: ‘The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit’ (Psalm 34:18; compare Isaiah 57:15; 66:2). Quarles notes that the phrase ‘poor in spirit’ also appears in one of the Dead Sea Scrolls (the War Scroll, 1QM 14:7) for God’s faithful, humble people. Luke’s version says simply ‘Blessed are you who are poor’ (Luke 6:20). Matthew’s wording draws out the inner attitude that God’s poor have always had.

To be poor in spirit is to know that you bring nothing to God: no goodness that earns his favour, no strength of your own. It is the opposite of pride. That is why this blessing comes first. The door into the kingdom is not achievement but need. Wesley described the poor in spirit as ‘they who are unfeignedly penitent, they who are truly convinced of sin’. Compare the tax collector who could only pray, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner’, and went home justified (Luke 18:13–14).

The promise is in the present tense: theirs is the kingdom. Quarles notes the echo of Daniel 7:22, 27, where the kingdom is given to ‘the saints of the Most High’. The humblest follower of Jesus already belongs to the kingdom that will outlast every empire.

vv.h: those who mourn, for they will be comforted
b: Isaiah 61:2–3 promised that God’s anointed one would ‘comfort all who mourn’ and give ‘the oil of joy for mourning’. Jesus announces that this comfort has arrived. The mourning may include every kind of grief in a broken world, but coming straight after ‘poor in spirit’ it surely includes grief over sin, our own and the world’s. John Stott calls it ‘the sorrow of repentance’. The psalmist wrote, ‘My eyes shed streams of tears because Your law is not obeyed’ (Psalm 119:136).

‘Will be comforted’ is what scholars call a divine passive: God is the one who will do it. Some comfort comes now, through forgiveness and the presence of God (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). Full comfort comes at the end, when ‘God will wipe away every tear from their eyes’ (Revelation 7:17; 21:4). Calvin noted that Christ does not merely say mourners are not unhappy; their very mourning prepares them ‘to receive eternal joy’.

vv.h: the meek, for they will inherit the earth
b: This Beatitude almost quotes Psalm 37:11: ‘But the meek will inherit the land’. Meekness is not weakness. The BSB footnote suggests ‘those who exercise strength under control’. Moses was called very meek or humble (Numbers 12:3), and Jesus describes himself as ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29) and comes to Jerusalem ‘gentle and riding on a donkey’ (21:5). The meek do not grab, push or take revenge. They trust God to put things right (Psalm 37:7–9). Wesley described them as ‘they that hold all their passions and affections evenly balanced’.

The promise is astonishing. In Psalm 37 the meek inherit the land of Israel. Jesus widens it to ‘the earth’ (the same Greek word can mean either). The people the world pushes aside will one day own the renewed creation (19:28; Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1). Calvin admitted that this seems ‘exceedingly foolish’ to the world, which thinks the aggressive rule the earth; but Christ declares that ‘the meek will be the lords and heirs of the earth’.

vv.h: those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled
b: Hunger and thirst are the strongest of desires; they are about staying alive. Jesus blesses those who want righteousness as badly as a starving person wants food. In Matthew, righteousness means doing God’s will (3:15; 5:20; 6:33): a life that is right with God and right with others. The blessing is not on people who have it all sorted, but on people who long for it.

Interpreters differ on how far this includes justice in society (see Where readings differ). Stott argued that biblical righteousness has three sides: being right with God, living a holy life, and seeking justice for others. Calvin read the verse mainly of people who suffer wrong and long for what is right. Either way, the promise is that God will fill them. Quarles notes another divine passive: God himself satisfies this hunger. Compare Isaiah 55:1–2 and Jesus’ words, ‘Whoever comes to Me will never hunger’ (John 6:35).

vv.h: the merciful, for they will be shown mercy
b: With verse 7 the Beatitudes turn outward, to how God’s people treat others. Mercy is kindness to people who do not deserve it or cannot repay it: forgiving the guilty, helping the needy. The Old Testament says, ‘Blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor’ (Proverbs 14:21), and God desires ‘mercy, not sacrifice’ (Hosea 6:6, quoted by Jesus in 9:13 and 12:7).

This is not a deal in which we earn God’s mercy by being merciful. People who have truly received mercy become merciful, and an unmerciful heart shows that God’s mercy has not been received. Jesus makes the same point in the Lord’s Prayer (6:12, 14–15) and in the parable of the unforgiving servant, who was forgiven a huge debt but would not forgive a small one (18:21–35). The mercy promised here is shown above all at the final judgement (James 2:13).

vv.h: the pure in heart, for they will see God
b: In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person: thoughts, desires and will, not only feelings. To be pure in heart is to be undivided and sincere, with no hidden agenda, wanting God above everything. The psalm asks, ‘Who may ascend the hill of the LORD?’ and answers, ‘He who has clean hands and a pure heart’ (Psalm 24:3–4). The Sermon will soon expose impure hearts: lust (5:28), showing off (6:1–18) and divided loyalty (6:22–24). Calvin observed that the world often admires clever deception, but Christ calls happy those ‘who take no delight in cunning’. Wesley described the pure in heart as ‘they who love God with all their hearts’.

To see God was the deepest longing of Israel’s saints (Psalm 27:4; 42:2), yet God told Moses, ‘no one can see Me and live’ (Exodus 33:20). Jesus promises that the pure in heart will see him. Christians see God now in Jesus (John 14:9), and will see him fully at the end: ‘They will see His face’ (Revelation 22:4; compare 1 John 3:2). No one is pure in heart by nature; that is why David prayed, ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God’ (Psalm 51:10).

vv.h: the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God
b: Peacemakers do more than keep the peace or avoid arguments. They work to bring peace where there is conflict, between people and God and between people and each other. Calvin described them as those who also ‘labor to settle differences among others’, and noted that it is tiring work that often earns complaints from both sides.

In the Bible, to be a ‘son’ of someone is to share his character. God is the great peacemaker: through Christ he made peace with his enemies ‘through the blood of His cross’ (Colossians 1:20; compare Ephesians 2:14–17). Jesus is the promised ‘Prince of Peace’ (Isaiah 9:6). People who make peace show the family likeness, and God will own them as his children. ‘Sons of God’ includes daughters too; it is a family title, used of all God’s children (Galatians 3:26–28).

vv.h: those who are persecuted because of righteousness
b: The last Beatitude is the most surprising. People who live God’s way will often be opposed, not for being difficult but because their lives challenge others. Stott calls it ‘the clash between two irreconcilable value-systems’. Jesus does not promise his followers an easy life; he promises them the kingdom.

The promise repeats the first: ‘theirs is the kingdom of heaven’. Together, verses 3 and 10 frame the whole list. Everything promised in between belongs to the kingdom, and it belongs to people the world looks down on or pushes out.

vv.h: Blessed are you … because of Me
b: Jesus now speaks directly to his disciples (‘you’), and he says that the persecution will be ‘because of Me’. In verse 10 it was ‘because of righteousness’. Loyalty to Jesus and living God’s way are treated as the same thing. No ordinary rabbi could say that suffering for him was the same as suffering for righteousness.

The response he asks for is astonishing: ‘Rejoice and be glad.’ Not because suffering is good, but because the reward in heaven is great, and because persecuted disciples stand in the line of the prophets. Jeremiah was beaten and put in stocks (Jeremiah 20:2) and later thrown into a pit (Jeremiah 38:6); Zechariah was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–21; compare 23:35). The apostles later did exactly this, ‘rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name’ (Acts 5:41). Calvin wrote that this teaching is hard for the flesh to accept, so ‘the more earnestly ought we to make it the subject of our meditation’.

5.diff: A ladder or a portrait? Augustine read the Beatitudes as stages in the Christian’s growth, beginning with humility, and matched them with the ‘sevenfold operation of the Holy Ghost’ in Isaiah 11:2–3. Wesley also saw an order, from conviction of sin to holiness of heart. Stott stressed that the Beatitudes are ‘not eight separate and distinct groups of disciples’ but eight qualities that belong together in every Christian. Catholic teaching says that ‘The Beatitudes are at the heart of Jesus’ preaching’ and that they ‘depict the countenance of Jesus Christ and portray his charity’ (Catechism 1716–1717). These are emphases rather than contradictions: all agree that the Beatitudes describe a God-given character, not a way to earn God’s favour. Which righteousness (verse 6)? Some read it mainly as a personal right standing and holy life given by God (Quarles; Protestants often add Christ’s righteousness counted to believers); Calvin read it mainly as longing for justice by those who suffer wrong; Stott included both, and social justice too. ‘Earth’ or ‘land’ (verse 5)? The BSB footnote allows ‘the land’, as in Psalm 37. Most read Jesus’ promise as the whole renewed earth.

b: Read side by side with Isaiah 61:1–3, the Beatitudes show Jesus announcing the arrival of the good news Isaiah promised: good news to the poor, comfort for those who mourn, a people called ‘oaks of righteousness’. At Nazareth Jesus read that passage and said, ‘Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing’ (Luke 4:21).

The Beatitudes are also a portrait of Jesus. He is ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29); he grieves in Gethsemane (26:37–38); he has mercy on the blind and the sick (9:27; 20:30–34); he makes peace through his cross; he is persecuted and insulted (27:27–31). Paul’s list of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23) describes the same character from another angle. What Jesus blesses, his Spirit produces.

The pattern of present and future in the promises is the pattern of the whole New Testament: the kingdom has come in Jesus, but not yet in its fullness. Christians are already God’s children (1 John 3:1) and already comforted, but they still wait to inherit the earth and see God face to face (Romans 8:18–25).

l.t: Good news to the poor and comfort for all who mourn: the background to verses 3–4.
‘The meek will inherit the land’: nearly quoted in verse 5.
Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? The one with clean hands and a pure heart.
Luke’s four blessings and four woes.
Jesus reads Isaiah 61 at Nazareth: ‘Today this Scripture is fulfilled.’
God has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom.
If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed.
The fruit of the Spirit: the same character, produced by God.
We are God’s children now; when Christ appears we will see him as he is.
The new heaven and new earth, where God wipes away every tear.

qs: Which Beatitude surprises you most, and why might Jesus call that kind of person ‘blessed’?
How do the Beatitudes describe Jesus himself? Which one do you see most clearly in his life?
Pick one Beatitude. What might it look like this week, at home or at work, to live it out?

5.ctx: In the ancient world salt was used to flavour food, to preserve it, and in sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13). Lamps were small clay bowls of olive oil with a wick, set on a stand to light a one-room house. Towns were often built on hills and could be seen for miles, especially at night.
5.mean: Straight after the Beatitudes, Jesus tells the same people what they are for. He does not say ‘try to become salt and light’; he says ‘You are’. The ‘you’ is plural: the whole community of his followers together. Salt was valuable. It gave food flavour and kept it from going bad. If salt lost its saltiness (many commentators explain that salt then was often impure, mixed with other minerals, and could lose its taste), it was useless and was thrown out onto the path. In the same way, disciples who lose what makes them different are no use to anyone. Then Jesus says, ‘You are the light of the world.’ Elsewhere he says, ‘I am the light of the world’ (John 8:12). His followers shine with his light, like the moon reflecting the sun. A city on a hill cannot be hidden, and no one lights a lamp only to cover it with a basket. Disciples are not meant to hide away. But notice the purpose: people are to see their good deeds and give glory not to them but to ‘your Father in heaven’. This does not contradict 6:1, where Jesus warns against doing good deeds to be seen by people. The difference is who gets the praise. The Beatitudes might make it sound as if Jesus’ people are weak and easily ignored. Here he says that this meek, merciful, persecuted community is the very thing the world needs.
5.big: Jesus’ followers are salt and light: by being different, they hold back the world’s decay and show God’s goodness so that people praise him.

vv.h: You are the salt of the earth
b: Salt had many uses, and Jesus does not say which one he means; perhaps all of them. Salt preserved meat and fish from going bad, so disciples may be pictured as holding back the moral decay of society. Salt also flavoured food, and Paul tells Christians to let their speech be ‘seasoned with salt’ (Colossians 4:6). Quarles points out that salt was also used to purify: Elisha threw salt into a spring and the water was healed (2 Kings 2:21). Salt was added to every grain offering as ‘the salt of the covenant’ (Leviticus 2:13), so it also spoke of lasting faithfulness to God.

vv.h: if the salt loses its savor
b: Pure salt cannot stop being salty. Many commentators explain that the salt people used was often mixed with other minerals; if the real salt dissolved away, what was left looked like salt but did nothing. Quarles notes that the Greek word for ‘loses its savor’ normally means ‘become foolish’. The same word is behind ‘foolish’ in 7:26, the man who heard Jesus’ words but did not do them. A disciple who stops living as a disciple has become foolish salt.
‘Thrown out and trampled by men’ is a sobering picture of uselessness. Jesus does not explain it further here, but the warning is clear: being Jesus’ people is not just a label; it shows.

vv.h: You are the light of the world
b: God called Israel to be ‘a light to the nations’ (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6), and the prophets pictured the nations streaming to Jerusalem, the city on God’s mountain, to learn his ways (Isaiah 2:2–3; 60:1–3). Jesus now gives that calling to his disciples, a small group of fishermen in Galilee. The light is not their own: Jesus is the light that has dawned on Galilee (4:16), and they shine because they belong to him.

vv.h: that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven
b: This is the first time in Matthew that Jesus calls God ‘your Father’. The Sermon will use the phrase again and again. The good deeds are not for the disciples’ reputation but for God’s. Peter writes the same: live such good lives among unbelievers that ‘they may see your good deeds and glorify God’ (1 Peter 2:12). In 6:1–18 Jesus will warn against the opposite: religion done to be seen by people, which gets their applause and nothing more.

The salt and light sayings show that Jesus’ followers are meant to be both different from the world and engaged with it. Salt that stays in the cellar does no good; salt that becomes like the food it is meant to season is useless. Light hidden under a basket helps no one. The two pictures guard against two opposite mistakes: withdrawing from the world, and blending into it.

Paul uses the same picture for a church in a pagan city: ‘you shine as lights in the world’ (Philippians 2:15). Jesus’ promise that the world would see his people’s deeds and glorify God begins to be fulfilled in Acts, where the first believers enjoyed ‘the favor of all the people’ (Acts 2:47).

l.t: God’s Servant, given as a light to the nations.
‘Arise, shine, for your light has come’: nations come to the light of God’s people.
Mark’s salt saying: ‘Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.’
Salt that loses its taste is thrown out.
Jesus: ‘I am the light of the world.’
Christians shine as lights in a crooked generation.
God’s people declare his praises, and others see their good deeds and glorify God.
Once darkness, now light in the Lord: live as children of light.

qs: What do salt and light each do? What might each picture mean for Christians at work or in the community?
How can we let our light shine without falling into the showing off that Jesus warns about in 6:1?
In what ways are Christians tempted to lose their ‘saltiness’, or to hide their light?

5.ctx: ‘The Law and the Prophets’ means the whole Old Testament (compare 7:12; 22:40). The scribes were experts who copied, studied and taught the Law; the Pharisees were a strict lay movement known for careful obedience to the Law and to the traditions built around it (see the glossary). People admired both groups as the most devout in Israel.
5.mean: Jesus has just announced a kingdom in which the poor and the gentle are blessed. Some might think he was throwing away the Old Testament. He says the opposite: ‘I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.’ To fulfil means to bring something to its intended goal, to fill it full. The Old Testament pointed forward, and everything in it finds its meaning in Jesus. Its promises come true in him. Its sacrifices point to his death. Its commands are explained by him in their deepest sense, and are kept by him perfectly. That is why not even the smallest letter of the Law will pass away until everything is accomplished: God’s word cannot fail. So disciples must not treat even the smallest of God’s commands as unimportant. Then comes a shocking sentence: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom. These were the most religious people anyone knew. How could anyone do better? Jesus means a different kind of righteousness, not just more rules. The examples that follow (5:21–48) show what he means. The scribes and Pharisees worked hard at outward obedience; Jesus looks at the heart, at anger, lust, honesty and love. This deeper righteousness is not something we can produce by trying harder. It is the obedience of a new heart that God promised to give (Jeremiah 31:33). Christians have discussed exactly how the Old Testament laws apply now (see Where readings differ), but all agree that Jesus is the key to reading them.
5.big: Jesus does not cancel the Old Testament; he fulfils it, and he calls his people to a righteousness of the heart that goes deeper than outward religion.

vv.h: I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them
b: ‘I have come’ hints that Jesus came from somewhere: he speaks as one sent by God (compare 9:13; 10:34; 20:28). ‘Fulfill’ is one of Matthew’s favourite words. It has been used of prophecies coming true (1:22; 2:15) and of Jesus’ baptism (‘to fulfill all righteousness’, 3:15). Here it covers all three: Jesus completes what the Old Testament promised, pictured and commanded.

Calvin, commenting on 5:21, put it simply: ‘We must not imagine Christ to be a new legislator, who adds any thing to the eternal righteousness of his Father.’ Jesus does not bring a new God or a new morality; he brings the old commands to their full meaning, and supplies by his Spirit the obedience the Law could not produce (Romans 8:3–4).

vv.h: not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen
b: The ‘jot’ is the yod, the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet, about the size of an apostrophe. The ‘stroke’ is a tiny mark that tells one Hebrew letter from another, like the tail that turns a Q into an O. Jesus is saying that God’s word stands down to its smallest detail. ‘Until everything is accomplished’ suggests that some parts of the Law reach their purpose and are completed in him; the letter to the Hebrews explains how the sacrifices and the priesthood are fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 8:13; 10:1–14).

vv.h: one of the least of these commandments
b: Rabbis sometimes graded commands as ‘light’ and ‘heavy’. Jesus does not deny that some matters are weightier (23:23), but he warns against treating any of God’s commands as unimportant and teaching others to do the same. Quarles notes that ‘these commandments’ probably points forward to Jesus’ own teaching in the rest of the Sermon. Being ‘least’ or ‘great’ is about rank within the kingdom, not whether someone gets in; getting in is the subject of verse 20.

vv.h: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees
b: Later Jesus will criticise the scribes and Pharisees for doing their deeds to be seen (23:5), for careful tithing of herbs while neglecting ‘justice, mercy, and faithfulness’ (23:23), and for being clean outside but full of greed inside (23:25–28). Their problem was not too much obedience, but obedience that stopped at the surface.

So the greater righteousness is not a longer list of rules but a deeper obedience: from the heart, motivated by love for God, and full of mercy. Who could have such righteousness? The prophets had promised a new covenant in which God would write his law on his people’s hearts (Jeremiah 31:33) and put his Spirit in them (Ezekiel 36:27). Protestants add that the righteousness that brings a person into God’s kingdom is finally Christ’s righteousness, counted to those who trust him (Philippians 3:9), and that a changed life is its fruit.

5.diff: How does Christ fulfil the Law? Reformed theology distinguishes the Law’s moral, ceremonial and civil parts: the ceremonial laws are fulfilled and ended in Christ, the civil laws expired with Israel’s state, and the moral law (summarised in the Ten Commandments) still binds believers as a rule of life, though not as a way of earning salvation (Westminster Confession 19). Lutherans emphasise the distinction between law and gospel and the law’s role in showing sin. Others, including New Covenant theologians and many dispensationalists, hold that the Mosaic law as a whole is fulfilled in Christ and that believers are now under ‘the law of Christ’ (1 Corinthians 9:21; Galatians 6:2), which includes many of the same moral commands. Calvin stressed that the new covenant God promised would write the same law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). All agree that Jesus shows what the Law really meant and that the sacrifices are ended in him; mainstream churches agree that Christians are not bound by the food laws.

b: Matthew 5:17 and 7:12 frame the main body of the Sermon: both speak of ‘the Law and the Prophets’. Everything in between explains what it means to fulfil them. Later Jesus sums them up in two commands: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself (22:37–40).

Paul says that faith does not ‘nullify the law’; ‘we uphold the law’ (Romans 3:31). He also says that ‘Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes’ (Romans 10:4). The word ‘end’ can mean goal as well as finish. Jesus is both: the goal the Law was heading for, and the end of the Law as a way of being right with God.

l.t: The Golden Rule is ‘the essence of the Law and the Prophets’: the other bookend of the Sermon.
All the Law and the Prophets hang on love for God and neighbour.
Jesus’ critique of the scribes and Pharisees: outward care, inward neglect.
It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to drop out.
Faith upholds the law; the Spirit fulfils its righteous standard in believers.
Christ is the end (goal) of the law for righteousness.
The Law was a shadow; Christ’s one sacrifice fulfils it.
The new covenant: the law written on the heart.

qs: What does it mean that Jesus ‘fulfils’ the Law and the Prophets? Can you think of examples?
What was wrong with the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, given how hard they worked at obedience?
How can a Christian take God’s commands seriously without falling into a rule-keeping religion?

5.ctx: This is the first of six examples (5:21–48), each beginning ‘You have heard that it was said… But I tell you’. ‘Do not murder’ is one of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:13; the sixth in the usual Protestant numbering). Local Jewish courts dealt with serious cases; the Sanhedrin was the highest Jewish council, in Jerusalem. Offerings were brought to the altar in the temple.
5.mean: Jesus begins his six examples with the commandment everyone thinks they have kept: ‘Do not murder.’ The scribes taught that a murderer would face the court. Jesus goes beneath the act to where it starts. Anyone who is angry with his brother will face judgement. Anyone who insults him with ‘Raca’ (an Aramaic word meaning roughly ‘empty-head’ or ‘worthless’) will face the highest court. Anyone who says ‘You fool!’ will face the fire of hell. Jesus is not making a new legal code with three levels of punishment. He is showing that anger and contempt are murder in seed form, and God sees the seed. Cain was angry before he killed Abel (Genesis 4:5–8). John says, ‘Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer’ (1 John 3:15). Then Jesus gives two pictures of what to do instead. First, if you are in the middle of worship and remember that someone has something against you, stop. Leave your gift, go and make peace, then come back. Putting things right with people matters more to God than religious ceremony. Second, if someone is taking you to court, settle with them quickly on the way, before it is too late. Many think this also points to a greater judgement: do not wait until you stand before God to deal with what is wrong. The person whose righteousness exceeds that of the Pharisees (5:20) does not just avoid violence; he takes the first step to end a quarrel, even when the other person is the one with the grievance.
5.big: God judges anger and contempt, not only murder, so Jesus’ followers must hurry to make peace with those they have wronged.

vv.h: You have heard that it was said to the ancients
b: Most of Jesus’ hearers could not read; they ‘heard’ the Law read and explained in the synagogue. ‘It was said’ refers to God’s command given at Sinai to the generation of Moses (‘the ancients’), together with the way it was being taught. The first half here is the commandment itself; ‘anyone who murders will be subject to judgment’ is a summary of the Law’s penalty (compare Exodus 21:12).

vv.h: But I tell you
b: Prophets said, ‘This is what the LORD says.’ Rabbis quoted earlier rabbis. Jesus simply says, ‘I tell you’, six times in this chapter. He does not contradict the commandment; he shows its full depth, and he does it on his own authority. No wonder the crowds were astonished (7:28–29).

vv.h: angry with his brother … ‘Raca’ … ‘You fool!’
b: ‘Brother’ here means a fellow member of God’s people. Some later manuscripts add ‘without cause’ (BSB footnote), probably to soften the saying; the earliest manuscripts do not have it. The New Testament does recognise anger at real evil (Mark 3:5; Ephesians 4:26), but it warns that ‘man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires’ (James 1:20). Jesus is targeting the anger that holds a grudge and despises.

‘Raca’ was a common insult. ‘Fool’ was worse. Quarles points out that in Matthew ‘fool’ describes someone outside the kingdom (7:26; 25:2–3): to call a brother ‘fool’ in this sense is to write him off, to treat him as damned. Jesus says that such contempt puts the speaker himself in danger of hell.

vv.h: the fire of hell
b: The Greek is literally ‘the Gehenna of fire’ (BSB footnote). Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom, outside Jerusalem, where some kings of Judah had burned children as sacrifices (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6; Jeremiah 7:31; 2 Kings 23:10). It became a picture of God’s final judgement. Jesus speaks of hell more than anyone else in the New Testament, and always as a warning to be taken with complete seriousness (5:29–30; 10:28; 18:9; 23:33).

vv.h: leave your gift there before the altar
b: Imagine a Galilean pilgrim who has travelled for days to Jerusalem with an animal for sacrifice, and is standing at the altar when he remembers a broken relationship. Jesus says: leave it there and go. The Law already required someone who had wronged a neighbour to put it right before bringing an offering (Leviticus 6:1–7; Numbers 5:5–8). God has always said that worship from a heart at war with others is hollow (Isaiah 1:11–17; Hosea 6:6).

Notice who has the grievance: ‘your brother has something against you’. Jesus tells the one who has caused the offence, or is thought to have, to take the first step. He does not wait for the other person to come to him.

vv.h: Reconcile quickly with your adversary
b: On the surface this is wise advice for anyone in debt: settle out of court, or you may end up in prison until you have paid ‘the last penny’ (the smallest Roman coin). In the flow of Jesus’ teaching it also points to God’s judgement. Do not put off dealing with sin and broken relationships, because a day is coming when it will be too late.

Jesus’ teaching here is the pattern for the whole New Testament on relationships between believers. Paul writes, ‘If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone’ (Romans 12:18), and ‘Do not let the sun set upon your anger’ (Ephesians 4:26). Jesus himself gives a step-by-step pattern for dealing with a brother who sins against you (18:15–17).

Behind it all is the gospel. God did not wait for his enemies to come to him: ‘when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son’ (Romans 5:10). People who have been reconciled to God become reconcilers (2 Corinthians 5:18–20). The peacemakers of 5:9 are the people who leave their gift at the altar and go.

l.t: ‘You shall not murder’: the sixth commandment.
Cain’s anger leads to the first murder.
Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.
Restitution to a wronged neighbour comes before the guilt offering.
How to go to a brother who has sinned against you.
Be slow to anger; human anger does not produce God’s righteousness.
Be angry yet do not sin; put away bitterness; forgive as God forgave you.
God reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.

qs: Why does Jesus treat anger and contempt so seriously? How are they related to murder?
Is there any kind of anger that is right? How can we tell the difference?
Is there anyone you need to go and be reconciled with? What would the first step be?

5.ctx: ‘Do not commit adultery’ is the commandment after it (Exodus 20:14). The tenth commandment already forbade coveting a neighbour’s wife (Exodus 20:17). For Jesus’ hearers the right eye and right hand were the most valued, the ones you could least spare.
5.mean: The second example takes the seventh commandment. Many thought that as long as they did not actually sleep with someone else’s wife, they had kept it. Jesus says that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. He is not talking about noticing that someone is attractive, or about a passing temptation, which even Jesus faced (Hebrews 4:15). He means looking in order to desire, deliberately feeding a fantasy. The commandment against coveting a neighbour’s wife already pointed this way (Exodus 20:17). Then Jesus uses deliberately shocking language. If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out. If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off. Better to lose one part of your body than for your whole body to go to hell. Jesus is not telling anyone to injure themselves; a blind man can still lust. He is using exaggeration, as teachers often did, to show how seriously we should take sin. Whatever leads us into sin, however precious it seems, must go: a habit, a website, a friendship, a way of spending time. Stopping sin at the source is costly, but the alternative is far worse. Jesus speaks to men here, in a culture where men held most of the power, but the principle applies to everyone. And for those who already feel guilty, the rest of the Gospel holds out hope: Jesus came to save his people from their sins (1:21).
5.big: Jesus says that lust in the heart is already adultery before God, and calls his followers to take drastic action against anything that leads them into sin.

vv.h: anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her
b: The Greek phrase means looking ‘with a view to’ desiring her. It is the deliberate, continued gaze, the kind of look David gave Bathsheba from his roof (2 Samuel 11:2). Job said, ‘I have made a covenant with my eyes. How then could I gaze with desire at a virgin?’ (Job 31:1). Quarles points out that Jesus’ words echo the tenth commandment, which uses the same verb in the Greek Old Testament for coveting a neighbour’s wife (Exodus 20:17).

vv.h: has already committed adultery with her in his heart
b: In the Bible the heart is where actions begin (15:19). Jesus does not say that lust is as harmful to others as adultery, but that before God it is the same sin in seed form. This is humbling: by this standard nobody can claim to have kept the commandment perfectly. The Sermon drives us to need mercy, and to seek a new heart.

vv.h: If your right eye causes you to sin, gouge it out
b: This is hyperbole, deliberate exaggeration to make a point, like the camel and the eye of a needle (19:24) or the beam in the eye (7:3). The eye and hand do not cause sin on their own; the heart does (15:19). The point is to take radical, costly action against whatever leads us to sin.
‘Causes you to sin’ is literally ‘makes you stumble’ or ‘trips you up’. Jesus repeats the picture in 18:8–9, in a passage that begins with warnings against causing others to stumble (18:6–7).

mis.t: Some readers have taken Jesus’ words about cutting off parts of the body literally.
mis.b: The New Bible Dictionary calls it ‘tragic’ that some in history took these sayings literally. The most famous case concerns a similar saying: Eusebius records that the young Origen took Matthew 19:12 ‘in too literal and extreme a sense’ and mutilated himself. The main Christian traditions read the eye and hand sayings as vivid exaggeration. The point is not self-harm, which cannot change the heart, but decisive action against what leads us into sin.

b: Jesus’ high view of sexual faithfulness flows from God’s design for marriage, which he will explain in 19:4–6: ‘the two will become one flesh’. Paul gives the same teaching to Christians in Corinth (1 Corinthians 6:12–20), and he too speaks of radical action: ‘Flee from sexual immorality’ (1 Corinthians 6:18). In Colossians he says, ‘Put to death’ what belongs to your earthly nature (Colossians 3:5).

The answer to lust is not only to cut out what tempts us but to be filled with something better. The Spirit produces self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), and the pure in heart are promised that they will see God (5:8).

l.t: The commandment against adultery, quoted in verse 27.
Do not covet your neighbour’s wife: echoed in verse 28.
Job’s covenant with his eyes.
David looks at Bathsheba from his roof, and lust leads to adultery and murder.
The same sayings, set in a warning about causing others to stumble.
Mark’s version: better to enter life maimed than to be thrown into hell.
Flee sexual immorality; your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
Put to death what belongs to your earthly nature.
Desire conceives and gives birth to sin.

qs: Where does Jesus say adultery begins? How does that change the way we think about purity?
What would it mean in practice today to ‘cut off’ what causes us to stumble?
How can Christians help each other in this area without shame, and how does the gospel give hope to those who have failed?

5.ctx: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 regulated divorce by requiring a written certificate, which protected a divorced woman and let her remarry. In Jesus’ day Jewish teachers argued about the grounds. The school of Shammai allowed divorce only for sexual unfaithfulness; the school of Hillel allowed it for almost anything, even a spoiled meal (Mishnah, Gittin 9:10). In Jewish law only a husband could issue a divorce, and a divorced woman often had to remarry to survive.
5.mean: The third example concerns divorce. People quoted Moses: ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’ Some used this to treat divorce as easy, as long as the paperwork was done. But Moses’ law did not command divorce; it limited the damage when it happened. Jesus goes back behind it to God’s purpose. Anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, brings adultery upon her. In that society a divorced woman usually had to remarry to survive. So a husband who sent her away without just cause pushed her into a new marriage that God did not recognise, because in God’s eyes the first marriage still stood. And the man who married her also committed adultery. Jesus takes marriage far more seriously than his hearers did. Marriage is not a contract to be ended when it suits the husband; it is a covenant before God. Jesus names one exception, sexual immorality (see Where readings differ for how churches understand it). Even then, he does not command divorce. In 19:3–9 he gives a longer explanation: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh, so ‘what God has joined together, let man not separate’. Moses allowed divorce only ‘because of your hardness of heart’. Notice that in a world where husbands held the power, Jesus’ teaching protected wives. Christians apply this teaching in different ways, and the pastoral situations are often painful (see Where readings differ).
5.big: Jesus restores God’s purpose for marriage as a lifelong covenant and protects the vulnerable from careless divorce.

vv.h: Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce
b: This summarises Deuteronomy 24:1. The certificate protected the woman: it proved she was free to remarry and could not be accused of adultery. The debate in Jesus’ day was over the phrase ‘some indecency’ in that verse. Shammai’s followers read it narrowly; Hillel’s read it so widely that almost any reason would do (Mishnah, Gittin 9:10). In 19:3 the Pharisees ask Jesus to take sides: ‘Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?’

vv.h: except for sexual immorality
b: The Greek word is porneia, a broad word for sexual sin, including adultery. Matthew alone records this exception (here and 19:9); Mark and Luke give the saying without it (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18). Most Protestants understand that Matthew makes explicit what Jesus’ hearers would assume, since adultery itself broke the marriage. Calvin wrote that ‘the woman, who has basely violated the marriage-vow, is justly cast off’. Others read the exception more narrowly (see Where readings differ).

vv.h: brings adultery upon her
b: The BSB footnote gives an alternative: ‘causes her to commit adultery’. The point is not that the innocent wife is guilty, but that the husband who divorces her unjustly is responsible for the situation he creates. The prophet Malachi had already said that God hates the kind of divorce in which a husband has ‘broken faith’ with ‘the wife of your youth’, his wife ‘by covenant’ (Malachi 2:14–16).

5.diff: The exception clause (here and 19:9) appears only in Matthew. Reformed and most Protestant churches read it as permitting divorce, and remarriage of the innocent party, for adultery; the Westminster Confession also allows divorce for wilful desertion that cannot be remedied (24.5–6; compare 1 Corinthians 7:15). Between the baptized, Catholic teaching holds that ‘a ratified and consummated marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power or for any reason other than death’ (Catechism 2382), and it does not read the exception as permitting remarriage; some Catholic scholars take porneia to mean a marriage that was unlawful from the start. Some Protestant scholars (for example Heth and Wenham in Jesus and Divorce) hold that Jesus allows no remarriage after divorce while the first spouse lives. The Orthodox Church opposes divorce but, as pastoral concession, ‘does permit divorced individuals to marry a second and even a third time’, with a service that ‘bears a penitential character’ (Orthodox Church in America). See also the notes on Mark 10:1 and Matthew 19:1.

b: Jesus’ teaching here is brief; the fuller discussion comes in 19:3–12, where he roots marriage in creation (Genesis 1:27; 2:24). Paul adds guidance for a situation Jesus did not address: a believer married to an unbeliever who leaves (1 Corinthians 7:10–16).

Throughout Scripture, marriage is also a picture of God’s covenant faithfulness. God speaks of Israel as his wife, and though she was unfaithful he did not abandon her for ever (Hosea 2:14–20). Paul says that Christian marriage reflects Christ’s love for the church (Ephesians 5:25–32). Faithfulness in marriage is a small picture of the faithfulness of God.

l.t: The law of the certificate of divorce.
Jesus’ fuller teaching on marriage and divorce.
Mark’s account, without the exception.
Luke’s short version of the saying.
God hates divorce in which a husband breaks faith with the wife of his youth.
Paul’s guidance on separation and on marriages to unbelievers.
Marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.
God’s faithfulness to his unfaithful people.

qs: What was the debate about divorce in Jesus’ day, and how does Jesus’ answer compare with both sides?
How did Jesus’ teaching protect women in his culture?
How can a church uphold Jesus’ high view of marriage while caring well for those who have been through divorce?

5.ctx: The Law forbade swearing falsely by God’s name (Leviticus 19:12) and required people to keep their vows (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23). By Jesus’ day some taught that an oath was binding only if it used God’s name, so people swore ‘by heaven’ or ‘by Jerusalem’ to sound serious while leaving themselves a way out (compare 23:16–22).
5.mean: The fourth example is about telling the truth. The saying people had heard, ‘Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord’, sums up several Old Testament laws. Quarles calls it a paraphrase of Leviticus 19:12, Numbers 30:2 and Deuteronomy 23:21–23. The trouble was what people did with it. They invented a scale of oaths. Swearing by God’s name was binding, but swearing by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem or by your own head was not, so you could sound solemn and still wriggle out. Jesus shuts every escape route. Heaven is God’s throne. The earth is his footstool. Jerusalem is the city of the great King. Even your own head is not really yours: you cannot make a single hair white or black. Everything you might swear by belongs to God, so every oath involves him. Then Jesus goes further: do not swear at all. Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No’. The need for oaths at all shows that people often lie; if we always told the truth, our plain word would be enough. ‘Anything more comes from the evil one’, the devil, whom Jesus calls ‘a liar and the father of lies’ (John 8:44). Jesus’ followers should be so honest that their word needs no extra guarantee. Whether this means Christians may never take an oath, for example in court, is a question on which churches differ (see Where readings differ).
5.big: Jesus’ followers should be so truthful that their plain ‘yes’ or ‘no’ can be trusted without any oath.

vv.h: Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord
b: An oath called God (or something sacred) to witness that you were telling the truth. A vow was a promise to God to do something. The Law took both seriously: ‘he must not break his word; he must do everything he has promised’ (Numbers 30:2). It also said that you did not have to make vows at all: ‘if you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin’ (Deuteronomy 23:22). Jesus’ teaching builds on that.

vv.h: by heaven … by the earth … by Jerusalem … by your head
b: Jesus draws on Isaiah 66:1 (‘Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool’) and Psalm 48:2 (Jerusalem, ‘the city of the great King’). In 23:16–22 he exposes the hair-splitting in more detail: some said swearing by the temple meant nothing, but swearing by the gold of the temple was binding. Calvin observed that ‘God condemned in the law not only acts of perjury, but lightness in swearing’.

vv.h: Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’
b: James repeats this almost word for word: ‘Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no, so that you will not fall under judgment’ (James 5:12). It is one of the clearest echoes of the Sermon in the rest of the New Testament. ‘The evil one’ may also be translated ‘evil’ (BSB footnote); either way, the need to bolster our words comes from a world where lying is normal.

5.diff: May Christians take oaths? The Anabaptist Schleitheim Confession (1527) held that Christ ‘prohibits all swearing’, and Mennonites and Quakers have refused oaths, affirming instead. Most churches hold that Jesus forbade casual or evasive swearing, not solemn oaths in court: Calvin pointed to the examples that follow, which show the target was ‘circuitous or indirect ways of swearing’; the Westminster Confession calls a lawful oath part of religious worship (22.1–2); and the Catholic Catechism says Jesus’ words do not exclude ‘oaths made for grave and right reasons (for example, in court)’ (2154). Jesus himself answered under oath at his trial (26:63–64), and Paul called God as witness (2 Corinthians 1:23). UK courts allow anyone to affirm instead of swearing.

b: Truthfulness reflects the character of God, ‘who cannot lie’ (Titus 1:2; compare Numbers 23:19). When God made promises to Abraham he swore by himself, ‘since He had no one greater to swear by’ (Hebrews 6:13). His word is utterly reliable. People who belong to him are called to be like him: ‘Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor’ (Ephesians 4:25).

Paul could say that his message was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ at the same time, because ‘all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ’ (2 Corinthians 1:18–20). Christian honesty rests on the faithfulness of God.

l.t: Do not swear falsely by God’s name.
Whoever makes a vow must keep his word.
Keep your vows; but there is no sin in not vowing.
Heaven is God’s throne and the earth his footstool.
Jesus exposes the hair-splitting over oaths.
Let your yes be yes and your no, no.
All God’s promises are ‘Yes’ in Christ.
Put off falsehood and speak truthfully.

qs: Why did people in Jesus’ day swear by heaven or Jerusalem instead of by God?
What are modern ways of making our words sound more reliable than they are?
What would it look like for our ‘yes’ to mean yes, at work, at home and in church commitments?

5.ctx: ‘Eye for eye’ is the law of equal justice in Exodus 21:24, Leviticus 24:19–20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. It was given to judges, to make punishment fit the crime and to stop revenge spiralling out of control. Soldiers and officials could press civilians into carrying loads, as Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry Jesus’ cross (27:32). A Roman mile was about 1,480 metres (BSB footnote).
5.mean: The fifth example takes a law that was meant for courts and shows what it means for personal life. ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth’ was a just and merciful law: it set a limit, so that punishment matched the wrong and no more. But people used it to excuse personal revenge: ‘He hit me, so I can hit him back.’ Jesus tells us ‘not to resist an evil person’, meaning do not take revenge or pay back evil with evil. Then he gives four pictures. If someone slaps you on the right cheek (probably a backhanded slap, an insult rather than an attack on your life), turn the other cheek. If someone sues you for your tunic, the inner garment, let him have your cloak too, the outer garment the Law said a poor man could keep overnight (Exodus 22:26–27). If someone forces you to carry a load for a mile (Roman soldiers often did), go two. Give to those who ask and lend to those who want to borrow. Each picture is about giving up your rights rather than standing on them. These are vivid examples, not a complete rulebook. Jesus is not saying that evil does not matter, or that society should have no police or courts; Paul says the state ‘does not carry the sword in vain’ (Romans 13:4). He is speaking to individuals about their own response to personal wrongs. Most Christians read it this way; the Anabaptist tradition reads it more strictly (see Where readings differ). And he lived it: when he was struck and mocked, ‘He did not retaliate’ (1 Peter 2:23). The disciple refuses to be ruled by revenge, and trusts God, the just Judge, to put things right.
5.big: Jesus calls his followers to give up personal revenge, absorbing wrongs and returning good for evil, as he himself did.

vv.h: Eye for eye and tooth for tooth
b: This law is sometimes called the lex talionis, Latin for ‘law of retaliation’. It is often misunderstood as harsh, but it was a big step forward from blood feuds, in which a family might kill many people to avenge one. Quarles notes that it was a principle for judges deciding cases, not permission for personal revenge. Even the Old Testament warned against that: ‘Do not say, “I will do to him as he has done to me”’ (Proverbs 24:29; compare Leviticus 19:18).

vv.h: not to resist an evil person
b: Calvin observed: ‘There are two ways of resisting’, and ‘The present subject is retaliation.’ The context is personal injury and insult. Jesus himself challenged the high priest’s servant who struck him unjustly (John 18:22–23), and Paul appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25; 25:11). So ‘do not resist’ does not mean ‘never speak up’. It means do not repay evil with evil (Romans 12:17–21).

vv.h: If someone slaps you on your right cheek
b: Most people are right-handed, so a blow to the right cheek was probably a backhanded slap, a deliberate insult. Jesus is not describing a violent attack on your life, but the kind of humiliation that makes us want to hit back. Turning the other cheek means refusing to answer insult with insult.

vv.h: your cloak as well … go with him two miles
b: A poor man might own only two garments. The Law protected his cloak: if he gave it as a pledge, it had to be returned by sunset, because it was his blanket (Exodus 22:26–27). Jesus says to give up even what the Law guaranteed you. The ‘mile’ refers to the common practice of soldiers and officials pressing civilians into service, as Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry Jesus’ cross (27:32); the same Greek verb is used there. Instead of resenting it, the disciple goes further than required.

vv.h: Give to the one who asks you
b: The Law commanded generous lending to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7–11). Jesus asks for a generous, open-handed spirit. This does not mean giving whatever anyone asks regardless of harm; elsewhere Scripture says that those unwilling to work should not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). But it rules out a tight-fisted heart (compare 6:22–23).

5.diff: Non-resistance and war. The Anabaptist tradition reads verse 39 as forbidding Christians to use force: the sword is ‘ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ’ (Schleitheim, 1527); Mennonites and Quakers are pacifist. Most churches hold that Jesus forbids personal revenge, not the state’s duty to punish wrongdoers and defend the innocent (Romans 13:4). The Westminster Confession allows magistrates to wage war ‘upon just and necessary occasion’ (23.2), and the Catholic Catechism sets out strict just-war conditions (2309). Calvin noted that a believer may still go to court for a just cause.

b: Paul’s teaching in Romans 12:14–21 is an extended comment on this passage: bless those who persecute you, do not repay evil for evil, leave room for God’s wrath, feed your enemy, ‘overcome evil with good’. Peter applies it to Christian slaves treated unjustly, pointing to Jesus as the example (1 Peter 2:18–24).

The cross is the ultimate turning of the other cheek. Jesus was struck, stripped and forced along the road. He did not retaliate, and prayed, ‘Father, forgive them’ (Luke 23:34). Yet the cross is not weakness: by it Jesus defeated evil. The disciple who refuses revenge is not passive; he is trusting God to judge justly and choosing to overcome evil with good.

l.t: Eye for eye: the law of equal justice for judges.
Do not say, ‘I will do to him as he has done to me.’
A poor man’s cloak must be returned by sunset.
Luke’s version of turning the other cheek.
Do not repay evil for evil; overcome evil with good.
Christ did not retaliate but entrusted himself to God.
The state is God’s servant to punish wrongdoing.
The Servant: ‘I offered My back to those who struck Me.’

qs: What was the ‘eye for eye’ law originally for, and how had people misused it?
What do the four pictures (cheek, cloak, mile, giving) have in common?
Where are you tempted to stand on your rights or pay someone back? What would going the second mile look like?

5.ctx: ‘Love your neighbor’ comes from Leviticus 19:18. The words ‘hate your enemy’ are not in the Old Testament; they summarise how some people limited ‘neighbour’ to their own people. Tax collectors worked for the Romans or for Herod and were despised as traitors and cheats. ‘Gentiles’ means non-Jews.
5.mean: The sixth and last example reaches the height of Jesus’ teaching. The Law said, ‘Love your neighbor’. Some had added, in practice if not in words, ‘and hate your enemy’, treating ‘neighbour’ as meaning only people like us. Quarles notes that the Law itself told Israel to love the foreigner living among them (Leviticus 19:34). Jesus says, ‘Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.’ This is love as action and choice, not warm feelings. You cannot pray sincerely for someone and keep hating them. Why love like this? So that you may be ‘sons of your Father in heaven’, showing the family likeness. God sends sunshine and rain on good and evil people alike. He gives good gifts to people who ignore and oppose him. Jesus then makes the point sharper. If you love only those who love you, what is special about that? Even tax collectors do the same. If you greet only your own people, so do pagans. God’s children are called to do ‘more’ than others, to love as God loves. Then the summary of the whole section: ‘Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.’ ‘Perfect’ here means complete, whole, undivided. In context it means love that has no limits, love that includes enemies, because God’s love is like that. Paul says God showed his love for us ‘while we were still sinners’ (Romans 5:8). This is the greater righteousness of 5:20. No one achieves it alone, but it is the goal toward which God’s Spirit is leading every child of his.
5.big: God’s children are to love even their enemies, as their Father does, aiming at the complete, undivided love that reflects his character.

vv.h: ‘Love your neighbor’ and ‘Hate your enemy’
b: Leviticus 19:18 says, ‘love your neighbor as yourself’; the context speaks of ‘your people’, but the same chapter commands love for the foreigner (Leviticus 19:33–34). Some groups did teach hatred of outsiders: one of the Dead Sea Scrolls (the Community Rule, 1QS 1:9–10) tells members to hate those it calls the sons of darkness. When a lawyer later asked Jesus, ‘And who is my neighbor?’, Jesus answered with the parable of the good Samaritan, in which the neighbour is a hated foreigner (Luke 10:29–37).

vv.h: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you
b: Love in the New Testament (agapē) is self-giving care for another’s good. It is something you do, not only something you feel. Prayer is where it starts. Jesus did this from the cross (Luke 23:34), and Stephen did it as he was stoned: ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them’ (Acts 7:60). The Old Testament already pointed this way: ‘If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat’ (Proverbs 25:21).

vv.h: He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good
b: Theologians call this God’s ‘common grace’: the good gifts he gives to all people, believers or not (Psalm 145:9; Acts 14:17). Every sunrise is a reminder that God is kind to his enemies. People who belong to him should be the same. ‘Sons of your Father’ means sharing his character, like the peacemakers in 5:9.

vv.h: Do not even tax collectors do the same?
b: Jesus uses two groups his hearers looked down on: tax collectors and Gentiles. Even they love their own friends. Ordinary human kindness only goes so far. Disciples are to do ‘more’, the same word that lies behind ‘exceeds’ in 5:20. Matthew himself had been a tax collector (9:9), and Jesus would be mocked as ‘a friend of tax collectors and sinners’ (11:19).

vv.h: Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect
b: The word teleios means complete, mature, whole. Quarles notes that the verse blends Leviticus 19:2 (‘Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy’) with Deuteronomy 18:13 (‘You must be blameless before the LORD your God’), where the Greek Old Testament uses the same word. Luke’s parallel says, ‘Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful’ (Luke 6:36). In context the perfection is above all a love that leaves no one out.

Calvin wrote: ‘This perfection does not mean equality, but relates solely to resemblance.’ We will never be God, but we are called to resemble him. Wesley read the verse as a promise as well as a command, part of his teaching that God can fill the believer with perfect love. Christians differ on how far this can be reached in this life (see Where readings differ), but all agree that it is the goal.

5.diff: ‘Be perfect’. Calvin: this ‘does not mean equality, but relates solely to resemblance’; the Reformed tradition holds that perfection is the goal toward which believers grow, but is not reached in this life (Westminster Confession 13.2). Wesley saw the command also as a promise, part of his teaching on Christian perfection: a heart made perfect in love, though not free from mistakes. The Catholic Catechism cites the verse for the universal call to holiness: all Christians are called ‘to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity’ (2013).

b: This is the heart of the gospel turned into a way of life. God loved his enemies: ‘God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us’ (Romans 5:8). The command to love enemies is not a burden laid on people who have never been loved; it is the overflow of having been loved by God while we were against him.

John draws the same line from God’s love to ours: ‘Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another’ (1 John 4:11). And Jesus gives a new command at the Last Supper: ‘As I have loved you, so you also must love one another’ (John 13:34).

l.t: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’.
Love the foreigner as yourself.
If your enemy is hungry, give him food.
Luke’s version: ‘Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.’
The good Samaritan: who is my neighbour?
Bless those who persecute you; feed your enemy.
Christ died for us while we were God’s enemies.
Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy.

qs: How had people narrowed the command to love their neighbour? Do we do something similar?
What does God’s sending of sun and rain on everyone teach us about his character?
Who is hard for you to love? What would it mean to pray for them this week?

6.ctx: Giving to the poor, prayer and fasting were the three great acts of devotion in first-century Judaism (compare Tobit 12:8 in the Apocrypha). The Law commanded generosity to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7–11). The temple and synagogues had collection chests for gifts.
6.mean: Chapter 5 described what the greater righteousness does. Chapter 6 asks why we do it. Jesus begins with a warning that covers the whole section: be careful not to do your righteous acts in front of people in order to be seen by them. If you do, you will have no reward from your Father. Jesus takes three examples, giving, prayer and fasting, and treats each the same way: do not do it like the hypocrites, to be admired; do it in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you. First, giving. Jesus takes it for granted that his followers will give to the poor; the question is how. Some made a show of it. ‘Do not sound a trumpet before you’ is probably a vivid way of saying ‘do not draw attention to yourself’. People like that get exactly what they wanted, the applause of others, and that is all they get. Scholars note that the verb in ‘they already have their full reward’ was used on business receipts to mean ‘paid in full’. Instead, give so quietly that your left hand does not know what your right hand is doing. This is a picture, not a rule about bookkeeping: do not even congratulate yourself. Is this a contradiction of 5:16, ‘let your light shine before men’? No. Our good deeds will often be seen, and that is fine, as long as the aim is God’s glory and not our own. The real question is the motive. And notice the promise. God sees what is done in secret, and he will reward it. Jesus does not ask us to stop wanting a reward, only to want the right one, from the right person.
6.big: Do good deeds, including giving, for God’s eyes and not for applause; the Father who sees in secret will reward his children.

vv.h: your righteous acts
b: Some later manuscripts read ‘charitable acts’ or ‘alms’ here (BSB footnote), but ‘righteousness’ is the better-supported reading and covers all three examples. The word links back to 5:20: the greater righteousness is not only deeper in what it does but purer in why it does it. Quarles notes that Jesus’ concern is motive, not location; good deeds done in public are fine (5:16), as long as they are not done to be seen.

vv.h: as the hypocrites do
b: ‘Hypocrite’ comes from the Greek word for an actor in the theatre, someone who wore a mask and played a part. Quarles notes that many actors lived for the applause of the crowd. Religious hypocrites are performers too: their giving is a show for an audience. Jesus uses the word more often in Matthew than in any other Gospel.

Some think ‘sound a trumpet’ refers to the trumpet-shaped collection boxes in the temple, which rattled when coins were thrown in. Quarles thinks this unlikely, since Jesus also mentions the streets, and takes it as a picture of drawing attention to yourself in any way.

vv.h: they already have their full reward
b: Scholars note that the verb was used on receipts to mean ‘paid in full’. The hypocrite gets what he was after, the admiration of people, and there is nothing more to come. Psalm 115:1 gives the opposite attitude: ‘Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory’.

vv.h: do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing
b: A humorous picture. Quarles takes it to mean keeping your giving secret even from yourself: not patting yourself on the back. Paul says, ‘God loves a cheerful giver’ (2 Corinthians 9:7), and Proverbs says, ‘Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender’ (Proverbs 19:17). The reward is not money in return, but God’s approval and the joys of his kingdom (compare 19:29; 25:21, 34–40).

Jesus repeats the same pattern three times in 6:1–18 (giving, prayer, fasting). Each time there is the wrong way, ‘as the hypocrites do’, their reward, ‘they already have their full reward’, the right way, in secret, and God’s reward, ‘your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you’. The repetition makes the point unforgettable.

The New Testament speaks freely of rewards (5:12; 10:41–42; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). They are not wages that earn salvation, which is God’s free gift, but the generous Father’s delight in the faithfulness of his children. The heart of the reward Jesus promises is the Father’s own approval and presence (compare 25:21, ‘Enter into the joy of your master’).

l.t: Be openhanded toward your poor brother.
Not to us, O LORD, but to your name be the glory.
The scribes and Pharisees do all their deeds to be seen.
The widow who gave two small coins, all she had.
Cornelius’s prayers and gifts to the poor rise as a memorial before God.
God loves a cheerful giver.
Whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me.

qs: What is the difference between letting our light shine (5:16) and doing righteous acts to be seen (6:1)?
Why is applause such a powerful motive, even in church life?
What could secret giving look like for you? How would you know if your motives were right?
