6.ctx: Devout Jews prayed at set times each day, often standing, and the synagogue was the centre of community prayer. ‘Pagans’ means non-Jews who worshipped other gods; their prayers often heaped up names and titles of the gods, or repeated formulas thought to have power.
6.mean: The second example is prayer, and Jesus warns against two opposite mistakes. The first is the mistake of the hypocrites. They love to pray standing up in the synagogues and on street corners, so that people will see them. Prayer has become a performance, aimed at an audience in the room rather than God. They get what they wanted, a reputation for holiness, and nothing more. Instead, says Jesus, go into your inner room, shut the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. The ‘inner room’ was the storeroom, often the only room in a house with a door. Jesus is not forbidding prayer together; he prayed with his disciples, and the prayer he teaches begins ‘Our Father’. He is saying that the heart of prayer is private, honest conversation with God. The second mistake is that of the pagans. They babble on, thinking they will be heard because of their many words, as if God had to be informed, flattered or worn down. The prophets of Baal shouted from morning until noon (1 Kings 18:26–29). Do not be like them, says Jesus, because your Father knows what you need before you ask him. Then why pray at all? Because prayer is not giving God information he lacks. It is a child speaking to a Father who already knows and cares, learning to trust him, and receiving what he loves to give. Long prayers are not wrong; Jesus sometimes prayed all night (Luke 6:12). What is wrong is thinking that words, by themselves, make God listen.
6.big: Prayer is not a performance for others or a technique to move God, but honest trust in a Father who sees in secret and knows what we need.

vv.h: they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners
b: Standing was a normal posture for prayer (Mark 11:25), and praying at set hours could mean being caught in the street when the time came. Jesus is not criticising posture or place, but the love of being seen. Quarles notes that the hypocrites chose the busiest places on purpose. Compare the Pharisee in Luke’s parable who ‘stood by himself and prayed’ about how good he was (Luke 18:11).

vv.h: go into your inner room, shut your door
b: Jesus may be echoing Isaiah 26:20 (‘enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you’), though there the point is shelter. The ‘inner room’ is a private place where no one will see. Quarles suggests the point is to avoid impressing even your own family. Jesus himself often withdrew to pray alone (14:23; Mark 1:35).

vv.h: do not babble on like pagans
b: The Greek word is unusual, possibly imitating the sound of meaningless repetition, like ‘blah blah’. Quarles notes that pagans piled up titles of their gods to win their favour, and that the Roman writer Seneca complained of people ‘fatiguing the gods’ with their prayers (as quoted by Quarles). The Old Testament already warned: ‘God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few’ (Ecclesiastes 5:2). Stott sums up the two errors: hypocrisy is a misuse of the purpose of prayer, and verbosity a misuse of its nature.

vv.h: your Father knows what you need before you ask Him
b: This is the reason for confident, simple prayer. God does not need persuading; he is already a loving Father. Calvin wrote that in prayer two things give us confidence, God’s ‘fatherly love toward us, and his boundless power’. Prayer changes us: it trains us to depend on God and to want what he wants.

Jesus’ teaching on prayer is spread through Matthew: pray for those who persecute you (5:44), ask, seek and knock (7:7–11), pray for workers for the harvest (9:38), agree together in prayer (18:19–20), pray with faith (21:22), and ‘watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation’ (26:41). In Gethsemane we see him pray, alone and in anguish, to his Father (26:36–46).

Paul’s great teaching on prayer stands on the same foundation: because God is our Father, we can pray with confidence and without anxiety (Philippians 4:6–7), and when we do not know what to pray, ‘the Spirit Himself intercedes for us’ (Romans 8:26).

l.t: ‘Enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you’.
God is in heaven and you are on earth; let your words be few.
The prophets of Baal shout for hours, but no one answers.
The Pharisee and the tax collector at prayer.
Jesus prays alone early in the morning.
The Spirit helps us in our weakness when we pray.
Do not be anxious; present your requests to God with thanksgiving.

qs: What two wrong approaches to prayer does Jesus warn against here?
If God already knows what we need, why should we pray?
What helps you to pray honestly and privately? What gets in the way?

6.ctx: Luke gives a shorter form of the prayer, taught when a disciple asked, ‘Lord, teach us to pray’ (Luke 11:1–4). Jewish prayers also praised God’s name and prayed for his kingdom: Quarles cites the Kaddish, a prayer whose core many scholars think is ancient, which asks God to let his kingdom rule ‘speedily and soon’. The closing doxology, words of praise (‘For Yours is the kingdom…’), is not in the earliest manuscripts (BSB footnote).
6.mean: Having warned against showy and wordy prayer, Jesus gives a model. ‘This is how you should pray’ means ‘pray like this’; it is a pattern as well as a prayer to say. It is short, simple and full of meaning. It begins ‘Our Father in heaven’. We come as children to a Father who loves us, and ‘in heaven’ reminds us that he is great, holy and able to help. ‘Our’ reminds us that we pray as a family. Then come six requests (some traditions, following Augustine, count seven). The first three are about God. ‘Hallowed be your name’ asks that God will be honoured as holy, in our lives and in the whole world. ‘Your kingdom come’ asks God to bring his rule fully, as he will when Jesus returns. ‘Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven’ asks that people on earth will obey God as completely as the angels do now. The last three are about us. ‘Give us this day our daily bread’ asks for what we need for today, trusting God for tomorrow. ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors’ asks for mercy for our sins, and reminds us that forgiven people forgive. ‘Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one’ asks God to protect us from sin and from the devil. Notice the order. God’s glory comes first, then our needs. Notice too how much of life it covers: body (bread), past (forgiveness), and future (temptation). Jesus then underlines one request. If you forgive others, your Father will forgive you; if you will not, he will not. Christians have prayed these words every day for two thousand years, and they have never run dry.
6.big: Jesus teaches us to pray as children to our Father: first for his name, kingdom and will, then for our daily bread, forgiveness and protection.

vv.h: this is how you should pray
b: Quarles notes that ‘like this’ suggests a model or guide for prayer rather than a script to recite without thinking. Yet Christians have always prayed the words themselves too: the Didache, an early Christian handbook from about AD 100, tells believers to pray this prayer three times a day. The Westminster Shorter Catechism calls it ‘the special rule of direction’ for prayer (Q. 99). It can be both a prayer to say and a pattern to pray by.

vv.h: Our Father in heaven
b: Israel sometimes called God Father (Isaiah 63:16; Malachi 1:6), but rarely in prayer. Jesus almost always addressed God as Father (the cry from the cross, quoting Psalm 22:1, is the exception, 27:46), using the Aramaic Abba in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and he invites his disciples to do the same. Paul says the Holy Spirit makes believers cry ‘Abba! Father!’ (Romans 8:15). This is the privilege of adoption into God’s family.

‘Our’ is plural, and Quarles notes there are seven more ‘us’ and ‘our’ words in the prayer. It is a family prayer. The Westminster Shorter Catechism says the opening teaches us to come to God ‘as children to a father able and ready to help us; and that we should pray with and for others’ (Q. 100).

vv.h: hallowed be Your name
b: To ‘hallow’ means to treat as holy. God’s ‘name’ means God himself as he has made himself known. Calvin explained: ‘To sanctify the name of God means nothing else, than to give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name’. Quarles hears an echo of Ezekiel 36:23, where God says, ‘I will show the holiness of My great name’, by cleansing his people and giving them a new heart. So the prayer asks God to act, and also asks that we and others will honour him.

vv.h: Your kingdom come
b: God already rules over all, but the kingdom Jesus announced (4:17) has come only in part. Stott says this request asks both that the kingdom may grow, as people submit to Jesus, and that it will soon be completed when he returns. The Shorter Catechism puts it this way: ‘that Satan’s kingdom may be destroyed; and that the kingdom of grace may be advanced … and that the kingdom of glory may be hastened’ (Q. 102). Compare the early Christian prayer ‘Come, Lord Jesus’ (Revelation 22:20).

vv.h: Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven
b: In heaven God’s will is done perfectly and gladly. This request asks for the same on earth. It is a prayer for the world, and also for ourselves: ‘that God, by his grace, would make us able and willing to know, obey and submit to his will in all things, as the angels do in heaven’ (Shorter Catechism, Q. 103). Jesus prayed it himself in Gethsemane at the greatest cost: ‘may Your will be done’ (26:42).
The phrase ‘on earth as it is in heaven’ probably belongs with all three of the first requests: may God’s name be honoured, his kingdom come and his will be done, on earth as in heaven.

vv.h: Give us this day our daily bread
b: The word translated ‘daily’ (epiousios) appears nowhere else in Greek before the Gospels, so its exact meaning is uncertain: ‘for today’, ‘for the coming day’, or ‘what we need’. Stott notes that Origen thought the Gospel writers had coined it. The request recalls the manna God gave Israel in the wilderness, enough for each day (Exodus 16:4), and the prayer in Proverbs 30:8: ‘feed me with the bread that is my portion’.

Stott quotes Luther, who said that ‘bread’ stands for ‘everything necessary for the preservation of this life’. Asking for it does not mean we stop working; it means we depend on God, who usually provides through ordinary means. Some early Christian writers also saw a spiritual meaning: the bread of God’s word, or the Lord’s Supper (see Where readings differ).

vv.h: forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors
b: Sin is pictured as a debt we owe God and cannot pay. Luke’s version says ‘sins’ (Luke 11:4), and verse 14 says ‘trespasses’; ‘trespasses’ became the familiar English form through Tyndale and the Book of Common Prayer, while many churches pray ‘debts’. Calvin wrote, ‘We ought always, therefore, to begin with the forgiveness of sins’.

Jesus is not saying that our forgiving earns God’s forgiveness. Stott explains: ‘God forgives only the penitent and that one of the chief evidences of true penitence is a forgiving spirit.’ The Catholic Catechism makes a similar point: God’s mercy ‘cannot penetrate our hearts as long as we have not forgiven those who have trespassed against us’ (2840).

vv.h: lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one
b: God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13). The word can mean ‘testing’ as well as ‘temptation’. The request asks God to keep us from situations where we will be overwhelmed by temptation, and to rescue us when we are in them. The Shorter Catechism puts it: ‘that God would either keep us from being tempted to sin, or support and deliver us when we are tempted’ (Q. 106). Quarles notes that the Spirit led Jesus into temptation (4:1); disciples, aware of their weakness, ask God not to do the same to them. In Gethsemane Jesus told his sleepy disciples, ‘Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation’ (26:41).

‘The evil one’ can also be translated ‘evil’ (BSB footnote). Matthew elsewhere uses the phrase for the devil (13:19, 38), and Stott and the Catholic Catechism (2851) both take it that way here. Calvin treated the two halves as one request: keep us from being overcome, by rescuing us from evil. Augustine counted them as two, making seven petitions in all.

vv.h: For Yours is the kingdom (footnote)
b: The BSB footnote notes that later manuscripts (the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus) add ‘For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.’ The earliest manuscripts end with ‘the evil one’. A form of the doxology appears in the Didache, and the New Bible Dictionary says it ‘has been used in the Christian church from the earliest times’. It echoes David’s prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11: ‘Yours, O LORD, is the kingdom’. Calvin was surprised that Latin copies left it out, since it ‘agrees so well with the rest of the prayer’.

vv.h: if you do not forgive men their trespasses
b: This is the only request Jesus comments on, which shows how important it is. The parable of the unforgiving servant (18:21–35) explains it. A servant forgiven a debt he could never repay refused to forgive a fellow servant a small sum. The master asks, ‘Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?’ The point is the difference in size between what God forgives us and what we forgive others. A person who has truly grasped God’s forgiveness cannot hold others’ debts against them for ever.

6.diff: Daily bread. Calvin called the early spiritualising of this request (‘supersubstantial’ bread) ‘exceedingly absurd’, and with Luther took it of ordinary bodily needs; the Shorter Catechism: ‘that of God’s free gift we may receive a competent portion of the good things of this life’ (Q. 104). The Catholic Catechism gives several senses at once: trust for each day, what is necessary for life, and also ‘the Bread of Life, the Body of Christ’; ‘The Eucharist is our daily bread’ (2837). Wesley also included ‘the sacramental bread, and thy grace’ alongside ‘All things needful for our souls and bodies’. Saying it or praying like it? Some Protestant traditions stress the prayer as a pattern and avoid frequent repetition; liturgical churches pray it at every service, and the Didache told Christians to pray it three times a day. Most hold both. The doxology. Not in the earliest manuscripts; most Protestants say it, Catholics use it at Mass after the prayer, and the Catechism says it ‘takes up again, by inclusion, the first three petitions’ (2855).

b: Tertullian, around AD 200, called the Lord’s Prayer ‘truly the summary of the whole gospel’ (quoted in the Catholic Catechism 2761). Each request opens onto a great theme of Scripture: God as Father (adoption), the holiness of his name, the kingdom, his will, his provision, forgiveness, and victory over evil.

Calvin, followed by Stott, compared the two halves of the prayer to the two tables of the Ten Commandments: first our duty to God, then our needs and our neighbour. The prayer trains our desires. If we pray it honestly, we learn to want God’s glory first, and to bring every need of body and soul to him.

In John 17 we hear Jesus himself pray for his disciples, in words that echo this prayer: he speaks of making the Father’s name known (17:6, 26), asks him to protect the disciples by that name (17:11), and prays, ‘keep them from the evil one’ (John 17:15).

l.t: Luke’s shorter form, followed by teaching on persistence in prayer.
God will show the holiness of his name by cleansing his people.
Bread from heaven, enough for each day.
Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with my portion.
‘Yours, O LORD, is the kingdom’: the background to the doxology.
The unforgiving servant: Jesus’ commentary on verses 12 and 14–15.
In Gethsemane Jesus prays ‘Your will be done’ and warns against temptation.
The Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry ‘Abba! Father!’
Jesus’ own prayer for his disciples.
God will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.

qs: Why do you think Jesus puts the requests about God’s name, kingdom and will before our own needs?
Which request do you find hardest to pray honestly, and why?
How could we use the Lord’s Prayer as a pattern for our own praying this week, alone and as a group?

6.ctx: The Law required fasting only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31), but by Jesus’ day devout people fasted often; the Pharisee in Luke’s parable boasts, ‘I fast twice a week’ (Luke 18:12). People who fasted sometimes stopped washing and put ashes on their heads as signs of grief.
6.mean: The third example is fasting, going without food for a time in order to seek God. Jesus says ‘when you fast’, not ‘if you fast’; he assumes his followers will. Elsewhere he says that his disciples will fast after he has been taken from them (9:15). The problem again is the hypocrites. They looked gloomy and made their faces unattractive, perhaps unwashed or smeared with ashes, so that everyone could see how much they were giving up. They get what they want, people’s admiration, and nothing more. Jesus says the opposite. When you fast, wash your face and put oil on your head, as people normally did to look after themselves. Look as you always do. Then no one will know but your Father, who sees in secret, and he will reward you. Fasting is not a way to impress God or to force his hand. It is a way of saying, with our bodies, that we need him more than food: to pray with focus, to grieve over sin, to seek his guidance, or to stand with others in need. The prophets warned that fasting without a changed life is worthless. Isaiah said the fast God wants is ‘to share your bread with the hungry’ (Isaiah 58:6–7). Fasting is between us and God. If we make it a show, we lose the point of it.
6.big: Fasting, like giving and prayer, is for God alone; done in secret, it expresses our hunger for him, and he rewards it.

vv.h: When you fast
b: The early church did fast. The leaders at Antioch were ‘worshiping the Lord and fasting’ when the Holy Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul, and they fasted and prayed again before sending them (Acts 13:2–3). The Didache, from about AD 100, told Christians not to fast on the same days as the hypocrites (Monday and Thursday) but on Wednesday and Friday, a sign that Christians took this passage seriously, if a little literally.

vv.h: they disfigure their faces
b: The word means to make something unrecognisable or to hide it. There is a wordplay in the Greek: they ‘make their faces disappear’ in order to ‘appear’ to people as fasting. Quarles suggests that ashes had become, in effect, theatrical make-up for the religious actor.

vv.h: anoint your head and wash your face
b: Oil was used to care for skin and hair, a normal part of grooming (2 Samuel 12:20; Psalm 104:15). Jesus is not asking people to look festive in order to hide their fast cleverly. He is saying: look normal, so that the fast is between you and God.

The prophets repeatedly warned against fasting that was only outward. Isaiah 58 is the classic passage: the people complained that God ignored their fasting, but on the day of their fast they oppressed their workers. Joel calls for a better fast: ‘rend your hearts and not your garments’ (Joel 2:13). Zechariah asks, ‘was it really for Me that you fasted?’ (Zechariah 7:5).

Jesus himself fasted for forty days in the wilderness (4:2). There he answered the tempter, ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God’ (4:4). That is the heart of fasting: feeding on God himself.

l.t: The Day of Atonement: the one fast the Law required.
The fast God chooses: justice and generosity, not only going without food.
Rend your hearts and not your garments.
Jesus’ disciples will fast when the bridegroom is taken away.
The church at Antioch fasts and prays before sending out missionaries.
Jesus fasts forty days and lives on every word from God.

qs: Why does Jesus assume that his disciples will fast?
What might be the modern equivalents of disfiguring your face to be noticed?
Have you ever fasted? What might help you, or your church or small group, to practise it well?

6.ctx: In the ancient world wealth was often kept as fine clothing, stored grain, or coins and jewellery hidden in the house. Houses had mud-brick walls, which a thief could literally dig through (the Greek for ‘break in’ means ‘dig through’).
6.mean: Having dealt with why we do good, Jesus turns to what we value. Quarles notes that 6:19–24 gives three contrasts: two treasures, two eyes and two masters. The first is about where we store our treasure. Do not store up treasures on earth. Everything on earth can be lost. Moths eat fine clothes. Rust, or vermin (the word can mean ‘eating’), destroys metal and stored food. Thieves dig through the wall and steal. Even what survives these will be left behind at death. Instead, store up treasures in heaven, where nothing can spoil or be stolen. What are treasures in heaven? In context, they are the rewards the Father gives for giving, prayer and fasting done for him (6:4, 6, 18), and more broadly a life spent for God and others. Jesus told a rich young man, ‘sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven’ (19:21). Then the key sentence: ‘where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.’ What we treasure captures our heart. Our heart follows our money. If our treasure is on earth, our hearts will be anxious and divided. If our treasure is with God, our hearts will be with him. Jesus is not condemning owning things or saving wisely. He is asking what we live for. Paul makes the same point: those who want to be rich fall into many traps, but those who are generous are ‘treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future’ (1 Timothy 6:9, 18–19).
6.big: Earthly wealth cannot last, so invest your life in what God values; your heart will follow your treasure.

vv.h: where moth and rust destroy
b: Quarles notes that fine fabrics could be worth their weight in gold, yet moths could ruin them. The word translated ‘rust’ literally means ‘eating’ (BSB footnote: ‘worm’), and may refer to vermin that eat stored food. The rich fool in Luke’s parable planned bigger barns for his grain, but God said, ‘This very night your life will be required of you’ (Luke 12:16–21).

vv.h: store up for yourselves treasures in heaven
b: Jesus does not tell us not to store up treasure; he tells us where to store it. It is right to want lasting riches. The question is whether we are wise enough to invest where they will last. Paul tells the rich ‘to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share’ (1 Timothy 6:18).

vv.h: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also
b: Notice the order: the heart follows the treasure. What we spend our money and time on shapes what we love. Quarles notes that greed is a form of idolatry (Ephesians 5:5; Colossians 3:5), because it puts something in the place of God. The first commandment, to love God with all your heart (Deuteronomy 6:5), leaves no room for loving things more.

Jesus says a great deal about money and possessions. In Matthew alone see the rich young man (19:16–26), the parable of the talents (25:14–30), and the woman who poured costly perfume on Jesus (26:6–13). The issue is always the heart: who or what do we trust and love?

The letter to the Hebrews gives the answer to the fear that drives us to hoard: ‘Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.”’ (Hebrews 13:5).

l.t: The rich fool who stored up treasure for himself but was not rich toward God.
Luke’s version: treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches.
The rich young man: ‘you will have treasure in heaven’.
The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil; be rich in good works.
Set your minds on things above; greed is idolatry.
Be content, for God will never leave you.

qs: What kinds of ‘treasures on earth’ are most tempting for us today?
What does it mean in practice to store up treasure in heaven?
Looking at how you spend your money and time, where would you say your heart is?

6.ctx: People in the ancient world often thought of the eye as a lamp that let light into the body. In Hebrew idiom a ‘good eye’ meant generosity and an ‘evil eye’ meant stinginess or envy (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 22:9; 23:6; BSB footnotes). ‘Money’ is the Aramaic word mammon, meaning wealth or possessions.
6.mean: The second and third contrasts go deeper into the same theme. First, the eye. ‘The eye is the lamp of the body.’ If your eye is good, your whole body is full of light; if your eye is bad, your whole body is full of darkness. At first this sounds like a saying about eyesight, but the surrounding verses are about money, and the BSB footnotes help. Literally, Jesus says ‘if your eye is sound’ and ‘if your eye is evil’. In Hebrew idiom a ‘good eye’ was a generous one (Proverbs 22:9), and an ‘evil eye’ was a greedy, stingy one (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 23:6). The word for ‘good’ also means ‘single’ or ‘undivided’. So Jesus is saying: how you look at money and possessions affects your whole life. Generosity fills a person with light. Greed fills them with darkness, and if what you thought was light is actually darkness, how great that darkness is! Then the third contrast: two masters. A slave could not belong to two owners; he would end up loving one and hating the other. In the same way, ‘You cannot serve both God and money.’ Money is not only a tool; it can become a master that demands our loyalty, time and trust. Jesus calls for a decision. We cannot give half our heart to God and half to wealth. Wesley noticed that Jesus places this teaching on single-minded intention between warnings about worldly desires (6:19–21) and worldly worries (6:25–34). Both greed and worry come from a divided heart.
6.big: A generous, undivided heart fills life with light; no one can serve both God and money, so we must choose whom we will serve.

vv.h: If your eyes are good … if your eyes are bad
b: Quarles explains that the ‘bad eye’ is the eye that delights in gazing at its own riches (compare Ecclesiastes 5:11), and the ‘healthy eye’ is generous. The word for ‘good’ (haplous) means ‘single’: an eye that sees clearly, not double. Wesley commented: ‘what the eye is to the body, the intention is to the soul.’ The point is the same either way: how we look at the world, and especially at money, shapes everything else.

vv.h: If then the light within you is darkness, how great is that darkness!
b: This is the frightening part. A person may think they see clearly while being blinded by greed. Quarles calls it the darkness of a cave untouched by the slightest ray. The love of money can blind people to their own spiritual danger (1 Timothy 6:9–10).

vv.h: No one can serve two masters
b: Jesus speaks of slavery, the strongest form of service. A part-time job for two employers is possible; being the property of two owners is not. Quarles notes that the Old Testament warned that prosperity makes people forget God (Deuteronomy 8:12–14; Proverbs 30:9). Money promises security, freedom and status, the very things God offers. That is why it so easily becomes a rival god.

The ‘single eye’ connects with the ‘pure in heart’ of 5:8: both describe an undivided devotion to God. James warns against being ‘double-minded’ (James 1:8; 4:8), and says friendship with the world is enmity with God (James 4:4).

Jesus will meet a man who tried to serve both masters: the rich young man, who went away sad ‘because he had great wealth’ (19:22). Zacchaeus, in Luke, shows the opposite: when Jesus came to his house, he gave away half his possessions (Luke 19:1–10).

l.t: A generous man (literally, a ‘good eye’) will be blessed.
Do not look on your poor brother begrudgingly (literally, with an ‘evil eye’).
Luke’s version of the eye as the lamp of the body.
No servant can serve two masters; the Pharisees, who loved money, sneered.
The rich young man who could not let go of his wealth.
Friendship with the world is enmity with God; purify your hearts, you double-minded.

qs: What does the Old Testament idea of a ‘good eye’ and ‘bad eye’ add to our understanding of this passage?
How can money become a master rather than a servant?
What practical steps help keep our hearts undivided?

6.ctx: Most people in Galilee lived close to the edge: a bad harvest could mean hunger. Food, drink and clothing were daily concerns. The ‘lilies of the field’ were wild flowers that covered the Galilean hills in spring; dried grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.
6.mean: ‘Therefore’ links this teaching to what came before. If God is your master and your treasure is in heaven, you do not need to worry. Jesus tells his followers not to worry about food, drink or clothes. He is not saying these things do not matter, or that we should not work or plan. He is talking about anxious fretting, the kind that takes over the mind. He gives several reasons. First, life is more than food. God gave us life and bodies, the greater gifts, so he can surely provide the lesser gifts of food and clothing. Second, look at the birds. They do not plant crops or fill barns, yet your heavenly Father feeds them, and you are worth much more than birds. Third, worry achieves nothing. No one can add a single hour to their life by worrying. Fourth, look at the wild flowers. They do not work, yet even King Solomon in all his splendour was not dressed like one of them. If God clothes grass that is here today and burned tomorrow, he will much more clothe you. Worry, says Jesus, shows ‘little faith’. It is how the Gentiles live, people who do not know God as Father. But your heavenly Father knows what you need. So, instead of worrying, ‘seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you.’ Make God’s rule and his ways your first priority, and trust him for the rest. And take one day at a time: tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own. This does not promise an easy life. It promises a Father who knows and cares.
6.big: Because our heavenly Father knows and cares for us, we can stop worrying, seek his kingdom first, and trust him for what we need, one day at a time.

vv.h: Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?
b: Quarles notes that Jesus uses a familiar form of argument, from the greater to the lesser. God gave life and formed the body, far greater gifts than food and clothes. If he did the greater, he will do the lesser.

vv.h: Look at the birds of the air
b: Birds are not lazy, but they do not store up for the future the way people do, and God feeds them (Psalm 104:27–28; 147:9). Luke has ‘ravens’ (Luke 12:24), which were unclean birds under the Law: God cares even for them. Elsewhere Jesus says not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father’s will, and ‘you are worth more than many sparrows’ (10:29–31).

vv.h: Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?
b: The BSB footnote gives an alternative: ‘a single cubit to his height’. The word can mean length of life or height of body; most think length of life fits best. Quarles adds that worry is not just useless but harmful. An earlier Jewish writer, Ben Sira (about 180 BC), said that anxiety brings on old age too soon (Sirach 30:24, in the Apocrypha).

vv.h: Consider how the lilies of the field grow
b: Solomon was the richest and most splendid king in Israel’s history (1 Kings 10:4–7, 21–23). Yet a wild flower, which lasts only a few days, is more beautiful. ‘O you of little faith’ is a phrase Matthew uses for disciples who believe but whose trust falters (8:26; 14:31; 16:8). Quarles points out that worry doubts God’s power, his knowledge or his love, and Jesus answers all three: he is able (birds and flowers), he knows (6:32), and he cares (‘Are you not much more valuable?’).

vv.h: For the Gentiles strive after all these things
b: Here ‘Gentiles’ means people who do not know the true God. Quarles notes that their gods were powerless, and they had no hope of resurrection, so the needs of this life were everything to them. Those who know God as Father have a different centre.

vv.h: But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness
b: This is the positive command at the heart of the passage. To seek the kingdom is to value it above everything (13:44–46), to pray for it to come (6:10), and to live under King Jesus. ‘His righteousness’ is the life that pleases God, which he himself gives (5:6). Some ancient manuscripts read ‘seek first His kingdom’ (BSB footnote), as in Luke 12:31; the meaning is the same.
‘All these things will be added’ means God will provide what we truly need, not every luxury we want. Wesley comments that whoever seeks the kingdom first ‘will soon come to seek this only’.

vv.h: tomorrow will worry about itself
b: Quarles enjoys the humour: Jesus pictures ‘tomorrow’ as a nervous person pacing the floor, doing enough worrying for everyone. Each day has its own troubles; we are given grace for today, as Israel was given manna for one day at a time (Exodus 16:4; compare 6:11).

Paul gives the same teaching: ‘Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus’ (Philippians 4:6–7). Peter: ‘Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you’ (1 Peter 5:7).

This passage does not deny that Christians face real hardship. Paul knew hunger and cold (2 Corinthians 11:27). Jesus himself had nowhere to lay his head (8:20). But it promises that our lives are held by a Father who knows our needs, and that nothing in all creation can separate us from his love (Romans 8:35–39). It is wise, too, to remember that some anxiety is an illness that needs care and treatment; Jesus’ words are an invitation to trust, not a rebuke to the suffering.

l.t: All creatures look to God for their food.
The splendour of King Solomon.
Luke’s version: consider the ravens.
Not one sparrow falls apart from the Father’s will.
Do not be anxious; pray, and God’s peace will guard you.
Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.
The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
God, who did not spare his Son, will graciously give us all things.

qs: What reasons does Jesus give for not worrying? Which one speaks most to you?
What is the difference between wise planning and anxious worry?
What would it look like for you to ‘seek first the kingdom of God’ this week?

7.ctx: Chapter 7 turns to relationships. The ‘beam’ was a large timber, the kind used to hold up a roof; Jesus grew up as a carpenter’s son (13:55). Dogs in that culture were mostly wild scavengers, and pigs were unclean animals under the Law; both were common pictures for those who despised holy things.
7.mean: ‘Do not judge’ may be one of the most quoted verses in the Bible, and one of the most misunderstood. Jesus is not forbidding all judgement. In this same chapter he tells his disciples to recognise false prophets by their fruit (7:15–20), and in the very next verse to tell the difference between ‘dogs’ and others (7:6). Elsewhere he says, ‘Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly’ (John 7:24). What he forbids is harsh, fault-finding, hypocritical judgement: the habit of looking down on others, assuming the worst about them, and setting ourselves up as their judge. Stott calls it ‘censoriousness’. The warning is serious. The standard you use on others will be used on you. If you are harsh with others, God will be harsh with you. If you are merciful, you will receive mercy (5:7). Then Jesus paints a comic picture. A man with a beam sticking out of his eye is trying to remove a speck of sawdust from his friend’s eye. It is ridiculous, and it is how we often behave: blind to our own big faults, sharp-eyed about others’ small ones. ‘You hypocrite!’ Jesus says. First deal with the beam in your own eye; then you will see clearly to help your brother. Notice that he does not say ‘never help with the speck’. Loving correction is good, but it starts with honest self-examination and humility. Verse 6 balances this. Do not give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls to pigs. Do not be naive. Some people will only mock and attack what is precious. Disciples must not be judgemental, but they must not be undiscerning either.
7.big: Jesus forbids harsh, hypocritical judgement of others; deal humbly with your own faults first, then help others gently, and use wise discernment.

vv.h: Do not judge, or you will be judged
b: The verb ‘judge’ can mean to discern or to condemn. Calvin wrote that these words ‘do not contain an absolute prohibition from judging, but are intended to cure a disease, which appears to be natural to us all’, the eagerness to find fault in others while excusing ourselves. Wesley added that we should not judge anyone ‘without full, clear, certain knowledge, without absolute necessity, without tender love.’

Paul applies the saying: ‘Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls’ (Romans 14:4). He also says that the church must deal with serious sin among its members (1 Corinthians 5:12). The difference is between condemning others from a position of superiority and caring for them under God’s word.

vv.h: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you
b: Quarles notes that the rabbis used the same saying to describe God’s fitting justice: the punishment matches the sin. Jesus applies it to judging others. David is a vivid example: when Nathan told him the story of a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb, David angrily condemned the man, only to hear Nathan say, ‘You are that man!’ (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

vv.h: the speck in your brother’s eye … the beam in your own eye
b: Quarles points out the humour: a carpenter’s image of someone with a roof-beam in his eye attempting delicate eye surgery. The three parts of the saying build up: ‘Why?’ asks about motive; ‘How can you say?’ is shock at the nerve of it; ‘You hypocrite!’ names the problem. The censorious person is acting a part, pretending to be holier than he is.

The goal is not to leave our brother with a speck in his eye, but to be able ‘to remove the speck’. Paul says the same: ‘you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted’ (Galatians 6:1).

vv.h: Do not give dogs what is holy; do not throw your pearls before swine
b: Holy food (from the sacrifices) must never be thrown to dogs; pearls are wasted on pigs, which cannot value them and may turn on you. Quarles takes the holy things and pearls to be the gospel of the kingdom (compare 13:45–46), and the dogs and pigs to be people who show only contempt for it. Disciples need not keep forcing the message on those who scorn it; Jesus told them to shake the dust off their feet and move on (10:14). Proverbs says, ‘Do not rebuke a mocker, or he will hate you’ (Proverbs 9:8).

mis.t: ‘Do not judge’ is often taken to mean that Christians should never say anything is wrong, or never evaluate anyone’s beliefs or behaviour.
mis.b: Stott writes that these words are ‘well known but much misunderstood’, and Calvin that they are not ‘an absolute prohibition from judging’. The same chapter tells disciples to recognise false prophets (7:15–20) and to use discernment (7:6), and Jesus elsewhere tells people to judge ‘justly’ (John 7:24). What he forbids is censorious, hypocritical condemnation of others, not moral discernment.

b: The passage connects to the Beatitudes and the Lord’s Prayer: the merciful will be shown mercy (5:7), and we ask to be forgiven as we forgive (6:12). People who know how much they have been forgiven find it hard to sit in judgement on others.

Ultimately, judgement belongs to God, and he has given it to Jesus (25:31–46; John 5:22). Paul tells the Corinthians to ‘judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes’, who ‘will expose the motives of men’s hearts’ (1 Corinthians 4:5). We cannot see hearts; he can.

l.t: Luke’s version, with ‘forgive, and you will be forgiven’.
You who judge others condemn yourself, for you do the same things.
Who are you to judge another’s servant? We will all stand before God.
Restore a sinning brother gently, watching yourself.
David condemns the rich man and hears, ‘You are that man!’
Do not judge by appearances, but judge justly.
Judge nothing before the time; the Lord will expose the heart.
There is one Lawgiver and Judge; who are you to judge your neighbour?

qs: What kind of judging does Jesus forbid, and what kind does he expect his disciples to do?
Why is it so easy to see others’ faults and miss our own?
Is there a ‘speck’ you have been focusing on in someone else? What might the ‘beam’ be in your own life?

7.ctx: Bread in Galilee was baked as small round loaves, which might look like the stones of the hillside (compare 4:3); fish from the lake might look something like snakes. Luke gives this teaching after the Lord’s Prayer and the parable of the friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–13).
7.mean: After the hard teaching of the Sermon, Jesus gives great encouragement. Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened. The Greek verbs suggest continuing action: keep on asking, seeking and knocking. And the promise is for everyone who asks. Why can we be so confident? Because of what God is like. Jesus asks the fathers listening: if your son asks for bread, would you give him a stone? If he asks for a fish, would you give him a snake? Of course not. Even sinful human parents know how to give good gifts to their children. ‘How much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!’ The argument moves from the lesser to the greater. If imperfect fathers love their children, how much more does the perfect Father love his. This does not mean that God gives us whatever we want. A good father does not give his child everything the child asks for; he gives what is good. Luke’s version says the Father will give ‘the Holy Spirit’ to those who ask (Luke 11:13), the greatest good gift of all. Some scholars think the asking here is especially about entering the kingdom and receiving the righteousness the Sermon describes (see Where readings differ). Either way, the Sermon’s demands are not meant to be met by our effort alone. We are to ask our Father for what only he can give. Then comes the Golden Rule: ‘do to others as you would have them do to you’. It sums up the whole Law and the Prophets, the whole teaching on how to treat people.
7.big: Keep asking, seeking and knocking, because your Father loves to give good gifts; and treat others as you would want to be treated, which sums up the Law and the Prophets.

vv.h: Ask … seek … knock
b: Each verb is in a form that suggests continuing action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. Luke places it after the parable of the man who knocks at his friend’s door at midnight and gets what he needs ‘because of the man’s persistence’ (Luke 11:8). Wesley comments: ‘Seek — Add your own diligent endeavours to your asking: and knock — Persevere importunately in that diligence.’

vv.h: if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone?
b: Quarles notes the visual similarity: small loaves might look like stones, and some fish like snakes. A loving father would never trick his hungry child with something useless or harmful. Isaiah uses an even stronger picture: ‘Can a woman forget her nursing child?’ Even if she could, God says, ‘I will not forget you’ (Isaiah 49:15).

vv.h: if you who are evil know how to give good gifts
b: Jesus casually calls his hearers ‘evil’. He is not insulting them; he is stating the truth about fallen human nature, even at its best. Yet even sinful parents love their children. The ‘how much more’ argument is one of Jesus’ favourites (compare 6:30; 10:25; 12:12). God is not a reluctant giver to be persuaded, but a Father far more generous than any human father.

vv.h: do to others as you would have them do to you
b: This saying is known as the Golden Rule. A famous Jewish story tells of Hillel, a leading rabbi of the generation before Jesus, who summed up the Law in a negative form: ‘That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.’ (Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Jesus puts it positively: not just avoiding harm, but actively doing the good you would want done to you.

‘This is the essence of the Law and the Prophets’ connects back to 5:17, where Jesus said he came to fulfil the Law and the Prophets. Quarles notes that 7:12 brings the main body of the Sermon to a close. Later Jesus says that the Law and the Prophets hang on two commands, love for God and love for neighbour (22:37–40); the Golden Rule is a practical way of doing the second.

7.diff: What are we to ask for? Most readers take verses 7–11 as a general encouragement to persistent prayer for every need, trusting the Father to give what is good; Wesley, for example, applies it to prayer for others as well as ourselves. Quarles argues that in the flow of the Sermon the asking, seeking and knocking are especially about entering the kingdom: seeking recalls 6:33 (‘seek first the kingdom’), knocking points ahead to the narrow gate (7:13–14), and the ‘good things’ are the righteousness and life the Sermon describes, which fits Luke’s ‘the Holy Spirit’ (Luke 11:13). The two readings overlap: God’s greatest gift is himself, and he also cares about our daily needs (6:11, 32).

b: The rest of the New Testament adds to Jesus’ teaching on prayer. James says, ‘You do not have, because you do not ask’, and also warns that we sometimes ask ‘with wrong motives’ (James 4:2–3). John says that if we ask ‘according to His will, He hears us’ (1 John 5:14). And James promises that anyone who lacks wisdom can ask God, ‘who gives generously to all without finding fault’ (James 1:5).

The Golden Rule echoes through the letters: ‘he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law’ (Romans 13:8–10); ‘The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”’ (Galatians 5:14).

l.t: The friend at midnight, and the Father who gives the Holy Spirit.
Luke’s form of the Golden Rule.
Can a mother forget her child? God will not forget you.
Ask God for wisdom, and he will give generously.
If we ask according to his will, he hears us.
Love is the fulfilment of the law.
He who did not spare his own Son will graciously give us all things.

qs: What does Jesus’ picture of a father and his son teach us about God?
Why might God not give us everything we ask for, even though he is a good Father?
How would you put the Golden Rule into practice in one relationship this week?

7.ctx: The Sermon now ends with a series of contrasts: two gates and roads (7:13–14), two kinds of tree and fruit (7:15–20), two kinds of followers (7:21–23), and two builders (7:24–27). The Old Testament often spoke of two ways, the way of life and the way of death (Deuteronomy 30:19; Psalm 1:6; Jeremiah 21:8).
7.mean: Jesus has finished his teaching. Now he calls for a decision. There are two gates and two roads. One gate is wide and the road broad, and many go through it, but it leads to destruction. The other gate is small and the road narrow, and only a few find it, but it leads to life. The picture is simple and searching. The broad road is easy to find and easy to walk. You do not need to think; you just go with the crowd. The narrow road is harder. It means following Jesus and living the life he has just described, from the Beatitudes onward: humility, mercy, purity, honesty, love for enemies, secret devotion, trust in the Father. The word for ‘narrow’ means cramped, hemmed in. Following Jesus has limits; not everything is allowed. But it leads to life, the life of the kingdom now and for ever. Jesus does not soften the warning. Most people, he says, are on the wrong road. This is not because God wants to keep people out; the gate is open, and Jesus has just told us to ask, seek and knock (7:7–8). It is because the narrow gate means turning away from the crowd and from ourselves. Elsewhere Jesus says, ‘I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved’ (John 10:9). The narrow gate is not a hard set of rules but a person: Jesus himself. To enter is to come to him and follow him.
7.big: Jesus calls everyone to choose: the easy, crowded road leads to destruction, but the narrow way of following him leads to life.

vv.h: Enter through the narrow gate
b: Quarles suggests that the picture is of a small door in a city wall, used when the main gates were shut, which only those who knew the city could find. Entering through the narrow gate means much the same as entering the kingdom of heaven (compare 19:17 and 19:23–24). Luke records a similar saying when someone asked, ‘will only a few people be saved?’ Jesus answered, ‘Make every effort to enter through the narrow door’ (Luke 13:23–24).

vv.h: wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction
b: The broad way is the way of the wicked in the Old Testament (Proverbs 4:14–19), the easy path of doing what we like. ‘Destruction’ means final ruin under God’s judgement, the opposite of ‘life’ in verse 14. Jesus does not describe it in detail here, but the contrast could not be sharper.

vv.h: small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life
b: Quarles notes that the word for ‘narrow’ (used of a road) means ‘tight’ or ‘cramped’, and probably refers to the moral boundaries of the path of righteousness, keeping to God’s commands without turning ‘to the right or to the left’ (Deuteronomy 5:32). The same word family is used elsewhere for hardship, and Paul taught new believers that ‘We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God’ (Acts 14:22). Following Jesus costs something, but it is the road to life.

The ‘two ways’ theme runs through the Bible. Moses set before Israel ‘life and death, blessing and cursing’ and urged them, ‘choose life’ (Deuteronomy 30:19). Psalm 1 contrasts the righteous person, like a fruitful tree, with the wicked, who are like chaff; ‘the way of the wicked will perish’ (Psalm 1:6). Jesus stands in this tradition, but with a difference: he himself is the way (John 14:6).

The early Christian manual called the Didache, from about AD 100, begins with the words ‘There are two ways, one of life and one of death’, and then draws heavily on the Sermon on the Mount to describe the way of life. From the beginning, Christians understood Jesus’ teaching as a path to walk.

l.t: Life and death set before Israel: choose life.
The way of the righteous and the way of the wicked.
‘I set before you the way of life and the way of death.’
Make every effort to enter through the narrow door.
Jesus: ‘I am the gate.’
Jesus: ‘I am the way and the truth and the life.’

qs: Why do you think the broad road is so popular, and the narrow one so hard to find?
How does John 10:9 (‘I am the gate’) help us understand what the narrow gate is?
Where do you feel the pull of the broad road in your own life?

7.ctx: Israel had a long history of false prophets who claimed to speak for God but did not (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Jeremiah 23:16). Shepherds wore sheepskin cloaks. Wolves were the great threat to flocks; Ezekiel compared corrupt leaders to wolves (Ezekiel 22:27).
7.mean: Jesus warns his followers to watch out for false prophets. They will not look dangerous. They come ‘in sheep’s clothing’, looking like part of the flock, but inside they are ravenous wolves. How can you tell? ‘By their fruit you will recognize them.’ Grapes do not grow on thornbushes, or figs on thistles. A healthy tree produces good fruit; a diseased tree produces bad fruit. What a tree is shows in what it produces. In the same way, what a teacher really is shows in their life and in the effect of their teaching: their character, their conduct, and the kind of disciples they produce. Then Jesus widens the warning to everyone who claims to follow him. ‘Not everyone who says to Me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father.’ On the last day many will protest: we prophesied in your name, drove out demons, did miracles. And Jesus will say, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!’ This is one of the most solemn warnings in the Bible. Calling Jesus ‘Lord’, even doing impressive things in his name, is not the same as belonging to him. Notice what Jesus claims here. He will be the judge on ‘that day’. People will call him ‘Lord’, a word used for God himself. And what matters is whether he knows them. True faith is not just words or spiritual gifts; it is a real relationship with Jesus that shows itself in doing the Father’s will.
7.big: False teachers, and false disciples, are known by their fruit; on the last day what counts is not impressive words or deeds but being known by Jesus and doing the Father’s will.

vv.h: in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves
b: False prophets look like believers. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that ‘savage wolves will come in among you’ (Acts 20:29), and John urges Christians to ‘test the spirits’, because ‘many false prophets have gone out into the world’ (1 John 4:1). Quarles notes that the false prophets here seem to have fairly orthodox words, since they call Jesus ‘Lord’ (7:21–22); their problem is a life that does not match.

vv.h: By their fruit you will recognize them
b: Quarles points out that Matthew’s grouping of grapes with thornbushes echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where God looked for good grapes but found only wild ones, and explained that the grapes were justice and righteousness (Isaiah 5:1–7). John the Baptist used the same picture: ‘every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire’ (3:10), and Jesus repeats it in verse 19.

The fruit includes behaviour, character and the results of a person’s teaching. Paul lists ‘the fruit of the Spirit’ (Galatians 5:22–23). Fruit takes time to grow and to see, which is why discernment needs patience.

vv.h: Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’
b: Quarles notes that in the Greek Old Testament ‘Lord’ (kyrios) translates God’s name, and that the double ‘Lord, Lord’ is used only of God there. Jesus accepts the title. He does not say the confession is unimportant; he says it is not enough on its own. Wesley explained the warning as aimed at anyone who ‘makes a mere profession of me and my religion’. Luke’s version puts it sharply: ‘Why do you call Me “Lord, Lord,” but do not do what I say?’ (Luke 6:46).

vv.h: I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!
b: ‘On that day’ is the day of judgement. The people Jesus describes did spectacular things in his name. Spiritual gifts and success in ministry are not proof that someone belongs to Jesus. Judas was one of the Twelve sent out to heal and drive out demons (10:1–4).

‘I never knew you’ is the heart of it. In the Bible, ‘know’ often means a close personal relationship. ‘The Lord knows those who are His’ (2 Timothy 2:19). ‘Lawlessness’ links back to the Law that Jesus came to fulfil (5:17): they claimed him as Lord but ignored his teaching.

7.diff: ‘I never knew you’. Reformed readers note that Jesus does not say ‘I once knew you’: those who fall away were never truly his, which fits the perseverance of true believers (compare 1 John 2:19). Arminian (Wesleyan) readers generally agree that these particular people were never truly Christ’s (Wesley: those who make ‘a mere profession’), so the verse does not settle the question; they base their view that a true believer can fall away on other warnings (for example Hebrews 6:4–6), and stress that this warning is meant for everyone who professes faith. Both agree that true faith shows itself in doing the Father’s will, that the warning should be taken to heart by all who call Jesus Lord, and that Jesus here speaks as the final Judge, a claim to divine authority.

b: Faith and fruit belong together throughout the New Testament. Jesus says, ‘a tree is known by its fruit’ (12:33) and ‘The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit’ (John 15:5). James writes, ‘faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead’ (James 2:17). Paul, who insists that we are saved by grace through faith, adds that we are ‘created in Christ Jesus to do good works’ (Ephesians 2:8–10).

Jesus’ words about ‘that day’ point ahead to the great judgement scene of 25:31–46, where the King separates the sheep from the goats. There too, what is revealed is a life that has served him, often without knowing it.

l.t: God’s vineyard produced wild grapes instead of justice and righteousness.
Israel’s leaders are like wolves tearing their prey.
Even a prophet who does signs must be rejected if he leads people away from God.
A tree is known by its fruit.
Luke’s version: ‘Why do you call Me “Lord, Lord”?’
Paul warns that savage wolves will come in among the flock.
Test the spirits; many false prophets have gone out.
Faith without deeds is dead.
The King judges the nations on ‘that day’.

qs: What ‘fruit’ should we look for to tell whether a teacher is genuine?
Why are words and even miracles not enough proof that someone belongs to Jesus?
How can we take this warning seriously without becoming fearful or suspicious of everyone?

7.ctx: In Galilee, dry riverbeds (wadis) could become raging torrents after heavy winter rain. A builder who wanted a lasting house would dig down to bedrock; one in a hurry might build on the sandy floor of a dry valley. Luke tells the same parable (Luke 6:47–49).
7.mean: Jesus ends the Sermon with a story everyone can picture. Two men build houses. From the outside, the houses may look the same. The difference is underneath. The wise man built on rock; the foolish man built on sand. Then the storm comes: rain pours down, the streams rise into torrents, the wind batters the walls. The house on the rock stands. The house on the sand collapses, ‘and great was its collapse!’ Jesus explains the meaning before he tells the story. The wise man is ‘everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them’. The foolish man is everyone who hears them and does not act on them. Both men heard Jesus. Both were in the crowd. The difference is not hearing but doing. The storm stands for the testing that comes to every life, and above all for the final judgement, which the Old Testament often pictured as a storm. On that day, only a life built on Jesus’ words will stand. This is an astonishing claim. Jesus says that his own words are the rock, the only safe foundation for life. He is not one more teacher offering helpful advice. His words decide our destiny. And the parable is a final, loving warning. It is possible to admire the Sermon on the Mount, quote it and even preach it, without building on it. Jesus does not want admirers but followers.
7.big: Hearing Jesus’ words is not enough; only the one who acts on them builds a life that will stand on the day of judgement.

vv.h: everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them
b: ‘These words of Mine’ means the whole Sermon. James puts it bluntly: ‘Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves’ (James 1:22). Quarles notes that the rabbis told a similar parable about hearing and doing the Law of God. If Jesus’ hearers knew it, they would notice that he puts his own words in the place of God’s Law.

vv.h: The rain fell, the torrents raged, and the winds blew
b: Quarles points out that the Old Testament often uses storms as pictures of God’s judgement (Isaiah 28:17; Ezekiel 13:10–14). Ezekiel spoke of a flimsy wall, whitewashed by false prophets, that would fall when God sent ‘torrents of rain’ and a windstorm (Ezekiel 13:11–13). Proverbs says, ‘The wicked are overthrown and perish, but the house of the righteous will stand’ (Proverbs 12:7). The storm also describes the trials of life, which test what we are built on.

vv.h: like a foolish man who built his house on sand
b: ‘Foolish’ in Matthew describes those who are unprepared for judgement, like the five foolish bridesmaids who had no oil (25:2–3). The parable ends with no happy twist: ‘it fell—and great was its collapse!’ Jesus wants the crash to ring in his hearers’ ears.

Paul says that there is only one foundation: ‘no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 3:11). Building on Jesus’ words and building on Jesus himself are the same thing, because his words are the expression of who he is.

This parable answers a question the Sermon raises: if the standard is so high, who can stand? Not those who claim to have kept it perfectly, but those who come to Jesus, hear him and keep putting his words into practice, trusting him to change them. The Sermon begins with the poor in spirit (5:3) and ends with doers of the word. The two belong together.

l.t: Luke’s version: the man who dug deep and laid his foundation on the rock.
The whitewashed wall that falls in the storm of God’s judgement.
The house of the righteous will stand.
Be doers of the word, not hearers only.
The wise and foolish bridesmaids.
Christ is the only foundation; each one’s work will be tested.
God lays in Zion a tested cornerstone; hail will sweep away the refuge of lies.

qs: What is the only difference between the two builders?
What ‘storms’ test the foundations of people’s lives today?
Which part of the Sermon on the Mount do you most need to start putting into practice?

7.ctx: The scribes taught by quoting earlier teachers, tracing their authority back through a chain of tradition to Moses (Mishnah, Avot 1:1). ‘When Jesus had finished saying these things’ is the phrase (with small variations) Matthew uses to close each of his five teaching blocks (see the introduction).
7.mean: The Sermon is over, and Matthew tells us how the crowds reacted: they were astonished at his teaching. The word means overwhelmed with amazement. Why? Because he taught ‘as one who had authority, and not as their scribes’. The scribes were respected teachers, but they did not speak on their own authority. They taught by quoting earlier teachers: Rabbi So-and-so said this, in the name of his teacher. Quarles notes that they traced their teaching back, link by link, to Moses at Sinai. Jesus did nothing of the kind. He said, ‘You have heard that it was said… But I tell you.’ He spoke as if he had the right to say what God’s Law meant. He said that the blessed are those who suffer ‘because of Me’ (5:11). He said that on the last day people would call him ‘Lord’, and that their destiny would depend on whether he knew them (7:21–23). He said that his words were the only rock to build a life on (7:24). No prophet or rabbi had ever spoken like this. The crowds sensed it. But being amazed is not the same as obeying. Matthew says the crowds followed him down the mountain (8:1), but not that they became disciples. The Sermon has just warned about hearing without doing. The question it leaves with every reader is not ‘Was that impressive?’ but ‘Will I build on it?’ By the end of the Gospel we learn where this authority comes from: the risen Jesus says, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me’ (28:18).
7.big: Jesus teaches with a unique, personal authority that astonishes the crowds; the right response is not only amazement but obedience.

vv.h: When Jesus had finished saying these things
b: This is the first of five places where Matthew uses this formula (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1), marking the end of a teaching block and a return to the story. Many see the five blocks as a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses, though scholars differ on how much to make of that.

vv.h: as one who had authority, and not as their scribes
b: Quarles quotes the opening of the Mishnah tractate Avot: ‘Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, and elders to prophets…’ The scribes’ authority was borrowed from the chain of tradition. Jesus’ authority is his own. Quarles suggests that the background is Deuteronomy 18:15–19: God promised a prophet like Moses and said, ‘I will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to My words that the prophet speaks in My name’ (Deuteronomy 18:19).
Mark records the same reaction in a synagogue in Capernaum (Mark 1:22). Even the officers sent to arrest Jesus came back saying, ‘Never has anyone spoken like this man!’ (John 7:46).

Jesus’ authority runs through the next two chapters: authority over disease (8:1–17), over storms (8:23–27), over demons (8:28–34) and even to forgive sins (9:6). The crowds who were astonished at his words will soon see his deeds. Matthew frames this whole section with matching summaries (4:23 and 9:35).

The final scene of Matthew brings the theme to its climax. On a mountain in Galilee, the risen Jesus says, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me’, and sends his disciples to teach the nations ‘to obey all that I have commanded you’ (28:18–20). The Sermon on the Mount is the first and fullest summary of what he commanded.

l.t: The prophet like Moses: God will hold accountable whoever does not listen.
In Capernaum the people are astonished at his authority.
‘Never has anyone spoken like this man!’
The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.
All authority has been given to Jesus: teach them to obey.
One like a son of man is given authority, glory and an everlasting kingdom.

qs: What was different about the way Jesus taught compared with the scribes?
Looking back over the Sermon, where do you see Jesus claiming an authority no ordinary teacher would claim?
Is it possible to be impressed by Jesus without obeying him? What would it take to move from one to the other?

8.ctx: Chapters 8–9 follow the Sermon with ten miracles, grouped in threes with teaching in between. In the Bible ‘leprosy’ covers a range of serious skin diseases (BSB footnote; Leviticus 13). The Law required a leper to tear his clothes, cover his mouth, cry ‘Unclean, unclean!’ and live alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46). Leviticus 14 set out how a priest confirmed that someone had been healed. Compare Mark 1:40–45 and Luke 5:12–16.
8.mean: Jesus has just taught with astonishing authority on the mountain. Now, as he comes down, Matthew shows the same authority in action. The first person to meet him is a leper. He was the most excluded person in Israel: not allowed in towns, not allowed to touch anyone, not allowed to worship at the temple, and treated almost as one of the living dead (compare Numbers 12:12). He kneels before Jesus and says, ‘Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.’ He has no doubt about Jesus’ power. His question is whether Jesus wants to help someone like him. Then Jesus does the unthinkable: he reaches out and touches him. Under the Law, touching a leper made a person unclean. But instead of the leper’s uncleanness passing to Jesus, Jesus’ cleanness passes to the leper. ‘I am willing,’ he says. ‘Be clean!’ And the man is healed at once. In the Old Testament only God healed lepers; when the king of Israel was asked to cure Naaman, he cried, ‘Am I God?’ (2 Kings 5:7). Jesus then tells the man to keep quiet and go to the priest with the offering Moses commanded. Jesus is not dismissing the Law; he is fulfilling it (5:17). The priest’s check would make the healing official, so that the man could return to his family, his village and the worship of God. It would also be ‘a testimony to them’: proof that something new had happened. This is a picture of what Jesus does for sinners. We cannot make ourselves clean. But he is willing, and his touch cleanses.
8.big: Jesus is both able and willing to make the unclean clean; his touch does not make him unclean but brings healing and restores outcasts to God’s people.

vv.h: a leper came and knelt before Him
b: The word for ‘knelt’ is the same word used for the Magi’s worship (2:11). Quarles argues that Matthew presents it as worship, and that ‘Lord’ here carries more than politeness. Calvin, comparing Mark and Luke, saw it at least as a gesture of deep reverence. Either way, the leper comes to Jesus as someone with God’s power.

vv.h: Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean
b: Notice the order: he does not doubt Jesus’ power, only his willingness. Years of being pushed away had taught him to expect rejection. Many people today feel the same way about God: sure he could help, unsure he would want to. Jesus’ answer, ‘I am willing’, speaks to them too.

vv.h: Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man
b: Jesus could have healed with a word, as he does in the next story. He chose to touch. The man may not have felt a human touch for years. Calvin observed that Christ’s purity is such that by touching he neither polluted himself nor broke the Law. Quarles notes that touching an unclean person normally made you unclean (Leviticus 5:3); here the opposite happens. Jesus’ holiness is contagious.

vv.h: show yourself to the priest and offer the gift prescribed by Moses
b: Leviticus 14 describes an eight-day ceremony for a healed leper, with sacrifices (the BSB footnote points to it). Quarles notes that in the Old Testament Miriam had to wait seven days outside the camp (Numbers 12:14–15), and Naaman had to wash seven times (2 Kings 5:14); this man is healed instantly. Priests could only declare someone clean; Jesus makes him clean.

Why tell him not to tell anyone? Jesus often asked people not to spread news of his miracles (9:30; 12:16). He did not want to be seen simply as a wonder-worker, or to stir up false hopes of a political Messiah before the time was right. See the note on Mark 1:40.

Leprosy in the Bible is more than a medical condition; it is a vivid picture of the effects of sin. It spreads, it defiles, and it cuts a person off from God’s people and God’s presence. The prophets promised a day when God would cleanse his people from all their uncleanness (Ezekiel 36:25). Jesus’ cleansing of lepers is a sign that this day has come (11:5).

The pattern of Jesus touching the untouchable runs through Matthew: he touches Peter’s feverish mother-in-law (8:15), is touched by a woman with bleeding (9:20), takes a dead girl by the hand (9:25) and touches blind eyes (9:29; 20:34). He brings God’s holiness into the places where uncleanness had shut people out.

l.t: The leper must cry ‘Unclean!’ and live alone outside the camp.
The ceremony for a healed leper, which Jesus tells the man to follow.
Naaman the leper healed through Elisha; ‘Am I God?’ asks the king.
Mark’s account: Jesus is moved with compassion.
Luke: the man was ‘covered with leprosy’.
Lepers are cleansed: a sign that Jesus is the Coming One.
The blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin.
A high priest who sympathises with our weakness: come with confidence.

qs: Why do you think the leper doubted Jesus’ willingness rather than his power?
What does it tell us about Jesus that he chose to touch the man?
Who are the ‘untouchables’ in our community, and how might we reach out to them?

8.ctx: A centurion was an officer in charge of around eighty to a hundred soldiers. In Galilee he probably served Herod Antipas rather than Rome directly, but he was a Gentile. Luke’s account says that he loved the Jewish nation and had built the local synagogue (Luke 7:1–10). Capernaum was Jesus’ base (4:13). Devout Jews avoided entering Gentile homes.
8.mean: The second miracle is for a Gentile, a foreign soldier. He comes to Jesus because his servant is lying at home paralysed and in terrible pain. Jesus at once offers to come and heal him. But the centurion says, ‘Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.’ He explains his reasoning from his own job. He is a man under authority: he obeys his superiors, and soldiers obey him. When he gives an order, it is done. He sees that Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness. Jesus does not need to be present; his word is enough. Jesus is amazed. On only two occasions in the Gospels is Jesus said to be amazed: here at a Gentile’s faith, and in Nazareth at his own people’s unbelief (Mark 6:6). ‘I have not found anyone in Israel with such great faith.’ Then he gives a startling picture. Many will come from east and west, from all the nations, and sit down at the great feast of God’s kingdom with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. But ‘the sons of the kingdom’, people who assumed they belonged by birth, will be thrown out into the darkness. Being born into God’s people is not enough; what matters is faith in Jesus. Then Jesus says to the centurion, ‘Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.’ And the servant is healed that very hour, at home, by a word. The Gospel that began with Gentile Magi worshipping the child (2:1–12) is already showing the door opening to the nations.
8.big: Faith that trusts the authority of Jesus’ word is what God looks for, and people from every nation who trust him will share the feast of his kingdom.

vv.h: my servant lies at home, paralyzed and in terrible agony
b: The word for ‘servant’ can also mean ‘child’ (BSB footnote); Luke’s word means a slave whom the centurion valued highly (Luke 7:2). Quarles notes that the word for ‘agony’ is used of torture. This hard soldier cares deeply about someone under his authority, a quiet picture of good leadership.

vv.h: Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof
b: He may be thinking of the Jewish custom against entering Gentile homes, but his words go further: he feels unworthy of Jesus himself, much as John the Baptist did (3:11). Calvin saw the healing as ‘a kind of first-fruits’ of Christ’s grace to the Gentiles. His words have entered Christian worship: the Catholic Mass, before Communion, echoes them: ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul will be healed’ (Catechism 1386).

vv.h: For I myself am a man under authority
b: His argument is simple. Authority works by word. He does not have to go and drag a soldier to his post; he gives an order. If Jesus has authority over disease, a word is enough. Quarles notes that the centurion calls himself a ‘man’, perhaps setting himself in contrast with Jesus, whom he addresses as ‘Lord’.

vv.h: He marveled
b: Calvin remarked that wonder cannot apply to God, but it could exist in Christ, ‘for he had clothed himself with our flesh, and with human affections’. Jesus is fully human: he can be genuinely surprised and moved.

vv.h: many will come from the east and the west … the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness
b: The great banquet of God’s kingdom was promised in Isaiah 25:6–8: ‘On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a lavish banquet for all the peoples’, and ‘He will swallow up death forever’. Jesus says Gentiles will sit at that table with Israel’s patriarchs. In his day many Jews would not even eat with Gentiles.

‘Sons of the kingdom’ means those who might be expected to inherit it, people of Israel who rely on their birth but reject Jesus. ‘Outer darkness’ and ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’ are among Jesus’ most sobering pictures of final judgement (13:42; 22:13; 25:30). The warning applies to anyone who assumes they are safe because of their background, including churchgoers.

This is the first of several Gentiles in Matthew whose faith outshines that of Israel: the Canaanite mother (15:21–28), and the Roman centurion at the cross who says, ‘Truly this was the Son of God!’ (27:54). The Gospel ends with Jesus sending his disciples to ‘all nations’ (28:19). Paul explains how Gentiles are grafted into God’s people by faith, while warning them too against pride (Romans 11:17–24).
The centurion’s faith rests entirely on the power of Jesus’ word. That is the faith every Christian is called to: we have not seen Jesus, but we trust his word (John 20:29; 1 Peter 1:8).

l.t: The LORD’s banquet for all peoples on his mountain.
Luke’s account: the centurion who built the synagogue.
People will come from east and west and recline in the kingdom; the last will be first.
The Canaanite woman’s great faith.
He sent forth his word and healed them.
Gentiles grafted in by faith; do not be arrogant.
The wedding supper of the Lamb.

qs: What did the centurion understand about Jesus that made his faith so great?
Why would Jesus’ words in verses 11–12 have shocked his hearers? What might shock us?
How can we grow in trusting Jesus’ word when we cannot see him at work?
