8.ctx: Peter grew up in Bethsaida (John 1:44) but now had a home in Capernaum, where his mother-in-law lived with the family. A high fever (Luke 4:38) could be deadly before modern medicine. In Mark’s account it was a Sabbath, which ended at sunset; that explains why crowds came in the evening (Mark 1:21, 32). Compare Mark 1:29–34 and Luke 4:38–41.
8.mean: The third miracle happens in Peter’s house. His mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. Jesus touches her hand, and the fever leaves her. She gets up immediately and begins to serve him, a sign that she is fully well, with no weakness left. Her response is also a model: those whom Jesus heals serve him. That evening the whole town comes. People bring many who are demon-possessed, and Jesus drives out the spirits ‘with a word’ and heals all the sick. Matthew then explains what this means. Matthew says this fulfils Isaiah 53:4, which he renders: ‘He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases’ (8:17). Isaiah 53 is the great chapter about God’s suffering Servant, who would be ‘pierced for our transgressions’ and ‘crushed for our iniquities’ (Isaiah 53:5). By quoting it here, Matthew tells us who Jesus is. He is the Servant. His healings are not just acts of kindness. They show that he has come to deal with everything that is wrong with the world: sin and its effects, including sickness, demons and death. He carries our burdens by taking them on himself, and this will reach its climax at the cross. Christians agree that Jesus’ death and resurrection will finally end all sickness, when God wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). They differ on how much healing believers should expect now (see Where readings differ).
8.big: Jesus is Isaiah’s suffering Servant, who takes up our sicknesses and sins; his healings preview the complete restoration his death will win.

vv.h: she got up and began to serve Him
b: Mark and Luke say she served ‘them’; Matthew, according to the oldest manuscripts, says ‘Him’. Quarles suggests Matthew is highlighting that service to Jesus is the right response to his healing. The same word for ‘serve’ is used of the angels serving Jesus after his temptation (4:11).

vv.h: He drove out the spirits with a word and healed all the sick
b: Jewish exorcists of the time used spells, roots and long incantations. Jesus uses a word, as God does: ‘He sent forth His word and healed them’ (Psalm 107:20). Quarles notes that Matthew stresses ‘all’: no illness was beyond him.

vv.h: He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases
b: Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4 in his own translation of the Hebrew (the BSB of Isaiah reads ‘carried our sorrows’). Calvin admitted that at first sight the quotation looks ‘inappropriate’, because Isaiah speaks of Christ’s death and spiritual grace; but he argued that Matthew looks at the purpose of the healings: ‘it would be idle to confine our view to a transitory advantage, as if the Son of God were a physician of bodies.’ Wesley said Isaiah ‘spoke it in a more exalted sense’, and Matthew applies it to a ‘lower meaning also’.

Quarles points out that Matthew is not proof-texting but pointing to the whole Servant Song (Isaiah 52:13–53:12): the one who heals is the one who will be punished for our sins. Peter quotes the next verse, ‘By His stripes you are healed’, of forgiveness through the cross (1 Peter 2:24).

8.diff: Healing in the atonement? Pentecostals such as the Assemblies of God cite this verse for their teaching that deliverance from sickness ‘is provided for in the Atonement, and is the privilege of all believers’, while admitting that not all are healed in this life. Most other traditions agree that Christ’s work will finally end all sickness (Revelation 21:4), but do not see physical healing as guaranteed now. Calvin argued that Matthew points to the purpose of the healings: Christ healed bodies to show he was sent ‘to relieve us from all evils and miseries’. Wesley saw a ‘lower sense’ here and a more exalted sense in Christ bearing our sins on the cross.

b: Isaiah 53 is quoted or echoed throughout the New Testament to explain Jesus’ death: Philip explains it to the Ethiopian official (Acts 8:32–35), Peter applies it to Christ’s suffering (1 Peter 2:21–25), and Jesus himself says, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors’ (Luke 22:37). Matthew is the only writer to apply it to the healings, showing that Jesus’ whole ministry is the work of the Servant.

The healings are a foretaste of the new creation. At the end, ‘there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain’ (Revelation 21:4). Christians pray for healing now, and God often answers; but every healing in this life is temporary, a sign pointing to the resurrection.

l.t: He took up our infirmities; he was pierced for our transgressions.
Mark’s account of the evening at Peter’s house.
Luke: Jesus rebuked the fever.
The LORD forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.
By his stripes you are healed: the cross and forgiveness.
No more death or pain in the new creation.

qs: What does Peter’s mother-in-law’s response teach us about how to respond to Jesus?
Why do you think Matthew connects Jesus’ healings with Isaiah 53?
How should we pray for healing, and how should we respond when healing does not come?

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 8
Assemblies of God, ‘Divine Healing’ (position paper, quoting the Statement of Fundamental Truths, sec. 12)

8.ctx: Jesus planned to cross the Sea of Galilee to the other side (BSB footnote), the eastern shore, a largely Gentile area. Burying one’s parents was one of the most sacred duties in Jewish life, part of honouring father and mother (Exodus 20:12). Jewish families, especially in Judea, often reburied the bones in a stone box about a year after death. Compare Luke 9:57–62.
8.mean: Between the miracles Matthew places two short conversations about following Jesus. As Jesus is about to cross the lake, a scribe comes and says, ‘Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go.’ It sounds wonderful. But Jesus answers with a warning: ‘Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.’ Following Jesus does not mean comfort or status. Jesus lived on the move, without the settled security even animals have. Anyone who follows him must be ready to give up security. Then another disciple says, ‘Lord, first let me go and bury my father.’ This seems a reasonable request; burying parents was a sacred duty. Perhaps his father had just died, or perhaps he meant he would wait until his father died, which could take years, or until the bones were reburied a year later. Jesus replies, ‘Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.’ It is one of his most shocking sayings. He probably means: let those who are spiritually dead, who do not follow me, take care of the funeral. Jesus is not against funerals or family; he upholds the command to honour parents (15:4). He is saying that following him must come first, before even the most sacred duty. Scholars know of no Jewish teacher of the time who made a demand like this; only God has the right to such loyalty. Matthew does not tell us how either man responded. The question is left for the reader: will you follow Jesus on his terms?
8.big: Following Jesus means putting him before comfort, security and even the most sacred family duties, because he has the right to our first loyalty.

vv.h: Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go
b: Students normally chose a teacher and asked to join his circle. Quarles notes that in Matthew only opponents and outsiders address Jesus as ‘Teacher’; disciples call him ‘Lord’ (as the second man does in verse 21). The scribe may have seen Jesus as just another rabbi. Admiring Jesus as a teacher is not enough to carry anyone through the cost of following him.

vv.h: the Son of Man has no place to lay His head
b: This is the first time in Matthew that Jesus calls himself ‘the Son of Man’, his favourite title for himself. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom and the service of every nation. Quarles points out the irony: the one destined to rule the universe has nowhere to sleep. Calvin wrote that Christ here ‘informs his disciples what sort of life they must be prepared to expect’.

vv.h: let the dead bury their own dead
b: Calvin wrote that ‘Christ does not condemn burial’; he intended to show that whatever draws us away from following him ‘deserves no other name than death’. Wesley: ‘When God calls, leave the business of the world to them who are dead to God.’ Compare Elijah’s call of Elisha, who asked to kiss his parents goodbye and was allowed to (1 Kings 19:20). Jesus asks for more than Elijah did, because he is more than a prophet.

Quarles notes that Jewish law exempted a son from almost every other religious duty until his father was buried. Jesus’ demand overrides even that. The point is urgency and priority: the kingdom has arrived, and nothing may come before following the King.

Luke adds a third conversation: a man who wants to say goodbye to his family first. Jesus replies, ‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God’ (Luke 9:62). Later Jesus will say that anyone who loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him (10:37).

Jesus’ homelessness was temporary and chosen. Paul says he ‘became poor’ for our sake, ‘so that you through His poverty might become rich’ (2 Corinthians 8:9). He gave up his place so that we could have a place in his Father’s house (John 14:2).

l.t: The Son of Man given an everlasting kingdom: the source of Jesus’ title.
Elijah calls Elisha, who first says goodbye to his parents.
Luke’s version, with a third would-be follower.
Whoever loves father or mother more than Jesus is not worthy of him.
Though rich, he became poor for our sake.
Paul counts everything loss compared with knowing Christ.

qs: What did each man need to understand about following Jesus?
How can Jesus’ words about burying the dead be both shocking and loving?
What ‘first let me…’ might hold you back from following Jesus wholeheartedly?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 8:19–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 8

8.ctx: The Sea of Galilee lies about 210 metres below sea level, surrounded by hills. Cold winds can rush down onto the warm water and whip up sudden, violent storms. Several of the disciples were experienced fishermen on this lake. In the Old Testament the sea often stands for chaos and danger that only God can control. Compare Mark 4:35–41 and Luke 8:22–25.
8.mean: The disciples follow Jesus into the boat, picking up the theme of the last passage. Following him leads straight into a storm. Matthew’s word for it is literally a ‘shaking’, the word for an earthquake. The waves sweep over the boat. Experienced fishermen are terrified. And Jesus is asleep. The disciples wake him: ‘Lord, save us! We are perishing!’ Their cry is like a prayer from the Psalms. Jesus answers first with a question: ‘You of little faith, why are you so afraid?’ Notice that in Matthew he says this while the storm is still raging. He is with them, so they are safe, even before anything changes. Then he gets up and rebukes the winds and the sea, and there is complete calm. The disciples are amazed: ‘What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!’ The Old Testament gives the answer. It is the LORD who stills the sea: ‘He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed’ (Psalm 107:29). Only God commands the wind and the waves. Jesus does what God does. This story speaks to every follower of Jesus. Following him does not mean there will be no storms. But he is in the boat. He may seem asleep, but he is not absent, and he is Lord of the storm.
8.big: Jesus commands the wind and the sea as only God can; his disciples may face storms, but with him in the boat they need not be ruled by fear.

vv.h: a violent storm came up on the sea
b: The word Matthew uses (seismos) normally means an earthquake. Quarles notes that ancient writers used it for huge waves. Mark and Luke call it a great windstorm. The disciples’ terror shows it was no ordinary squall.

vv.h: But Jesus was sleeping
b: Some see an echo of Jonah, asleep in the storm (Jonah 1:5–6). Quarles points out the differences: Jonah was running from God, and the storm stopped only when he was thrown overboard; Jesus calms it with a word. His sleep shows his true humanity (he was exhausted) and his perfect trust in his Father (Psalm 4:8).

vv.h: Lord, save us! We are perishing!
b: In Mark the disciples call Jesus ‘Teacher’; in Luke, ‘Master’. In Matthew they cry, ‘Lord, save us!’ Quarles notes that in the Greek Old Testament nearly every cry of ‘Lord, save’ is a prayer to God (for example Psalm 12:1; 118:25). Matthew’s readers would hear the disciples praying to Jesus.

vv.h: You of little faith … Then He got up and rebuked the winds
b: Wesley commented: ‘First, he composed their spirits, and then the sea.’ Matthew places Jesus’ question before the miracle, which suggests that faith should hold even before the storm stops. ‘Rebuked’ is the word used for God rebuking the waters (Psalm 104:7; 106:9) and for Jesus rebuking demons (17:18). Calvin noted that the elements, ‘devoid of feeling’, obey Christ’s voice.

vv.h: What kind of man is this?
b: The question hangs over the rest of the Gospel. After Jesus walks on water, the disciples will answer it: ‘Truly You are the Son of God!’ (14:33).

The Psalms praise the LORD as the one who rules the raging sea: ‘when its waves mount up, You still them’ (Psalm 89:9; compare 65:7; 107:23–30). In Genesis God brought order out of the watery chaos (Genesis 1:2, 6–10), and at the exodus he split the sea (Exodus 14:21). Jesus’ command over the sea is a clear sign that God himself has come among his people.

Many Christians have found comfort in this story in their own storms. The promise of Isaiah 43:2 fits it well: ‘When you pass through the waters, I will be with you’. The promise is not that there will be no storms, but that God will be with us in them.

l.t: Sailors cry to the LORD, and he calms the storm to a whisper.
You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, you still them.
Jonah asleep in the storm.
Mark: ‘Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?’
Jesus walks on the water; ‘Truly You are the Son of God!’
When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.

qs: What does this story reveal about who Jesus is?
Why do you think Jesus speaks to the disciples about their fear before he calms the storm?
What storms are you facing? What would it mean to trust Jesus in the middle of them?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 8:23–27 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 8

8.ctx: The region on the eastern shore was mostly Gentile, part of the Decapolis; the pig herds show it was not a Jewish area, since pigs were unclean under the Law. Manuscripts name the region differently: Gadarenes, Gergesenes or Gerasenes (BSB footnote). Tombs cut into the hillsides could shelter the homeless. Compare Mark 5:1–20 and Luke 8:26–39, which focus on one man.
8.mean: Having shown his authority over the sea, Jesus now shows his authority over the powers of evil. As soon as he lands on the eastern shore, two men possessed by demons come out from the tombs to meet him. They are so violent that no one dares to go that way. Mark describes one of them breaking chains and cutting himself with stones (Mark 5:3–5). This is what evil does to people: it isolates, degrades and destroys. The demons know exactly who Jesus is. ‘What do You want with us, Son of God? Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?’ They know a day of judgement is coming for them (25:41). They see that Jesus can bring it forward. They beg to be sent into a large herd of pigs nearby. Jesus says one word: ‘Go!’ The demons leave the men and enter the pigs, and the whole herd rushes down the steep bank into the lake and drowns. The demons’ destructive nature is plain for all to see. The townspeople come out, hear what has happened, and beg Jesus to leave. It is a tragic ending. They are more upset about the loss of their pigs, or more frightened of Jesus’ power, than glad that two men have been set free. Matthew leaves us with the contrast: the demons recognise Jesus as Son of God, and the people ask him to go away. Jesus’ power over evil is total. But people can still choose to push him away.
8.big: Jesus has complete authority over evil powers and can set its victims free with a word, yet people can still choose to send him away.

vv.h: two demon-possessed men
b: Mark and Luke tell of one man. Calvin followed Augustine’s suggestion that there were two, and that Mark and Luke mention only the one who ‘was more generally known’ and worse afflicted. Quarles agrees, noting that Mark and Luke never say only one was healed. Matthew records pairs elsewhere too (9:27; 20:30). Where there were two, there was one.

vv.h: Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?
b: Demons in the Gospels often recognise Jesus before people do (Mark 1:24; 3:11). Their question shows that they know their final judgement is fixed: ‘the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’ (25:41). Quarles notes that ‘Son of God’ is the title the devil used in the wilderness (4:3, 6). Knowing who Jesus is does not save them; James says, ‘Even the demons believe that—and shudder’ (James 2:19).

vv.h: Go!
b: One word. Quarles contrasts Jewish exorcists, who used magical roots, long spells and the names of angels. Jesus needs nothing but his own command. Why did he allow the demons into the pigs? Matthew does not say. Perhaps it showed beyond doubt that the men were truly free, and showed the destructive purpose of the demons, who destroy whatever they possess.

vv.h: they begged Him to leave their region
b: The whole town comes out, but not to welcome him. Fear, the loss of income, or simple unwillingness to have their lives disturbed: whatever the reason, they ask Jesus to go. Mark adds that the healed man wanted to go with Jesus, but Jesus sent him home to tell his people what God had done (Mark 5:18–20).

8.diff: One man or two? Mark and Luke tell of one man, Matthew of two. Calvin followed Augustine in holding that there were two, and that Mark and Luke mention only the better-known one; Quarles agrees. Some critical scholars think Matthew doubled the number, as perhaps also in 20:30. Where? The manuscripts give ‘Gadarenes’, ‘Gergesenes’ or ‘Gerasenes’ (BSB footnote). Gadara and Gerasa were both cities of the Decapolis, and many think the names refer to the wider district; others locate the event at a small town on the lake shore.

b: Jesus came ‘to destroy the works of the devil’ (1 John 3:8). His exorcisms show that the stronger man has come to tie up the strong man and plunder his house (12:28–29). Paul says that at the cross Christ ‘disarmed the powers and authorities’ and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15).

The Bible takes evil spiritual powers seriously, but never presents them as equal rivals to God. Christians are told to resist the devil, who will flee (James 4:7), and to stand firm in God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18). They need not be fascinated by the demonic or afraid of it: Jesus’ one word is enough.

l.t: Mark’s fuller account: ‘My name is Legion’.
Luke: the healed man sitting at Jesus’ feet, dressed and in his right mind.
Jesus binds the strong man: the kingdom of God has come.
The eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.
Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them at the cross.
The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
Even the demons believe, and shudder.

qs: What do the demons know about Jesus? Why is that knowledge not enough?
Why do you think the townspeople asked Jesus to leave?
In what ways might people today prefer that Jesus stay away from their lives?

‘Gerasenes’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

9.ctx: Jesus’ ‘own town’ is Capernaum (4:13). Mark and Luke add that the man’s friends lowered him through the roof because of the crowd (Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26). Many people then assumed that serious illness was a punishment for sin. The Old Testament teaches that only God can forgive sins against him (Psalm 130:3–4; Isaiah 43:25).
9.mean: Some men bring a paralysed man to Jesus on a mat. Jesus sees their faith, and says something nobody expects: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.’ They came for healing; Jesus begins with forgiveness. He shows what the man needs most. Some of the scribes are horrified. ‘This man is blaspheming!’ they think. They are right about one thing: only God can forgive sins. If Jesus is just a man, he is claiming what belongs to God alone. Jesus knows what they are thinking, which is itself something the Old Testament says only God can do (1 Kings 8:39; compare 1 Chronicles 28:9). He asks, ‘Which is easier: to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” or to say, “Get up and walk”?’ Anyone can say ‘your sins are forgiven’; no one can see whether it has happened. But ‘get up and walk’ can be tested at once. So Jesus does the visible thing to prove the invisible: ‘So that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…’ He tells the paralysed man to get up, take his mat and go home. And the man does. The crowd are filled with awe and praise God for giving such authority to men. Matthew’s point is clear. Jesus’ healings are signs of something deeper. The Son of Man has authority to forgive sins, here on earth, now. That is the good news the paralysed man received first, and it is offered to everyone who comes to Jesus.
9.big: Jesus, the Son of Man, has authority on earth to forgive sins, and he proves it by healing a paralysed man; forgiveness is our deepest need.

vv.h: When Jesus saw their faith
b: Faith can be seen in action: Mark tells how the friends dug through the roof to reach Jesus (Mark 2:4). Calvin observed that ‘It is God alone, indeed, who knows faith’, but the friends ‘had given evidence of faith by the laboriousness of that attempt’. Wesley understood ‘their faith’ to include the faith of the paralysed man too. Those who bring others to Jesus are doing something precious.

vv.h: Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven
b: ‘Son’ (literally ‘child’) is a word of warm affection. ‘Take courage’ echoes the reassurances of Moses and the prophets when God was about to act (for example Exodus 14:13). Does this mean the man’s illness was caused by his sin? Jesus does not say. Quarles thinks Jesus links the two in this case; elsewhere Jesus clearly denies that suffering is always caused by personal sin (John 9:2–3; Luke 13:1–5). What is certain is that sin is the deeper problem behind all the world’s suffering, and that Jesus deals with it first.

vv.h: This man is blaspheming!
b: Mark records their reasoning: ‘Who can forgive sins but God alone?’ (Mark 2:7). They are right in principle. If Jesus is not God, his words are blasphemy. The charge of blasphemy will come back at his trial (26:65).

vv.h: the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
b: In Daniel 7:13–14 the Son of Man is given authority, glory and kingship. Quarles notes that in Daniel’s vision of the heavenly court ‘the books were opened’ for judgement (Daniel 7:10), and the Son of Man shares in the throne. The judge of all can forgive. And Jesus does it ‘on earth’, not just at the last day.

vv.h: glorified God, who had given such authority to men
b: The crowd do not yet understand that Jesus is more than a man, but they rightly praise God. The plural ‘men’ may also hint at what comes later: Jesus will give his followers authority over forgiveness in his name (16:19; 18:18; John 20:23).

The Old Testament links forgiveness and healing: ‘He who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases’ (Psalm 103:3), and Isaiah pictures a restored people of whom ‘no resident of Zion will say, “I am sick.” The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity’ (Isaiah 33:24). Jesus brings both, but forgiveness comes first.

Christians differ on how forgiveness is declared in the church today (for example in confession and absolution, or in the preaching of the gospel), but all agree that the authority to forgive sins belongs to Jesus, and that the forgiveness he gives is real and complete (1 John 1:9).

l.t: The heavenly court; the Son of Man given authority.
Mark’s account: the friends lower the man through the roof.
Luke’s account: ‘We have seen remarkable things today.’
He forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.
God: ‘I am He who blots out your transgressions.’
Neither this man nor his parents sinned: suffering is not always punishment.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us.

qs: Why do you think Jesus spoke of forgiveness before healing?
Were the scribes right that only God can forgive sins? What does that tell us about Jesus?
Who are the people you could ‘carry’ to Jesus in prayer or practical help?

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 9

9.ctx: Tax collectors bought the right to collect tolls and taxes for the authorities, and made their living by charging more. They were seen as traitors and thieves, and were widely regarded as ritually unclean. Mark and Luke call this man Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). Sharing a meal was a sign of acceptance and friendship.
9.mean: Jesus walks past a tax booth and sees a man named Matthew sitting there. He says two words: ‘Follow Me.’ And Matthew gets up and follows him. It is the same call the fishermen received (4:19), but this man was far more shocking. Tax collectors were despised. They worked for the hated ruling powers and grew rich by overcharging their own people. Later rabbinic writings, Quarles notes, compared meeting one to meeting a bear. Rabbis would not accept their testimony in court. Jesus calls one to be his disciple, and later one of the Twelve (10:3). Then Matthew throws a party. Many tax collectors and ‘sinners’ (people known for breaking God’s Law) come and eat with Jesus and his disciples. The Pharisees are scandalised: ‘Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?’ Eating with someone meant accepting them. Jesus answers with a simple picture: ‘It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.’ A doctor who avoided sick people would be useless. Then he quotes Scripture back at them: ‘Go and learn what this means: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice”’ (Hosea 6:6). These Pharisees were careful about religious rules but showed no mercy to sinners. Finally: ‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.’ He is not saying the Pharisees were righteous; he is saying that only people who admit they are sick will come to the doctor. The Gospel we are reading was traditionally linked with this very tax collector. If so, Matthew is telling the story of his own rescue.
9.big: Jesus calls the despised and the sinful to follow him and welcomes them to his table, because he came as a doctor for the sick, not for those who think they are well.

vv.h: a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth
b: Capernaum was on a trade route, and a toll booth there would tax goods crossing between territories. Quarles notes that ‘Matthew’ means ‘gift of the LORD’, and may have been a name Jesus gave him, as he named Simon ‘Peter’ (16:18). Only this Gospel calls him ‘Matthew the tax collector’ in the list of the Twelve (10:3), as if he never forgot where Jesus found him.

vv.h: Follow Me … and Matthew got up and followed Him
b: Fishermen could go back to their boats (John 21:3); a tax collector who walked away from his booth could not easily get it back. Quarles notes that Jewish tradition said repentance was very hard for a tax collector, because he could never repay everyone he had cheated. Jesus calls him anyway. Compare Zacchaeus, another tax collector whose life was turned upside down by Jesus (Luke 19:1–10).

vv.h: Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?
b: The name ‘Pharisee’ probably means ‘separated one’. They kept away from anyone and anything that might make them unclean. To them, a holy teacher eating with sinners was a contradiction. Jesus was later mocked as ‘a friend of tax collectors and sinners’ (11:19). He took it as a description of his mission.

vv.h: I desire mercy, not sacrifice
b: This quotes Hosea 6:6, where God tells Israel that he wants faithful love more than religious rituals. Wesley explained it as ‘I will have mercy rather than sacrifice’: God values acts of mercy even above the sacrifices he commanded. Calvin wrote that the Pharisees were ‘contending with God and the Prophet’ when they objected to help being given to the wretched. Jesus quotes the same verse again in 12:7.
Some later manuscripts add ‘to repentance’ after ‘sinners’ (BSB footnote; compare Luke 5:32). Jesus calls sinners not to stay as they are, but to turn and follow him, as Matthew did.

Jesus’ meals with sinners are a preview of the great banquet of the kingdom (8:11). They show the shape of the gospel: God welcomes sinners not after they have cleaned themselves up, but in order to make them clean. Paul calls himself the worst of sinners and says, ‘Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners’ (1 Timothy 1:15).
Luke gathers three parables around the same complaint, that Jesus ‘welcomes sinners and eats with them’: the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son (Luke 15). Each ends with a party.

l.t: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’.
Mark’s account: the call of Levi.
Luke: Levi leaves everything and holds a great banquet.
Zacchaeus: the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.
Jesus welcomes sinners; the lost sheep.
Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 again.
Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.

qs: Why were tax collectors so despised? Who might be the equivalent today?
What does Jesus mean by ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’?
Is there anyone you find it hard to imagine Jesus welcoming? What does this passage say to that?

9.ctx: John the Baptist’s disciples, like the Pharisees, fasted often (compare Luke 18:12). Jewish weddings lasted up to a week, and wedding guests were excused some religious duties while the feast lasted. Wine was stored in goatskins; new wine was still fermenting and expanding, so it needed new, stretchy skins. Compare Mark 2:18–22 and Luke 5:33–39.
9.mean: Now John the Baptist’s disciples come with a question: ‘Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast so often, but your disciples do not fast?’ John lived simply in the wilderness, and his followers fasted. Jesus had just been at a party with tax collectors. What was going on? Jesus answers with a picture from a wedding. Guests do not mourn while the bridegroom is with them; a wedding is a time for joy. Jesus is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament God pictured himself as Israel’s husband (Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20), so this is a remarkable claim. While he is present, it is a time of celebration, not mourning. ‘But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.’ This is the first hint in Matthew that Jesus will be violently taken away: his death. Christians do fast now, between his going and his return. Then come two short pictures. No one sews a patch of new, unshrunk cloth on an old garment; when it is washed, the new cloth shrinks and tears the old. No one pours new wine into old, brittle wineskins; the fermenting wine would burst them. New wine needs new skins. Something new has come with Jesus. It cannot simply be added to old habits and expectations. Interpreters differ on exactly what the old and new stand for (see Where readings differ), but all agree that Jesus brings something that changes everything.
9.big: Jesus is the bridegroom whose presence brings joy; his coming is something new that cannot simply be patched onto the old, and his followers fast in longing while he is away.

vv.h: How can the guests of the bridegroom mourn while He is with them?
b: John the Baptist himself had called Jesus the bridegroom and himself the bridegroom’s friend (John 3:29). Calvin noted that Chrysostom made that connection. Wesley: ‘While I am with them, it is a festival time, a season of rejoicing, not mourning.’ The Bible ends with the wedding of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9).

vv.h: the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast
b: ‘Taken from them’ suggests removal by force, perhaps echoing Isaiah 53:8, ‘He was cut off from the land of the living’. Jesus is not against fasting; he taught his disciples how to fast (6:16–18). He is saying that fasting must fit the moment in God’s plan. The early church fasted (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23).

vv.h: new wine into new wineskins
b: Old goatskins became dry and brittle; fermenting wine gave off gas and stretched the skin. Pour new wine into an old skin, and you lose both. ‘Both are preserved’ shows that Jesus cares about keeping the new wine safe.

Quarles takes the old garment and wineskins as the traditions of the Pharisees, and the new as Jesus’ teaching, which needs new forms. Calvin and Wesley read it differently: Jesus is protecting his young, weak disciples from demands they are not yet ready for. Wesley: ‘Give harsh doctrines to such as have strength to receive them.’ (See Where readings differ.)

9.diff: What are the old and the new? Many interpreters, including Quarles, take the old garment and old wineskins to be the religious traditions of the Pharisees (and of John’s disciples), and the new cloth and new wine to be the life of the kingdom Jesus brings, which needs new forms rather than being patched onto the old. Calvin rejected the view that the old garments stand for the Pharisees and the new for the gospel; he read the sayings as Jesus protecting his ‘weak and tender disciples’ from severe disciplines they were not yet ready for. Wesley took a similar line. Both readings agree that Jesus’ coming changes the way God’s people live.

b: The bridegroom picture runs through the whole Bible. God says to Israel, ‘as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you’ (Isaiah 62:5). Jesus tells parables of a wedding feast (22:1–14) and of bridesmaids waiting for the bridegroom (25:1–13). Paul says Christ loves the church as a husband loves his wife (Ephesians 5:25–27), and Revelation ends with ‘the marriage of the Lamb’ (Revelation 19:7).

The new wine picture also points to the new covenant. At the Last Supper Jesus takes the cup and speaks of ‘My blood of the covenant’ and of drinking new wine with his disciples in his Father’s kingdom (26:28–29).

l.t: As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so God rejoices over his people.
God will betroth his people to himself for ever.
Mark’s account of the question about fasting.
Luke adds: ‘No one after drinking old wine wants new.’
John the Baptist: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices.
The wedding supper of the Lamb.
If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.

qs: Why does Jesus compare himself to a bridegroom? What does that say about life with him?
What does verse 15 suggest about fasting after Jesus’ departure?
What ‘old wineskins’ might make it hard for us to receive what Jesus is doing?

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 9

9.ctx: A synagogue leader was an important, respected figure who organised worship in the local synagogue; Mark and Luke name him Jairus (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41). A woman with continual bleeding was ritually unclean under the Law, and anyone who touched her, or her bed or seat, became unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:19, 25–27). Jewish men wore tassels on the corners of their cloaks as a reminder of God’s commands (Numbers 15:38–39). Professional mourners and flute players were hired for funerals.
9.mean: Two stories are woven together, both about women; Mark and Luke add that the girl was twelve, the same number of years the woman had been ill. A synagogue leader kneels before Jesus. His daughter has just died, but he believes that if Jesus lays his hand on her, she will live. Jesus gets up and goes with him. On the way a woman comes up behind Jesus. She has had bleeding for twelve years. That meant twelve years of being unclean: unable to go to the temple, and making anyone she touched unclean too. People would have expected her to keep her distance. But she says to herself, ‘If only I touch His cloak, I will be healed.’ She touches the fringe of his cloak. Jesus turns and sees her and, instead of rebuking her, says, ‘Take courage, daughter; your faith has healed you.’ The word ‘healed’ is the same word as ‘saved’. Her uncleanness does not defile Jesus; his power makes her clean. He calls her ‘daughter’, welcoming her back into God’s family. At the leader’s house the funeral has already begun. Flute players and mourners are making a noise. Jesus says, ‘Go away. The girl is not dead, but asleep.’ They laugh at him, because they know she is dead. Jesus means that for him death is like sleep, something from which he can wake a person. He puts the crowd out, takes the girl by the hand, and she gets up. Touching a corpse, like touching the woman, should have made Jesus unclean. Instead, his touch brings life. Matthew’s account is brief, and he focuses on one thing: faith that comes to Jesus finds him able to deal with uncleanness and even death.
9.big: Jesus’ touch cleanses the unclean and raises the dead; those who come to him in faith, however desperate, find him able to save.

vv.h: My daughter has just died … come and place Your hand on her, and she will live
b: In Mark the girl is dying when her father first comes (Mark 5:23), and messengers later bring news of her death. Matthew, telling the story briefly, gives the outcome straight away. The father’s faith is remarkable: he believes Jesus can raise the dead. The word for ‘knelt’ is again the word for worship.

vv.h: touched the fringe of His cloak
b: The ‘fringe’ was probably one of the tassels God commanded Israelites to wear, ‘so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD’ (Numbers 15:39). Quarles points out that people expected even accidental contact with such a woman to make a man unclean. The opposite happened. Later many sick people begged just to touch the fringe of Jesus’ cloak, and all who touched him were healed (14:36).

vv.h: Take courage, daughter, … your faith has healed you
b: Calvin noted that ‘Take courage’ shows her faith was mixed with fear, yet Jesus commends it. Faith does not have to be strong or perfect to reach Jesus; it has to reach him. Quarles notes that her faith was the condition, not the cause: Jesus healed her in response to her faith. The word for ‘healed’ (sōzō) also means ‘saved’, and Matthew’s readers would hear both senses.

vv.h: The girl is not dead, but asleep
b: Jesus speaks the same way of Lazarus (John 11:11–14). For him death is not the end; he can wake the dead as easily as we wake someone from sleep. The New Testament often speaks of Christians who have died as having ‘fallen asleep’ (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), because they will be raised.

Jesus raises the dead three times in the Gospels: this girl, the widow’s son at Nain (Luke 7:11–17) and Lazarus (John 11). Each was raised to ordinary life and would die again. They point ahead to Jesus’ own resurrection, after which death has no more power over him (Romans 6:9), and to the resurrection of all who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

Both stories show Jesus reversing the uncleanness laws. In Haggai 2:12–13, uncleanness spreads by touch and holiness does not; many interpreters see Jesus reversing that pattern. In Jesus, holiness becomes contagious. This anticipates the cleansing that comes through his death (Hebrews 9:13–14).

l.t: A woman with prolonged bleeding is unclean, and so is anyone who touches her.
Tassels on garments to remember God’s commands.
Mark’s fuller account: Jairus and the woman.
Luke’s account: ‘Who touched Me?’
All who touched the fringe of his cloak were healed.
Jesus: ‘I am the resurrection and the life.’
Those who have fallen asleep in Jesus will rise.

qs: What do the synagogue leader and the woman have in common, and how are they different?
Why is it significant that Jesus calls the woman ‘daughter’?
How does this passage give hope in the face of death?

9.h: Jesus Heals the Blind and Mute
9.ctx: ‘Son of David’ was a title for the Messiah, the promised king from David’s line (see 1:1). The prophets promised that when God came to save, the eyes of the blind would be opened and the mute would sing (Isaiah 35:5–6). Matthew records another healing of two blind men in 20:29–34.
9.mean: Two blind men follow Jesus, shouting, ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David!’ They cannot see him, but they see who he is: the promised King. Jesus goes indoors, and they follow him in. He asks, ‘Do you believe that I am able to do this?’ ‘Yes, Lord,’ they answer. He touches their eyes and says, ‘According to your faith will it be done to you.’ Their eyes are opened. Jesus warns them strictly not to tell anyone, but they go out and spread the news everywhere. Then a man who cannot speak, because of a demon, is brought to Jesus. When the demon is driven out, the man speaks. The crowds are amazed: ‘Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!’ But the Pharisees say, ‘It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons.’ These two reactions bring the section of miracles (chapters 8–9) to a close. The same deeds lead some to wonder and others to hostility. Jesus has shown authority over disease, nature, demons and death, and has forgiven sins. The evidence is there. But evidence alone does not make people believe. The Pharisees cannot deny the miracles, so they explain them away. This accusation will come back with full force in chapter 12. Meanwhile, Isaiah’s promise is coming true: blind eyes are opened, and the mute speak. The blind men saw more than the Pharisees did.
9.big: Jesus, the Son of David, opens blind eyes and gives speech to the mute as the prophets promised; the same works lead some to faith and others to harden their hearts.

vv.h: Have mercy on us, Son of David!
b: This is the first time anyone in the story calls Jesus ‘Son of David’ (compare 1:1); it will come again in healing stories (15:22; 20:30–31) and at his entry into Jerusalem (21:9). Quarles suggests the link between the Son of David and healing comes from Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s shepherds for not healing the sick and promises to set over his flock ‘one shepherd, My servant David’ (Ezekiel 34:4, 23).

vv.h: Do you believe that I am able to do this? … According to your faith
b: Jesus does not need their faith to have power. But he often looks for faith in those he heals (8:13; 9:2, 22; 15:28). Faith is the hand that receives what he gives. In Nazareth, where people did not believe, he did few miracles (13:58).

vv.h: See that no one finds out about this!
b: Jesus often told people to keep quiet about his healings (8:4; 12:16). He did not want crowds who only wanted miracles, or a popular movement to make him a political king (John 6:15). The men disobeyed, perhaps out of sheer joy, but disobedience is still disobedience.

vv.h: It is by the prince of demons that He drives out demons
b: The Pharisees cannot deny that something supernatural is happening, so they claim it comes from Satan. Jesus will answer this charge in 12:22–32: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and to call the Spirit’s work evil is a dreadful sin.

Isaiah 35 is the background to these healings: ‘Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer, and the mute tongue will shout for joy’ (Isaiah 35:5–6). When John the Baptist later asks whether Jesus is the Coming One, Jesus points to exactly these signs (11:4–5).

Physical blindness becomes a picture of spiritual blindness throughout the Gospels. In John 9, a man born blind comes to see and worship Jesus, while the Pharisees who claim to see are shown to be blind (John 9:39–41).

l.t: The eyes of the blind opened and the mute tongue shouting for joy.
The failed shepherds of Israel, and God’s servant David as shepherd.
Two more blind men cry out to the Son of David.
Jesus answers the charge that he drives out demons by Satan.
The blind see: Jesus’ answer to John the Baptist.
Spiritual sight and spiritual blindness.

qs: What did the blind men ‘see’ about Jesus that others missed?
Why do you think the same miracles produced such different reactions?
How can we pray for people who are spiritually blind to Jesus?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos

9.ctx: Verse 35 repeats almost word for word the summary in 4:23, framing the Sermon (chapters 5–7) and the miracles (chapters 8–9). ‘Sheep without a shepherd’ is an Old Testament picture of God’s people without good leaders (Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5).
9.mean: Matthew sums up Jesus’ ministry again: teaching, preaching and healing in all the towns and villages. Then he shows us Jesus’ heart. When he sees the crowds, he is ‘moved with compassion’. The word describes a gut-deep feeling of pity. He sees them as ‘harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd’. Israel had religious leaders, teachers of the Law in every town, but, as Wesley put it, none who truly cared for their souls. Ezekiel had condemned Israel’s leaders as shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock, and God had promised to come and shepherd his people himself (Ezekiel 34:11–16). Jesus is that shepherd. Then he changes the picture from sheep to a harvest field. ‘The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.’ The crowds are like a field of ripe grain ready to be gathered in. The problem is not a lack of people ready to respond, but a lack of workers. So Jesus tells his disciples to pray: ‘Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.’ The harvest belongs to God. He is the one who sends the workers. And in the very next chapter Jesus sends out the Twelve. The disciples who pray for workers become the answer to their own prayer. This passage is the bridge between Jesus’ own ministry (chapters 4–9) and the mission he gives his followers (chapter 10). Compassion leads to prayer, and prayer leads to mission.
9.big: Jesus’ compassion for helpless people moves him to call his disciples to pray for workers, and then to send them out; the harvest is God’s and it is ready.

vv.h: He was moved with compassion for them
b: The Greek verb comes from the word for a person’s inner organs, the gut. In the Gospels it is used only of Jesus and of characters in his parables, such as the forgiving master, the good Samaritan and the father of the lost son (18:27; Luke 10:33; 15:20). It describes deep, active mercy.

vv.h: harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd
b: Moses prayed that God would appoint a leader ‘so that the congregation of the LORD will not be like sheep without a shepherd’ (Numbers 27:17), and God gave Joshua, whose name is the same as Jesus’ in Greek (compare Hebrews 4:8). Wesley noted that ‘they had many teachers’, scribes in every city, ‘But they had none who cared for their souls’. Jesus is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

vv.h: The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few
b: In the Bible harvest can be a picture of judgement (Joel 3:13; Matthew 13:39), but here it is a picture of gathering people into God’s kingdom. Quarles notes Jeremiah 2:3, where Israel is ‘the firstfruits of His harvest’; the mission begins with Israel (10:6). Jesus says the same in John: ‘Lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest’ (John 4:35).

Ezekiel 34 is essential background for this passage and for chapter 10. God condemns the shepherds of Israel who have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick or searched for the lost, and says, ‘I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out’ (Ezekiel 34:11). Jesus does what Israel’s leaders failed to do, and then sends his disciples to do the same.

Prayer for mission has been at the heart of the church from the beginning. Paul asked for prayer that ‘the word of the Lord may spread quickly’ (2 Thessalonians 3:1). Jesus’ command here is still one of the simplest and most urgent prayers a church can pray.

l.t: Failed shepherds, and God who will shepherd his flock himself.
Moses prays that Israel will not be like sheep without a shepherd.
The matching summary before the Sermon on the Mount.
Jesus sends the seventy-two: ‘The harvest is plentiful.’
The fields are ripe for harvest.
Jesus the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

qs: What did Jesus see when he looked at the crowds? What do we tend to see?
Why does Jesus tell his disciples to pray before he sends them out?
Who are the ‘harassed and helpless’ around you? How might you pray, and be part of the answer?

Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 9:35–38 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 9

10.ctx: Chapter 10 is the second of Matthew’s five teaching blocks, Jesus’ instructions for mission. Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from Jacob’s twelve sons (Genesis 49:28). Lists of the Twelve also appear in Mark 3:16–19 and Luke 6:14–16, with Peter first and Judas Iscariot last; Acts 1:13 lists the Eleven, again with Peter first.
10.mean: Jesus has told his disciples to pray for workers (9:38). Now he calls twelve of them and sends them out. First he gives them his own authority: authority to drive out evil spirits and to heal every disease and sickness, exactly the ministry Jesus himself has been doing (4:23; 9:35). Then Matthew names them. The number twelve is deliberate. Israel had twelve tribes, and Jesus later says that the Twelve will sit on twelve thrones ‘judging the twelve tribes of Israel’ (19:28). By choosing twelve, Jesus shows that he is gathering and renewing God’s people around himself. These men are called ‘apostles’ here for the only time in Matthew. An apostle is someone sent with authority to represent the sender. Look at who they are. Four fishermen. A tax collector, Matthew, who had worked for the hated ruling powers. Simon the Zealot, a name that may point to fierce zeal for God’s Law, or to links with those who wanted to drive out the Romans by force. If so, a tax collector and a zealot in the same group would once have been enemies. Most were ordinary working men from Galilee. And the last name is Judas Iscariot, ‘who betrayed Jesus’. Jesus chose him too, knowing what was in him (John 6:70–71). This is the kind of group Jesus builds his church with: ordinary, mixed, flawed people, held together by their calling to him. Peter is named ‘first’, and he leads the group throughout the Gospels. Christians differ on what that means for church leadership later (see Where readings differ).
10.big: Jesus chooses twelve ordinary, very different men, gives them his authority and sends them out, gathering and renewing God’s people around himself.

vv.h: gave them authority over unclean spirits … and heal every disease and sickness
b: The words repeat exactly what Matthew said of Jesus in 4:23 and 9:35. The disciples’ ministry is an extension of his. Quarles notes the repeated ‘every’: no disease would be too hard. The authority is given; it is not their own.

vv.h: first Simon, called Peter, and his brother Andrew
b: Matthew alone adds ‘first’. Peter is the leader and spokesman of the Twelve throughout the Gospels (16:16; 17:4; 26:33) and in the early church (Acts 1–12). He is also the one who denies Jesus three times (26:69–75) and is restored (John 21:15–19). Calvin readily allowed ‘That Simon Peter was the first among the apostles’, but denied that being named first gave him ‘authority over his companions’.

vv.h: Thomas and Matthew the tax collector
b: Mark and Luke list Matthew without his old job. Only this Gospel adds ‘the tax collector’, as if the writer wanted to remember where Jesus found him (9:9). Thaddaeus seems to be the same man as ‘Judas son of James’ in Luke 6:16; people in that time often had more than one name.

vv.h: Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus
b: ‘Zealot’ translates a word meaning ‘zealous one’ (BSB footnote: ‘Simon the Cananean’; the word comes from the Aramaic for zealous). It may describe his religious zeal or his past in the movement that opposed Rome. ‘Iscariot’ probably means ‘man from Kerioth’, a town in southern Judea, which may have made Judas the only non-Galilean in the group. Matthew never lets us forget how his story ends.

10.diff: ‘First, Simon’. Catholic teaching sees Peter’s place at the head of every list as reflecting the primacy Christ gave him, which continues in the bishop of Rome, ‘Peter’s successor’ (Catechism 552–553; 880–882). Protestants agree that Peter was the leading apostle, but, with Calvin, hold that ‘the circumstance of his being mentioned first, does not imply that he possessed authority over his companions’, nor a continuing office. See the note on 16:13.

b: Jesus’ choice of twelve signals the renewal of Israel. When Judas died, the apostles chose Matthias to restore the number (Acts 1:21–26). In Revelation, the new Jerusalem has twelve gates named for the twelve tribes and twelve foundations bearing ‘the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb’ (Revelation 21:12–14). The people of God in both covenants are one people, built on Christ.
Paul reminds the Corinthians that God chose ‘the foolish things of the world to shame the wise’ (1 Corinthians 1:26–29). The list of the Twelve is a living example.

l.t: The twelve tribes of Israel.
Mark: Jesus appointed the Twelve to be with him and to be sent out.
Luke: Jesus prayed all night before choosing the Twelve.
The Twelve will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes.
The eleven pray and choose Matthias to replace Judas.
The new Jerusalem: twelve tribes and twelve apostles.
God chose the weak and lowly.

qs: Why do you think Jesus chose twelve apostles?
What does the mix of people in this list (a tax collector and a zealot, fishermen and Judas) tell us about the church?
What authority and mission has Jesus given to ordinary Christians today?

Catechism of the Catholic Church 552–553 (Peter and the keys)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 880–882 (the Pope as Peter’s successor)

10.ctx: Galilee was surrounded by Gentile territory and, to the south, by Samaria. Jews and Samaritans had been bitter rivals for centuries (compare John 4:9). Travellers depended on hospitality, and a greeting of ‘Peace’ (Hebrew shalom) was a blessing. Sodom and Gomorrah were the cities God destroyed for their wickedness (Genesis 19). Compare Mark 6:7–13 and Luke 9:1–6; 10:1–12.
10.mean: Jesus gives the Twelve their instructions. First, where to go: not to Gentile areas or Samaritan towns, but ‘to the lost sheep of Israel’. This sounds narrow, but it is about timing, not favouritism. God’s promises were made to Israel first, and the mission begins there. After the resurrection, Jesus will send them to ‘all nations’ (28:19). Second, what to do: preach the same message as John and Jesus, ‘The kingdom of heaven is near’, and show it in action: heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, drive out demons. ‘Freely you have received; freely give.’ They must not charge for God’s gifts. Third, how to travel: lightly. No money, no bag, no spare clothes or sandals or staff. They are to depend on God, working through the hospitality of those who welcome them, because ‘the worker is worthy of his provisions’. In each town they should find a ‘worthy’ person, someone open to their message, and stay there. If a home welcomes them, their blessing of peace rests on it. If not, the blessing comes back to them. And if a town rejects them and their message, they are to shake the dust off their feet as a sign that the town has rejected God’s offer. On the day of judgement it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. Rejecting Jesus’ messengers is serious, because the message is his. Some of these instructions were for this particular mission; later Jesus allowed a bag and money (Luke 22:35–36). But the principles remain: urgency, simplicity, generosity and dependence on God.
10.big: Jesus sends his disciples to announce and show the kingdom, travelling light, giving freely and trusting God, while warning that rejecting the message is serious.

vv.h: Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles … Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel
b: Quarles notes that this did not ban helping a Gentile or Samaritan who lived among Jews; it limited the mission field for now to Galilee. Jesus himself says, ‘I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’ (15:24), yet he helps the Canaanite woman. Paul describes the order: the gospel is ‘first to the Jew, then to the Greek’ (Romans 1:16).

‘Lost sheep’ echoes Ezekiel 34, where God promises to seek his lost and scattered flock. Quarles points out that the phrase means all Israel, not a special group: ‘We all like sheep have gone astray’ (Isaiah 53:6).

vv.h: The kingdom of heaven is near … Freely you have received; freely give
b: ‘Preach’ means to announce publicly, like a king’s herald. The message is about God’s reign arriving through Jesus. The signs show what that reign is like: healing, life, cleansing, freedom. ‘Freely you have received’ covers both the authority they were given and the grace they themselves received. Peter later refused money from Simon the sorcerer who wanted to buy the Spirit’s power (Acts 8:18–20).

vv.h: the worker is worthy of his provisions
b: Paul quotes this saying, ‘The worker is worthy of his wages’, and seems to count it as Scripture (1 Timothy 5:18; compare Luke 10:7). He teaches that ‘those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel’ (1 Corinthians 9:14), though he often chose not to use that right.

vv.h: shake the dust off your feet
b: Many commentators suggest that it echoes the idea that Gentile soil was unclean, which devout Jews would not want to bring home. For the disciples to do this to a Jewish town was a vivid warning: by rejecting the Messiah, the town had put itself outside God’s people. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

Jesus’ words ‘Freely you have received; freely give’ sum up the whole Christian life. Everything we have from God is grace (1 Corinthians 4:7), so we give freely to others, whether time, money, help or the gospel itself.

The mission here is the first step in a widening circle. In Acts the risen Jesus tells the apostles they will be his witnesses ‘in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth’ (Acts 1:8). Samaria, off limits now, is part of the plan later (Acts 8:4–25).

l.t: God will seek his lost sheep.
Mark: Jesus sends them out two by two.
The sending of the seventy-two.
‘I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’, yet Jesus helps a Canaanite.
After the resurrection: go to all nations.
Those who preach the gospel should live by the gospel.
Witnesses to Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth.

qs: Why do you think Jesus told the Twelve to go only to Israel at this stage?
What does ‘Freely you have received; freely give’ mean for you?
Which of Jesus’ instructions are for that mission only, and which principles still apply to us?

Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 10:1–8 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

10.ctx: Local Jewish councils could sentence offenders to flogging with thirty-nine lashes (compare Deuteronomy 25:2–3; 2 Corinthians 11:24). ‘Governors and kings’ were Roman officials and client rulers such as the Herods. ‘Beelzebul’ was a name for the prince of demons (12:24). Much of this passage looks beyond the first mission to the persecution that would come later (compare 24:9–14).
10.mean: Jesus now warns his disciples honestly about what lies ahead. ‘I am sending you out like sheep among wolves.’ A shepherd among sheep is safe; a sheep among wolves is in mortal danger. So they must be ‘as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves’: wise and alert to danger, but pure and harmless, never using wrong methods to protect themselves. They will be handed over to councils and flogged in synagogues. They will be dragged before governors and kings. But even this will be an opportunity: they will be witnesses to them and to the Gentiles. And they need not worry about what to say, because ‘the Spirit of your Father’ will speak through them. Persecution will reach into families. Brother will betray brother; children will turn against parents. ‘You will be hated by everyone because of My name.’ But ‘the one who perseveres to the end will be saved’. When persecuted in one town, they should move on to the next; there will still be towns left ‘before the Son of Man comes’ (a hard saying; see Where readings differ). Why should they expect such treatment? Because a disciple is not above his teacher. If they called Jesus, the head of the house, ‘Beelzebul’, they will insult his household too. To be treated like Jesus is the disciple’s honour. This passage was fulfilled in the lives of the apostles, as Acts shows, and it has been the experience of Christians in many places ever since. Jesus does not hide the cost. But he promises his Spirit, his presence and final salvation.
10.big: Jesus sends his disciples out vulnerable among hostile people, calling them to be wise and pure, promising the Spirit’s help and final salvation to those who endure.

vv.h: as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves
b: Quarles suggests the snake’s wisdom here is the good sense to escape danger, which fits the command to flee in verse 23. Calvin explained: ‘You have need of wisdom and of harmlessness, because you will be like sheep in the midst of wolves.’ The word for ‘innocent’ literally means ‘unmixed’: pure, with no hidden motives. Wisdom without innocence becomes cunning; innocence without wisdom becomes naivety. Jesus asks for both.

vv.h: you will be brought before governors and kings as witnesses
b: Acts shows this coming true: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4), Paul before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa (Acts 24–26). Persecution became an opportunity to bear witness at the highest levels.

vv.h: it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you
b: This is a promise for times of trial, not an excuse for lazy preparation in ordinary teaching. When Peter and John, ‘unschooled, ordinary men’, spoke boldly before the council, the rulers were astonished (Acts 4:13). Note ‘your Father’: the disciples face their accusers as children of God.

vv.h: the one who perseveres to the end will be saved
b: Jesus repeats this in 24:13. Quarles takes ‘the end’ to mean the end of the trial (even death), and ‘saved’ to mean eternal salvation. Christians differ on how perseverance and salvation relate (see the glossary on perseverance): Reformed Christians hold that every true believer will endure, while Arminian and Catholic Christians hold that a believer can fall away. All agree that the call to endure is real and that God gives strength to endure (1 Corinthians 10:13).

vv.h: A disciple is not above his teacher
b: Jesus repeats this at the Last Supper: ‘No servant is greater than his master. If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well’ (John 15:20). Paul calls it a gift: ‘it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him’ (Philippians 1:29).

10.diff: ‘Before the Son of Man comes’ (verse 23) is one of the hardest sayings in Matthew. Quarles lists four main views: (1) Jesus would catch up with the disciples during this mission; (2) the resurrection, when Jesus received ‘all authority’ (28:18), as in Daniel 7, where the Son of Man comes to God to receive the kingdom (Quarles’ own view); (3) the judgement on Jerusalem in AD 70, which was Wesley’s view (‘To destroy their temple and nation’); (4) Christ’s return at the end, meaning the mission to Israel will continue until then. Each has defenders among careful interpreters.

b: Persecution for Christ is a constant theme of the New Testament. Paul writes, ‘all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted’ (2 Timothy 3:12). Peter tells suffering believers not to be surprised, but to rejoice in sharing Christ’s sufferings (1 Peter 4:12–14). The Beatitudes already said it: ‘Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness’ (5:10).

Jesus’ honesty is striking. He does not recruit followers with promises of an easy life. Yet alongside the warnings come three promises: the Spirit will speak through you (verse 20), the one who endures will be saved (verse 22), and, in the next paragraph, your Father knows every hair on your head (verse 30).

l.t: Like lambs among wolves.
The Holy Spirit will teach you what to say.
Hated by all nations; the one who perseveres will be saved.
If the world hates you, it hated me first.
Peter and John before the Sanhedrin, speaking boldly.
The apostles flogged, rejoicing to suffer for the Name.
All who live godly lives will be persecuted.
The Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives the kingdom.

qs: What does it mean to be ‘shrewd as snakes and innocent as doves’ in our setting?
How have these warnings been fulfilled in church history and today?
Which promise in this passage would most help you if you faced opposition for your faith?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 10:16–20 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 10

10.ctx: Houses in Galilee had flat roofs, used for work, rest and conversation; an announcement from a rooftop would be heard across a village. Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food: two for an assarion, a small copper coin (BSB footnote). ‘Hell’ translates Gehenna (BSB footnote; see the note on 5:21).
10.mean: Three times Jesus says, ‘Do not be afraid’ (verses 26, 28, 31). He has just warned of persecution; now he gives reasons not to be ruled by fear. First, the truth will come out. ‘There is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed.’ So what Jesus has taught them privately they must proclaim openly, from the housetops. Fear tempts us to keep quiet; the gospel must be spoken. Second, fear the right one. People can kill the body, but they cannot touch the soul. ‘Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell’: God. This is not a fear that drives us away from God, but a reverent awe that puts every human threat in perspective. ‘The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high’ (Proverbs 29:25). Third, God cares for you. Two sparrows were sold for a tiny coin, yet not one falls to the ground ‘apart from the will of your Father’. Even the hairs on your head are numbered. If God watches over sparrows, how much more his children? ‘So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.’ Then comes the challenge. Everyone who confesses Jesus before people, he will confess before his Father in heaven. Whoever denies him before people, he will deny before his Father. Jesus places himself at the centre of the final judgement. What we say about him now matters for ever. Peter would deny Jesus three times and later be restored (26:69–75; John 21:15–19). The warning is serious, but the door of repentance stays open.
10.big: Do not fear people: the truth will come out, God alone holds our eternal destiny, and he cares for us in every detail, so we can confess Jesus openly.

vv.h: What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight
b: Jesus often taught his disciples privately (13:10–17). They are not to keep it private. Quarles notes that fear chokes a disciple into silence just when it is most important to speak. The apostles said, ‘we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard’ (Acts 4:20).

vv.h: fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell
b: Most interpreters understand ‘the One’ to be God, who alone has power over eternal destiny (compare Isaiah 8:13, ‘Only He should be feared’). Wesley noted that ‘our Lord commands those who love God, still to fear him’. The fear of God and love for God belong together; the next verses speak of him as ‘your Father’. This verse also raises the question of what ‘destroy’ means (see Where readings differ).

vv.h: not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father
b: Wesley called this ‘The particular providence of God’, which ‘extends to the very smallest things’. Calvin wrote that tyrants, whatever their madness, are not outside God’s control, and that ‘As God is the guardian of our life’, we need not dread human cruelty. Quarles notes that a sparrow cost less than half an hour’s wage. Luke has ‘five sparrows sold for two pennies’ (Luke 12:6): the fifth thrown in free, and still God remembers it.

vv.h: everyone who confesses Me before men
b: To ‘confess’ is to declare openly that you belong to Jesus. In court, Jesus will be the advocate for those who have owned him. Paul writes, ‘if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved’ (Romans 10:9). He also warns, ‘if we deny Him, He will also deny us’ (2 Timothy 2:12). Peter’s restoration shows that a moment of failure need not be final.

10.diff: ‘Destroy both soul and body in hell’. Those who hold conditional immortality, including Seventh-day Adventists and some evangelicals (John Stott tentatively favoured it), read ‘destroy’ here as meaning that the lost will finally perish rather than suffer for ever. Those who hold the traditional view of hell as eternal punishment (the historic position of Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches) read ‘destroy’ as ruin, not ceasing to exist, alongside texts such as 25:46. See the note on Mark 9:42.

b: The doctrine of God’s providence, his care and control over all things, is one of the great comforts of Scripture. Joseph could say to his brothers, ‘what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good’ (Genesis 50:20). Paul writes that ‘God works all things together for the good of those who love Him’ (Romans 8:28). The sparrow saying brings this down to the smallest details of our lives.

Isaiah 8:12–13 lies behind Jesus’ teaching: ‘Do not fear what they fear … The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared.’ Peter quotes it to persecuted Christians and adds, ‘in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord’ (1 Peter 3:14–15).

l.t: Do not fear what they fear; the LORD alone is to be feared.
The fear of man is a snare.
Luke’s version: five sparrows sold for two pennies.
Peter denies Jesus three times.
Peter restored: ‘Feed My sheep.’
Do not fear; sanctify Christ as Lord; be ready to give a defence.
Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ.
Confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord.

qs: What three reasons does Jesus give for not being afraid?
What is the difference between the fear of God and being afraid of God?
In what situations are you tempted to keep quiet about Jesus? How might these verses help?
