Seventh-day Adventist Church, 28 Fundamental Beliefs, nos. 26–27
David L. Edwards and John Stott, Essentials: A Liberal–Evangelical Dialogue (Hodder & Stoughton, 1988), ch. 6 (Stott’s tentative case for annihilation)
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)

10.ctx: Many Jews expected the Messiah to bring peace on earth (Isaiah 9:6–7; Zechariah 9:10). Jesus quotes Micah 7:6, which describes families torn apart in a time of moral collapse (BSB footnote: Micah 7:6). Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels; condemned men had to carry their own crossbeam to the place of execution.
10.mean: Jesus says something that sounds shocking: ‘Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.’ Did he not come as the Prince of Peace? Yes, and in the end his reign will bring perfect peace. But his coming also divides. The ‘sword’ is not violence; Jesus later tells a follower to put his sword away (26:52; John 18:10–11 names Peter). It is a picture of division, as Luke’s version says (Luke 12:51). People must decide about Jesus, and not everyone will decide the same way, even in the same family. Jesus quotes Micah: a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, ‘A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.’ Christians in many parts of the world know exactly what this means: to follow Jesus can cost them their families. Then Jesus asks for first place. ‘Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me.’ Only God can rightly demand a love greater than for parents and children. Jesus is not telling us to love our families less, but to love him most. ‘Anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me.’ His hearers knew what that meant: a condemned man carrying his crossbeam to his death. Following Jesus means being ready to lose everything, even life, for him (see Where readings differ on how widely this applies). And then the great paradox: ‘Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.’ Clinging to our own life and comfort ends in losing what matters. Giving our life to Jesus, whatever it costs, is how we find true life.
10.big: Jesus divides people because he demands first place, above family and life itself; those who lose their life for him find true life.

vv.h: I have not come to bring peace, but a sword
b: Quarles notes that the sword stands for division: it cuts in two. The word in verse 35 translated ‘turn’ means to divide. Jesus does bring peace with God (Romans 5:1) and will bring peace to the world in the end (Colossians 1:20). But in this age his coming forces a choice, and choices divide.

vv.h: a man against his father … A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household
b: Micah 7:6 described a society falling apart. Quarles notes that later rabbis read it as a sign of the times just before the Messiah comes. Jesus says that the division will be over him. Wesley adds that the foes are the foes of a man ‘That loves and follows me’. Psalm 27:10 gives comfort: ‘Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.’

vv.h: Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me
b: Luke’s version uses the strong Semitic idiom ‘hate’ (Luke 14:26), meaning ‘love less by comparison’. In the Ten Commandments, honouring parents is a command from God (Exodus 20:12), and Jesus upholds it (15:4–6). For Jesus to claim a love greater than this is to claim the place of God.

vv.h: anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me
b: This is the first mention of the cross in Matthew, before Jesus has predicted his death (16:21; his crucifixion in 20:19). Quarles reads it strictly: the disciple must be ready to choose death rather than deny Jesus. Calvin applied it more widely: ‘we cannot be reckoned his disciples unless we are prepared to endure many afflictions’. Wesley explained the cross as ‘whatever pain or inconvenience cannot be avoided, but by doing some evil, or omitting some good’. Luke adds ‘daily’ (Luke 9:23).

vv.h: whoever loses his life for My sake will find it
b: This saying appears more often in the Gospels than almost any other (16:25; Mark 8:35; Luke 9:24; 17:33; John 12:25). ‘Life’ translates a word that also means ‘soul’ or ‘self’. Living for ourselves leads to losing ourselves; giving ourselves to Jesus is how we truly find ourselves, now and for ever.

10.diff: Taking up the cross. Quarles argues that Jesus meant readiness for martyrdom, choosing death rather than denying him, and rejects reading it simply as dying to self-interest. Calvin and Wesley applied it more broadly to all the afflictions and costs that come from following Christ; Luke’s ‘take up his cross daily’ (Luke 9:23) points that way too. Many interpreters hold both: the call includes willingness to die for Jesus, and the daily self-denial that prepares for it.

b: Jesus does not ask anything of his disciples that he did not do himself. He took up his cross and lost his life, and the Father raised him (16:21). Paul can say, ‘I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me’ (Galatians 2:20), and ‘I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord’ (Philippians 3:8).

Jesus also promised that no one who leaves family for his sake will lose out: they will receive a hundredfold, a new family in the people of God, ‘along with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life’ (Mark 10:29–30).

l.t: A man’s enemies are the members of his own household; but I will watch for the LORD.
Not peace but division.
Count the cost; whoever does not carry his cross cannot be my disciple.
Deny yourself, take up your cross; what good is it to gain the world?
A hundredfold now, with persecutions, and eternal life.
I have been crucified with Christ.
Unless a grain of wheat falls and dies, it remains alone.

qs: How can Jesus be the Prince of Peace and also say he brings a sword?
What does it look like in practice to love Jesus more than family, without loving family less?
What might ‘taking up your cross’ mean in your life this week?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 10:37–42 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 10

10.ctx: In the ancient world a messenger represented the one who sent him: to welcome or insult the messenger was to welcome or insult the sender (compare 2 Samuel 10:1–5). Hospitality for travelling teachers was vital to the early church’s mission (3 John 5–8). Cold water was precious in a hot climate.
10.mean: Jesus ends his mission instructions not with warning but with promise. ‘He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me.’ The disciples go out as Jesus’ representatives, and he goes with them in a real sense. To welcome them is to welcome Jesus, and to welcome Jesus is to welcome God the Father. This is both an encouragement to the messengers and an invitation to those who hear them. Jesus then speaks of rewards. Whoever welcomes a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. Whoever welcomes a righteous person because he is righteous will receive a righteous person’s reward. Those who support God’s messengers share in their reward, even if they are not prophets or preachers themselves. And then the smallest act of all: ‘if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is My disciple, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.’ ‘Little ones’ means ordinary, humble disciples, not only children. No act of kindness to one of Jesus’ people is too small for God to notice. This is the other side of the hard sayings just before. Following Jesus may cost family and life, but it also brings us into a family where the smallest kindness counts for eternity. In 25:31–46 Jesus will say that whatever was done for ‘the least of these brothers of Mine’ was done for him.
10.big: Jesus is present in his messengers, so welcoming them is welcoming him and his Father; no act of kindness to his people, however small, will go unrewarded.

vv.h: he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me
b: Quarles notes that Matthew usually presents Jesus as the one who sends; here he is the one sent by the Father (compare 15:24; 21:37). Receiving Jesus is the only way to a relationship with the Father. John records the same saying (John 13:20), and Luke has its opposite: ‘whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me’ (Luke 10:16).

vv.h: a prophet’s reward … a righteous man’s reward
b: The widow of Zarephath fed Elijah and was kept alive through famine (1 Kings 17:8–16); the Shunammite woman made a room for Elisha and received a son (2 Kings 4:8–17). Those who support God’s servants share in their work and in their reward. John says that those who support travelling Christian workers become ‘fellow workers for the truth’ (3 John 8).

vv.h: even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones
b: ‘Little ones’ is Jesus’ name for his ordinary followers (18:6, 10, 14). Wesley explained it as ‘The very least Christian’. The reward is not earned by the size of the gift but given by the generosity of God, who notices everything done for Jesus’ sake (compare Mark 9:41).

The idea that Jesus is present in his people runs through Matthew. He promises to be with two or three gathered in his name (18:20) and with his disciples always (28:20). On the last day he will say that whatever was done for the least of his brothers was done for him (25:40). When the risen Jesus confronted Saul, he asked, ‘why do you persecute Me?’ (Acts 9:4).

Hospitality is one of the most practical marks of Christian love: ‘Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it’ (Hebrews 13:2).

l.t: Whoever receives the one I send receives me.
Whoever rejects you rejects me.
A cup of water given in my name will not lose its reward.
The widow who fed Elijah.
Whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me.
Show hospitality to strangers.
Support Christian workers as fellow workers for the truth.

qs: What does it mean that welcoming Jesus’ messengers is welcoming Jesus himself?
Why do you think Jesus ends his hard teaching on persecution with these promises?
What ‘cup of cold water’ could you offer to a fellow Christian this week?

11.ctx: Verse 1 closes Jesus’ second teaching block (chapter 10). John the Baptist had been arrested by Herod Antipas (4:12); Matthew explains why in 14:3–5. Josephus says John was held at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Compare Luke 7:18–23.
11.mean: Jesus finishes instructing the Twelve and goes on teaching and preaching in the towns of Galilee. Meanwhile John the Baptist is in prison. He hears about ‘the works of Christ’, and sends his disciples with a question: ‘Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?’ It is a surprising question from the man who baptised Jesus and heard the voice from heaven (3:13–17). John had preached that the Coming One would baptise with the Spirit and with fire, and clear his threshing floor (3:11–12). Yet here he was in prison, and the judgement had not come. Isaiah had promised that the Anointed One would ‘proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners’ (Isaiah 61:1), and John was still a prisoner. Jesus does not rebuke the question. He answers with evidence. ‘Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.’ Almost every phrase echoes Isaiah. Isaiah 35 promised that when God comes to save, the blind will see, the deaf hear, the lame leap and the mute shout for joy. Isaiah 26 promised that the dead will rise. Isaiah 61 promised good news to the poor. Jesus is saying: look at what is happening; the promises are coming true. Then a gentle warning: ‘Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.’ Jesus is not the kind of Messiah many expected. He came first to heal and save, not yet to judge. Those who stumble over that will miss him.
11.big: When doubts come, Jesus points to his works, which fulfil the prophets’ promises; blessed are those who trust him even when he does not act as they expected.

vv.h: John heard in prison about the works of Christ
b: Quarles notes that ‘the works of Christ’ links with 11:19, ‘wisdom is vindicated by her actions’ (the same Greek word): Jesus’ deeds show who he is. Matthew calls him ‘Christ’ here, the Messiah, telling the reader the answer to John’s question before it is asked.

vv.h: Are You the One who was to come?
b: ‘The One who was to come’ (or the Coming One) echoes John’s own words in 3:11 and Psalm 118:26, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD’, which the crowds will sing at Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem (21:9).

Did John himself doubt? Quarles thinks he did, understandably, since the Spirit and the fire he had announced had not yet come and he was still in prison. Calvin thought otherwise: he called the idea that John asked partly for his own sake ‘exceedingly foolish’, and argued that John sent his disciples to Jesus because they ‘remained in a state of hesitation’. Either way, the right place to take doubts is to Jesus.

vv.h: The blind receive sight … the good news is preached to the poor
b: Quarles shows how Jesus weaves together promises about God’s own coming (Isaiah 35:4–6; 26:19) and about the Messiah, the Anointed One (Isaiah 61:1). One of the Dead Sea Scrolls (4Q521) also links these signs with the Messiah. Jesus’ answer quietly claims both: in him the Messiah has come, and God has come. Matthew has already shown each sign in chapters 5–9: the blind (9:27–31), the lame (9:1–8), lepers (8:1–4), the deaf and mute (9:32–33), the dead (9:18–26), and the good news preached to the poor (5:3).

vv.h: Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me
b: The BSB footnote gives ‘who is not offended by Me’. The word is the root of our word ‘scandal’: a stumbling block. Calvin read it as a warning that believers ‘must encounter offenses, which will tend to interrupt the progress of faith’, such as Jesus’ lowliness and the cross. Paul says that Christ crucified is ‘a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles’ (1 Corinthians 1:23).

11.diff: Did John doubt? Many modern commentators, including Quarles, think John genuinely wavered, since the judgement he had announced had not come and he was still in prison. An older view, held by several early Christian writers and by Calvin, is that John was not in doubt himself but sent his disciples so that they would see Jesus for themselves; Calvin called the opposite view ‘exceedingly foolish’. Both agree that Jesus answers with gentle evidence, not rebuke.

b: John’s question is an encouragement to anyone who struggles with doubt. Most modern commentators think that even the greatest of the prophets (11:11) was shaken by suffering and unanswered expectations, though Calvin disagreed (see Where readings differ). Jesus does not condemn him; in the very next breath he praises him. Faith is not the absence of questions but bringing our questions to Jesus and looking at the evidence he gives.

Isaiah 35, which Jesus echoes, goes on to describe a highway in the desert on which ‘the redeemed’ will return to Zion with everlasting joy, and ‘sorrow and sighing will flee’ (Isaiah 35:8–10). Jesus’ healings are the first signs of that great homecoming.

l.t: God comes to save: the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap.
Your dead will live; their bodies will rise.
Good news to the poor, liberty to the captives.
Luke’s account: Jesus heals many in that hour.
John’s announcement of the Coming One.
Why John was in prison, and his death.
Christ crucified: a stumbling block, yet the power and wisdom of God.

qs: Why might John, of all people, have asked this question?
How does Jesus answer, and why does he answer that way rather than simply saying ‘Yes’?
What do you do with your doubts? How does this passage help?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 11:1–6 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119 (Whiston): John the Baptist

11.ctx: Crowds had gone out to the Jordan wilderness to hear John (3:5). Malachi, the last book of the Old Testament in our Bibles, promised a messenger to prepare the way of the LORD, and named him ‘Elijah the prophet’ (Malachi 3:1; 4:5). John wore clothing like Elijah’s (3:4; 2 Kings 1:8). Compare Luke 7:24–35.
11.mean: As John’s disciples leave, Jesus speaks to the crowd about John, and it is high praise. He asks three times what they went out into the wilderness to see. A reed shaking in the wind, someone weak who bends to every pressure? No; John was a rock who told a king he was wrong, and was in prison for it. A man in fine clothes? No; people like that live in palaces, flattering kings. A prophet? Yes, and more than a prophet. John is the messenger Malachi promised, who would prepare the way. Jesus quotes Malachi 3:1, but with a striking change. In Malachi, God says the messenger will prepare the way ‘before Me’. Jesus quotes it as ‘prepare Your way before You’: the LORD’s coming is Jesus’ coming. No one born of a woman is greater than John. ‘Yet even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.’ This is not a put-down of John. It shows how great the new age is. John stood at the turning point, pointing to the King; the humblest disciple who lives after the cross and resurrection knows more of God’s salvation than John could. If they are willing to accept it, John is ‘the Elijah who was to come’. Then Jesus turns to the crowd. This generation is like children in the marketplace who will not join any game. Some play wedding music and others refuse to dance; some play funeral songs and others refuse to mourn. John came fasting, and people said he had a demon. Jesus came eating and drinking with sinners, and they called him a glutton and a drunkard. Nothing pleased them. But ‘wisdom is vindicated by her actions’: in the end, the results of God’s ways prove them right.
11.big: John was the greatest of the prophets, the promised forerunner, yet the kingdom Jesus brings is greater still; people who will not respond to God find fault with every messenger.

vv.h: A reed swaying in the wind?
b: Quarles notes that in the Old Testament a reed pictured weakness and unreliability; Egypt was ‘that splintered reed of a staff’ (Isaiah 36:6). John was the opposite. To borrow the picture from 7:24–25, he was a house on the rock, not a reed in the wind.

vv.h: Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You
b: Malachi 3:1 reads, ‘Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.’ Jesus changes ‘before Me’ to ‘before You’. Quarles points out what this means: a prophecy of the LORD himself coming to his temple is applied to Jesus. Jesus takes the place of God in the prophecy.

vv.h: even the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he
b: Wesley explained that ‘the least true Christian believer has a more perfect knowledge of Jesus Christ’ than John had. The point is the privilege of living in the age of fulfilment: we know the cross and resurrection that John only pointed to.

vv.h: the kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence
b: One of the hardest verses in Matthew (see Where readings differ). The BSB footnote offers ‘has been forcefully advancing’. Quarles takes it negatively: the kingdom’s herald and its King suffer at the hands of violent men, as John’s imprisonment and Jesus’ cross show.

vv.h: he is the Elijah who was to come
b: Malachi ended the Old Testament with the promise, ‘I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD’ (Malachi 4:5). The angel told Zechariah that John would go ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah’ (Luke 1:17). John himself denied being literally Elijah returned (John 1:21); he fulfilled Elijah’s role but was not Elijah returned in person.

vv.h: They are like children sitting in the marketplaces
b: Interpreters divide. Some take the children calling out as John and Jesus, and ‘this generation’ as those who refuse to play along. Others, including Quarles, read it the other way round: the complaining children are the critics, who wanted John to dance and Jesus to mourn. Either way the point is the same: some people will reject any messenger God sends.

‘Wisdom is vindicated by her actions’ (Luke: ‘by all her children’). Quarles argues that Jesus is quietly identifying himself with the personified Wisdom of Proverbs 8, a theme that becomes clearer in 11:25–30.

11.diff: ‘The kingdom of heaven has been subject to violence’ (verse 12) is obscure. Some take it negatively: violent men (such as Herod) attack the kingdom and its messengers; Quarles reads it this way. Others take it positively (BSB footnote: ‘has been forcefully advancing’), with the ‘violent’ as those who press eagerly into it: Wesley wrote that people ‘rush into my kingdom with a violence like that of those who are taking a city by storm.’ Compare Luke 16:16, ‘everyone is forcing his way into it’.

b: John’s greatness lay in pointing away from himself. He said, ‘Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!’ (John 1:29), and ‘He must increase; I must decrease’ (John 3:30). That is the calling of every Christian witness.

The identification of Jesus with God’s Wisdom (11:19) is developed elsewhere in the New Testament: Christ is ‘the wisdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 1:24), ‘in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge’ (Colossians 2:3).

l.t: ‘Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.’
Elijah the prophet sent before the Day of the LORD.
Luke’s account: wisdom is vindicated by all her children.
John will go in the spirit and power of Elijah.
Elijah has already come, and they did not recognise him.
Wisdom calls out, and was with God before creation.
Christ is the wisdom of God.

qs: What qualities of John does Jesus praise?
In what sense is the least in the kingdom greater than John?
Are there ways we, like ‘this generation’, find excuses not to respond to God?

11.ctx: Chorazin was a small town about two miles north of Capernaum; Bethsaida, on the north shore of the lake, was the home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Tyre and Sidon were wealthy Gentile ports to the north, condemned by the prophets for pride (Ezekiel 26–28). Sodom was the city destroyed for its wickedness (Genesis 19). Compare Luke 10:13–15.
11.mean: Now Jesus speaks words of judgement. He denounces the towns where he had done most of his miracles, because they did not repent. ‘Woe to you’ is the language of the prophets announcing God’s judgement, but it carries grief too. Chorazin and Bethsaida had seen extraordinary things. Matthew does not even record the miracles done in Chorazin, a reminder that Jesus did far more than the Gospels describe (John 21:25). Yet the people did not turn to God. Jesus says that if the same miracles had been done in Tyre and Sidon, pagan cities, they would have repented long ago, in sackcloth and ashes, the signs of deep sorrow. So on the day of judgement it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for these Jewish towns. Then Capernaum, Jesus’ own base: ‘will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!’ These words echo Isaiah’s taunt against the proud king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:13–15). If Sodom had seen what Capernaum saw, it would still be standing. The principle is clear and sobering. The more God shows us, the more he holds us responsible. Those who have heard the gospel many times and seen God at work are not safer than those who have never heard; they are more accountable. Capernaum’s sin, as Jesus names it, was not open wickedness. Its sin was indifference: it saw and did not change. Today little remains of these towns but ruins.
11.big: The greater the light people have received, the greater their responsibility; seeing God at work and not repenting brings heavier judgement than the sins of pagan cities.

vv.h: because they did not repent
b: Repentance was at the heart of Jesus’ preaching from the start (4:17). Quarles notes that the miracles were meant to lead to repentance and faith. Miracles alone do not change hearts; they confirm a message that must be received.

vv.h: they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes
b: Sackcloth was rough cloth made of goat hair, worn in mourning; ashes were sprinkled on the head. When Jonah preached, the pagan Ninevites repented in sackcloth (Jonah 3:5–6), a story Jesus will use in 12:41.

vv.h: will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!
b: Isaiah pictured the king of Babylon saying, ‘I will ascend to the heavens’, and God answering, ‘you will be brought down to Sheol’ (Isaiah 14:13–15). Hades is the Greek word for the realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol). Capernaum, proud of being Jesus’ home, faced a fall like Babylon’s.

11.diff: What would have happened? Jesus says Tyre, Sidon and Sodom ‘would have repented’. Molinists (following Luis de Molina, and today William Lane Craig) cite this verse for God’s ‘middle knowledge’: he knows what free people would do in any situation. Reformed theologians reject that idea, and Calvin read the saying not as revealing what God foresaw but as speech ‘accommodated to the ordinary capacity of the human mind’, warning against raising ‘thorny questions’ about God’s secret decrees. Both sides agree the main point is the guilt of those who saw and did not repent.

b: Jesus repeatedly teaches that responsibility matches privilege: ‘From everyone who has been given much, much will be required’ (Luke 12:48). Hebrews warns those who have heard the gospel: ‘how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?’ (Hebrews 2:3).

Jesus’ words of judgement are not cold. Luke records him weeping over Jerusalem because it did not recognise the time of God’s visitation (Luke 19:41–44). The ‘woe’ of judgement and the tears of compassion come from the same heart.

l.t: The proud king who would ascend to heaven is brought down to Sheol.
Luke’s version, in the sending of the seventy-two.
Pagan Nineveh repents in sackcloth.
The destruction of Sodom.
To whom much is given, much will be required.
How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem.

qs: Why does Jesus say Tyre, Sidon and Sodom will be better off at the judgement than these towns?
What was Capernaum’s real sin?
How might Christians who have heard the gospel many times be in danger of the same indifference?

11.ctx: Jesus’ prayer (verses 25–26) is followed by a statement about himself (verse 27) and an invitation (verses 28–30). A ‘yoke’ was a wooden frame joining two animals to pull a plough; Jewish teachers spoke of taking on the yoke of the Law. In the next chapter two arguments about the Sabbath, the day of rest, follow straight on. Compare Luke 10:21–22.
11.mean: Straight after the woes on the unrepentant towns, Jesus prays, and his prayer is pure praise. ‘I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children.’ The ‘wise and learned’ are not people who are truly wise, but people who are wise in their own eyes, like the scholars who rejected Jesus. The ‘little children’ are his disciples: ordinary people who know they need to be taught. God shows himself not to the clever and self-sufficient, but to the humble. And Jesus delights in this: ‘Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.’ Then he makes one of the greatest claims in the first three Gospels. All things have been entrusted to him by his Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Jesus knows the Father as only the Son can, and the Father knows him in the same way. The only way to know God truly is through Jesus. And then, astonishingly, the invitation goes out to everyone: ‘Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.’ The teachers of the day loaded people with heavy rules (23:4). Jesus offers a different yoke. Take my yoke, he says, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; you will find rest for your souls. Following Jesus is still a yoke: it means discipleship, obedience and learning. But his yoke is easy and his burden light, because he carries it with us, and because he is gentle. The God who reveals himself to the humble invites the weary to come.
11.big: God reveals himself to the humble through his Son, who alone truly knows the Father; and Jesus invites all who are weary to come to him for rest.

vv.h: hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children
b: Quarles notes that ‘these things’ are the knowledge of the Father and the Son (verse 27). The Old Testament prizes true wisdom, but warns, ‘Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes’ (Isaiah 5:21). Paul makes the same point: God chose what the world thinks foolish to shame the wise (1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

vv.h: No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son
b: This verse sounds like John’s Gospel (compare John 10:15; 14:6). It claims a unique, mutual knowledge between the Father and the Son: Jesus is not merely one of God’s children but the Son. Wesley commented that the knowledge of God comes to ‘none but those to whom he revealeth it’.

vv.h: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest
b: Calvin took the weary to be people whose consciences are burdened by sin and fear of God’s judgement. Wesley spoke of ‘rest from the guilt of sin by justification, and from the power of sin by sanctification.’ Quarles connects the promise with the Sabbath stories that follow (12:1–14): Jesus gives the true rest that the Sabbath pointed to (compare Hebrews 4:9–10).

vv.h: Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me
b: Jewish writings speak of ‘the yoke of the commandments’ and ‘the yoke of the Torah’. At the Jerusalem council Peter called the burden of the Law ‘a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear’ (Acts 15:10). Jesus’ yoke is discipleship to him. Calvin stressed that it is still a yoke, a discipline, not freedom from the fight against sin. ‘You will find rest for your souls’ quotes Jeremiah 6:16, where God tells his people to walk in the good way.

vv.h: For My yoke is easy and My burden is light
b: The word for ‘easy’ also means kind or good. Wesley: ‘gracious, sweet, benign, delightful’. John says, ‘His commandments are not burdensome’ (1 John 5:3). Quarles notes that Jesus’ invitation echoes Wisdom’s invitation in Jewish writings (Sirach 51), another hint that Jesus is God’s Wisdom in person.

11.diff: Election and invitation side by side. Reformed readers see in verses 25–27 God’s sovereign choice: Calvin says it is ‘a distinction which depends entirely on the will of God, that the wise remain blind, while the ignorant and unlearned receive the mysteries of the Gospel’. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers stress the universal invitation of verse 28; Wesley read verse 25 permissively, as God having ‘suffered these things to be hid’ from people ‘who are in other respects wise and prudent’. Both views hold the two truths together: God reveals, and all who are weary are invited.

b: Verse 27 is one of the clearest statements in the first three Gospels of the relationship between the Father and the Son that the church later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity. The Son is known fully only by the Father, and reveals the Father to whom he chooses (compare John 1:18; 17:25–26).

‘Gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29) is one of the very few places where Jesus describes his own heart. It is the heart of the one who invites. Isaiah described the Servant who would not break a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3), a passage Matthew quotes a few verses later (12:20).

l.t: Walk in the good way, and you will find rest for your souls.
Luke: Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit.
The scribes and Pharisees tie up heavy loads on people’s shoulders.
A yoke neither we nor our fathers could bear; saved by grace.
As the Father knows me and I know the Father.
A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.
God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise.

qs: Why does God reveal himself to ‘little children’ rather than to ‘the wise and learned’?
What does verse 27 tell us about who Jesus is?
In what ways are you weary or burdened? What would it mean to take Jesus’ yoke?

12.ctx: The Law allowed people to pick ears of grain by hand from a neighbour’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25). The Sabbath commandment forbade work on the seventh day (Exodus 20:8–11; compare 34:21), but did not list in detail what counted as work. Later Jewish teaching listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work, including reaping and threshing (Mishnah, Shabbat 7:2). Compare Mark 2:23–28 and Luke 6:1–5.
12.mean: Jesus has just offered rest to the weary (11:28). Now come two arguments about the Sabbath, the day of rest. Jesus and his disciples are walking through grainfields on the Sabbath. The disciples are hungry, so they pick some heads of grain and eat them. Picking grain from a field was allowed; the problem for the Pharisees was the day. To them, picking and rubbing grain counted as reaping and threshing, two kinds of forbidden work. ‘Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.’ Jesus answers with four arguments. First, David: when he and his men were hungry, the priest gave them the holy bread that only priests were allowed to eat (1 Samuel 21:1–6). Human need came before a rule about worship, and David was not condemned. Second, the priests: every Sabbath they work harder than usual in the temple, offering extra sacrifices (Numbers 28:9–10), yet they are innocent, because temple service comes first. And ‘One greater than the temple is here.’ If temple service outranks the Sabbath, how much more does Jesus? Third, Scripture: ‘If only you had known the meaning of “I desire mercy, not sacrifice,” you would not have condemned the innocent’ (Hosea 6:6). The Pharisees cared more about their rules than about hungry people. Fourth, and greatest: ‘the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.’ God gave the Sabbath; Jesus claims to be its Lord. In this story he does not set the Sabbath aside; he shows what it is for, and claims the right to say so.
12.big: Jesus is greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath; God gave the day of rest for mercy and blessing, not as a burden, and Jesus alone has authority to say what it means.

vv.h: Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath
b: Quarles notes that the Old Testament forbids only a few specific activities on the Sabbath, such as cooking, lighting a fire and buying and selling (Exodus 16:23; 35:3; Nehemiah 13:15). The later list of thirty-nine kinds of work included reaping, threshing and winnowing; picking and rubbing grain could be counted as all three. Quarles argues that the disciples had broken the Pharisees’ interpretation, not God’s command.

vv.h: what David did when he and his companions were hungry
b: The ‘consecrated bread’ (BSB footnote: ‘the Bread of the Presence’) was twelve loaves set out before the LORD each week and then eaten by the priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). Ahimelech the priest gave it to David in an emergency (1 Samuel 21:6). Quarles points out the implication: if David could do this, the Son of David has at least the same freedom.

vv.h: One greater than the temple is here
b: The temple was the holiest place on earth, where God was present among his people. Jesus claims to be greater. In him God is present in a fuller way: he is Immanuel, ‘God with us’ (1:23). John says that Jesus spoke of his body as the temple (John 2:19–21).

vv.h: I desire mercy, not sacrifice
b: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 for the second time (compare 9:13). Wesley explained: ‘I always prefer acts of mercy, before matters of positive institution’. God’s laws were meant to serve love, not to replace it.

vv.h: the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath
b: Mark adds, ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath’ (Mark 2:27). Wesley noted that Jesus’ claim ‘certainly implies, that the Sabbath was an institution of great and distinguished importance’: only someone with divine authority could be its Lord.

12.diff: The Sabbath and the Lord’s Day. Christians apply this passage differently. The Reformed tradition holds that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday as ‘the Christian Sabbath’, to be kept holy with rest and worship, while works of necessity and mercy are allowed (Westminster Confession 21.7–8). The Lutheran Augsburg Confession (art. 28) teaches that Scripture has done away with the Sabbath and that the church set Sunday apart for worship; many Baptists and New Covenant theologians likewise see the Sabbath fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:9–10). Catholic teaching holds that Sunday fulfils the Sabbath and asks the faithful to rest from unnecessary work (Catechism 2175, 2185). Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday. All agree that Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and that mercy is never forbidden. See the note on Mark 2:23.

b: The Sabbath goes back to creation: God rested on the seventh day and blessed it (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:11). It was also a sign of redemption from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). Jesus, the Lord of the Sabbath, brings the rest it pointed to. Hebrews says, ‘There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God’ (Hebrews 4:9).
Jesus’ claims in this passage are breathtaking: greater than David, greater than the temple, Lord of God’s own holy day. In the next verses the Pharisees begin to plot his death (12:14).

l.t: David eats the consecrated bread.
The priests’ extra Sabbath offerings.
‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’.
Mark: the Sabbath was made for man.
Jesus speaks of his body as the temple.
God rests on the seventh day and blesses it.
A Sabbath rest remains for God’s people.

qs: What was the Pharisees’ objection, and how does each of Jesus’ four answers deal with it?
What does it mean that Jesus is ‘Lord of the Sabbath’?
How can Christians today receive God’s gift of rest as a blessing rather than a burden?

12.ctx: A ‘withered’ hand was shrunken and useless, perhaps through paralysis. Some Jewish teachers allowed medical help on the Sabbath only when a life was in danger. Breaking the Sabbath deliberately was, in principle, a capital offence under the Law (Exodus 31:14–15). Compare Mark 3:1–6 and Luke 6:6–11.
12.mean: Jesus goes into a synagogue, and a man with a withered hand is there. The Pharisees ask, ‘Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?’ Matthew tells us why: in order to accuse him. The man is not life-threateningly ill; his healing could wait a day. If Jesus heals him, they can charge him with breaking the Sabbath deliberately. Jesus answers with an everyday example. If one of you has a sheep that falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will you not lift it out? Of course you will. ‘How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.’ The Sabbath is not a day when doing good is forbidden; it is a day for doing good. Then Jesus tells the man, ‘Stretch out your hand.’ He stretches it out, and it is completely restored. Jesus does not even touch him. He did nothing that even their rules called work. The response is chilling. The Pharisees go out and plot how they might kill Jesus. They were angry that he healed on the Sabbath, and on that same Sabbath they planned a murder. This is the first plot against Jesus’ life during his ministry (compare Herod in 2:13–16). From here the opposition grows until the cross. The story shows the difference between religion that serves people and religion that uses rules against them. Jesus valued the man above the rule. The Pharisees valued the rule above the man, and in the end above God’s own Son.
12.big: It is always right to do good on the Sabbath; Jesus restores a man’s hand, while those who put rules above mercy begin to plot his death.

vv.h: In order to accuse Jesus, they asked Him
b: Quarles explains the trap: an unintentional Sabbath breach could be forgiven with a sin offering, but if Jesus defended healing before doing it, the act would be deliberate. Their question was not a search for truth but a snare.

vv.h: If one of you has a sheep and it falls into a pit
b: Jewish teachers debated whether an animal could be rescued on the Sabbath; many allowed it. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater, as he often does (6:26; 10:31). Luke records a similar argument about untying an ox or donkey to give it water (Luke 13:15–16).

vv.h: Stretch out your hand
b: Quarles notes that the description recalls King Jeroboam, whose hand withered when he stretched it out against a man of God (1 Kings 13:4–6) and was restored when the prophet prayed. Here the man stretches out his hand in obedience, and it is made whole.

vv.h: the Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus
b: Mark adds that they joined with the Herodians, supporters of Herod’s family (Mark 3:6), two groups who normally disliked each other. Hostility to Jesus made strange allies. The irony is sharp: on the day of rest they plotted death.

Jesus healed on the Sabbath several times (Mark 1:21–31; Luke 13:10–17; 14:1–6; John 5:1–18; 9:1–16), as if deliberately. The Sabbath celebrated God’s good creation and his rescue of his people; what better day to restore a man’s hand? Isaiah said the Sabbath should be called ‘a delight’ (Isaiah 58:13).

The conflict over the Sabbath is really a conflict over who Jesus is. In John, when Jesus heals on the Sabbath and says, ‘To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working’, his opponents seek to kill him because he was ‘making Himself equal with God’ (John 5:17–18).

l.t: Mark: Jesus looks at them with anger, grieved at their hard hearts.
Luke: ‘Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil?’
A woman bent over for eighteen years healed on the Sabbath.
Jeroboam’s withered hand restored.
Sabbath healing and the claim to be equal with God.
Call the Sabbath a delight.

qs: Why did the Pharisees ask their question, and how does Jesus expose their motives?
What does ‘it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath’ teach about the purpose of God’s commands?
Where might we be tempted to value rules or routines above people?

12.ctx: Isaiah 40–55 contains four ‘Servant Songs’ about a mysterious Servant of the LORD; Isaiah 52:13–53:12, the fourth, describes his suffering and death. Matthew quotes the first, Isaiah 42:1–4, his longest Old Testament quotation, in a form that differs in places from both the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament (see BSB footnote).
12.mean: Knowing that the Pharisees are plotting against him, Jesus withdraws. Large crowds follow, and he heals them all, but warns them not to make him known. Why the secrecy? Matthew explains with a long quotation from Isaiah 42. Jesus is God’s chosen Servant. ‘Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights.’ These words echo the voice at Jesus’ baptism, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (3:17). ‘I will put My Spirit on Him’: the Spirit came on Jesus at his baptism. ‘He will proclaim justice to the nations’: his mission reaches beyond Israel. Then comes the key to this passage: ‘He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets.’ Jesus does not push himself forward, stir up crowds, or fight for power. He does not answer his enemies’ plot with a rival campaign. He withdraws and quietly goes on healing. ‘A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish.’ A bruised reed is almost broken; a smoking wick is almost out. Jesus is gentle with the weak, the damaged and the nearly hopeless. He does not crush them; he restores them. Yet he is not weak himself. He will lead justice to victory, and the nations will put their hope in his name. This picture of the gentle Servant comes right between two scenes of fierce hostility (12:14 and 12:24). Jesus answers hatred not with force but with quiet, persistent mercy.
12.big: Jesus is Isaiah’s gentle Servant, filled with God’s Spirit, who does not crush the weak but quietly brings justice and hope to the nations.

vv.h: warning them not to make Him known
b: Quarles suggests that open publicity about Jesus’ identity would have brought an early showdown with the authorities, before the right time. Jesus’ quiet ministry fitted the Servant Isaiah described.

vv.h: Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved
b: Matthew’s wording ‘My beloved’ links the quotation to the Father’s words at the baptism (3:17) and transfiguration (17:5). Quarles notes that by Matthew’s time some of the prophecy was already fulfilled: the Spirit had come on Jesus (3:16).

vv.h: justice to the nations … In His name the nations will put their hope
b: The Servant’s mission reaches the Gentiles. Quarles takes ‘justice’ here to include Jesus’ role as judge of the nations (compare 25:31–46). Isaiah’s last line reads ‘In His law the islands will put their hope’; Matthew follows the Greek Old Testament’s ‘in his name’, pointing to Jesus himself as the hope of the world.

vv.h: A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish
b: Wesley explained the bruised reed as ‘A convinced sinner: one that is bruised with the weight of sin’, and the smoking wick as ‘One that has the least good desire, the faintest spark of grace’. Jesus does not finish off the weak; he fans the faintest spark into flame.

The four Servant Songs (Isaiah 42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12) reach their climax in the suffering Servant who bears the sins of many. Matthew has already applied Isaiah 53 to Jesus’ healings (8:17). Here he shows the Servant’s character: gentle, humble, Spirit-filled. In 20:28 Jesus will say that he came ‘to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many’.

This passage matches Jesus’ own description of himself just before: ‘I am gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29). The church is called to the same gentleness with the weak: ‘Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness’ (Galatians 6:1).

l.t: The first Servant Song: a bruised reed he will not break.
The Spirit descends; ‘This is My beloved Son’.
Gentle and humble in heart.
Mark: crowds, healings and a command to silence.
The suffering Servant who bears the sin of many.
The Son of Man came to serve and to give his life.

qs: Why does Matthew quote Isaiah 42 at this point in the story?
What do the pictures of a bruised reed and a smouldering wick tell us about how Jesus treats weak people?
Who around you feels like a bruised reed? How could you show them Jesus’ gentleness?

12.ctx: ‘Son of David’ was a title for the Messiah (see 9:27). ‘Beelzebul’ (BSB footnote: also spelled Beezeboul or Beelzebub) was a name for the prince of demons; it probably comes from a title of the Canaanite god Baal. Some Jewish exorcists of the time drove out demons by spells and appeals to more powerful spirits. Compare Mark 3:20–27 and Luke 11:14–23.
12.mean: A man is brought to Jesus who is demon-possessed, blind and mute. Jesus heals him, and he can see and speak. The crowds are astounded: ‘Could this be the Son of David?’ They are starting to wonder if Jesus is the Messiah. The Pharisees move quickly to stop the idea. They cannot deny the miracle, so they explain it away: ‘Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons.’ In other words, Jesus is in league with Satan. Jesus knows their thoughts and answers with three arguments. First, it makes no sense. Every kingdom divided against itself will be ruined. If Satan were driving out his own demons, he would be destroying his own kingdom. Second, it is inconsistent. ‘By whom do your sons drive them out?’ Some of the Pharisees’ own followers practised exorcism; would they say the same about them? Third, there is another explanation: ‘if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.’ The exorcisms are proof that God’s reign has broken in. Then a picture: no one can rob a strong man’s house unless he first ties up the strong man. Satan is the strong man; Jesus is the stronger one who has come to bind him and set his captives free. Finally, there is no neutral ground: ‘He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.’ Everyone must decide. The Pharisees thought they were judging Jesus; in fact they were standing on the wrong side of the greatest battle in history.
12.big: Jesus drives out demons by the Spirit of God, proving that God’s kingdom has come and that the stronger one has bound Satan; no one can stay neutral about him.

vv.h: Could this be the Son of David?
b: The question in Greek expects a hesitant answer, something like ‘This couldn’t be the Son of David, could it?’ The crowd is wondering but not yet convinced. Quarles notes that the Pharisees refuse even to use Jesus’ name, calling him ‘this man’.

vv.h: Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons
b: Quarles notes that the Old Testament treats pagan gods as demons (Deuteronomy 32:17; compare 1 Corinthians 10:20), so naming Baal’s title was naming Satan. To accuse Jesus of using Satan’s power was to accuse him of sorcery, a capital crime. They had already made a similar charge (9:34).

vv.h: if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you
b: This is one of Jesus’ clearest statements that the kingdom is already present in his ministry. Luke has ‘by the finger of God’ (Luke 11:20), recalling the Egyptian magicians’ words about the plagues (Exodus 8:19). Calvin noted that ‘come’ is emphatic: God appears as Redeemer ‘without any request from them’. Matthew here uses ‘kingdom of God’ instead of his usual ‘kingdom of heaven’.

vv.h: unless he first ties up the strong man
b: Isaiah asked, ‘Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty?’ and God answered that the captives would be taken away and the plunder retrieved (Isaiah 49:24–25). Jesus is the stronger one. His victory over Satan began in the wilderness (4:1–11), shows itself in every exorcism, and is decisively won at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

vv.h: He who is not with Me is against Me
b: In the battle between God’s kingdom and Satan’s, there is no middle ground. ‘Gather’ is a shepherd’s word (compare 9:36–38): Jesus is gathering God’s scattered flock, and anyone who does not join him is scattering it.

The theme of Christ’s victory over Satan runs through the New Testament. Jesus says, ‘now the prince of this world will be cast out’ (John 12:31). Hebrews says that through his death Jesus destroyed ‘him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil’ (Hebrews 2:14). Revelation pictures Satan bound and finally defeated (Revelation 20:1–3, 10).
The Old Testament promised a stronger one from the very beginning: the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15).

l.t: The captives of the mighty will be taken away.
Mark: ‘He is out of His mind’; the strong man bound.
Luke: ‘by the finger of God’; a stronger man attacks and overpowers him.
The first accusation that Jesus drives out demons by the prince of demons.
The offspring of the woman will crush the serpent’s head.
Christ disarmed the powers at the cross.
Through death he destroyed the one who holds the power of death.

qs: What three answers does Jesus give to the accusation that he works by Satan’s power?
What does the picture of the strong man tell us about what Jesus came to do?
Why is there no neutral position about Jesus?

12.ctx: The scene continues from the Pharisees’ charge that Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul (12:24). Some Jewish teachers listed sins that could never be forgiven, or taught that certain sins were atoned for only by the sinner’s death. ‘Brood of vipers’ was John the Baptist’s phrase for the Pharisees and Sadducees (3:7). Compare Mark 3:28–30 and Luke 12:10; 6:43–45.
12.mean: Jesus now gives a solemn warning to the Pharisees. First, the good news, which would have astonished his hearers: ‘every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men.’ There is no sin so great that God cannot forgive it. Even speaking against the Son of Man can be forgiven. Paul was once a blasphemer and persecutor, but he received mercy because he acted in ignorance (1 Timothy 1:13). But there is one exception: ‘the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven’, and whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven ‘either in this age or in the one to come’. What is it? In context it is what the Pharisees had just done. They saw the Spirit of God plainly at work, setting a man free, and deliberately called it the work of the devil. This is not a careless word or a moment of doubt. It is a settled, wilful refusal to recognise God’s work even when it is obvious, calling good evil and light darkness. Why can it not be forgiven? Not because God’s grace runs out, but because a heart so hardened will not repent, and refuses the only way of forgiveness. Then Jesus turns to the link between the heart and the mouth. A tree is known by its fruit. ‘You brood of vipers, how can you who are evil say anything good? For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.’ Our words reveal what is inside us. And we will give account on the day of judgement for every careless word, because our words show what we really are. A pastoral note: people who are worried that they have committed this sin almost certainly have not. Those who have hardened their hearts in this way do not care; concern itself is a sign of the Spirit at work.
12.big: Every sin can be forgiven except the hardened refusal to recognise the Spirit’s work in Jesus; our words reveal our hearts and will be judged.

vv.h: every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men
b: Quarles points out how stunning this was. Some rabbis taught that certain sins could never be forgiven, or only through the sinner’s death. Jesus declares that every sin and blasphemy can be forgiven, and the passive ‘will be forgiven’ means God will forgive. The conditions are repentance and faith (4:17), not the size of the sin.

vv.h: whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven
b: Calvin described it as the sin of those who ‘maliciously turn to his dishonor the perfections of God, which have been revealed to him by the Spirit’, people who slander God’s gifts and power ‘contrary to the conviction of their own mind’. He stressed that the Spirit is not higher than Christ; the difference is that such people ‘cannot be excused on the plea of ignorance’. Wesley wrote that it is ‘neither more nor less than the ascribing those miracles to the power of the devil’. Quarles adds that it is unforgivable because such hardness never repents; Mark calls it ‘eternal sin’ (Mark 3:29).

vv.h: either in this age or in the one to come
b: Wesley explained this as ‘a proverbial expression among the Jews, for a thing that would never be done.’ Quarles notes that some rabbis taught that death would wipe out the sin of profaning God’s name; Jesus says that not even death atones for this sin. (On a Catholic reading of this phrase, see Where readings differ.)

vv.h: out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks
b: Quarles notes that ‘brood of vipers’ pictures them spitting venom, like the wicked of Psalm 140:3: ‘the venom of vipers is on their lips’. James warns that the tongue ‘is a fire’ (James 3:6). Words are not small things; they come from the heart.

vv.h: every careless word they have spoken
b: ‘Careless’ means idle, useless. Wesley applied it broadly: ‘every discourse which is not conducive to the glory of God’. Jesus is not teaching salvation by words; he is saying that words are evidence of the heart, and the heart is what God judges.

12.diff: ‘In the one to come’ (verse 32). Catholic teaching, following Gregory the Great, draws from this saying that ‘certain offenses can be forgiven in this age, but certain others in the age to come’, part of its teaching on purification after death (Catechism 1031). Protestant interpreters generally read the phrase as a Jewish way of saying ‘never’, as Wesley did. What is the sin, and who can commit it? Some hold that it could be committed only by eyewitnesses during Jesus’ ministry; Augustine understood it as final impenitence, refusing God’s forgiveness to the end; Calvin, as malicious slander of the Spirit’s work against one’s own conviction. Reformed theology holds that a true believer cannot commit it; some Arminians hold that an apostate could. Some link it with Hebrews 6:4–6 and 1 John 5:16. See also the note on Mark 3:28.

b: The New Testament speaks elsewhere of a hardening that puts a person beyond repentance: Hebrews warns of those who ‘have fallen away’ and cannot be ‘restored to repentance’ (Hebrews 6:4–6), and John mentions ‘a sin that leads to death’ (1 John 5:16). Christians differ on how these passages relate, but all hold out the open invitation of the gospel to anyone who wants to come.

The teaching on words echoes the Sermon on the Mount: anger and insults are murder in the heart (5:22), and a tree is known by its fruit (7:16–20). Luke gives the saying about the heart and mouth in his Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:45).

l.t: Mark: ‘eternal sin’, because they said he has an unclean spirit.
Luke’s version of the saying.
Paul, once a blasphemer, shown mercy because he acted in ignorance.
Out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.
The power of the tongue.
A warning about falling away.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful to forgive.

qs: What had the Pharisees done that led Jesus to give this warning?
Why does Jesus begin with ‘every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven’? How is that good news?
What do your words reveal about your heart? What would it mean to have our words changed?

Catechism of the Catholic Church 1030–1032 (purification after death)

12.ctx: Jonah was the prophet who ran from God, was swallowed by a great fish for three days and nights, and then preached to Nineveh, which repented (Jonah 1–3). The Queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, who travelled to test Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10:1–13). Compare Luke 11:29–32 and Matthew 16:1–4.
12.mean: Some scribes and Pharisees come to Jesus: ‘Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.’ He has just healed a blind and mute man in front of them, and they explained it away. Now they want more proof. Jesus refuses. ‘A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign.’ ‘Adulterous’ is the prophets’ word for unfaithfulness to God, like a wife unfaithful to her husband. People who will not believe the signs they have seen will not believe another one. But Jesus promises one sign: the sign of the prophet Jonah. ‘For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.’ Jonah was swallowed and, as he says in his prayer, brought up from the depths as if from the grave (Jonah 2:2–6). Jesus will be buried and will rise. His resurrection will be the great sign. Then Jesus turns the tables. At the judgement the men of Nineveh will stand up and condemn this generation, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, ‘and now One greater than Jonah is here.’ The queen of Sheba will condemn it too, because she travelled from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, ‘and now One greater than Solomon is here.’ Pagan Ninevites and a foreign queen responded to lesser messengers. These religious leaders have the greatest prophet and the wisest king standing in front of them, and they ask for a sign. The problem is not a lack of evidence, but an unwilling heart.
12.big: Jesus refuses signs to those who will not believe, but offers the sign of his death and resurrection; he is greater than Jonah and Solomon, so rejecting him is graver than any pagan’s unbelief.

vv.h: Teacher, we want to see a sign from You
b: Quarles thinks this particular request may have been sincere, unlike the later testing in 16:1. Even so, Jesus knows their hearts. Signs alone do not produce faith; Jesus later says that if people do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31).

vv.h: A wicked and adulterous generation
b: Moses called the wilderness generation ‘a perverse generation’ (Deuteronomy 32:20), and the prophets pictured Israel’s unfaithfulness as adultery (Hosea 3:1; Ezekiel 16). Jesus places his generation in the same line.

vv.h: three days and three nights in the heart of the earth
b: This quotes Jonah 1:17. Jesus died on Friday and rose on Sunday, which by modern counting is less than three full days (see Where readings differ). Jonah’s prayer describes his rescue in the language of resurrection: ‘You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God’ (Jonah 2:6).

vv.h: One greater than Jonah … One greater than Solomon is here
b: Jonah was a reluctant prophet; Solomon was the wisest king. Jesus is greater than both, prophet and king in one, just as he is greater than the temple (12:6). Quarles notes that ‘greater’ refers to Jesus himself. Both examples are Gentiles who responded to God, again showing that the door is open to the nations.

12.diff: ‘Three days and three nights’. Jesus died on Friday afternoon and rose early on Sunday. Wesley explained that ‘It was customary with the eastern nations to reckon any part of a natural day of twenty-four hours, for the whole day’; the Gospels themselves use ‘after three days’ and ‘on the third day’ interchangeably (compare Mark 8:31 and Matthew 16:21). A few have argued for a Wednesday crucifixion (for example R. A. Torrey) or a Thursday one, but most interpreters accept the Friday dating.

b: The resurrection is the sign to which all Jesus’ other signs point. Peter preached at Pentecost that God raised Jesus because ‘it was impossible for death to keep Him in its grip’ (Acts 2:24). Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:17).
The book of Jonah ends with God’s compassion for the great pagan city of Nineveh (Jonah 4:11). Jesus, greater than Jonah, brings that compassion to all nations (28:19).

l.t: Jonah three days and three nights in the belly of the fish.
Jonah’s prayer: raised from the pit.
Nineveh repents at Jonah’s preaching.
The queen of Sheba visits Solomon.
Luke’s version: Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites.
A second demand for a sign; again only the sign of Jonah.
Christ raised on the third day; if not, faith is futile.

qs: Why does Jesus refuse to give the sign they asked for?
What is ‘the sign of Jonah’, and why is it the greatest sign?
What do the Ninevites and the queen of Sheba teach us about how to respond to Jesus?

12.ctx: Some Jewish exorcists of the time drove out demons (12:27); Quarles suggests that Jesus’ story may reflect cases where an exorcism brought no lasting change. Compare Luke 11:24–26.
12.mean: Jesus tells a short, unsettling story. An evil spirit leaves a man and wanders through dry places looking for rest, but finds none. So it decides to go back to the ‘house’ it left. When it returns, it finds the house vacant, swept clean and put in order. It brings seven other spirits even worse than itself, and they all move in. The man ends up worse off than before. Then Jesus applies it: ‘So will it be with this wicked generation.’ The point is that clearing out evil is not enough. The house was clean but empty. Nothing good had moved in to fill it. A person can give up bad habits, tidy up their life, even become religious, but if their heart is not filled by God himself, they are vulnerable to something worse. Jesus is speaking first about his generation. They had seen God at work in John the Baptist and in Jesus. Many had been stirred, and perhaps some outward reform had happened. But they did not receive Jesus himself. A people who have been swept clean but remain empty will end up worse than before. The same is true for individuals. What fills the empty house is the Holy Spirit, given to those who trust Jesus. Moral reform without new life is a house swept clean and left empty.
12.big: Reform without new life leaves a person or people empty and in greater danger; the cleansed heart must be filled by God himself.

vv.h: it passes through arid places seeking rest
b: Quarles suggests that the story may describe a real situation, where a demon was driven out by an exorcist other than Jesus, without lasting freedom. Once, Jesus ordered a spirit never to return (Mark 9:25).

vv.h: it finds the house vacant, swept clean, and put in order
b: ‘Vacant’ is the key word. Quarles suggests that it points to the absence of the Holy Spirit, whom the Messiah came to give (3:11). The house had been tidied, a picture of temporary reform, but not occupied.

vv.h: seven other spirits more wicked than itself
b: Seven often stands for completeness in the Bible. Wesley noted that this implies ‘there are degrees of wickedness among the devils themselves’. The point is that the last state is far worse than the first. Peter warns of those who escape the world’s corruption through knowing Christ and are then entangled again: ‘their final condition is worse than it was at first’ (2 Peter 2:20).

Paul describes the positive side of this picture: Christians are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), and are to ‘be filled with the Spirit’ (Ephesians 5:18). Putting off the old life must be matched by putting on the new (Ephesians 4:22–24; Colossians 3:5–14).

Many interpreters see Jesus’ warning about ‘this wicked generation’ fulfilled within forty years. Many who had heard him later rejected the apostles’ message, and Jerusalem was destroyed in AD 70, an event Jesus foretold with tears (Luke 19:41–44).

l.t: Luke’s version of the story.
The final condition worse than the first.
Jesus commands a spirit never to return.
Put off the old self; put on the new.
Be filled with the Spirit.
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

qs: What is the point of the story of the empty house?
How can someone ‘clean up’ their life without truly coming to Jesus?
What fills the ‘house’ of a Christian’s life, and how can we keep it filled?

12.ctx: Jesus’ family lived in Nazareth, about twenty miles (thirty kilometres) from Capernaum. Mark says they had come because they thought he was ‘out of His mind’ (Mark 3:21, 31). His brothers are named in 13:55; John says that at first they did not believe in him (John 7:5). Christians understand these ‘brothers’ in different ways (see the note on Mark 6:1). Compare Mark 3:31–35 and Luke 8:19–21.
12.mean: While Jesus is still speaking to the crowds, his mother and brothers arrive and stand outside, wanting to speak to him. Someone tells him. Jesus answers with a question: ‘Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?’ Then, pointing to his disciples, he says, ‘Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.’ At first this may sound harsh. Is Jesus rejecting his family? No. He loved his mother, and from the cross he made sure she would be cared for (John 19:26–27). But he is saying something important about the family of God. His truest family is not defined by blood but by relationship to his Father. Anyone who does the Father’s will belongs to Jesus as closely as a brother, a sister or a mother. Notice that he says ‘sister’ too, though only his brothers were mentioned; women disciples are part of his family. This ends a section full of conflict and rejection (11:2–12:50). The religious leaders have rejected him, and even his own family do not yet understand him. But a new family is forming around him: people who hear his words and do his Father’s will. This is a great comfort to anyone whose own family has turned away because of their faith (10:35–37). In Jesus they gain a family of brothers and sisters, and God as their Father. And it is good news that his brothers later believed: James became a leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14; 15:13; 1 Corinthians 15:7).
12.big: Jesus’ true family are those who do the will of his Father; everyone who follows him becomes his brother, sister or mother in the family of God.

vv.h: His mother and brothers stood outside
b: Quarles notes that Jesus was probably teaching in a house, which fits 13:1, where he ‘went out of the house’. Mark explains that his family thought he had lost his mind and came to take him home (Mark 3:21). Standing ‘outside’ is a quiet picture of their position at this point.

vv.h: Pointing to His disciples, He said, ‘Here are My mother and My brothers.’
b: Wesley commented: ‘See the highest severity, and the highest goodness!’ Jesus is not denying his natural family, but putting his spiritual family first, just as he put his heavenly Father’s business first as a boy (Luke 2:49).

vv.h: whoever does the will of My Father in heaven
b: Doing the Father’s will was the mark of a true disciple in the Sermon on the Mount (7:21). It is not a way of earning a place in the family, but the sign of belonging. Jesus himself is the perfect example: ‘not as I will, but as You will’ (26:39).

The New Testament everywhere treats believers as a family: God is our Father (6:9), Christians are brothers and sisters, and the church is ‘God’s household’ (1 Timothy 3:15). Jesus ‘is not ashamed to call them brothers’ (Hebrews 2:11).

Jesus promised that anyone who leaves family for his sake will receive ‘a hundredfold in the present age—houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children’ (Mark 10:29–30). The church is meant to be that family.

l.t: Mark: his family thought he was out of his mind.
Luke: those who hear God’s word and do it.
Even his brothers did not believe in him.
Mary and Jesus’ brothers praying with the disciples after the resurrection.
From the cross, Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple.
Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.
A hundredfold: brothers, sisters, mothers and children.

qs: Was Jesus rejecting his family? How do you know?
What does it mean to be part of Jesus’ family?
How can our church be a true family, especially for those whose own families have rejected them?

13.ctx: Chapter 13 is the third of Matthew’s five teaching blocks, a collection of parables about the kingdom of heaven. A parable is a short story or picture from everyday life that teaches a spiritual truth. Farmers in Galilee scattered seed by hand (scholars debate whether before or after ploughing), so some inevitably fell on paths, rocky patches and weedy corners. Compare Mark 4:1–9 and Luke 8:4–8.
13.mean: After two chapters of growing opposition (11–12), Jesus begins to teach in a new way. He goes out to the lake, so many people gather that he sits in a boat and teaches the crowd standing on the shore. Matthew says he told them ‘many things in parables’. The first is about a farmer sowing seed. As he scatters it, some falls on the hard path, where birds eat it. Some falls on rocky ground with only a thin layer of soil; it springs up fast but withers in the sun because it has no root. Some falls among thorns, which grow up and choke it. And some falls on good soil and produces a crop, a hundred, sixty or thirty times what was sown. Then: ‘He who has ears, let him hear.’ Jesus will explain the parable in verses 18–23, but even without the explanation the main point is clear. The seed is the same everywhere; the difference is the ground. The same message of the kingdom meets very different responses. Some people never let it in. Some respond with excitement that does not last. Some let other things crowd it out. And some receive it and bear fruit beyond all expectation. This parable explains what the disciples have been seeing: why so many who hear Jesus do not follow him, even though his word is powerful. It also encourages them. Most of the seed may seem wasted, but the harvest from the good soil is enormous. Quarles estimates a normal harvest in Israel at about ten times the seed sown. Ancient writers occasionally report a hundredfold in exceptionally fertile places, but thirty, sixty or a hundred was a rich harvest. God’s word will not fail to bear fruit.
13.big: The message of the kingdom meets different kinds of hearts; much seed seems wasted, but where it is received it produces an astonishing harvest.

vv.h: He got into a boat and sat down, while all the people stood on the shore
b: Quarles notes the eyewitness detail, found only in Matthew, that the people stood on the shore (Mark 4:1 says they crowded along it). Sitting was the teacher’s posture (5:1). A boat a little way out made a natural platform, and the water may have carried his voice.

vv.h: He told them many things in parables
b: The Hebrew word for parable (mashal) covers proverbs, riddles and stories. Quarles notes that Solomon, the son of David, was famous for his proverbs (1 Kings 4:32); the Son of David now teaches in parables. Wesley commented that this way of speaking ‘drew and fixed the attention of many, and occasioned the truths delivered to sink the deeper into humble and serious hearers’.

vv.h: along the path … on rocky ground … among thorns
b: Paths ran through and around fields, trodden hard by feet and animals. Much of Galilee has limestone close beneath the surface, so seed can sprout quickly in warm, shallow soil and then dry out. Thorny weeds grow faster than grain and starve it of water and light. Every listener would have recognised the scene.

vv.h: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold
b: Quarles estimates a normal yield in Israel at around tenfold. Ancient writers occasionally report a hundredfold in exceptionally fertile places, but the harvest here is still remarkable. Isaac reaped ‘a hundredfold’ in a year when the LORD blessed him (Genesis 26:12). The parable ends not with failure but with abundance.

vv.h: He who has ears, let him hear
b: Jesus often ended his teaching this way (11:15; 13:43). Everyone has ears; not everyone truly listens. The call echoes Moses: ‘the LORD has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear’ (Deuteronomy 29:4).

The Bible often pictures God’s word as seed or rain that brings growth: ‘so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please’ (Isaiah 55:10–11). Peter says that believers have been born again ‘not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God’ (1 Peter 1:23).

Mark adds a related parable about seed growing secretly while the farmer sleeps (Mark 4:26–29): the growth belongs to God. Paul makes the same point about ministry: ‘I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow’ (1 Corinthians 3:6).

l.t: Mark’s account of the parable of the sower.
Luke’s account.
God’s word will not return to him empty.
Isaac reaps a hundredfold, and the LORD blessed him.
The seed grows by itself while the farmer sleeps.
Born again through the living and enduring word of God.
One plants, another waters, but God gives the growth.

qs: What are the four kinds of ground, and what happens to the seed in each?
Why do you think Jesus began teaching in parables at this point in his ministry?
Where have you seen God’s word produce an unexpected harvest?
