13.ctx: The disciples ask privately why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables. Jesus answers by quoting Isaiah 6:9–10, words God spoke when he called Isaiah to preach to a people who would refuse to listen until judgement came (Isaiah 6:11–13). The same passage is quoted in John 12:40 and Acts 28:26–27. Compare Mark 4:10–12 and Luke 8:9–10.
13.mean: The disciples ask, ‘Why do You speak to the people in parables?’ Jesus’ answer is startling. ‘The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you, but not to them.’ A ‘mystery’ in the Bible is not a puzzle to be cracked but a secret of God’s plan that people can know only if God reveals it. The disciples have been given that knowledge; the crowds have not. Then a principle: whoever has will be given more; whoever does not have will lose even what he has. Those who receive the truth Jesus gives will grow in understanding; those who refuse it will end up with nothing. So Jesus speaks to the crowds in parables, because ‘though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand.’ He quotes Isaiah. God told Isaiah that his preaching would harden a people whose hearts had grown callous: they had closed their own eyes, so that they would not see and turn and be healed. The parables work in two ways at once. For those who come to Jesus wanting to understand, as the disciples do, the parables open up the truth, and Jesus explains them. For those who have set their hearts against him, the parables hide the truth: they hear stories about farmers and fish and go away unchanged. This is both mercy and judgement. Then Jesus turns to his disciples with deep joy: ‘blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear.’ Many prophets and righteous people longed to see what they are seeing, the promised King and his kingdom, but did not. Christians disagree about how God’s choice and human response fit together in this passage (see Where readings differ). All agree that the right response is to listen, seek and ask.
13.big: Jesus’ parables reveal the secrets of the kingdom to those who come to him and hide them from those who have hardened their hearts; his disciples are blessed to see what prophets longed to see.

vv.h: The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven has been given to you
b: ‘Has been given’ implies God as the giver. Quarles notes that ‘mysteries’ are God’s secret plans, which can be known only by revelation: who the King is, when the kingdom comes, and what it is like, the subject of this chapter. Paul uses the word for the gospel now revealed (Romans 16:25–26; Colossians 1:26–27).

vv.h: Whoever has will be given more
b: Wesley explained: ‘Whosoever hath — That is, improves what he hath, uses the grace given according to the design of the giver’, and called it ‘the grand rule of God’s dealing with the children of men’. Jesus repeats the principle in the parable of the talents (25:29). Quarles notes that in Mark and Luke it is the devil who ‘takes away’ the word from the hard-hearted hearer (Mark 4:15; Luke 8:12).

vv.h: Though seeing, they do not see
b: In Isaiah 6 God tells the prophet, ‘Make the hearts of this people calloused’ (Isaiah 6:10). Matthew quotes the Greek Old Testament, which puts it this way: ‘this people’s heart has grown callous … they have closed their eyes’. Both are true: people harden their hearts, and God gives them over to the hardness they choose (compare Romans 1:24–28). Calvin wrote that ‘the word of God, in its own nature, is always bright, but its light is choked by the darkness of men’.
Isaiah’s message of hardening was not the end of the story: even after judgement, ‘the holy seed will be a stump in the land’ (Isaiah 6:13). A faithful remnant would remain, as the disciples now are.

vv.h: blessed are your eyes because they see
b: Peter writes that the prophets ‘searched and investigated carefully’ about the coming grace, and that even angels long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:10–12). The disciples live in the time of fulfilment. Quarles notes that ‘your’ is emphatic in Greek: you, unlike the crowds, have been given eyes to see.

13.diff: Why do some understand and others not? Reformed readers see here God’s sovereign grace: the knowledge ‘has been given’ to the disciples and not to others. Quarles, for example, links it with 11:27 and 25:34 and says that God had selected particular people to inherit the kingdom; Calvin says Christ ‘intentionally spoke obscurely’ to many. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers stress human responsibility: Wesley paraphrases, ‘I do not give more knowledge to this people, because they use not that which they have already’, and says they were ‘unwilling to understand the things of God’. Both note that Matthew’s form of Isaiah 6 says the people ‘have closed their eyes’, and both hold that Jesus’ explanations are open to all who come and ask. See also the note on Mark 4:10.

b: Isaiah 6:9–10 became one of the key Old Testament texts by which the early church understood why many in Israel did not believe in Jesus. John quotes it after Jesus’ signs (John 12:37–41), and Paul quotes it at the very end of Acts, as he turns to the Gentiles in Rome (Acts 28:25–28). Paul also teaches that Israel’s hardening is partial and temporary, ‘until the full number of the Gentiles has come in’ (Romans 11:25).
The pattern of revealing and concealing fits Jesus’ prayer in 11:25: the Father has hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children.

l.t: Isaiah’s call: a people hardened, yet a holy seed remains.
Mark’s version: ‘so that they may be ever seeing’.
John quotes Isaiah 6 to explain unbelief.
Paul quotes Isaiah 6 in Rome.
Hidden from the wise, revealed to little children.
Israel’s hardening is partial, until the full number of the Gentiles comes in.
The prophets searched; angels long to look into these things.

qs: What does Jesus mean by ‘the mysteries of the kingdom’?
How do the parables both reveal and hide the truth?
What would it look like for you to have ‘ears to hear’ when you read Jesus’ words?

13.h: The Parable of the Sower Explained
13.ctx: This is one of the few parables that Jesus explains in detail; Matthew records his explanation of the parable of the weeds too (13:36–43). In Mark the disciples ask for the explanation privately (Mark 4:10–20). Compare Luke 8:11–15.
13.mean: Jesus explains the parable of the sower. The seed is ‘the message of the kingdom’, the word. The four kinds of ground are four kinds of hearers. First, the path: someone hears the message but does not understand it, and the evil one snatches it away. The word never gets beneath the surface. Second, the rocky ground: someone hears the word and at once receives it with joy. But there is no root. When trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he quickly falls away. Third, the thorns: someone hears the word, but ‘the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth’ choke it, so that it bears no fruit. Jesus has already warned about both in the Sermon on the Mount: worry about food and clothing (6:25–34), and treasures on earth (6:19–24). Fourth, the good soil: someone hears the word and understands it, and bears fruit, a hundred, sixty or thirty times over. Notice that every hearer hears; the difference is what happens next. Understanding in Matthew means more than grasping an idea. It means taking the word to heart and acting on it, like the wise builder who heard Jesus’ words and put them into practice (7:24). Notice too that the good soil does not all produce the same amount. What matters is fruit, not comparison. This parable is a mirror. It asks every reader: what kind of soil am I? It also explains to Christians why many who start well do not continue, and encourages them to keep sowing, because good soil exists and the harvest is real.
13.big: The same word is heard by everyone; the devil, persecution and worldly cares can stop it bearing fruit, but those who truly hear and understand it produce a rich harvest.

vv.h: the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart
b: Quarles links the hard path with the Isaiah quotation just before: hearing without understanding. Mark names Satan and Luke the devil (Mark 4:15; Luke 8:12). Wesley warned that the wicked one comes ‘either inwardly; filling the mind with thoughts of other things; or by his agent’, such as people who change the subject when the word should be considered. Calvin observed that human wickedness does not make the word ‘lose its own nature, or to cease to have the character of seed’.

vv.h: receives it with joy. But since he has no root
b: Joy is not a bad sign; the problem is the lack of root. Jesus warned that persecution would come ‘because of My name’ (10:22). Quarles calls these hearers ‘fair-weather friends’ who leave when following Jesus becomes costly. Jesus’ own disciples would fall away for a time on the night of his arrest (26:31, 56).

vv.h: the worries of this life and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word
b: Quarles notes how wealth deceives: it promises a security it cannot give (6:19), persuades us that we can serve God and money (6:24), and offers happiness it cannot deliver (Ecclesiastes 5:10). The rich young man is a sad example (19:22). Paul warns that ‘the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil’ (1 Timothy 6:10).

vv.h: the one who hears the word and understands it
b: In Matthew, understanding is the key difference (13:13, 15, 19, 23, 51). It is the opposite of the hard heart of Isaiah 6. Fruit in Matthew means a changed life of obedience (3:8; 7:16–20; 21:43).

13.diff: Do the rocky and thorny hearers lose salvation? Reformed readers usually see the rocky and thorny ground as people who were never truly converted; their joy was temporary because there was no root of real faith. Calvin says such hearers ‘are not truly regenerated by the incorruptible seed’. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers more often see some of them as people who truly believed for a time and then fell away; Luke says they ‘believe for a season’ (Luke 8:13). Wesley drew the line between the soils: the rocky-ground hearer had ‘No deep work of grace’, but the thorny-ground hearer ‘hath root in himself, is deeply convinced, and in a great measure inwardly changed’, and is still choked. All agree that the parable calls every hearer to examine whether the word has taken root and is bearing fruit.

b: The New Testament repeatedly calls for perseverance that shows the reality of faith: ‘continue in your faith, established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel’ (Colossians 1:23). Hebrews uses a similar farming picture: land that drinks the rain and produces useful crops receives a blessing, but land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless (Hebrews 6:7–8).
Jesus says that fruitfulness comes from remaining in him: ‘The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5).

l.t: Mark’s explanation of the parable.
Luke: those who hold fast the word with a noble and good heart.
Treasure in heaven and freedom from worry.
The rich young man goes away sad.
The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil.
Remain in me and you will bear much fruit.
Land that bears useful crops, and land that bears thorns.

qs: What helps God’s word take root in your life, and what hinders it?
What ‘worries of this life’ or deceptions of wealth most threaten to choke the word today?
How can we help each other to become ‘good soil’?

13.ctx: The ‘weeds’ were probably darnel, a kind of rye grass that looks much like wheat in its early stages; it often carries a poisonous fungus. Sowing weeds in an enemy’s field was a known act of malice. The parable is explained in 13:36–43.
13.mean: Jesus tells another story. A man sows good seed in his field. But at night, while everyone is asleep, his enemy comes and sows weeds among the wheat and slips away. When the plants grow and the grain appears, the weeds appear too. The owner’s servants are puzzled: ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?’ He replies, ‘An enemy did this.’ The servants want to pull up the weeds at once. But the owner says no: if you pull up the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest. Then the harvesters will gather the weeds to be burned and bring the wheat into the barn. This is the first parable in the chapter that begins ‘The kingdom of heaven is like’. It answers a question that may lie behind John the Baptist’s doubts (11:3): if the kingdom has come, why is there still so much evil in the world? Why has the Messiah not swept it all away? The answer is that God’s kingdom has come, but not yet in its final form. For now, good and evil grow side by side. Evil does not come from the owner; it comes from an enemy. And judgement is certain, but it is God’s work at the right time, not ours. Jesus’ own explanation follows in verses 36–43.
13.big: God’s kingdom has come, yet evil still grows alongside it, sown by the enemy; God will separate the two at the harvest, so his servants must wait patiently for his judgement.

vv.h: The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field
b: ‘Is like’ does not mean that the kingdom is like the man himself, but that the whole story shows what the kingdom is like. Jesus later explains that the sower is the Son of Man (13:37). Quarles notes that the Old Testament pictures God as the sower (Jeremiah 31:27; Hosea 2:23); Jesus takes that role.

vv.h: his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat
b: Darnel was hard to tell from wheat when young, but became clear when the grain formed (13:26). Wesley: ‘It was not discerned before: it seldom appears, as soon as the good seed is sown: all at first appears to be peace, and love, and joy.’ Quarles stresses that the parable is not saying true and false disciples can never be told apart (compare 7:16–20).

vv.h: Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field?
b: The question raises the problem of evil. The owner’s answer, ‘An enemy did this’, shows that God is not the source of evil. Quarles calls it a ‘mini-theodicy’, a short defence of God’s goodness in the face of evil (compare James 1:13–17). Wesley called it ‘A plain answer to the great question concerning the origin of evil’: God ‘implanted no evil in the human soul: An enemy (with man’s concurrence) hath done this.’

vv.h: Let both grow together until the harvest
b: The roots of the two plants intertwined, so pulling one would damage the other. Patience is not approval of evil; it is waiting for the right time. Peter explains that the Lord ‘is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance’ (2 Peter 3:9).

Jesus’ disciples struggled with God’s timing. James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54–55), and Peter drew his sword (John 18:10–11; compare Matthew 26:51–52). Jesus repeatedly taught that judgement belongs to God and will come at the end of the age.
Paul says that the Lord will ‘bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts’ (1 Corinthians 4:5), so we should not pass final judgement before the time.

l.t: Jesus explains the parable of the weeds.
John: the wheat gathered, the chaff burned.
James and John want to call down fire; Jesus rebukes them.
God’s patience: not wanting anyone to perish.
Judge nothing before the appointed time.
God tempts no one; every good gift is from above.

qs: What does this parable say about where evil comes from?
Why does the owner tell the servants to wait?
How should Christians respond to evil in the world while they wait for God’s final judgement?

13.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed
13.ctx: The mustard plant of Galilee, usually identified as black mustard, grows from a tiny seed into a large bush, often two or three metres tall in a single season (Quarles). Birds perch in it and eat its seeds. This and the next parable form a pair: compare Mark 4:30–32 and Luke 13:18–21.
13.mean: Jesus tells two short parables about how the kingdom grows. The first is about a mustard seed. A man plants it in his field. It is ‘the smallest of all seeds’, meaning the smallest seed people commonly sowed, yet it grows into the largest of garden plants and becomes like a tree, so that birds come and nest in its branches. The kingdom of heaven started tiny. A carpenter from Nazareth gathered a handful of followers, one of whom would betray him. Most people hardly noticed. The religious leaders opposed him, and Herod had just killed his forerunner. It did not look like the start of anything great. But Jesus says that is exactly how God’s kingdom works. The picture of birds nesting in a great tree comes from the prophets. In Daniel and Ezekiel a great tree sheltering birds pictures a mighty empire (Daniel 4:10–12; Ezekiel 31:6). Ezekiel also uses it for the kingdom God himself would plant: a tender shoot set on the mountain of Israel that becomes a majestic cedar, where ‘Birds of every kind will nest under it’ (Ezekiel 17:22–23). Jesus is saying that his small beginning is the start of that kingdom. This parable answered a real question for Jesus’ first followers. If he is the King, why is his kingdom so small and unimpressive? Where are the armies, the crowds, the power? The answer is that God’s kingdom does not arrive with fanfare. It begins small, and it grows. It is also an encouragement to Christians today in small churches and hard places. Zechariah asked, ‘who has despised the day of small things?’ (Zechariah 4:10). What God plants, however small it looks, will grow beyond anything we could imagine. Wesley applied it two ways: ‘So will the Christian doctrine spread in the world, and the life of Christ in the soul.’
13.big: God’s kingdom begins as small as a mustard seed but grows into a great tree; what God plants will become far greater than its beginnings suggest.

vv.h: The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man took and planted in his field
b: Wesley thought the parables so far ‘relate chiefly to unfruitful hearers; these that follow, to those who bear good fruit.’ Calvin saw the point of this one: though the kingdom looks despised at first, it will become great.

vv.h: Although it is the smallest of all seeds
b: Quarles points out that Jesus means the smallest seed his hearers knew, not the smallest in the world (some orchid seeds are smaller). He was speaking in everyday terms, not giving a botany lesson. Wesley: ‘That is, one of the least: a way of speaking extremely common among the Jews.’

vv.h: it becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches
b: A mustard plant is not strictly a tree, and many take this as a clue that Jesus is pointing to Scripture. In Daniel 4 and Ezekiel 31 a great tree sheltering birds pictures a world empire; in Ezekiel 17:22–24 God plants a cedar on Israel’s mountain where ‘Birds of every kind will nest under it’. Many see the birds as the nations finding shelter in God’s kingdom (compare 8:11; 28:19). The Scofield Reference Bible, by contrast, saw the birds as a sign of an ‘insecure’ refuge, in keeping with its reading of the leaven (see 13:33).

Daniel saw a stone ‘cut out, but not by human hands’ that struck the statue of the world empires and ‘became a great mountain and filled the whole earth’ (Daniel 2:34–35). Jesus’ parables of growth fit that vision: God’s kingdom begins humbly and ends filling the world.
Revelation sees ‘a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue’ standing before the throne (Revelation 7:9). The handful in Galilee became that multitude.

l.t: Mark: the mustard seed puts out great branches.
Luke’s account of the mustard seed.
God plants a cedar on Israel’s mountain where birds of every kind nest.
Nebuchadnezzar’s dream of a great tree sheltering the birds.
The stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth.
Do not despise the day of small things.
A great multitude from every nation.

qs: What does the mustard seed teach about how God’s kingdom grows?
Why might Jesus’ first followers have needed this parable?
Where do you need to trust that something God has planted will grow, even though it looks small?

13.ctx: Leaven was a lump of sourdough kept back from the previous baking and worked into new dough to make it rise. ‘Three measures’ (Greek sata) was a large amount, enough to feed a hundred people or more. Sarah used the same quantity to bake for Abraham’s three visitors (Genesis 18:6). Compare Luke 13:20–21.
13.mean: The second parable of growth comes from the kitchen. ‘The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.’ A small lump of sourdough is worked into a great mass of flour. At first nothing seems to happen. You cannot see the leaven once it is mixed in. But slowly it works through the whole batch, until all of it has risen. The mustard seed showed the kingdom growing outwardly, from small to great. The leaven shows it working inwardly, quietly and unseen, until its effect is everywhere. The kingdom of God does not usually come with headlines. It works through the word preached, through prayer, through ordinary believers living faithfully, through changed hearts. Its progress is often hidden. But it is real, and it spreads. The word translated ‘mixed’ is literally ‘hid’. The woman hid the leaven in the flour. The kingdom is present now, but hidden; one day it will be fully revealed. The quantity matters too. Three measures of flour would make bread for a crowd. A little leaven does a great work. Some readers have objected that leaven in the Bible usually stands for evil, so this parable must be about evil spreading in the church (see the verse notes below). Most interpreters reject that reading, because Jesus says plainly that the kingdom of heaven is like the leaven. This parable encourages patience. We may not see much happening in our own lives, our church or our town. The leaven is still at work. Wesley put it simply: ‘Thus will the Gospel leaven the world and grace the Christian.’
13.big: Like a little leaven working through a great batch of dough, God’s kingdom works quietly and unseen until its influence spreads through everything.

vv.h: leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour
b: Wesley: ‘This was the quantity which they usually baked at once’. The Greek for ‘mixed’ is literally ‘hid’, perhaps hinting that the kingdom works unseen. Jesus often drew his pictures from women’s work as well as men’s (compare 24:41; Luke 15:8–10).

vv.h: until all of it was leavened
b: Leaven elsewhere in the Bible often pictures the spread of evil (16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). The Scofield Reference Bible, a classic dispensational study Bible, argued that it must mean evil here too, saying the other view ‘does violence to the unvarying symbolical meaning of leaven’. Quarles, like most interpreters, rejects that: here Jesus says the kingdom is like the leaven, and the point is its quiet, pervasive spread. Wesley also read it as the gospel spreading.

The same picture can work for good or ill. A little leaven of false teaching can corrupt a whole church (Galatians 5:9); the leaven of the kingdom can transform a whole life. Paul prays that Christ may dwell in believers’ hearts and that they may be ‘filled with all the fullness of God’ (Ephesians 3:17–19).
Isaiah foresaw that ‘the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water’ (Isaiah 11:9). Habakkuk repeats the promise (Habakkuk 2:14).

l.t: Luke’s account of the leaven.
Sarah bakes with three measures of flour.
The earth full of the knowledge of the LORD.
The leaven of the Pharisees: the same picture used for evil.
A little leaven works through the whole batch.
Christ dwelling in the heart; filled with the fullness of God.

qs: How is the kingdom like leaven in dough?
Why do you think Jesus used a picture that usually stood for something bad?
Where might God be quietly at work in your life or church, even if you cannot see much happening?

13.h: I Will Open My Mouth in Parables
13.ctx: Matthew pauses to explain Jesus’ use of parables, quoting Psalm 78:2. Psalm 78 is headed ‘A Maskil of Asaph’; it retells Israel’s history to teach the next generation. Compare Mark 4:33–34.
13.mean: Matthew steps back from the parables to make a comment. ‘Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables. He did not tell them anything without using a parable.’ At this point in his ministry, his public teaching came entirely in parables. Wesley added that this was ‘not at that time; at other times he did’ teach plainly. Then Matthew explains why: ‘So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.”’ He is quoting Psalm 78. That psalm begins with the psalmist promising to speak in parables and riddles. But the ‘riddles’ turn out to be the story of Israel: God’s mighty acts in the exodus and the wilderness, and Israel’s repeated failure to trust him. The psalmist tells the story so that the next generation will ‘put their confidence in God’ and not be like their stubborn ancestors (Psalm 78:7–8). Matthew sees Jesus doing the same thing on a greater scale. Through parables he is revealing what God has kept hidden from the beginning: the secret of the kingdom, now arriving in Jesus himself. And as in Psalm 78, the story is told to a generation that is in danger of hardening its heart. Notice how Matthew can call the psalmist ‘the prophet’. Chronicles says that Asaph ‘prophesied’ and calls him ‘the seer’ (1 Chronicles 25:2; 2 Chronicles 29:30). For Matthew, all Scripture speaks of Christ. This short passage invites us to read the Old Testament as Matthew did: as a story whose deepest meaning is revealed in Jesus. The things ‘hidden since the foundation of the world’ are now being made known, and we are among those privileged to hear them (13:16–17).
13.big: Matthew explains that Jesus’ parables fulfil Psalm 78: through them Jesus reveals what God had kept hidden from the beginning.

vv.h: He did not tell them anything without using a parable
b: Wesley: ‘That is, not at that time; at other times he did.’ Mark adds that ‘He explained everything to His own disciples’ privately (Mark 4:34).

vv.h: I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world
b: Matthew’s wording differs slightly from the Psalm, which in the BSB reads ‘I will utter things hidden from the beginning’ (Psalm 78:2). Psalm 78 is headed ‘of Asaph’, and Chronicles says Asaph ‘prophesied’ and calls him ‘the seer’ (1 Chronicles 25:2; 2 Chronicles 29:30), so Matthew can call the psalmist ‘the prophet’. Some manuscripts and modern editions lack ‘of the world’ (BSB footnote).

Paul speaks of ‘the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints’ (Colossians 1:26), and of ‘the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past’ (Romans 16:25). The parables are part of that unveiling.

Jesus taught that all the Scriptures point to him (Luke 24:27; John 5:39). Psalm 78 itself warns against forgetting God’s works, a warning the disciples will need when they forget the feedings (16:9).

l.t: Mark: he explained everything privately to his disciples.
‘I will open my mouth in parables’; teach the next generation.
The words of David and of Asaph the seer.
The mystery hidden for ages, now revealed.
The revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past.
Blessed are your eyes; many prophets longed to see what you see.

qs: Why does Matthew connect Jesus’ parables with Psalm 78?
What things ‘hidden since the foundation of the world’ does Jesus reveal?
How does reading the Old Testament with Jesus at the centre change the way you read it?

13.h: The Parable of the Weeds Explained
13.ctx: Jesus leaves the crowds and goes into the house with his disciples. The ‘fiery furnace’ echoes Daniel 3:6. ‘The end of the age’ is Matthew’s phrase for the final judgement and Christ’s return (13:39, 40, 49; 24:3; 28:20).
13.mean: In private, the disciples ask Jesus to explain the parable of the weeds, and he does so point by point. The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man, Jesus himself. The field is the world. The good seed are ‘the sons of the kingdom’, people who belong to God. The weeds are ‘the sons of the evil one’. The enemy who sows them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the harvesters are angels. Then Jesus describes the judgement plainly. At the end of the age the Son of Man will send out his angels. They will remove from his kingdom every cause of sin and all who practise lawlessness, and throw them into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. ‘Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.’ Notice who is in charge. The Son of Man sows, the Son of Man sends the angels, and the kingdom is called ‘His kingdom’. Jesus is not only the farmer; he is the Judge of the world. The explanation is sobering and hopeful. Sobering, because evil is real, it has a personal source, and it will be judged; Jesus uses the strongest pictures of judgement. Hopeful, because evil will not have the last word. Those who belong to God, who now live among weeds and sometimes feel overwhelmed, will one day shine like the sun. Daniel had promised, ‘the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens’ (Daniel 12:3). Jesus ends again with the call: ‘He who has ears, let him hear.’
13.big: Jesus, the Son of Man, will judge the world at the end of the age, removing all evil and making the righteous shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom.

vv.h: The field is the world
b: This detail matters for one of the main debates about the parable (see Where readings differ). Quarles notes that the good seed here stands for people, not the word as in the sower parable. Wesley: ‘The good seed are the children of the kingdom — That is, the children of God, the righteous.’

vv.h: every cause of sin and all who practice lawlessness
b: Quarles notes the probable echo of Zephaniah 1:3 in the Hebrew, where God threatens to sweep away the wicked with their idols. ‘Lawlessness’ is the word Jesus used of false disciples in 7:23. The Son of Man has ‘His kingdom’ and ‘His angels’: Jesus is Lord of heaven and earth.

vv.h: they will throw them into the fiery furnace
b: The wording echoes Daniel 3:6, where those who would not worship the king’s image were thrown into ‘the blazing fiery furnace’. Quarles notes that the word can mean a smelting furnace, and suggests Malachi 4:1 as background: ‘the day is coming, burning like a furnace’. Jesus uses the image to show the seriousness of final judgement.

vv.h: the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father
b: The BSB footnote points to Daniel 12:3. The righteous share the glory of their Lord, whose face ‘shone like the sun’ at his transfiguration (17:2). Paul says Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

13.diff: What does the parable say about the church? Jesus says the field is the world (13:38), but many have also applied the parable to the visible church. Calvin: ‘So long as the pilgrimage of the Church in this world continues, bad men and hypocrites will mingle in it with those who are good’, though he insisted the parable does not forbid church discipline, and does not mean false doctrine must be tolerated. Wesley distinguished hypocrites, who have ‘the form of godliness, without the power’, from open sinners, who ‘ought to be rooted up without delay, and not suffered in the Christian community’. Catholic teaching describes the Church as ‘embracing in its bosom sinners, at the same time holy and always in need of being purified’ (Lumen Gentium 8). The Anabaptist tradition stresses that the church should be a disciplined community of committed believers, using the ban (Schleitheim, art. 2). Many modern commentators, including Quarles, think the parable is about the world, and so says nothing against church discipline. All agree that only God can finally judge hearts.

b: Jesus’ teaching on the final judgement in Matthew comes to its climax in 25:31–46, where the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne and separates the nations. The weeds and the net (13:47–50) prepare for that scene.

The hope of shining glory runs through the New Testament: ‘When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory’ (Colossians 3:4). Meanwhile Paul calls believers to ‘shine as lights in the world’ (Philippians 2:15).

l.t: The wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens.
The blazing fiery furnace.
The day burning like a furnace; the righteous go free.
The Son of Man judges the nations.
Jesus’ face shines like the sun.
When Christ appears, you will appear with him in glory.
The Lord Jesus revealed from heaven with his mighty angels.

qs: What does Jesus’ explanation tell us about who he is?
How do the warning of the furnace and the promise of shining fit together?
How should the certainty of final judgement shape the way we live and speak about Jesus now?

13.h: The Parables of the Treasure and the Pearl
13.ctx: Ordinary people had no safe place for valuables, especially in time of war, so they often buried them (compare 25:18), and treasure was sometimes forgotten when its owner died. Pearls were among the most valuable objects in the ancient world. The Roman writer Pliny tells how Cleopatra won a bet that she could spend ten million sesterces on one meal, by dissolving one of her two great pearls in vinegar and drinking it (Natural History 9.58).
13.mean: Two very short parables, spoken to the disciples, make one point: the kingdom of heaven is worth more than everything else. In the first, a man finds treasure hidden in a field, perhaps while ploughing someone else’s land. He hides it again, and then, ‘in his joy’, goes and sells everything he has and buys the field, so that the treasure is legally his. In the second, a merchant is searching for fine pearls. When he finds one of great value, he sells all he has and buys it. The two stories differ in one way. The first man stumbles on the treasure by surprise; the merchant has been searching. Some people find the kingdom when they are not looking for it; others find it after a long search. But both respond in the same way. They give up everything to gain it, and they do it gladly. Notice the words ‘in his joy’. Jesus is not describing grim sacrifice. The man does not feel he is losing anything; he knows he is gaining far more. That is what discovering the kingdom is like. Following Jesus costs everything (10:37–39; 16:24–26), but compared with what we receive it is no loss at all. Paul knew this: ‘I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord’ (Philippians 3:8). The parables ask a searching question: do we value Jesus and his kingdom like that?
13.big: The kingdom of heaven is a treasure worth more than everything we have; those who truly see its worth gladly give up all to gain it.

vv.h: treasure hidden in a field
b: Quarles notes that the same word, ‘treasure’, was used for the Magi’s treasure chests (2:11). He argues that buying the field was the honest, legal way to claim the find, not trickery. Proverbs urges us to seek wisdom ‘like hidden treasure’ (Proverbs 2:4). Wesley described the kingdom as ‘a treasure hid from the world, and from the most wise and prudent in it’.

vv.h: in his joy he went and sold all he had
b: Calvin wrote that ‘the Gospel does not receive from us the respect which it deserves, unless we prefer it to all the riches, pleasures, honors, and advantages of the world’. He added that this does not mean every believer must literally sell everything, but that the kingdom must come first.

vv.h: a merchant in search of fine pearls … one very precious pearl
b: Quarles notes that the merchant’s searching recalls ‘seek first the kingdom of God’ (6:33) and ‘seek, and you will find’ (7:7). Jesus has already used pearls as a picture of something precious that must not be thrown to pigs (7:6).

13.diff: Who is the buyer? Most interpreters, including Calvin, Wesley and Quarles, take the man and the merchant to be people who find the kingdom and give up everything for it. A minority of interpreters have read the buyer as Christ, who gave everything to purchase his people. The Scofield Reference Bible, for example, saw the treasure as Israel and the pearl as the church, both bought by Christ ‘at the awful cost of His blood’. The first reading fits the setting among the disciples better, though the second expresses a truth taught elsewhere (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 1:18–19).

b: The theme of joyful sacrifice runs through Jesus’ teaching. He promised that anyone who leaves houses or family for his sake will ‘receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life’ (19:29). Hebrews says that Jesus himself ‘for the joy set before Him … endured the cross’ (Hebrews 12:2).
The rich young man (19:16–22) is the opposite of the man in the parable: offered the treasure of the kingdom, he would not sell what he had, and went away sad.

l.t: Seek wisdom like hidden treasure.
Treasure in heaven; seek first the kingdom.
The rich young man; a hundredfold for those who leave all.
I count all things as loss compared with knowing Christ.
For the joy set before him he endured the cross.
Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.

qs: What is the difference between the man who finds the treasure and the merchant? What do they have in common?
Why is ‘in his joy’ so important in this parable?
What would it look like for you to value the kingdom above everything else?

13.ctx: Fishermen on the Sea of Galilee used a large dragnet, with floats along the top and weights along the bottom, pulled between two boats or hauled to the shore. It caught every kind of fish, some of which were unclean under the Law (Leviticus 11:9–12) and had to be thrown away. Several of the disciples were fishermen (4:18–22).
13.mean: The last parable of the chapter returns to the theme of judgement. The kingdom of heaven is like a large net cast into the lake that catches fish of every kind. When it is full, the fishermen drag it to shore, sit down and sort the catch, keeping the good fish and throwing the bad away. ‘So will it be at the end of the age.’ The angels will separate the wicked from the righteous and throw the wicked into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Like the weeds, the net shows that in this age the good and the bad are gathered together, and that a day of separation is coming. The fishermen among the disciples would have known the scene well. Jesus had called them to be ‘fishers of men’ (4:19); here he reminds them that the final sorting is not their job but the angels’, at God’s command. Then Jesus asks, ‘Have you understood all these things?’ They say, ‘Yes.’ So he tells them a last parable about themselves. Every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old. A scribe was an expert in the Scriptures. A disciple who understands Jesus’ teaching becomes a new kind of scribe, who can bring out the old treasures of the Old Testament and the new treasures of Jesus’ teaching, and show how they fit together. That is exactly what Matthew himself does throughout his Gospel.
13.big: At the end of the age God will separate the wicked from the righteous; disciples who understand Jesus become teachers who bring out treasures old and new.

vv.h: a net that was cast into the sea and caught all kinds of fish
b: Quarles describes the dragnet, which caught everything in its path. Unlike a casting net aimed at a shoal, it was indiscriminate. Sorting happened on shore, not in the boat. The picture fits a world in which the gospel goes out to all kinds of people.

vv.h: The angels will come and separate the wicked from the righteous
b: This repeats the ending of the weeds parable almost word for word (13:40–42). The repetition underlines the certainty of judgement. In 25:31–33 the Son of Man separates people ‘as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats’.

vv.h: Have you understood all these things? ‘Yes,’ they answered.
b: Understanding is the mark of the good soil (13:23). The disciples’ understanding is still partial, as later chapters show (15:16; 16:9), but they are on the right side of the line drawn in 13:11–16.

vv.h: every scribe who has been discipled in the kingdom of heaven
b: Calvin rejected reading ‘new and old’ as simply the Law and the Gospel, and took it to mean teaching that is varied and ‘wisely and properly adapted to the capacity of every individual’. Wesley applied it to ‘every duly prepared preacher of the Gospel’. Many see here a self-portrait of Matthew, the scribe of the kingdom who brings out Old Testament treasures and new ones.

Jesus shows what it means to bring out treasures old and new when, after his resurrection, he explains to the disciples on the road to Emmaus ‘what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself’ (Luke 24:27). Paul tells Timothy that the Scriptures ‘are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus’ (2 Timothy 3:15).
The parables of the weeds and the net prepare for Jesus’ final discourse on the end of the age (chapters 24–25), where the same themes of waiting, watchfulness and separation return.

l.t: Jesus calls fishermen to fish for people.
The same pattern of separation in the weeds parable.
The sheep and the goats.
Jesus opens the Scriptures about himself.
The Scriptures make us wise for salvation.
Fish of many kinds in the river of life.

qs: How is the parable of the net similar to the parable of the weeds?
What does it mean to bring out ‘new treasures as well as old’?
How well do you know the old treasures of the Old Testament? How could you grow in this, on your own or with others?

13.ctx: ‘When Jesus had finished these parables’ marks the end of Matthew’s third teaching block. Nazareth was Jesus’ home town (2:23). Christians understand Jesus’ ‘brothers’ and ‘sisters’ in different ways (see the note on Mark 6:1). Compare Mark 6:1–6 and Luke 4:16–30.
13.mean: After the parables, Jesus goes home to Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue. The people are astonished. ‘Where did this man get such wisdom and miraculous powers?’ But their astonishment turns sour. ‘Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t His mother’s name Mary, and aren’t His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? Aren’t all His sisters with us as well?’ They know his family. They watched him grow up. How can this ordinary local man be someone special? ‘And they took offense at Him.’ Jesus answers with a proverb: ‘Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor.’ And he did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief. This short scene is a living example of the parables just told. The same seed falls on hard ground. The people saw his wisdom and his power, and could not deny either, yet familiarity bred contempt. They thought they knew all about him, and so they could not see who he really was. It is a warning to anyone who has grown up around Christian things. It is possible to be so familiar with Jesus that we never truly meet him. Notice too the effect of unbelief. Jesus’ power is not weakened, but he does not force his works on people who reject him. Mark says that he ‘could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick’ (Mark 6:5). Matthew puts it more gently, but the point is the same: unbelief shuts the door on what God is ready to do.
13.big: Familiarity can blind people to who Jesus is; his own town took offence at him, and their unbelief kept them from seeing his mighty works.

vv.h: Where did this man get such wisdom and miraculous powers?
b: The question is the right one, as Quarles notes: are Jesus’ words and works from God or from somewhere else (compare 12:24; 21:23–25)? The people of Nazareth were impressed by both his teaching and his miracles, but would not follow the evidence to its conclusion.

vv.h: Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?
b: The word for carpenter (tektōn) can mean a builder or craftsman in wood or stone (see History below). Mark has ‘Isn’t this the carpenter?’ (Mark 6:3): Jesus himself worked at the trade. Some later manuscripts give ‘Joses’ for Joseph (BSB footnote). James later led the church in Jerusalem, and the letter of Jude, whose author calls himself ‘a brother of James’ (Jude 1), is traditionally ascribed to him.

vv.h: Only in his hometown and in his own household is a prophet without honor
b: Luke records the same proverb at Nazareth (Luke 4:24), and John says that even Jesus’ brothers did not believe in him at first (John 7:5). Nathanael once asked, ‘Can anything good come from Nazareth?’ (John 1:46).

vv.h: He did not do many miracles there, because of their unbelief
b: Calvin explained Mark’s stronger wording: ‘unbelievers, as far as lies in their power, bind up the hands of God by their obstinacy; not that God is overcome’. Wesley applied it to every age: the reason why many mighty works are not done now is ‘that unbelief every where prevails’.

Nazareth was a small Jewish farming village on a ridge in Lower Galilee: current estimates suggest 200–500 people in Jesus’ day. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus (who names many Galilean villages) or in early rabbinic writings, which fits a place of no importance (compare John 1:46). Excavations under the Church of the Annunciation found silos, cisterns, tombs and simple houses.

About 6 km away stood Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital after 4 BC. The word translated ‘carpenter’ (Greek tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Building work at Sepphoris would have drawn craftsmen from the surrounding villages, and many scholars think Joseph and Jesus may have worked there, though the Gospels never mention it.

src.l: ‘Nazareth’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Reed; Bagatti)
‘Sepphoris’, Lexham Bible Dictionary
Josephus, Antiquities 18.27 (Whiston): Antipas makes Sepphoris his capital

b: The rejection at Nazareth foreshadows the wider rejection of Jesus by his own people: ‘He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him’ (John 1:11). Yet John adds, ‘to all who did receive Him … He gave the right to become children of God’ (John 1:12).

Isaiah described the Servant of the LORD as one who ‘grew up before Him like a tender shoot’, with ‘no stately form or majesty to attract us’, ‘despised and rejected by men’ (Isaiah 53:2–3). Nazareth saw only the ordinary carpenter’s son.

l.t: Mark: ‘He could not perform any miracles there’; he marvelled at their unbelief.
Luke: the synagogue at Nazareth tries to throw Jesus off a cliff.
Even his brothers did not believe in him.
He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.
No stately form to attract us; despised and rejected.
His family thought he was out of his mind; his true family.

qs: Why did the people of Nazareth take offence at Jesus?
In what ways can familiarity with Christian things make it harder to truly know Jesus?
What does this passage teach about the effect of unbelief?

14.ctx: Herod here is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea. Matthew tells the story of John’s death as a flashback: it explains why Herod thinks Jesus is John raised from the dead. John had been arrested back in 4:12, and had sent messengers from prison in 11:2. Compare Mark 6:14–29 and Luke 9:7–9.
14.mean: News about Jesus reaches Herod the tetrarch, and it frightens him. ‘This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!’ Matthew then goes back to tell what happened to John. Herod had taken Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, while his brother was still alive. The law of Moses forbade this (Leviticus 18:16), and John had told Herod plainly, ‘It is not lawful for you to have her.’ So Herod put John in prison. He wanted to kill him, but he was afraid of the people, who regarded John as a prophet. Then came Herod’s birthday feast. Herodias’ daughter danced, and Herod was so pleased that he swore to give her anything she asked. Her mother told her what to ask for: John’s head on a platter. The king was grieved, but he had sworn an oath in front of his guests, and he would not lose face. So the greatest of those born of women (11:11) was beheaded in a prison cell to satisfy a grudge and a rash promise. His disciples buried his body and went and told Jesus. This is one of the darkest scenes in the Gospels, and Matthew does not soften it. A faithful man dies for telling the truth to a powerful man, and God does not step in to save him. Yet the story is not just about John. John was the forerunner, and his death points ahead to Jesus’ own. Like John, Jesus will be arrested, will face a ruler who knows he is innocent, and will be killed because a leader fears people more than God (27:24). Herod’s guilty conscience shows that the truth John spoke would not stay buried. And Jesus’ response, in the next verse, is to withdraw to a quiet place, knowing that his own hour is coming.
14.big: John the Baptist was killed for speaking God’s truth to a powerful man; his death foreshadows the death of Jesus, and shows the cost of faithfulness.

vv.h: This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!
b: Matthew and Luke give Herod his exact title, ‘tetrarch’ (ruler of a quarter of a kingdom); Mark and Matthew 14:9 use the popular title ‘king’. Calvin thought the idea came from rumours among the people, born of ‘the hatred which they bore to the tyrant, and their detestation of so shocking a murder’. Wesley, who took Herod to be a Sadducee, remarked: ‘Sadduceeism staggers when conscience awakes.’
Quarles notes that John himself did no miracles (John 10:41), so the guess makes little sense. It shows a guilty conscience rather than careful thought.

vv.h: It is not lawful for you to have her
b: Herodias had been married to Herod’s half-brother, who was still alive. The law said, ‘You must not have sexual relations with your brother’s wife’ (Leviticus 18:16; compare 20:21). Josephus adds that Herod divorced his first wife to marry Herodias (see History below).
Wesley wrote: ‘John’s words were rough, like his raiment. He would not break the force of truth by using soft words, even to a king.’

vv.h: Although Herod wanted to kill John, he was afraid of the people
b: Mark adds a more mixed picture: Herod ‘feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man’, and ‘listened to him gladly’ (Mark 6:20). A man can enjoy hearing the truth and still refuse to obey it.

vv.h: Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist
b: Rash oaths are a theme in Scripture. Jephthah’s vow cost him his daughter (Judges 11:30–35), and Jesus has already warned his followers not to swear oaths at all (5:33–37). Mark records that Herod even promised ‘up to half my kingdom’ (Mark 6:23), the same offer King Xerxes made to Esther (Esther 5:3). But this time the request brings death, not rescue.

vv.h: The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests
b: Calvin saw the vanity behind it: Herod acted ‘as if it were more dishonorable to retract a rash and foolish promise than to persist in a heinous crime’. Wesley was more biting: ‘So he murdered an innocent man from mere tenderness of conscience.’ A wicked promise should be broken, not kept.

vv.h: Then John’s disciples came and took his body and buried it. And they went and informed Jesus
b: Wesley reflected on the mystery of it: ‘How mysterious is the providence, which left the life of so holy a man in such infamous hands!’ But he added: ‘we are sure the Almighty will repay his servants in another world for whatever they suffer in this.’ John’s disciples did the last loving thing they could, and then went to the right person.

hist.t: Herod Antipas, Herodias and John’s death
b: The Herod of Matthew 14 is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. After his father died in 4 BC, Augustus made him tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of Galilee and Perea, which he governed for 43 years. Matthew and Luke give his exact title, ‘tetrarch’; Mark (and Matthew 14:9) use the popular ‘king’. He rebuilt Sepphoris and founded Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee.

Josephus confirms the outline of the Gospel account. Antipas divorced his first wife, daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. Josephus calls that first husband Herod; the Gospels call him Philip (Matthew 14:3; Mark 6:17). Since several of Herod the Great’s sons were called Herod, some suggest he bore both names. Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, and Josephus says many Jews saw the defeat as God’s punishment for his killing of ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who called the Jews to righteousness and baptism.

Josephus gives a political reason for the execution: Antipas feared John’s influence over the crowds might lead to a revolt. The Gospels give the personal story. The two fit together easily. Josephus says John was held and killed at Machaerus, Antipas’s fortress east of the Dead Sea.

b: John stands in a long line of prophets who were persecuted for speaking God’s word to rulers. Elijah was hunted by Ahab and his wife Jezebel (1 Kings 19:1–2), a pair often compared with Herod and Herodias. Jesus himself said that Elijah had come in John, and ‘they did not recognize him, but have done to him whatever they wished’; ‘In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands’ (17:12).

Jesus taught that the prophets were persecuted in every generation (5:12; 23:29–37), and promised a reward to those who suffer for righteousness. Hebrews lists faithful people who were killed for their faith and says that ‘the world was not worthy of them’ (Hebrews 11:36–38).

l.t: Mark’s fuller account of John’s death.
Luke: John rebuked Herod for Herodias and for all his evil deeds.
Elijah confronts Ahab; Jezebel is behind the evil.
The law against marrying a brother’s wife.
Jesus: Elijah has already come, and they did to him whatever they wished.
Blessed are those persecuted for righteousness.
The faithful who suffered, of whom the world was not worthy.

qs: Why did John speak so plainly to Herod, and what did it cost him?
How does Herod show that knowing the truth is not the same as obeying it?
Where might fear of what others think lead you to do something you know is wrong?

14.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
14.ctx: This is the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels: compare Mark 6:30–44, Luke 9:10–17 and John 6:1–15. Luke places it near Bethsaida, at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. John adds that the loaves were barley loaves brought by a boy, and that afterwards the crowd wanted to make Jesus king by force.
14.mean: When Jesus hears that John has been killed, he withdraws by boat to a quiet place. Perhaps he wants to grieve, to pray, and to be away from Herod for a while. But the crowds find out and walk round the lake to meet him. When he steps ashore and sees them, he does not send them away. He has compassion on them and heals their sick. As evening comes, the disciples make a sensible suggestion: this is a desolate place and it is late; send the people away to buy food in the villages. Jesus’ reply astonishes them: ‘They do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.’ All they have is five loaves and two fish. ‘Bring them here to Me,’ he says. He has the people sit on the grass. He takes the loaves and fish, looks up to heaven, gives thanks, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to hand out. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. About five thousand men eat, besides women and children. This miracle shows who Jesus is. In the wilderness God fed Israel with manna (Exodus 16). The prophet Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves and had some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Here Jesus feeds thousands with five. He is the shepherd God promised, who would feed his flock himself (Ezekiel 34:15, 23). The miracle also shows how Jesus works through his people. He tells the disciples to feed the crowd, knowing they cannot. Then he takes what little they have, blesses it, and gives it back to them to give away. They are the waiters at his table, not the source of the food. Christians still face needs far bigger than their resources. The lesson is not to pretend we have enough, but to bring what we have to Jesus.
14.big: Jesus, the compassionate Shepherd, feeds thousands from five loaves; he takes the little his disciples bring and makes it more than enough.

vv.h: When Jesus heard about John, He withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place
b: Matthew links the withdrawal directly to John’s death. Quarles notes that it foreshadows Jesus’ own death. Wesley gave three reasons for it: ‘1. To avoid Herod: 2. Because of the multitude pressing upon him … 3. To talk with his disciples’, who had just returned from their mission (Mark 6:30–31). Jesus knew grief and the need to be alone with his Father.

vv.h: He had compassion on them and healed their sick
b: His plans for rest were interrupted, yet he did not resent the crowd. Mark says he had compassion ‘because they were like sheep without a shepherd’ (Mark 6:34; compare Matthew 9:36). Quarles contrasts him with the selfish shepherds of Israel condemned in Ezekiel 34, who fed themselves and not the flock. Herod has just held a feast that ended in murder; Jesus holds a feast that brings life.

vv.h: This is a desolate place … Dismiss the crowds
b: The disciples’ idea was practical and kind. But ‘desolate place’ (the same word as ‘wilderness’) is a reminder of Israel in the desert, where God fed his people every day for forty years.

vv.h: You give them something to eat
b: The ‘you’ is emphatic. Quarles notes that the command exposes the disciples’ inability: they could not do it. Calvin observed that ‘Hitherto Christ had bestowed his whole attention on feeding souls, but now he includes within his duties as a shepherd the care even of their bodies.’ He added a careful warning: ‘We have no right, indeed, to expect that Christ will always follow this method’, though he will never fail his people.

vv.h: We have here only five loaves of bread and two fish … Bring them here to Me
b: Bread and dried or salted fish were everyday food around the lake. The disciples’ ‘only’ meets Jesus’ ‘bring them here’. What is not enough in our hands becomes enough in his.

vv.h: Looking up to heaven, He spoke a blessing. Then He broke the loaves
b: Jewish families blessed God before meals; in the Mishnah the blessing over bread ends ‘who brings forth bread from the earth’ (Berakhot 6:1). Calvin notes that ‘blessing denotes thanksgiving’, and draws the lesson that ‘we cannot partake of our food with holiness and purity, unless we express our gratitude to God’.

Matthew uses the same four actions at the Last Supper: Jesus ‘took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples’ (26:26). In Mark and Luke the Greek verb for ‘gave’ suggests ongoing action (‘kept giving’); Quarles takes this to mean the bread multiplied as it was handed out.

vv.h: They all ate and were satisfied … twelve basketfuls of broken pieces
b: Everyone had as much as they wanted, and there was more left over than there had been at the start. Quarles notes that the word for basket (kophinos) was a large basket with straps, carried by travellers and soldiers. Some see a link between the twelve baskets and the twelve tribes of Israel or the twelve apostles. At the least, nothing God gives is wasted (John 6:12).

vv.h: About five thousand men were fed, besides women and children
b: Only Matthew adds ‘besides women and children’. The whole crowd may have been well over ten thousand people, probably more than lived in most towns in Galilee.

mis.t: ‘The real miracle was that everyone shared their packed lunches’
mis.b: Some modern writers have suggested that the people had hidden food and were moved by the boy’s example to share it. Quarles notes that such explanations come from a prior belief that miracles cannot happen, not from the text. All four Gospels tell it as a miracle, John says the crowd saw it as ‘the sign that Jesus had performed’ (John 6:14), and the disciples remembered it as a display of his power (16:9).

b: In John’s account the feeding leads into Jesus’ teaching that he himself is the true bread from heaven: ‘I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger’ (John 6:35). The bread in the wilderness pointed to Christ, who gives his life for the world (John 6:51).

The meal looks ahead to the messianic banquet, when God will prepare a feast for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6), and Jesus will eat and drink with his people in his Father’s kingdom (26:29). Psalm 23 pictures the LORD as a shepherd who makes his sheep lie down in green pastures and prepares a table before them.

l.t: John’s account: the boy’s barley loaves, and the crowd’s wish to make Jesus king.
Mark: sheep without a shepherd; groups of hundreds and fifties.
God feeds Israel with manna in the wilderness.
Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves, with some left over.
God promises to shepherd and feed his flock himself, through ‘My servant David’.
Jesus, the true bread from heaven.
The LORD is my shepherd; he prepares a table before me.
God is able to make all grace abound, supplying seed to the sower and bread for food.

qs: What did Jesus want his disciples to learn when he said, ‘You give them something to eat’?
How does this miracle show Jesus as the shepherd God promised in Ezekiel 34?
What ‘five loaves’ do you have that you could bring to Jesus for the needs around you?

14.ctx: This happens the same night as the feeding of the five thousand. John says the crowd wanted to make Jesus king by force (John 6:15), which may explain why Jesus sent the disciples away so quickly. The Sea of Galilee is about 13 miles long and 8 miles wide; sudden strong winds are common. Only Matthew tells of Peter walking on the water. Compare Mark 6:45–52 and John 6:16–21.
14.mean: Straight after the feeding, Jesus makes the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him across the lake. He sends the crowds home and goes up the mountain alone to pray. By night the boat is far from land, battered by waves, with the wind against it. Between three and six in the morning Jesus comes to them, walking on the sea. The disciples are terrified and cry out, ‘It’s a ghost!’ At once Jesus speaks: ‘Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.’ Peter answers, ‘Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You on the water.’ Jesus says, ‘Come.’ Peter climbs out and walks on the water towards Jesus. But when he sees the strength of the wind, he is afraid and begins to sink. ‘Lord, save me!’ Immediately Jesus reaches out and catches him: ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’ When they climb into the boat, the wind dies down, and those in the boat worship him, saying, ‘Truly You are the Son of God!’ In the Old Testament only God rules the sea. Job says that God alone ‘treads on the waves of the sea’ (Job 9:8). Jesus’ words ‘It is I’ can also be translated ‘I am’, echoing the name God gave himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). Jesus is doing what only God does, and the disciples respond with worship. Peter’s story is a picture of faith that every believer knows. While he looks to Jesus, he does what he could never do by himself. When he looks at the wind, he sinks. Yet even his sinking leads to a short, honest prayer, and Jesus answers at once. ‘Little faith’ is a rebuke, but it is spoken by a hand that is already holding him. The storm did not stop before Jesus came, and it did not stop before Peter sank. But Jesus came through it to them, and he did not let go.
14.big: Jesus walks on the sea as only God can; when Peter looks away from him and sinks, Jesus saves him, and the disciples worship him as the Son of God.

vv.h: Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat
b: ‘Made’ is a strong word. Wesley explained that the disciples ‘were unwilling to leave him’. John tells us that the crowd wanted to make Jesus king by force (John 6:15). Jesus would not be the kind of king they wanted, and he got his disciples away from that excitement.

vv.h: He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray
b: Quarles notes the echo of Moses going up the mountain alone to meet God (Exodus 24:2), and that Jesus here practises what he taught about praying in private (6:6). Calvin saw both natures of Christ here: ‘he showed himself to be a man by praying; and this he did not hypocritically’. He also thought it likely that Jesus prayed for his disciples as the storm came on.

vv.h: The boat was already far from land, buffeted by the waves because the wind was against it
b: The Greek says ‘many stadia’ from land (BSB footnote); a stadion was about 185 metres. John says they had rowed three or four miles (John 6:19). ‘Buffeted’ is the word for being tormented. They were where Jesus had sent them, and they were in trouble. Obedience does not guarantee calm water.

vv.h: During the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea
b: The fourth watch was ‘between three and six in the morning’ (BSB footnote). They had struggled for most of the night. Quarles rejects attempts to explain the miracle away (for instance, that Jesus was walking on a sandbar): the Creator is not bound by the ordinary patterns he sustains (Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3). In the Old Testament God makes a path through the sea: ‘Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters’ (Psalm 77:19).

vv.h: It’s a ghost!
b: The word means an apparition or terrifying sight. Fishermen who knew the lake well knew that people do not walk on water. Their fear shows they had not yet understood the feeding they had just seen (Mark 6:52).

vv.h: Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid
b: ‘It is I’ is literally ‘I am’ (egō eimi). Quarles hears an echo of God’s name in Exodus 3:14, ‘I AM WHO I AM’, and of God’s words in Isaiah: ‘Do not fear … When you pass through the waters, I will be with you’ (Isaiah 43:1–2). Calvin noted that the disciples’ confidence is ‘founded on his presence’. Courage comes not from a calmer sea but from knowing who is with us.

vv.h: Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You on the water
b: Commentators have read Peter differently. Calvin was critical: ‘The condition which he lays down shows that his faith was not yet fully settled’; Peter, ‘without the wings of faith, … desires to fly at will.’ Yet Calvin granted that ‘this longing sprung from a good principle’. Wesley read ‘if’ as ‘since’: ‘St. Peter was in no doubt, or he would not have quitted the ship.’ Either way, Peter wisely asked Jesus to command him rather than simply jumping.

vv.h: Come
b: One word from Jesus was enough. For a few steps a fisherman did what only God does, because he was obeying Jesus’ word. Calvin added that Christ’s power ‘shone more brightly in the person of Peter’ than if he had walked alone.

vv.h: When he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, ‘Lord, save me!’
b: Nothing about the wind had changed; what changed was where Peter looked. Wesley noted that Peter ‘had been used to the sea, and was a skilful swimmer’, yet ‘When grace begins to act, the natural courage and strength are withdrawn.’ ‘Lord, save me!’ is one of the shortest prayers in the Bible. Quarles notes that in the Greek Old Testament such cries are prayers to the LORD. Compare Psalm 69:1: ‘Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck.’

vv.h: Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter. ‘You of little faith,’ He said, ‘why did you doubt?’
b: Jesus rescued first and rebuked second. ‘Little faith’ is a favourite phrase in Matthew (6:30; 8:26; 16:8; 17:20). Calvin explained that not all doubt is sinful: ‘A man may sometimes doubt without any fault on his part; and that is, when the word of the Lord does not speak with certainty on the matter.’ But Peter had an express command from Christ and had seen his power.

vv.h: When they had climbed back into the boat, the wind died down
b: Psalm 107 describes sailors in a storm who ‘cried out to the LORD in their trouble’, and ‘He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed’ (Psalm 107:28–29). The disciples saw that psalm acted out.

vv.h: Those who were in the boat worshiped Him, saying, ‘Truly You are the Son of God!’
b: This is the first time in Matthew that the disciples call Jesus the Son of God. They worship him, and he accepts it, though he had told Satan that only God is to be worshipped (4:10). Calvin thought ‘those who were in the boat’ might include sailors and passengers. On what they understood by ‘Son of God’, see Where readings differ.

14.diff: What did the disciples mean by ‘Son of God’ (14:33)? Calvin and Wesley both took the disciples’ words chiefly as a confession that Jesus is the Messiah. Wesley: ‘They mean, the Messiah.’ Calvin: by this title they ‘render to him the honor of the Messiah’, since ‘at that time this lofty mystery was not generally known, how God was to be manifested in the flesh’. Quarles reads the scene as a revelation of God himself: Jesus walks on the sea as only God does, speaks the divine ‘I am’, and receives worship, so the confession points to his deity. These readings are not as far apart as they look. All three affirm that Jesus is God the Son. The question is how much the disciples grasped that night, and how much Matthew’s readers, who know the whole story, are meant to see in their words.

b: The Old Testament repeatedly pictures God as Lord of the sea: he divided the Red Sea (Exodus 14), ‘stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea’ (Job 9:8), and ‘You rule the raging sea’ (Psalm 89:9). Mark’s account adds, ‘He intended to pass by them’ (Mark 6:48), which may recall God passing by Moses and Elijah to reveal his glory (Exodus 33:19–22; 1 Kings 19:11).

Peter’s experience is a picture of the Christian life: ‘Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith’ (Hebrews 12:2). Isaiah promised that the LORD will be with his people when they pass through deep waters (Isaiah 43:2).

l.t: Mark: he intended to pass by them; their hearts were hardened.
John: ‘It is I; do not be afraid’, and the boat reaches land at once.
God alone treads on the waves of the sea.
God reveals his name, I AM.
‘When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.’
Sailors cry to the LORD, and he calms the storm.
Fixing our eyes on Jesus.
Jesus calms the storm: ‘What kind of man is this?’

qs: Why do you think Jesus sent the disciples into a storm and then came to them so late in the night?
What does Jesus do in this passage that the Old Testament says only God does?
What ‘wind’ tends to take your eyes off Jesus, and what does his response to Peter teach you?

14.ctx: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, between Capernaum and Magdala. The lake was sometimes called the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1). Compare Mark 6:53–56.
14.mean: After the night on the lake, Jesus and the disciples land at Gennesaret. As soon as the people recognise Jesus, they send word all round the region and bring all their sick to him. They beg him just to let them touch the fringe of his cloak, and everyone who touches it is healed. This short summary comes after two great miracles and before a long argument with the Pharisees about what makes a person clean or unclean. It reminds us how freely Jesus gave his power. The people did not come with long prayers or great understanding. They simply came, and trusted that even the edge of his clothes was enough. Earlier a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years did the same and was healed (9:20–22); the news had clearly spread. The ‘fringe’ was probably one of the tassels that faithful Jews wore on the corners of their garments, as the law commanded, to remind them of God’s commands (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus kept the law and wore them. There is a contrast here with the scene that follows. Ordinary people press close to Jesus, wanting to touch him. In the next passage, religious leaders come all the way from Jerusalem to find fault with his disciples for not washing their hands. The sick knew they needed him; the experts thought they did not. Jesus is the shepherd who, as Ezekiel promised, binds up the broken and strengthens the weak (Ezekiel 34:16). His power was not rationed. ‘All who touched Him were healed.’
14.big: Sick people throughout the region came to Jesus and were healed by touching the edge of his cloak; his power flowed freely to all who came to him in need.

vv.h: When the men of that place recognized Jesus, they sent word to all the surrounding region
b: Jesus had become well known. People did not keep the news to themselves but sent for everyone who needed him. That is still the right instinct when we know where help is found.

vv.h: and begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed
b: The law commanded Israelites to wear ‘tassels for the corners of their garments, with a blue cord on each tassel’, so that they would ‘remember all the commandments of the LORD’ (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus’ power did not lie in the cloth: it was his power, received by trust (9:22). Quarles notes that the words for the sick echo Ezekiel 34:4, where Israel’s shepherds failed to strengthen the weak or heal the sick.
Matthew often gives short summaries of Jesus’ healing (4:23–24; 8:16–17; 9:35; 15:30–31). He explains them with Isaiah 53:4: ‘He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases’ (8:17).
The healings point forward to the day when there will be ‘no more death or mourning or crying or pain’ (Revelation 21:4).

l.t: Mark: people laid the sick in the marketplaces wherever he went.
The woman who touched the fringe of his cloak.
The command to wear tassels.
The failed shepherds and the Shepherd who heals.
He took our infirmities and carried our diseases.
No more death, mourning, crying or pain.

qs: Why do you think the people asked only to touch the fringe of Jesus’ cloak?
What contrast do you notice between this scene and the one that follows in 15:1–9?
Who could you ‘send word’ to about Jesus this week?
