15.ctx: The ‘tradition of the elders’ was a large body of rules handed down by Jewish teachers to apply the law of Moses to daily life. It was passed on by word of mouth and later written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200). Ritual hand-washing before meals was about religious purity, not hygiene. These Pharisees and scribes had come from Jerusalem, perhaps sent to investigate Jesus. Compare Mark 7:1–13.
15.mean: A group of Pharisees and scribes arrive from Jerusalem with a complaint. ‘Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat.’ They are not talking about dirty hands. Their tradition required a ritual washing to remove any religious uncleanness picked up from the world. Jesus answers with a question of his own: ‘And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?’ He gives an example. God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’, and he took this so seriously that cursing a parent was punishable by death. But the tradition allowed a man to declare his money or property ‘a gift devoted to God’ (Mark calls it ‘Corban’). Once it was declared, he no longer had to use it to support his elderly parents. A religious-sounding vow became a way of escaping a plain duty. ‘Thus you nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition.’ Then Jesus calls them hypocrites and quotes Isaiah: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’ Jesus does not condemn every tradition. He went to the synagogue and kept the feasts. The problem was that human rules had been raised to the level of God’s word, and were then used to cancel it. Worship had become a matter of outward correctness while the heart was far away. This is a warning to every religious person and every church. It is easy to add our own rules to God’s, to judge others by them, and to forget the weightier matters of love and mercy. It is just as easy to honour God with words while our hearts are elsewhere. Christians differ on how Scripture and church tradition relate (see Where readings differ). But all agree that no tradition may be used to set aside a plain command of God.
15.big: Jesus condemns human traditions that cancel God’s commands, and worship that honours God with the lips while the heart is far from him.

vv.h: Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders?
b: Wesley explains ‘the elders’ as ‘The chief doctors or, teachers among the Jews.’ Josephus says the Pharisees kept rules received from their fathers that were not written in the law of Moses; later rabbis traced this oral tradition back to Moses himself (Mishnah Avot 1:1). The charge is against the disciples, but it is aimed at their teacher.

vv.h: And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?
b: Calvin notes that the Pharisees ‘did not openly or professedly set aside the law of God … but there was an indirect transgression of it’. That is how tradition usually goes wrong: not by open rejection of God’s word, but by quietly making room to avoid it.

vv.h: Honor your father and mother … Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death
b: Jesus quotes Exodus 20:12 and 21:17 (BSB footnotes). Wesley adds that honour ‘implies all such relief as they stand in need of’. In a world with no pensions, honouring parents meant supporting them in old age (compare 1 Timothy 5:4, 8).

vv.h: Whatever you would have received from me is a gift devoted to God
b: Mark gives the Hebrew word: ‘Corban’ (that is, a gift devoted to God) (Mark 7:11). Quarles notes that the Mishnah discusses such vows. Wesley paraphrases: ‘I have given, or at least, purpose to give to the treasury of the temple, what you might otherwise have had from me.’ The money might never actually reach the temple; the vow simply kept it from the parents.

vv.h: These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me
b: Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13, following the Greek Old Testament (BSB footnote). Wesley: ‘without this all outward worship is mere mockery of God.’ On ‘the precepts of men’ he asks, ‘As equal with, nay, superior to, those of God. What can be a more heinous sin?’

Calvin drew a wider principle: ‘in vain is God worshipped, when the will of men is substituted in the room of doctrine’, for ‘since God chooses to be worshipped in no other way than according to his own appointment, he cannot endure new modes of worship to be devised.’ This became known in Reformed churches as the ‘regulative principle’ of worship.

15.diff: Scripture and tradition. Reformed and other Protestants read this passage as a warning that every church tradition must be tested by Scripture, the only infallible rule. The Westminster Confession says nothing is to be added to Scripture ‘whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men’, and that the supreme judge of all controversies ‘can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture’ (1.6, 1.10). Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree that merely human traditions can contradict God’s word, but distinguish them from apostolic Tradition, which hands on what the apostles received and which they hold together with Scripture. The Orthodox Longer Catechism says divine revelation is preserved ‘By two channels—holy tradition and holy Scripture’ (Q. 16), and the Catholic Catechism distinguishes that Tradition from ‘the various theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions, born in the local churches over time’ (80–83). All agree that no tradition may be used to cancel a plain command of God, as the Corban rule did. See also the note on Mark 7:1.

b: Isaiah’s complaint is repeated through the prophets: God desires a true heart more than outward ritual (1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8). Jesus will later accuse the scribes and Pharisees of tithing herbs while neglecting ‘justice, mercy, and faithfulness’ (23:23).

Paul warns against rules that ‘have an appearance of wisdom’ but are ‘based on human commands and teachings’ (Colossians 2:20–23), and tells Timothy that caring for one’s own family is a basic Christian duty (1 Timothy 5:8).

l.t: Mark’s account, with an explanation of Jewish washing customs.
Lip-service and rules taught by men.
Honour your parents; the penalty for cursing them.
Human rules with an appearance of wisdom.
Providing for one’s own family.
Woe to you, hypocrites: clean outside, unclean within.

qs: What was wrong with the Pharisees’ Corban rule, according to Jesus?
What is the difference between a helpful tradition and one that cancels God’s word?
Are there ways in which you honour God with your lips while your heart is far from him?

15.ctx: Under the law of Moses some foods, such as pork, were ‘unclean’ (Leviticus 11), and many things made a person ritually unclean for a time. Jesus now teaches where real uncleanness comes from. Mark adds the comment, ‘Thus all foods are clean’ (Mark 7:19). Compare Mark 7:14–23.
15.mean: Jesus calls the crowd and gives them a short saying to think about: ‘A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.’ The disciples are worried. ‘Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?’ Jesus is not troubled. ‘Every plant that My heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots. Disregard them! They are blind guides. If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.’ Peter asks him to explain the saying, and Jesus does so plainly. Food goes into the stomach and passes out of the body; it does not touch the heart. But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and the heart is where evil starts: ‘evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander.’ These are what make a person unclean before God, not eating with unwashed hands. This was revolutionary. Jewish life was full of careful rules about food and washing, meant to keep people pure. Jesus says the real problem is inside us. We cannot make ourselves clean by avoiding the right foods or performing the right rituals, because the source of uncleanness is our own heart. That is bad news and good news. It is bad news because no amount of outward religion can fix us. It is good news because Jesus came to deal with the heart itself, to give what God promised through Ezekiel: ‘a new heart’ and ‘a new spirit’ (Ezekiel 36:26). After his resurrection the church came to see that the food laws had done their work and were no longer binding (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). But Jesus’ main point still stands. Notice the list begins with ‘evil thoughts’. Wesley commented, ‘First evil thoughts — then murders — and the rest.’ Sin starts long before it is seen.
15.big: Real uncleanness comes not from food or unwashed hands but from the human heart; only God can make the heart clean.

vv.h: A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it
b: Jesus speaks this to the whole crowd, not just the disciples. Quarles notes that Peter calls it a ‘parable’ (15:15) because it is a short, puzzling saying that needs explaining.

vv.h: Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended?
b: Quarles points out that the disciples were not being oversensitive: Jesus had called these respected teachers hypocrites, accused them of breaking a commandment that carried the death penalty, and placed their tradition below God’s word.

vv.h: Every plant that My heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots
b: Isaiah described God’s restored people as ‘the branch of My planting, the work of My hands’ (Isaiah 60:21). Quarles notes that the Mishnah used this verse to say that all Israel has a share in the world to come. Jesus says these leaders are not God’s planting. ‘Disregard them’ uses the same verb as the master’s ‘Let both grow together’ in the parable of the weeds (13:30).

Interpreters differ on what the ‘plant’ is. Calvin: ‘it was rather to men that Christ referred’, the people God has not grafted into his tree of life. Wesley: ‘Every plant — That is, every doctrine.’ Both readings warn that what God has not planted will not last.

vv.h: Disregard them! They are blind guides. If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit
b: Wesley takes ‘Let them alone’ as ‘a plain direction how to behave with regard to all such’: do not be anxious about them. Quarles notes that a pit was a trap or a prison (Psalm 7:15), and that Ezekiel uses a similar word for the grave (Ezekiel 32:18). Jesus will say more about blind guides in 23:16–26.

vv.h: Do you still not understand?
b: Wesley admired the honesty of the Gospel writers: ‘How fair and candid are the sacred historians? Never concealing or excusing their own blemishes.’ The disciples’ slowness is recorded, not hidden.

vv.h: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander
b: The list moves from thoughts to deeds to words, and roughly follows the order of the sixth to ninth commandments (Exodus 20:13–16). Calvin: ‘all sins proceed from the wicked and corrupt affections’ of the heart. Wesley notes that ‘slander’ (railings) ‘includes all reviling, backbiting, and evil speaking.’
Scripture says, ‘The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure’ (Jeremiah 17:9), and ‘Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life’ (Proverbs 4:23).

vv.h: These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him
b: Matthew ends where the argument began, with the hand-washing tradition. Mark adds, ‘Thus all foods are clean’ (Mark 7:19). Quarles suggests Matthew, writing for Jewish Christians, focuses on the tradition rather than on the food laws. Peter himself had to learn this lesson later: ‘Do not call anything impure that God has made clean’ (Acts 10:15).

God promised to deal with the heart: ‘I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you’ (Ezekiel 36:26). David prayed, ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God’ (Psalm 51:10). The New Testament teaches that Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience (Hebrews 9:13–14).

Paul taught that ‘nothing is unclean in itself’ (Romans 14:14), but that Christians should not use their freedom in food to harm a weaker brother (Romans 14:13–21). James warns that the tongue reveals the heart (James 3:5–12).

l.t: Mark: ‘Thus all foods are clean’; a longer list of sins.
God promises a new heart and a new spirit.
The heart is deceitful; the LORD searches it.
Peter’s vision: do not call unclean what God has made clean.
Nothing is unclean in itself, but walk in love.
Out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.

qs: Why does Jesus say that what comes out of a person, not what goes in, makes them unclean?
Why do you think the list of sins begins with ‘evil thoughts’?
What outward things do people today rely on to feel clean before God?

15.h: The Faith of the Canaanite Woman
15.ctx: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities on the Mediterranean coast, north-west of Galilee. The prophets had condemned them (Ezekiel 26–28), yet Jesus said they would have repented if they had seen his miracles (11:21–22). Mark calls her ‘a Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin’ (Mark 7:26); Matthew uses the old name ‘Canaanite’, recalling Israel’s ancient enemies. After teaching about what really makes people unclean, Jesus goes to a region the Pharisees considered unclean. Compare Mark 7:24–30.
15.mean: Jesus leaves Galilee and goes north into Gentile territory. A local woman comes crying out, ‘Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon.’ She is a Canaanite, from a people who were Israel’s enemies for centuries. Yet she calls Jesus by a Jewish title for the Messiah, and pleads for mercy. At first Jesus says nothing. The disciples, irritated by her shouting, urge him to send her away. Jesus says, ‘I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.’ But she will not give up. She kneels in front of him: ‘Lord, help me!’ Jesus replies, ‘It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.’ She answers, ‘Yes, Lord, even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table.’ And Jesus exclaims, ‘O woman, your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire.’ Her daughter is healed at that moment. Jesus’ words can sound harsh, and Christians have explained them in different ways (see Where readings differ). But the shape of the story is clear. Jesus came first to Israel, as God had promised. That was the order of God’s plan: the gospel is ‘first to the Jew, then to the Greek’ (Romans 1:16). The woman accepts that order. She does not argue that she deserves equal treatment. She simply trusts that there is so much grace at the Master’s table that even a crumb is enough for her, and that Jesus will not refuse it. Her faith is humble, persistent and bold all at once. Only two people in Matthew are praised by Jesus for great faith: a Gentile centurion (8:10) and this Canaanite woman. Both are Gentiles. The children of the kingdom are proving slow to believe, while outsiders are coming in.
15.big: A Gentile mother refuses to give up, trusting that even a crumb of Jesus’ grace is enough; he praises her great faith and heals her daughter.

vv.h: Jesus withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon
b: Quarles notes that strict Pharisees avoided Gentile lands for fear of becoming ritually unclean; later rabbis even advised travellers there to stay on an animal’s back, be carried on someone’s shoulders, or walk only on the beach washed by the tide (Mishnah Ohalot 18:6). Having just taught that defilement comes from the heart, Jesus walks straight into ‘unclean’ territory.

vv.h: Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon
b: Calvin: ‘without some knowledge of the promises, she would not have called Christ the Son of David.’ Quarles notes that David drove away the evil spirit troubling Saul (1 Samuel 16:23), and that later Jewish writings remembered David’s son Solomon as a great exorcist, so the title fitted her request.

Her cry for mercy is the language of the Psalms, where it is always addressed to God (Psalm 6:2; 41:4; 86:3). She prays to Jesus as people prayed to the LORD. Her daughter’s suffering has become her own: ‘have mercy on me’.

vv.h: But Jesus did not answer a word
b: Silence can feel like refusal. Calvin wrote that ‘the silence of Christ was a sort of refusal’, yet ‘her continuance in prayer was a proof of her perseverance.’ Wesley: ‘He sometimes tries our faith in like manner.’ Quarles takes the silence as a test meant to draw out her faith, not as coldness. The disciples, by contrast, just wanted the noise to stop.

vv.h: I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel
b: Quarles notes that the phrase is drawn from Ezekiel 34, where God promises to ‘seek the lost’ (Ezekiel 34:16) and to set over them ‘one shepherd, My servant David’ (34:23). Jesus had given the Twelve the same limit on their first mission (10:5–6). Wesley: ‘Not primarily; not yet.’ Calvin agreed that ‘present circumstances rendered it necessary that he should begin with the Jews’; the wall between Jew and Gentile came down through the cross (Ephesians 2:14).

vv.h: The woman came and knelt before Him. ‘Lord, help me!’
b: The word translated ‘knelt’ is the word Matthew uses for worship (as in 14:33). Quarles hears an echo of prayers in the Psalms, such as ‘Help me, O LORD my God’ (Psalm 109:26). Her prayer is now only three words long. Desperation strips prayer down to its core.

vv.h: It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs
b: Jews sometimes called Gentiles ‘dogs’. But the word here is a diminutive, meaning small dogs or household pets; the BSB footnote gives ‘Or puppies’. Mark adds the word ‘first’: ‘First let the children have their fill’ (Mark 7:27). Quarles reads it as a picture of priority: a good father feeds his children before his pets, but the pets are still fed.
Calvin heard it more severely: ‘Christ’s reply is harsher than ever’, comparing her to a dog to show that what belonged to Israel’s covenant was not hers by right. See Where readings differ.

vv.h: Yes, Lord, even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table
b: Quarles stresses that she agrees with Jesus (‘Yes, Lord’) rather than contradicting him. She accepts that the children come first, but points out that the pets do not have to wait until the meal is over: they can eat the crumbs while the children eat. Jesus has more than enough grace for Israel and for her.

vv.h: O woman, your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire
b: Calvin praised the way she ‘so tempered her confidence with humility, that, while she advanced no unfounded claim, neither did she shut against her the fountain of the grace of Christ, by a sense of her own unworthiness.’ Wesley defined her faith as ‘Thy reliance on the power and goodness of God.’
Jesus heals the daughter at a distance, by his word alone, as he did the centurion’s servant (8:13). Contrast ‘O woman, your faith is great!’ with Peter’s ‘little faith’ on the lake (14:31).

15.diff: Was Jesus being harsh? Readers have heard Jesus’ silence and his words about ‘dogs’ in different ways. Calvin took them as genuinely severe: Jesus ‘disdainfully compares the woman herself to a dog’, showing that the blessings of the covenant belonged to Abraham’s family, though Calvin stresses that this was only ‘at that time’ and was meant to test and display her faith. Wesley also read it as a trial of faith: ‘He sometimes tries our faith in like manner.’ Quarles, like many modern commentators, notes the diminutive word (‘little dogs’, household pets) and Mark’s ‘first’, and reads the saying as a gentle picture of priority rather than an insult. All agree that Jesus intended to help her, that the order ‘Israel first, then the nations’ was God’s plan, and that the story ends with some of the highest praise Jesus gives anyone.

b: From the beginning God promised that through Abraham ‘all the families of the earth will be blessed’ (Genesis 12:3). Matthew’s genealogy includes Gentile women such as Rahab, a Canaanite (1:5). The Gospel ends with Jesus sending his disciples to ‘make disciples of all nations’ (28:19).

Elijah was sent to a widow in Zarephath, in the region of Sidon, and raised her son (1 Kings 17:8–24); Jesus pointed to that story when his own town rejected him (Luke 4:25–26). Paul explains the order of salvation history in Romans 1:16 and 11:11–24.

l.t: Mark’s account: ‘First let the children have their fill.’
Elijah and the Gentile widow of Zarephath, near Sidon.
God will seek the lost sheep and set David his servant over them.
The centurion’s great faith; many will come from east and west.
First to the Jew, then to the Greek; Gentiles grafted in.
Jesus’ parable about always praying and not giving up.
Make disciples of all nations.

qs: How does the woman show her faith at each stage of the conversation?
Why do you think Jesus answered her first with silence and then with a hard saying?
What do you do when God seems silent in answer to your prayers?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 15:21–28 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 15

15.h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
15.ctx: Mark says Jesus went through the region of the Decapolis, ten mainly Gentile cities east and south of the Sea of Galilee (Mark 7:31). Many think the crowd here was largely Gentile. Mark also records the healing of a deaf and mute man at this point (Mark 7:31–37). Compare Mark 8:1–10.
15.mean: Jesus returns to the Sea of Galilee, goes up on a mountain and sits down. Large crowds come, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute and many others, and lay them at his feet. He heals them all, and the crowd is amazed to see the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking and the blind seeing. ‘And they glorified the God of Israel.’ This is exactly what Isaiah said would happen when God came to save: ‘Then the eyes of the blind will be opened … Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy’ (Isaiah 35:5–6). The crowd stays with Jesus for three days, and their food runs out. Jesus calls his disciples: ‘I have compassion for this crowd … I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint along the way.’ The disciples ask where they could find enough bread in such a remote place. They seem to have forgotten what happened before. They have seven loaves and a few small fish. Jesus gives thanks, breaks them, and the disciples hand them out. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and seven large baskets of leftovers are gathered. Four thousand men are fed, besides women and children. Some readers think this is the same event as the feeding of the five thousand, told twice. But the numbers, places and details differ, and Jesus himself later refers to both (16:9–10). If the crowd was mainly Gentile, as their praise of ‘the God of Israel’ suggests, the point is powerful. Jesus has just told the Canaanite woman that the children must be fed first. Now, after feeding Israel, he spreads a table for the nations too. They receive not crumbs, but a full meal, with baskets left over. The compassion that moved Jesus for Israel moves him for the Gentiles as well.
15.big: Jesus heals many and feeds four thousand; the compassion he showed Israel reaches this crowd too, which may have been largely Gentile.

vv.h: He went up on a mountain and sat down
b: Quarles notes that these are the same words that began the Sermon on the Mount (5:1), recalling Moses on Sinai. Moses’ signs in Egypt brought plagues on Gentiles; Jesus’ signs bring healing to them.

vv.h: the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and laid them at His feet
b: The word translated ‘laid’ normally means ‘threw’. Quarles takes it to suggest haste: people put the sick down one after another as fast as they could. Quarles also notes that people healed of long-term disabilities usually need months to learn to walk or speak; these were restored instantly.

vv.h: And they glorified the God of Israel
b: Matthew uses this phrase only here. Quarles notes that Josephus used it when contrasting Israel’s God with pagan gods, and that the Philistines were once told to ‘Give glory to the God of Israel’ (1 Samuel 6:5). The phrase suggests Gentiles turning from idols, which ‘have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see’ (Psalm 115:5), to the living God who makes the mute speak and the blind see.

vv.h: I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days
b: Wesley: ‘It was now the third day since they came.’ This time it is Jesus, not the disciples, who raises the problem. His compassion reaches to tired bodies and empty stomachs as well as to sickness.

vv.h: Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread?
b: Calvin was blunt: ‘The disciples manifest excessive stupidity in not remembering’ the earlier miracle. But he turned the point on himself and his readers: we too forget, and should let ‘the experience of the past’ lead us ‘to expect for the future the same assistance’.

vv.h: Seven, they replied, and a few small fish … He gave thanks and broke them
b: The pattern is the same as before: what the disciples have, Jesus’ thanksgiving, the breaking, and the disciples handing it out. Wesley: ‘he praised God for it, and prayed for a blessing upon it.’

vv.h: seven basketfuls of broken pieces … four thousand men were fed, besides women and children
b: A different word for ‘basket’ is used here (spyris), a large hamper. Paul was let down from the wall of Damascus in one (Acts 9:25). Quarles cites a papyrus from AD 29 showing that such a basket could hold fifty loaves. Some see a link between the seven baskets and the nations, as the twelve recalled Israel, but Matthew does not say so.

vv.h: He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan
b: Magadan is not otherwise known. Quarles and many others think it is another spelling of Magdala, on the west shore of the lake, probably the home of Mary Magdalene; some later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘Magdala’. Mark calls the place Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10).

15.diff: Two feedings, or one? Some scholars, as Quarles notes, have suggested that the feedings of the five thousand and the four thousand are two versions of a single event. Most interpreters, including Calvin and Quarles, treat them as two events: the numbers, places and even the words for ‘basket’ differ, and Jesus refers to both separately (16:9–10). Quarles also notes that Moses, Elijah and Elisha were each linked with more than one miraculous feeding. Interpreters also differ on whether this crowd was mainly Gentile. Quarles thinks so, pointing to the Decapolis setting (Mark 7:31) and the praise of ‘the God of Israel’; he acknowledges that others take the crowd to be mainly Jewish. Either way, Jesus’ compassion and power are the same.

b: Isaiah 35 describes the coming of God to save, when the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap and the mute sing (Isaiah 35:4–6). Jesus pointed to these signs when John the Baptist asked if he was the one to come (11:4–5).

The prophets foresaw the nations coming to worship Israel’s God: ‘Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth’ (Isaiah 45:22); ‘all nations will stream to it’ (Isaiah 2:2). Psalm 115 contrasts lifeless idols with the living God.

l.t: Mark: the deaf man healed in the Decapolis, then the four thousand fed.
The blind will see, the lame leap, the mute sing.
Idols have mouths but cannot speak.
Manna and quail: God feeds Israel in the wilderness.
The blind see and the lame walk: the signs of the Messiah.
All nations will stream to the mountain of the LORD.

qs: What do the people’s praise of ‘the God of Israel’ and the earlier story of the Canaanite woman suggest about who was in this crowd?
Why do you think the disciples forgot what Jesus had done before?
What past experiences of God’s help could strengthen your trust for a present need?

Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 15:29–39 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 15
‘Magdala’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

16.ctx: The Pharisees and Sadducees were rival parties who disagreed on major questions, such as the resurrection and angels (Acts 23:8). Here they join forces against Jesus. A similar demand was made in 12:38–42. Some manuscripts do not include the words about the weather in verses 2–3 (BSB footnote). Compare Mark 8:11–13 and Luke 12:54–56.
16.mean: The Pharisees and Sadducees come to Jesus together, which is surprising: on most questions they were opponents. They test him by asking for ‘a sign from heaven’. Jesus has done many miracles, but they want something more: a spectacular proof, clearly from God, that would settle the matter on their terms. Perhaps they wanted bread to fall from the sky like manna, or a sign in the heavens like the hail and darkness in Moses’ day. Jesus answers with a picture from everyday life. When the evening sky is red, you say the weather will be fair; when the morning sky is red and overcast, you say it will be stormy. ‘You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but not the signs of the times.’ They can read the weather, but they cannot read what God is doing in front of them. The ‘signs of the times’ are everywhere: the sick healed, demons driven out, the poor hearing good news, the Scriptures being fulfilled. Many ordinary people have recognised them. The experts have not. Jesus then repeats what he said before: ‘A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.’ Jonah came back after three days in the fish; Jesus will rise on the third day (12:40). That will be the sign. And then, Matthew says, ‘He left them and went away.’ The conversation was over. There is a warning here for anyone who says, ‘I would believe if God would just show me a sign.’ The problem is rarely a lack of evidence. Calvin said they were hypocrites ‘because they pretend to ask that which, if it were exhibited to them, they are resolved not to observe.’ Jesus gives signs freely to those in need, but he will not perform on demand for those who have already made up their minds.
16.big: Jesus refuses to perform a sign on demand for those who will not believe; they can read the sky but not what God is doing, and the only sign they will get is his resurrection.

vv.h: The Pharisees and Sadducees came and tested Jesus by asking Him to show them a sign from heaven
b: Quarles notes that Josephus says the Sadducees usually went along with the Pharisees in public because the Pharisees were more popular. Opposition to Jesus brought these rivals together, as it later brought Herod and Pilate together (Luke 23:12). ‘Tested’ is the same word used of Satan’s testing in the wilderness (4:1).

Wesley thought they asked for a sign from heaven because it was something ‘they imagined Satan could not counterfeit’, since they had already put down his miracles to the devil (12:24). Quarles notes a Jewish expectation that the Messiah, like Moses, would bring down manna: ‘I will rain down bread from heaven for you’ (Exodus 16:4).

vv.h: You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but not the signs of the times
b: Quarles notes that ancient weather handbooks gave the same rule as the English saying, ‘Red sky at night, shepherd’s delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd’s warning.’ The word for ‘times’ (kairos) means seasons or appointed times in God’s plan. Wesley: ‘The signs which evidently show, that this is the time of the Messiah.’
Several manuscripts do not include the words from ‘When evening comes’ to ‘the signs of the times’ (BSB footnote). Luke records a similar saying on another occasion (Luke 12:54–56).

vv.h: A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah
b: ‘Adulterous’ means unfaithful to God, as Israel was often described in the prophets. Wesley: ‘your love of the world, which is spiritual adultery, blind your understanding.’ Quarles hears Moses’ words about the wilderness generation, ‘a perverse and crooked generation’ (Deuteronomy 32:5). On the sign of Jonah, see 12:38–42.
‘He left them and went away.’ Quarles takes this as the end of a fruitless debate, and an example for the disciples, who must also leave behind the influence of these leaders (16:5–12).
Paul wrote that ‘Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified’ (1 Corinthians 1:22–23). The greatest sign God has given is the death and resurrection of Jesus.

In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, Abraham says that those who will not listen to Moses and the Prophets ‘will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead’ (Luke 16:31). Evidence alone does not change a heart that refuses to see.

l.t: The earlier demand for a sign; the sign of Jonah explained.
Mark: Jesus sighed deeply in his spirit.
Luke: you can interpret the earth and sky but not the present time.
Three days and nights in the fish, and then out again.
Jews demand signs; we preach Christ crucified.
Not persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.

qs: Why did Jesus refuse to give these leaders the sign they asked for?
What were the ‘signs of the times’ that they failed to see?
Do you ever find yourself asking God for proof on your own terms?

16.h: The Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
16.ctx: Leaven was a small piece of fermented dough kept back from a previous batch and worked into new dough to make it rise. A little leaven affects the whole batch. In Scripture it often pictures a corrupting influence (1 Corinthians 5:6–8), though Jesus also used it in a good sense (13:33). Compare Mark 8:14–21 and Luke 12:1.
16.mean: After leaving the Pharisees and Sadducees, Jesus and the disciples cross the lake. On the way the disciples realise that they have forgotten to bring bread. Jesus says to them, ‘Watch out! Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.’ The disciples misunderstand completely. They think he is scolding them for forgetting the bread, or perhaps warning them not to buy bread from these groups. Jesus knows what they are saying and rebukes them: ‘You of little faith, why are you debating among yourselves about having no bread?’ Have they forgotten the five loaves for the five thousand and the twelve baskets left over? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand and the seven baskets? Jesus is not worried about bread; he has shown twice that he can provide it. Then they understand. He is warning them about ‘the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.’ Like leaven, false teaching is small and hidden at first, but it spreads quietly until it affects everything. The disciples had just seen these leaders demand a sign while refusing to believe. That attitude, along with their teaching, could seep into the disciples’ own hearts. This passage shows two dangers. One is false teaching that slowly spreads in a church. The other is the disciples’ own forgetfulness. They had seen Jesus feed thousands twice, and still they worried about lunch. Worry about our needs can make us deaf to what Jesus is really saying. Calvin noted that leaven usually stands for ‘some foreign substance, by which the native purity of any thing is impaired.’ The cure for both dangers is the same: remember what Jesus has done, and listen carefully to what he actually says.
16.big: Jesus warns his disciples against the spreading influence of the Pharisees’ and Sadducees’ teaching, and rebukes them for forgetting how he has provided for them.

vv.h: Watch out! Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
b: Quarles notes that ‘Watch out’ is a call to be alert, and ‘Beware’ a call to keep away. Wesley explains leaven as ‘their false doctrine: this is elegantly so called; for it spreads in the soul, or the Church, as leaven does in meal.’ Mark has ‘the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod’ (Mark 8:15); Luke, on another occasion, ‘the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy’ (Luke 12:1).

vv.h: It is because we did not bring any bread
b: Quarles suggests the disciples may have thought Jesus was forbidding them to buy bread from these groups, much as strict Jews avoided bread made by Gentiles, which might not have been purged of leaven at Passover (Exodus 13:7).

vv.h: You of little faith … Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand?
b: The rebuke is not for forgetting bread but for forgetting Jesus. Wesley paraphrases: ‘Am I not able, if need so require, to supply you by a word?’ Quarles notes that ‘little faith’ recalls 6:30, where Jesus rebuked anxiety about food and clothing.

vv.h: Then they understood that He was not telling them to beware of the leaven used in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees
b: Calvin: ‘The word leaven is very evidently used by Christ as contrasted with the pure and uncorrupted word of God.’ Jesus did not reject everything these teachers said (23:2–3), but he warned against their way of reading Scripture, their love of tradition, the Sadducees’ denial of the resurrection, and their refusal to believe.

Paul uses the same picture: ‘a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough’ (1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9). At Passover Israel had to clear all leaven from their homes (Exodus 12:15), which Paul applies to the Christian life: not ‘the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness’, but ‘the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth’ (1 Corinthians 5:8).
The New Testament repeatedly warns against false teaching that spreads quietly (Acts 20:29–31; 2 Timothy 2:16–18; 2 Peter 2:1).

l.t: Mark: ‘Do you still not understand?’
Luke: the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.
Removing leaven at Passover.
A little leaven works through the whole batch.
False teaching spreads like leaven.
Do not worry about what you will eat; you of little faith.

qs: Why did the disciples misunderstand Jesus’ warning?
In what ways is false teaching like leaven?
How can remembering what God has done in the past help you trust him now?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 16

16.ctx: Caesarea Philippi lay about 25 miles north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, in mainly Gentile territory ruled by Herod’s son Philip. It had a shrine to the god Pan and a temple to the emperor Augustus (see History below). This is a turning point in Matthew: from now on Jesus begins to teach openly about his death (16:21). Compare Mark 8:27–30 and Luke 9:18–21.
16.mean: Far from the crowds, Jesus asks his disciples, ‘Who do people say the Son of Man is?’ They report what people are saying. Some think he is John the Baptist come back to life, others Elijah, others Jeremiah or one of the prophets. These are all compliments. People can see that Jesus speaks with God’s authority. But they are all wrong, because they all put him in the same category as other great men. Then Jesus asks the question that matters most: ‘But what about you? Who do you say I am?’ Simon Peter answers for them all: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ Jesus is the Messiah, the anointed King promised to David’s line. More than that, he is the Son of the living God, sharing his Father’s life in a way no prophet ever did. Jesus responds, ‘Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven.’ Peter did not work this out by his own cleverness; God opened his eyes. Then Jesus makes a promise: ‘you are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.’ He will give Peter ‘the keys of the kingdom of heaven’, with authority to ‘bind’ and ‘loose’. Christians have long disagreed about what exactly the rock and the keys mean (see Where readings differ). But several things are clear. Jesus is the builder, and the church is his: ‘My church’. Peter’s confession of Jesus is its foundation truth. Nothing, not even death, will overcome it. And this confession is the heart of the Christian faith. Every person must answer Jesus’ question for themselves. It is not enough to know what others say about him. Finally, Jesus tells the disciples not to tell anyone yet. They know who he is, but they do not yet know what kind of Messiah he is. That lesson begins in the next verse.
16.big: Peter, taught by the Father, confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus promises to build his church, which nothing will overcome.

vv.h: Who do people say the Son of Man is?
b: Mark has ‘Who do people say I am?’ and Luke ‘Who do the crowds say I am?’ Matthew’s wording uses Jesus’ own favourite title for himself, drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where ‘One like the Son of Man’ receives an everlasting kingdom. Quarles notes that this keeps the Messiah title in its highest sense: a king over all nations, not just a liberator from Rome.

vv.h: Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets
b: Herod had said John (14:2). Malachi promised that Elijah would come before ‘the great and awesome Day of the LORD’ (Malachi 4:5), but Jesus taught that John was the Elijah who was to come (11:14; 17:12–13). Wesley mentions ‘a current tradition among the Jews, that either Jeremiah, or some other of the ancient prophets would rise again before the Messiah came.’ Quarles suggests Jeremiah came to mind because he was the prophet of judgement on Jerusalem and its temple.

vv.h: But what about you? Who do you say I am?
b: In Greek ‘you’ is emphatic and plural: Jesus asks all the disciples. Calvin saw here the call for believers to hold to Christ even ‘though the whole world may be carried away by its own inventions’. Quarles notes that Jesus asks what they ‘say’, not just what they think: true faith speaks (10:32–33).

vv.h: Simon Peter answered, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’
b: ‘Christ’ (Greek) and ‘Messiah’ (Hebrew) both mean ‘anointed one’: the promised King from David’s line (1:1; 2:2–4). ‘Son of God’ was a royal title (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), but Quarles argues that in Matthew it means far more: the Son alone knows the Father (11:27), shares one name with the Father and the Spirit (28:19), and is Immanuel, ‘God with us’ (1:23).

‘The living God’ contrasts the true God with idols (Joshua 3:10; Jeremiah 10:10). In Caesarea Philippi, with its temple to Augustus, ‘son of the divine one’, Peter confesses Jesus as Son of the living God (see History below). Wesley adds simply that Peter was the one ‘generally the most forward to speak.’

vv.h: This was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven
b: ‘Flesh and blood’ means human ability. Wesley: ‘thy own reason, or any natural power whatsoever.’ Calvin: ‘In the person of one man Christ reminds all that we must ask faith from the Father’, for ‘all the senses of men are deficient in this respect, till God opens our eyes to perceive his glory in Christ.’ Compare 11:25–27: only the Father reveals the Son.
‘Simon son of Jonah’ is in Greek ‘Simon Bar-Jonah’ (BSB footnote). Quarles notes that Simon was the most common Jewish man’s name of the time, which is why Jesus adds his father’s name.

vv.h: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church
b: There is a play on words. ‘Peter’ (Petros) means ‘rock’ or ‘stone’; ‘rock’ here is petra. In Aramaic, the language Jesus probably spoke, both would be kepha, the source of Peter’s other name, Cephas (John 1:42). Who or what the rock is has been debated for centuries; see Where readings differ.

‘Church’ (ekklēsia) means an assembly. Quarles notes that the Greek Old Testament used it for the assembly of Israel gathered before God (Deuteronomy 4:10; 31:30). Jesus is gathering a new people of God around himself. He calls it ‘My church’: he is the builder and owner. In the Gospels the word appears only here and in 18:17.

Paul says the church is ‘built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone’ (Ephesians 2:20), and that ‘no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 3:11). Peter himself calls Jesus ‘the living stone’ and believers ‘living stones’ (1 Peter 2:4–5).

vv.h: and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it
b: Hades is the realm of the dead (the BSB keeps the Greek word; older versions say ‘hell’). The Old Testament speaks of ‘the gates of Sheol’ (Isaiah 38:10) and ‘the gates of death’ (Job 38:17) for the power of death. Quarles points out that gates keep people in, so this is a promise that death will not hold Christ’s people: a promise of resurrection.

Calvin and Wesley took the gates as the power of Satan. Calvin: ‘every kind of power and of weapons of war’; the church ‘will prove to be invincible, because the truth of God, on which the faith of the Church rests, will ever remain unshaken.’ He added that this promise is ‘the sound of a trumpet, calling us to be always ready and prepared for battle.’ Wesley: the church universal has never been destroyed; ‘There hath been a small remnant in all ages.’

vv.h: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven
b: Quarles explains the picture from Isaiah 22:22, where God gives his steward Eliakim ‘the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open.’ The king’s steward held the keys and acted with the king’s authority. ‘Bind’ and ‘loose’ were terms Jewish teachers used for forbidding and permitting.

The Greek verbs can be rendered ‘will have been bound … will have been loosed’; Quarles takes this to mean Peter announces on earth what heaven has already decided. In 18:18 Jesus gives the same authority to the disciples together, and after the resurrection he tells them, ‘If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven’ (John 20:23). Wesley notes that Peter first opened the kingdom by preaching, ‘both to the Jews, Acts ii, and to the Gentiles, Acts x.’

vv.h: Then He admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ
b: Wesley explains that it was not right to proclaim it ‘before that grand proof of it, his resurrection’; otherwise some would try to ‘make him a king’ and others would oppose him all the more. Quarles adds that an early arrest would cut short the teaching the disciples still needed, as the next scene shows.

16.diff: Who or what is the rock, and what are the keys? This verse lies at the centre of one of the main divisions in Christianity. Catholic teaching: ‘The Lord made Simon alone, whom he named Peter, the “rock” of his Church. He gave him the keys of his Church and instituted him shepherd of the whole flock’, and ‘This pastoral office of Peter and the other apostles … is continued by the bishops under the primacy of the Pope’ (Catechism 881); the Pope is ‘Peter’s successor’ (882). The Catechism also says, ‘Because of the faith he confessed Peter will remain the unshakeable rock of the Church’, and that binding and loosing ‘connotes the authority to absolve sins, to pronounce doctrinal judgements, and to make disciplinary decisions in the Church’ (552–553). Orthodox teaching holds that ‘the Church, as the Body of Christ, can have no other Head than Jesus Christ’ (Longer Catechism 259). John Chrysostom, much honoured in the East, read ‘this rock’ as ‘the faith of his confession’ (Homily 54 on Matthew). Protestants have read the rock in three main ways. Calvin took it as the faith Peter confessed, ‘the common foundation of the whole Church’, adding that ‘Rank is a different thing from power’ and that nothing given to Peter passes to successors ‘by hereditary right’; the keys are ‘the office of teaching’. Wesley took it as ‘the faith which thou hast now professed’, or Christ pointing to himself, and said the keys were ‘not to him alone’. Many modern Protestant commentators, including Quarles, take the rock to be Peter himself, as the leading apostle and first confessor, on grammatical grounds, while insisting this describes ‘a person, not an office’, with no successors and no infallibility (16:23 follows at once). The Westminster Confession says, ‘There is no other head of the church but the Lord Jesus Christ’, and that the keys are committed to church officers for preaching and discipline (25.6; 30.2). All agree that Christ is the builder of his church, that Peter’s confession is its foundation truth, and that the church will not be overcome.

hist.t: Caesarea Philippi, Pan and the ‘son of god’ Augustus
b: The city stood beside a large cave from which one of the sources of the Jordan flowed. In the Greek period the cave became a shrine to the god Pan, and the place was called Panias (the modern name is still Banias). About 20 BC the emperor Augustus gave the area to Herod the Great, who built a temple ‘of the whitest stone’ to Augustus ‘near the place called Panium’, according to Josephus. Herod’s son Philip developed the town into a city and named it Caesarea in honour of the emperor, adding his own name to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast.

After Julius Caesar was murdered, the Roman Senate declared him a god (42 BC). Augustus, his adopted son, then called himself divi filius, ‘son of the divine one’, a title found on his coins and inscriptions. Quarles points out the contrast: in a town with a temple to the son of a dead man declared divine, Peter confesses Jesus as ‘the Son of the living God’.
The cave can still be seen at Banias. Many preachers draw out the setting: among shrines to Pan and to a deified emperor, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ.

b: Peter’s confession is the climax of the first half of Matthew. The question ‘Who is this?’ has been building (8:27; 11:3; 12:23; 14:33). From here the Gospel turns towards Jerusalem and the cross (16:21).

Peter later used his ‘keys’ in Acts: preaching at Pentecost, when about three thousand were added (Acts 2:41), and opening the door to the Gentiles in the house of Cornelius (Acts 10:34–48). Yet he also had to be corrected by Paul (Galatians 2:11–14). In Revelation the twelve foundations of the city bear ‘the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb’ (Revelation 21:14).

16.ctx: ‘From that time on Jesus began’ is a phrase Matthew uses to mark a new stage (compare 4:17). This is the first of several clear predictions of Jesus’ death and resurrection (17:22–23; 20:18–19; 26:2). The elders, chief priests and scribes together made up the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem. Compare Mark 8:31–33 and Luke 9:22.
16.mean: Peter has just confessed Jesus as the Christ. Now Jesus begins to show the disciples what that means: he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and on the third day be raised to life. The word ‘must’ is important. Jesus is not saying this might happen, or that he is likely to be caught. It must happen, because it is God’s plan, foretold in Scripture. Isaiah had said of the Servant of the LORD, ‘it was the LORD’s will to crush Him’, and that his soul would be ‘a guilt offering’ (Isaiah 53:10). Peter cannot accept it. He takes Jesus aside and rebukes him: ‘Far be it from You, Lord! This shall never happen to You!’ It must have seemed loyal and loving. How could the Messiah, the Son of the living God, be killed? But Jesus turns and says to Peter, ‘Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me. For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.’ These are some of the hardest words Jesus ever spoke to a friend. Moments before, Peter had spoken by revelation from the Father. Now he is speaking Satan’s lines. In the wilderness Satan had offered Jesus a way to be King without suffering (4:8–9). Peter offers the same thing, out of love, and Jesus recognises the temptation at once. The rock has become a stumbling stone. This passage teaches that the cross was not an accident or a defeat. It was the path God chose, and Jesus walked it willingly. It also warns us that human thinking, even well-meant, can oppose God’s purposes. The natural human concern is to protect ourselves and those we love from suffering. God’s concern was to save his people from their sins (1:21), and that required the cross.
16.big: Jesus begins to teach that he must suffer, die and rise; when Peter tries to stop him, Jesus rebukes him for thinking in human terms instead of God’s.

vv.h: He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things … and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life
b: Quarles notes that ‘must’ expresses divine necessity, what God has ordained. Wesley saw the change in Jesus’ teaching: ‘Hitherto he had mainly taught them only one point, That he was the Christ. From this time he taught them another, That Christ must through sufferings and death enter into his glory.’

Wesley also noted who would reject him: the elders (‘The most honourable and experienced men’), the chief priests (‘Accounted the most religious’) and the scribes (‘The most learned’). ‘Would not one have expected, that these should have been the very first to receive him?’ ‘Be raised’ implies that God the Father will raise him.

vv.h: Far be it from You, Lord! This shall never happen to You!
b: The Greek phrase is literally ‘Mercy to you’, a short way of saying ‘May God be merciful to you’, much like ‘God forbid!’ (Quarles). Calvin’s translation has ‘Lord, spare thyself’. The second phrase is a very strong denial: ‘this will absolutely not happen’. Quarles notes the irony: Jesus was going to Jerusalem not to seek mercy for himself, but to bring God’s mercy to others.
Wesley calls ‘favour thyself’ ‘The advice of the world, the flesh, and the devil, to every one of our Lord’s followers.’

vv.h: Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me
b: Jesus uses almost the same words he spoke to Satan in the wilderness (4:10). Wesley: ‘Thou art my enemy, while thou fanciest thyself most my friend’; Peter was ‘acting the very part of Satan’ by trying ‘to hinder the redemption of mankind.’ Wesley adds that the rebuke was sharper than any other Jesus is recorded as giving his apostles, because Peter’s heart was ‘puffed up with the commendation lately given him.’

Quarles hears ‘Get behind me’ as a reminder that a disciple walks behind his master (compare ‘come after Me’ in 16:24). Calvin disagreed: ‘It is idle to speculate … about the word … behind’; the phrase simply means ‘go away’. Either way, the stumbling block (skandalon, a trap or an obstacle to trip over) is an ironic contrast with the rock of 16:18.

Isaiah 52:13–53:12 foretells a Servant who would be ‘pierced for our transgressions’ and ‘crushed for our iniquities’ (53:5), whose death would ‘justify many’ (53:11), and who would afterwards ‘prolong His days’ (53:10). On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus asked, ‘Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?’ (Luke 24:26).

Peter later learned this lesson deeply. He wrote that Christ ‘Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree’ (1 Peter 2:24), and told suffering Christians that they shared in Christ’s sufferings (1 Peter 4:13).

l.t: Mark: he spoke plainly about this; turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter.
The suffering Servant of the LORD.
Satan offers the kingdoms of the world without the cross.
Gethsemane: ‘Yet not as I will, but as You will.’
Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer?
Peter on Christ’s suffering for us.

qs: Why was it necessary for Jesus to suffer and die?
Why did Jesus speak so sharply to Peter, who meant well?
When might loving advice from others, or our own instincts, pull us away from God’s will?

16.ctx: Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals. The condemned man usually carried the crossbeam of his cross through the streets to the place of execution. Jesus has already said something similar to the Twelve (10:38–39); here it is for all who would follow him. Compare Mark 8:34–9:1 and Luke 9:23–27.
16.mean: Jesus has just told the disciples that he must suffer and die. Now he tells them that his followers must be ready to do the same. ‘If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.’ To deny yourself is to stop living for yourself: to say no to the self that wants its own way, and yes to Jesus. To take up your cross is to be ready even to die for him. Jesus’ first hearers knew what a man carrying a cross meant. He was on his way to execution, and he was not coming back. To follow Jesus is to go where he goes, and he is going to the cross. Then come three reasons. First: ‘whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.’ The person who holds on to his life at all costs, even denying Christ to keep it, will lose real life for ever. The one who gives his life to Jesus will find it. Second: ‘What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?’ Nothing in this world is worth that trade, and nothing can buy the soul back. Third: ‘the Son of Man will come in His Father’s glory with His angels, and then He will repay each one according to what he has done.’ The cross is not the end of the story. The one who suffers will return as Judge and King. Then Jesus adds a puzzling promise: ‘some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom’ (see Where readings differ). For many Christians in history, and many today, taking up the cross has meant real persecution and even martyrdom. For all of us, it means daily choosing Christ’s will over our own. Wesley noted that ‘little’ crosses ‘which come daily, and even hourly, make up in number what they want in weight.’
16.big: To follow Jesus is to deny yourself and take up your cross; those who lose their lives for him will find true life when he returns in glory.

vv.h: If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me
b: Wesley: ‘None is forced; but if any will be a Christian, it must be on these terms’: ‘let him in all things deny his own will, however pleasing, and do the will of God, however painful.’ Calvin: ‘none can be reckoned to be the disciples of Christ unless they are true imitators of him’; self-denial means ‘to be reduced to nothing, provided that God lives and reigns in us.’
Jesus taught and healed freely and told his disciples to do the same (10:8). Grace is free, yet following him asks for everything.

vv.h: Whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it
b: The word for ‘life’ (psychē) is the same word translated ‘soul’ in 16:26. Wesley explains ‘save his life’ as ‘At the expense of his conscience’, and the promise as ‘What he loses on earth he shall find in heaven.’ The saying appears in all four Gospels in various forms (10:39; Mark 8:35; Luke 17:33; John 12:25).

vv.h: What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?
b: Satan once offered Jesus ‘all the kingdoms of the world and their glory’ (4:8). Quarles links the second question to Psalm 49: ‘No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. For the redemption of his soul is costly’ (Psalm 49:7–8). Only Christ could pay that ransom (20:28).

vv.h: The Son of Man will come in His Father’s glory with His angels, and then He will repay each one according to what he has done
b: This draws on Daniel 7:9–14, where the Son of Man comes before the Ancient of Days. Quarles notes that ‘His angels’ makes the angels belong to the Son of Man, and that ‘repay each one’ quotes Psalm 62:12, which says this of God: ‘For You will repay each man according to his deeds.’ Wesley: ‘For there is no way to escape the righteous judgment of God.’ Salvation is by grace, but our deeds show whether our faith is real (7:21–23; 25:31–46).

vv.h: Some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom
b: ‘Taste death’ means to die. Calvin dismissed the idea that this referred to the apostle John living to the end of the world: that notion ‘is ridiculous’. In all three Gospels this saying is followed straight away by the Transfiguration (17:1–8). For different views of what Jesus meant, see Where readings differ.

16.diff: ‘Some who are standing here’ (16:28). Since Jesus has not yet returned, what did he mean? Many interpreters, ancient and modern, connect it with the Transfiguration that follows six days later, when three disciples saw Jesus’ glory (17:1–8; compare 2 Peter 1:16–18). Calvin took it as ‘the manifestation of heavenly glory, which Christ began to make at his resurrection, and which he afterwards made more fully by sending the Holy Spirit’. Wesley saw ‘the Messiah coming to set up his mediatorial kingdom, with great power and glory, by the increase of his Church, and the destruction of the temple, city, and polity of the Jews’ in AD 70. Quarles sees a series: the Transfiguration as a preview, then the resurrection (28:18), then the judgement on Jerusalem, leading to the final judgement. Some critical scholars, following Albert Schweitzer, have held that Jesus expected the end within a generation and was mistaken; Quarles answers that ‘will not taste death before’ implies these disciples would die afterwards, so the saying cannot mean the final return. Each of the main Christian views finds a real coming of the kingdom in the disciples’ lifetime. See also the note on Mark 9:1.

b: Paul described the Christian life as dying and rising with Christ: ‘I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me’ (Galatians 2:20). He counted everything as loss ‘compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord’ (Philippians 3:8).

Jesus’ call echoes through Christian history. The early martyrs, including Peter himself (John 21:18–19), took it literally. Ecclesiastes reminds us that all our gains are left behind at death (Ecclesiastes 5:15), and Jesus told of a rich fool who gained much but lost his soul (Luke 12:16–21).

l.t: Mark: whoever is ashamed of me and my words.
Luke: take up his cross daily.
Anyone who does not take up his cross is not worthy of me.
No one can pay the ransom for a soul; God will redeem.
You will repay each man according to his deeds.
The Son of Man comes before the Ancient of Days.
Crucified with Christ; Christ lives in me.
Counting everything as loss for Christ.
Unless a grain of wheat falls and dies.

qs: What does it mean, in practice, to deny yourself and take up your cross?
Why is it foolish to gain the whole world and lose your soul?
What is one way you could choose Christ’s will over your own this week?

17.ctx: This happens six days after Peter’s confession and Jesus’ first prediction of his death (16:13–28). The mountain is not named; Wesley suggested Mount Tabor, others Mount Hermon near Caesarea Philippi. The scene recalls Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 24 and 34). Peter later wrote that he was an eyewitness of it (2 Peter 1:16–18). Compare Mark 9:2–13 and Luke 9:28–36.
17.mean: Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain by themselves. There he is transfigured before them. His face shines like the sun, and his clothes become as white as light. Suddenly Moses and Elijah appear, talking with him. Peter, overwhelmed, offers to put up three shelters, one each for Jesus, Moses and Elijah. While he is still speaking, a bright cloud surrounds them, and a voice from the cloud says, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!’ The disciples fall face down in terror. Jesus comes, touches them and says, ‘Get up. Do not be afraid.’ When they look up, they see no one except Jesus. A week earlier Jesus had spoken of his coming death and of his future glory (16:21, 27). Now three disciples see that glory with their own eyes. Jesus did not borrow this light from outside, as Moses’ face once reflected God’s glory (Exodus 34:29). It shone out from within. For a moment the glory hidden in his ordinary human life shone through, and they saw that this man is also God’s eternal Son. Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets. Both had met God on a mountain, and both now talk with Jesus. Luke tells us the subject: his ‘departure’, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Then the Father speaks, using the same words as at Jesus’ baptism (3:17), and adds three more: ‘Listen to Him!’ Moses had promised that God would raise up a prophet like him: ‘You must listen to him’ (Deuteronomy 18:15). Jesus is that prophet, and more: he is God’s beloved Son. Moses and Elijah fade, and Jesus alone remains. All the Old Testament pointed to him. On the way down, Jesus tells them to say nothing until he has risen. The disciples ask about Elijah, and Jesus explains that Elijah has already come in John the Baptist, and was rejected, as the Son of Man will be. Glory and suffering belong together. The mountain does not cancel the cross; it shows who is going to the cross.
17.big: On the mountain three disciples see Jesus’ divine glory, Moses and Elijah bear witness to him, and the Father commands, ‘Listen to Him!’; the glorious Son must still go the way of suffering.

vv.h: After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John
b: Quarles hears an echo of Exodus 24:16, where the cloud covered Sinai ‘For six days’, and ‘on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud’. Moses also took three named companions, Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, with seventy elders, part of the way (Exodus 24:1, 9). Peter, James and John are the inner circle who will also be with Jesus in Gethsemane (26:37).

vv.h: There He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun
b: ‘Transfigured’ (metamorphoō) means his outward form was changed. Quarles notes that this does not mean Jesus became divine at this moment; rather his appearance now matched what he truly was, the glory he had with the Father ‘before the world existed’ (John 17:5). Wesley: ‘The indwelling Deity darted out its rays through the veil of the flesh’, so that ‘his clothes could not conceal its glory’.

Calvin adds that this was only ‘a taste of his boundless glory, such as they were able to comprehend. Then his face shone as the sun; but now he is far beyond the sun in brightness.’ Quarles compares Daniel’s vision of the Ancient of Days, whose ‘clothing was white as snow’ (Daniel 7:9), and the psalm: ‘He wraps Himself in light as with a garment’ (Psalm 104:2).

vv.h: Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus
b: Moses gave the Law; Elijah was the great prophet whom Malachi promised would come before the Day of the LORD (Malachi 4:4–5). Wesley: Moses, Elijah ‘and God speaking from heaven, all bore witness to him.’ Calvin thought it ‘more probable that they were actually brought to that place’, not just a vision, and that they came ‘in order to wait upon Christ.’ Luke says they spoke about his ‘departure’ (the Greek word is exodos) at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).

vv.h: Lord, it is good for us to be here. If You wish, I will put up three shelters
b: Readers have judged Peter differently. Mark says Peter ‘did not know what else to say’ (Mark 9:6), and Calvin thought ‘his desire was foolish’, partly because ‘he absurdly put the servants on a level with their Lord’. Wesley called it ‘The words of rapturous surprise’, noting that Peter asked for three shelters, not six, ‘because the apostles desired to be with their Master.’ Quarles points to ‘If You wish’, found only in Matthew, as a sign of Peter’s humble eagerness to serve. ‘Shelters’ can also be translated ‘tabernacles’ (BSB footnote), the word used for Israel’s tents in the wilderness.

vv.h: This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!
b: The cloud is the cloud of God’s glory, as on Sinai and over the tabernacle, when ‘Moses was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting because the cloud had settled on it’ (Exodus 40:35). The Father’s words join Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1, as at the baptism (3:17). The BSB notes that Peter cites this verse in 2 Peter 1:17.

‘Listen to Him!’ echoes Deuteronomy 18:15: ‘The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me … You must listen to him.’ Wesley: ‘As superior even to Moses and the prophets.’ Calvin observed that the voice of God was heard ‘but that neither a body nor a face was seen’.

vv.h: they fell facedown in terror. Then Jesus came over and touched them
b: Only Matthew records that they fell facedown at the voice, and that Jesus came and touched them (Mark 9:6 and Luke 9:34 also mention their fear). Quarles compares Israel’s fear at Sinai, when the people begged that God would not speak to them directly (Exodus 20:18–19). The one whose glory terrifies them is the same one who stoops to touch them. Wesley: ‘doubtless the same moment he gave them courage and strength.’

vv.h: when they looked up, they saw no one except Jesus
b: Moses and Elijah have done their work of pointing to him. Calvin noted that the cloud taught the disciples ‘they must return to their former warfare, and therefore must not expect a triumph before the time.’ The vision ends, but Jesus remains with them.

vv.h: Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead
b: Quarles notes that the word for ‘vision’ (horama) means something actually seen, not a dream. Wesley suggests reasons for the silence: the other disciples might be ‘grieved and discouraged because they were not admitted to the sight’, and only the resurrection would ‘make it credible, and confirm their testimony about it.’

vv.h: Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first? … Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things
b: The scribes taught from Malachi 4:5–6 that Elijah would come before the Messiah. The disciples have just seen Elijah, and Jesus has spoken of suffering; how do these fit? Quarles, against most translations, thinks verse 11 repeats the scribes’ teaching, which Jesus then corrects with ‘But I tell you’ (17:12): Malachi spoke of turning the hearts of fathers and children, not of restoring everything. Calvin: John did not restore all things perfectly, but ‘conveyed and handed them over to Christ, who would complete the work which he had begun.’ See Where readings differ.

vv.h: Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him … In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands
b: John the Baptist dressed and preached like Elijah (3:4; 2 Kings 1:8). When asked, ‘Are you Elijah?’ John said, ‘I am not’ (John 1:21). Wesley explains: ‘I am not Elijah the Tishbite, come again into the world. But he was the person of whom Malachi prophesied under that name.’ If the forerunner was rejected and killed, the Messiah will be too. Quarles notes this is the first time Matthew speaks of the Son of Man suffering.

17.diff: Will Elijah come again? Most modern interpreters, including Calvin, Wesley and Quarles, hold that Malachi’s promise of Elijah was fulfilled in John the Baptist, as Jesus says here and in 11:14. Calvin wrote that the scribes had ‘rashly interpreted’ Malachi ‘as if Elijah the Tishbite … were to return a second time to the world.’ Many early church writers expected Elijah himself to come before Christ’s return; Chrysostom wrote, ‘Elias indeed comes then, before my second advent’ (Homily 57 on Matthew). Dispensationalist interpreters have revived this view and often expected a further, personal coming of Elijah before Christ’s return. The Scofield Reference Bible called Malachi 4:5–6 a ‘still unfulfilled prophecy’, fulfilled in John only ‘in an adumbrative and typical sense’ (that is, as a foreshadowing). All agree that John came ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah’ (Luke 1:17) and that the restoration of all things will be completed by Christ (19:28).

b: Peter later appealed to this event as eyewitness evidence: ‘we were eyewitnesses of His majesty … we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain’ (2 Peter 1:16–18). John wrote, ‘We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father’ (John 1:14).

The transfiguration is also a promise for believers. Paul says Christ ‘will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body’ (Philippians 3:21), and that even now believers are ‘being transformed into His image’ (2 Corinthians 3:18, using the same Greek verb). John: ‘when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is’ (1 John 3:2).

l.t: Mark: his clothes became radiantly white; Peter did not know what to say.
Luke: while he was praying; they spoke of his departure at Jerusalem.
Moses on Sinai: the cloud, the glory, the seventh day.
Moses’ face shines after speaking with the LORD.
A prophet like Moses: you must listen to him.
Remember Moses; I will send you Elijah.
Eyewitnesses of his majesty on the holy mountain.
Being transformed into his image.
The same words from heaven at Jesus’ baptism.

qs: What did Peter, James and John learn about Jesus on the mountain?
Why do you think the Father added ‘Listen to Him!’ to the words he spoke at Jesus’ baptism?
How does seeing Jesus’ glory help us to face suffering, as the disciples soon would?
