17.ctx: While Jesus was on the mountain, the other nine disciples had tried and failed to help a boy troubled by a demon. Mark gives a much fuller account, including the father’s cry, ‘I do believe; help my unbelief!’ (Mark 9:14–29). Compare Luke 9:37–43.
17.mean: Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets a crowd. A man kneels before him: ‘Lord, have mercy on my son. He has seizures and is suffering terribly. He often falls into the fire or into the water. I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.’ Jesus’ reply is startling: ‘O unbelieving and perverse generation! How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy here to Me.’ He rebukes the demon, it comes out, and the boy is healed from that moment. Moving from the glory of the mountain to this scene is like moving from heaven to earth. On the mountain there was light, worship and the Father’s voice. Below there is a suffering child, a desperate father, a curious crowd and helpless disciples. Jesus is not dragged down by it. He does not leave the boy in his misery. But he does feel the weight of the unbelief around him. His words echo God’s complaint about Israel in the wilderness: Moses called them ‘a perverse and crooked generation’ (Deuteronomy 32:5), and God asked, ‘How long will this wicked congregation grumble against Me?’ (Numbers 14:27). Jesus speaks as God speaks. The boy’s condition sounds like what we would call epilepsy, and the Greek word for ‘has seizures’ literally means ‘moonstruck’. Some modern readers think Matthew simply mistook epilepsy for a demon. But Matthew distinguishes the two elsewhere: people brought to Jesus ‘the demon-possessed, those having seizures, and the paralyzed’ (4:24). Here a demon was at work. In the ancient world such a condition had no reliable cure, and open fires and wells made it deadly. The father did the right thing. When the disciples failed, he did not give up; he came to Jesus himself. Even when Christians fail, Christ does not. He still says, ‘Bring the boy here to Me.’
17.big: Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets human misery and unbelief; where his disciples fail, he frees a tormented boy with a word.

vv.h: a man came up to Jesus and knelt before Him. ‘Lord, have mercy on my son’
b: Quarles notes that ‘Lord, have mercy’ is the language of the Greek Psalms addressed to the LORD (compare Psalm 6:2, ‘Be merciful to me, O LORD’). The father prays to Jesus as people prayed to God. He also describes the danger: the boy ‘often falls into the fire or into the water.’

vv.h: He has seizures and is suffering terribly
b: The Greek word means ‘moonstruck’ (older versions say ‘lunatic’), because people linked such fits with the moon. Mark’s fuller description leads most scholars to think of epileptic seizures (Mark 9:18, 20). Quarles points out that Matthew does not confuse epilepsy with demons, since he lists them separately in 4:24; in this case the seizures had a demonic cause. Nolland, cited by Quarles, notes that Matthew uses ‘terribly’ almost only of people Jesus heals: his compassion goes out to those who suffer most.

vv.h: I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him
b: Jesus had given the Twelve ‘authority over unclean spirits, so that they could drive them out and heal every disease and sickness’ (10:1). Their failure is not a failure of Jesus’ power, as the next verses explain.

vv.h: O unbelieving and perverse generation! How long must I remain with you?
b: Commentators differ on whom Jesus was rebuking. Calvin thought the words were aimed mainly at the scribes, ‘not against ignorant and weak persons, but against those who, through inveterate malice, obstinately resist God.’ Wesley: ‘Our Lord speaks principally this to his disciples.’ Quarles thinks it includes the father, the crowd and the disciples. Quarles hears in the words the voice of God in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5, 20) and in Numbers 14:27.

vv.h: Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy, and he was healed from that moment
b: Matthew tells it briefly. One word from Jesus did what his disciples could not. Quarles notes that ‘from that moment’ implies a lasting cure: the boy was healed and stayed healed.

Mark records the father’s honest prayer, ‘I do believe; help my unbelief!’ (Mark 9:24). Jesus accepted that mixture of faith and doubt, and healed the boy. It is a prayer many believers have made their own.

Jesus’ authority over demons shows that the kingdom of God has come (12:28). The New Testament promises that Christ has disarmed the powers of evil (Colossians 2:15) and will finally destroy the devil’s works (1 John 3:8).

l.t: Mark’s fuller account: ‘I do believe; help my unbelief!’
Luke: all were astonished at the majesty of God.
A perverse and crooked generation, children of unfaithfulness.
‘How long will this wicked congregation grumble against Me?’
Demon-possessed and those with seizures listed separately.
The Twelve given authority over unclean spirits.
The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.

qs: What contrasts do you notice between the scene on the mountain and the scene below?
Why do you think Jesus spoke so strongly about the unbelieving generation?
When other Christians have failed you, how can you still bring your needs to Jesus?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 17:14–18 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 17

17.ctx: Some later manuscripts add verse 21, ‘But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting’ (BSB footnote; compare Mark 9:29). Jesus uses the same mustard-seed picture for faith in Luke 17:6, and speaks of moving mountains again in Matthew 21:21.
17.mean: Afterwards the disciples come to Jesus privately. They are embarrassed and puzzled: ‘Why couldn’t we drive it out?’ Jesus answers plainly: ‘Because you have so little faith.’ Then he makes a remarkable promise: ‘if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, “Move from here to there,” and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you.’ The disciples had been given authority over demons (10:1). They had used it before. But this time, it seems, they relied on themselves, or doubted that the authority Jesus gave them would work in so hard a case. Their problem was not that they lacked some special technique. It was that they were not trusting Jesus. Notice the size of the faith Jesus asks for: as small as a mustard seed, the smallest seed people knew (13:32). The point is not that we need great faith. It is that even tiny faith, if it is real faith in the great God, can do what seems impossible. The power is not in the faith but in the One trusted. Moving mountains was a well-known picture for doing the impossible; Paul uses it too (1 Corinthians 13:2). Jesus may have pointed to the very mountain they had just come down from. He is not promising that Christians can rearrange the landscape for fun, or get anything they want by believing hard enough. Calvin warned: ‘He does not mean that God will give us every thing that we may mention.’ Faith trusts God to do his will, not ours. Christians differ on how far promises like this apply to miracles today (see Where readings differ). But every believer can take this to heart. The size of our faith is not the issue. The question is whether we are actually relying on Jesus, especially when the problem in front of us is big.
17.big: The disciples failed because they did not truly trust Jesus; even faith as small as a mustard seed, placed in God, can do what seems impossible.

vv.h: Why couldn’t we drive it out?
b: They asked privately, Quarles suggests to avoid further embarrassment. Calvin: the power ‘they once possessed’ had not simply been taken from them; ‘they had lost it by their own fault.’

vv.h: Because you have so little faith
b: Quarles notes this is the fifth time in Matthew that Jesus speaks of ‘little faith’ (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). Each time the disciples doubt his care or power in a specific situation. Wesley: ‘Because in this particular they had not faith.’

vv.h: if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move
b: Wesley: ‘To remove mountains was a proverbial phrase among the Jews … to express a thing which is very difficult, and to appearance impossible.’ Calvin: ‘It is a hyperbolical mode of expression, no doubt’, but ‘the meaning amounts to this, that God will never forsake us, if we keep the door open for receiving his grace.’

Wesley added a caution: this kind of faith ‘does not always imply saving faith’; it is ‘a supernatural persuasion given a man, that God will work thus by him at that hour.’ Paul agrees that faith to move mountains without love is nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2).

vv.h: Nothing will be impossible for you
b: The angel told Mary, ‘no word from God will ever fail’ (Luke 1:37). The promise rests on God’s power, not ours. In Mark, Jesus adds, ‘This kind cannot come out, except by prayer’ (Mark 9:29). Calvin: ‘For the weakness of faith he prescribes prayer as a remedy’.

17.diff: Do Christians still move mountains? Quarles argues that the ‘you’ here means the Twelve, whom Jesus had specially empowered to heal and drive out demons (10:1), and that the promise was fulfilled in the miracles of Acts; Paul shows that not every believer works miracles (1 Corinthians 12:29–30). Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe that the Spirit still gives ‘gifts and ministries as in New Testament times’, and that believers may evangelize ‘with accompanying supernatural signs’ (Assemblies of God, Fundamental Truths, sec. 10). Calvin read the saying as a hyperbole teaching that God will never fail those who trust him, but not that he will give whatever we ask. Wesley distinguished miracle-working faith, given for a particular moment, from saving faith. All agree that God still answers prayer, that nothing is impossible for him, and that faith rests on God’s will, not on our wishes.

b: The disciples’ failure did not end their calling. After the resurrection and Pentecost they healed and drove out demons in Jesus’ name (Acts 3:1–10; 5:12–16). Their faith grew as they saw the risen Lord.

Hebrews defines faith as ‘the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see’ and says that ‘without faith it is impossible to please God’ (Hebrews 11:1, 6). Abraham is the great example of faith in the God who does the impossible (Romans 4:18–21).

l.t: Mark: this kind cannot come out except by prayer.
‘Increase our faith!’ Faith like a mustard seed uprooting a tree.
Faith that can say to a mountain, ‘Be lifted up.’
The smallest of seeds.
Faith to move mountains without love is nothing.
Different gifts given by the Spirit; not all work miracles.
Abraham trusts God to do what he promised.

qs: Why did the disciples fail, according to Jesus?
What is the difference between great faith and faith in a great God?
Where do you need to trust Jesus with something that looks like a mountain?

17.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion
17.ctx: This is the second time Jesus plainly foretells his death and resurrection (16:21; compare 20:18–19). Jesus and the disciples are back in Galilee, on the way to Jerusalem. Compare Mark 9:30–32 and Luke 9:43–45.
17.mean: Back in Galilee, Jesus tells the disciples again what is going to happen: ‘The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life.’ This time Peter does not argue. Instead, ‘the disciples were deeply grieved.’ This short passage adds something new to the first prediction. The word translated ‘delivered’ means ‘handed over’. Jesus will be handed over by Judas to the chief priests (26:15–16), by the Jewish council to Pilate (27:2), and by Pilate to the soldiers (27:26). But behind all these human hands is another. Isaiah said of the suffering Servant, ‘the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all’ (Isaiah 53:6), and the Greek version of Isaiah uses this same verb: the Lord ‘handed him over’ for our sins. Peter preached at Pentecost that Jesus ‘was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge’, and yet those who killed him were guilty (Acts 2:23). God was in control, and people were responsible. Both are true. The disciples grieved, because they heard ‘kill’ and seem not to have heard ‘raised to life’. Mark says they did not understand and were afraid to ask (Mark 9:32). Many Jews expected a resurrection of all the dead at the end of time, not of one man after three days. Their sorrow is understandable, but it was sorrow that did not yet see the whole picture. Jesus did not hide the cost from them. He told them again and again, so that afterwards they would remember and understand that none of it took him by surprise. Christians today can face hard news in the same light. God’s purposes include suffering, but they do not end there. ‘On the third day He will be raised to life.’
17.big: Jesus again foretells that he will be handed over, killed and raised; God’s hand is behind the human hands, and the story does not end in death.

vv.h: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men
b: Quarles notes that ‘delivered’ (paradidōmi) can mean ‘betrayed’ or simply ‘handed over’, and that the passive may hint at God as the one who hands him over. Matthew later says the Son of Man goes ‘just as it is written about Him’ (26:24), and Jesus prays in Gethsemane, ‘Yet not as I will, but as You will’ (26:39). The Son of Man, who will rule all nations (Daniel 7:14), will first be given into human hands.

vv.h: They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life. And the disciples were deeply grieved
b: The disciples’ grief shows they understood he would die but not that he would rise. Quarles suggests they could not imagine one person rising before the general resurrection at the end of time. Many commentators compare Hosea 6:2: ‘on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence.’

The New Testament repeatedly holds together God’s plan and human guilt in Jesus’ death: Acts 2:23; 4:27–28. Paul says God ‘did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all’ (Romans 8:32), using the same verb ‘handed over’.
The risen Jesus reminded his followers that he had told them all this beforehand: ‘Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?’ (Luke 24:26).

l.t: Mark: they did not understand and were afraid to ask.
Luke: the meaning was hidden from them.
The first prediction, and Peter’s rebuke.
The LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all.
Delivered up by God’s set plan; God raised him up.
He did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all.

qs: What new detail does this second prediction add to the first one in 16:21?
How can God be in control of Jesus’ death while the people who killed him are still responsible?
Why do you think the disciples heard only the sad part of what Jesus said?

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 17

17.ctx: Exodus 30:13–15 required half a shekel from every man aged twenty or over when Israel was counted; by Jesus’ day this had become a yearly temple tax. In Jesus’ day this was two drachmas, so it was called ‘the two-drachma tax’ (BSB footnote). This story is found only in Matthew. Capernaum was Jesus’ home base in Galilee (4:13).
17.mean: When Jesus and the disciples arrive in Capernaum, the men collecting the temple tax ask Peter, ‘Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?’ Peter says, ‘Yes.’ When he goes into the house, Jesus speaks first, before Peter can raise the matter. ‘What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes: from their own sons, or from others?’ ‘From others,’ Peter answers. ‘Then the sons are exempt,’ Jesus says. Kings do not tax their own children. The temple tax was paid to God for his house. But Jesus is God’s Son. It makes no sense for the Son to pay tax to his own Father for his own Father’s house. Wesley summed it up: ‘I am the Son of God. Therefore I am free from any obligation of paying this to my own Father.’ And because Jesus’ followers are now God’s children too, they share in that freedom. Then comes the surprise. ‘But so that we may not offend them,’ Jesus tells Peter to go fishing. The first fish he catches will have a four-drachma coin in its mouth, enough to pay for both of them. Jesus was free, but he did not insist on his rights. He chose to pay rather than put an unnecessary stumbling block in front of people who would not understand. Calvin put it this way: Christ paid ‘not by obligation or necessity, but by a free and voluntary submission’. This is a pattern for Christians. We may be free in Christ, but love will often lay that freedom aside for the sake of others (Romans 14:13–21; 1 Corinthians 9:19). We should be willing to offend when the truth requires it, as Jesus did with the Pharisees (15:12–14), but never needlessly. The story also shows Jesus’ knowledge and power. He knew what Peter had been asked, and he knew which fish would bite. Even the fish of the sea serve the Son of God.
17.big: As God’s Son, Jesus is free from the temple tax, yet he pays it to avoid needless offence; he provides the coin in a fish’s mouth, showing his authority over all creation.

vv.h: Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas? ‘Yes,’ he answered
b: The tax was collected each spring. Quarles notes that the collectors’ question expects the answer ‘yes’. Calvin took it to be a tribute paid to the ruling powers, so that ‘they paid to tyrants what they were formerly in the habit of paying to God alone’; most modern scholars, including Quarles, think it was still the temple tax, which Rome took over only after AD 70 (see History below). Wesley thought it ‘a voluntary thing, which custom rather than any law had established’; Exodus 30 commands the half-shekel only at a census, and the yearly collection grew up later (compare Nehemiah 10:32).

vv.h: Jesus preempted him. ‘What do you think, Simon?’
b: Jesus spoke before Peter could ask. He knew the conversation that had taken place outside. Wesley: ‘Just when St. Peter was going to ask him for it.’

vv.h: Then the sons are exempt
b: Quarles notes that ‘kings of the earth’ invites comparison with the King of heaven. Jesus is the Son of the King to whom the temple belongs, and his disciples, who call God ‘your Father’ (5:16; 6:9), are sons too. Calvin saw a lesson in humility: Christ had ‘taken upon him the form of a servant’ (Philippians 2:7), but paid freely.

vv.h: But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish you catch
b: Wesley: ‘do not contest it with them, but rather yield to their demand, than violate peace or love. O what would not one of a loving spirit do for peace! Any thing which is not expressly forbidden in the word of God.’

The coin was a stater, worth about a shekel, (BSB footnote), exactly enough for two people. Matthew does not describe the catch; the point is Jesus’ word. Calvin thought Jesus did this not out of poverty but ‘to prove by a miracle, that he had a more extensive dominion than all earthly kings, since he had even fishes for his tributaries.’ Wesley marvelled at his ‘Knowledge, penetrating into this animal, though beneath the waters; and power, in directing this very fish to Peter’s hook’.

After the temple was destroyed, the emperor Vespasian ordered every Jew everywhere to pay the same two drachmas each year to the Capitol in Rome instead, as Josephus records. For Matthew’s Jewish-Christian readers, this story about the tax would have had a sharp relevance either way: before 70 as a question of the temple, after 70 as a question of avoiding needless offence.

src.l: Josephus, Jewish War 7.218 (Whiston): the two-drachma tax diverted to the Capitol

b: God gave humans rule ‘over the fish of the sea’ (Genesis 1:28), and once ‘appointed a great fish’ for Jonah (Jonah 1:17). Quarles sees in Jesus both the true man who exercises that rule and the Creator whom the creatures obey.

Paul applies Jesus’ example: ‘Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible’ (1 Corinthians 9:19). Peter writes, ‘Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil; live as servants of God’ (1 Peter 2:16).

l.t: The half-shekel offering for the tabernacle.
The LORD appoints and commands a great fish.
Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.
Pay taxes to whom taxes are due.
Do not put a stumbling block in a brother’s way.
Free, yet a servant of all.

qs: What does Jesus’ question about kings and their sons reveal about who he is?
Why did Jesus pay a tax he did not owe?
Where might you need to set aside your rights to avoid giving needless offence?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 17:24–27 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 17

18.ctx: Chapter 18 is the fourth of Matthew’s five teaching blocks, about life together in the community of Jesus’ followers. Jesus calls them ‘little ones’, ‘brothers’ and ‘fellow servants’: a family. Mark and Luke say the disciples had been arguing about which of them was the greatest (Mark 9:33–37; Luke 9:46–48).
18.mean: The disciples come to Jesus with a question: ‘Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?’ Perhaps they had noticed that Peter, James and John had been taken up the mountain, or that Peter had been singled out (16:17–19; 17:24–27). Mark tells us they had been arguing about it on the road. Jesus answers with an object lesson. He calls a little child and stands the child in the middle of them. Then he says, ‘Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.’ The disciples were asking about rank in the kingdom. Jesus tells them that, with their present attitude, they will not even get in. They must ‘change’, a word that means a complete turnaround. In Jesus’ world, children had no status. They could not earn, could not argue their case, and depended entirely on others. Jesus is not praising children for being innocent or for never asking questions. He says what he means in the next sentence: ‘whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.’ The point is humility: knowing we are small and needy, and depending wholly on our Father. Wesley put it this way: ‘lowly in heart, knowing yourselves utterly ignorant and helpless, and hanging wholly on your Father who is in heaven’. Then Jesus adds, ‘whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me.’ The humble, the overlooked and the weak in his family are so precious to him that to welcome them is to welcome him. This turns the world’s ladder upside down. In the kingdom, greatness is not about position, influence or being noticed. It belongs to those who stop trying to be great. Jesus himself is the supreme example. He ‘humbled Himself and became obedient to death—even death on a cross’ (Philippians 2:8), and God exalted him.
18.big: The way into the kingdom, and the way to greatness in it, is to humble yourself like a little child; Jesus counts the welcome given to his humble followers as given to him.

vv.h: Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?
b: Wesley: ‘Which of us shall be thy prime minister? They still dreamed of a temporal kingdom.’ Quarles points out the irony: the answer should have been obvious. The greatest in the kingdom of heaven is the King himself. The disciples were thinking only of one another.

vv.h: Jesus invited a little child to stand among them
b: The Greek word is a diminutive: ‘little child’; it can be used of any young child. In the house at Capernaum (17:25), the child may have belonged to the family. Jesus does not just tell the disciples about humility; he shows them.

vv.h: unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven
b: ‘Never’ is very strong in Greek: ‘you absolutely will not’. ‘Change’ means turn around completely; Quarles compares Saul, who was ‘transformed into a different person’ (1 Samuel 10:6). Calvin: ‘Christ does not allot even the lowest place to any man who does not lose sight of distinctions and humble himself.’

Quarles notes that this verse is often taken to praise a ‘childlike faith’ that asks no questions. But verse 4 shows that Jesus means a child’s humility, not naivety. Wesley adds that, though it is doubtful whether this text says so much, every person must be ‘inwardly changed, renewed in the image of God’ to enter the kingdom of glory.

vv.h: whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven
b: Calvin gave a ‘short definition’ of humility: ‘That man is truly humble who neither claims any personal merit in the sight of God, nor proudly despises brethren, or aims at being thought superior to them, but reckons it enough that he is one of the members of Christ’. Scripture repeats it: ‘God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble’ (1 Peter 5:5).

vv.h: whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me
b: The ‘child’ now stands for any humble disciple. Wesley: ‘all who are in this sense little children are unspeakably dear to me. Therefore help them all you can, as if it were myself in person’. Compare 10:40: ‘He who receives you receives Me’.

Jesus returns to greatness again when James and John ask for the best seats: ‘whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant’, for ‘the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve’ (20:26–28). At the Last Supper he washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:12–15).

God says through Isaiah: ‘I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit’ (Isaiah 57:15). Paul tells the Philippians to have the same mind as Christ, who ‘humbled Himself’ (Philippians 2:3–8).

l.t: Mark: they had argued on the road about who was greatest.
Luke: whoever is least among you is the greatest.
Jesus welcomes the little children.
Greatness through service; the Son of Man came to serve.
God dwells with the humble in spirit.
Christ humbled himself, and God exalted him.
Clothe yourselves with humility.

qs: Why do you think the disciples were asking who was the greatest?
What does it mean to become like a little child, according to verse 4?
Who are the ‘little ones’ in your church or community who most need to be welcomed?

18.ctx: ‘Causes … to stumble’ translates a Greek word (skandalizō) meaning to trip someone up, or to make them fall away from faith. A ‘large millstone’ was the kind turned by a donkey, far heavier than a hand mill. Jesus said something similar about the eye and hand in the Sermon on the Mount (5:29–30). Compare Mark 9:42–48 and Luke 17:1–2.
18.mean: Jesus has just said that whoever welcomes one of his little ones welcomes him. Now he gives the opposite warning: ‘if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.’ The ‘little ones’ here are not only children but humble believers, ‘who believe in Me’. To cause them to stumble means to lead them into sin or to turn them away from Christ. Jesus says that a terrible death would be better than facing God’s judgement for that. Then: ‘Woe to the world for the causes of sin. These stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come!’ In a fallen world there will always be things that trip people up: temptation, false teaching, bad example, persecution. That is no excuse for the person who causes them. Then Jesus turns the warning inward. ‘If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away.’ Better to enter life crippled than to be thrown into eternal fire. The same goes for the eye. Jesus does not mean literal self-harm; he is using the strongest picture possible to show how seriously we must deal with anything that leads us away from God. If something as precious as a hand or an eye would cost us eternal life, it must go. Interpreters read the details in different ways (see Where readings differ). But the main lines are clear. Jesus cares fiercely for the weakest of his people. He warns those who would lead them astray. And he calls every disciple to radical seriousness about sin in their own life. There is real comfort here too. Calvin saw that this was said ‘for the consolation of the godly’: if the world despises Christ’s humble followers, God does not.
18.big: Jesus fiercely protects his humble followers, warning of judgement on anyone who causes them to fall, and calls every disciple to deal ruthlessly with whatever leads them into sin.

vv.h: if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble
b: Quarles notes that ‘who believe in Me’ shows that the little ones are Jesus’ disciples, not only literal children. The verb is used in Matthew for falling away from faith (13:21; 24:10; 26:31). Wesley explains: ‘turn them not out of the right way, neither hinder them in it.’ Calvin heard comfort in it: ‘if their mean condition draws upon them the insults of the world, God does not despise them.’

vv.h: a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea
b: The Greek says literally a ‘donkey millstone’, the large stone turned by an animal. Quarles notes that drowning was one of the most dreaded deaths in the ancient world. Jesus is not recommending it; he is saying that even this would be better than God’s judgement on those who lead his people astray.

vv.h: These stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the man through whom they come!
b: Wesley: ‘Such is the nature of things, and such the weakness, folly, and wickedness of mankind, that it cannot be but they will come’. He defined offences as ‘all things whereby any one is turned out of, or hindered in the way of God.’ Calvin took the first ‘woe’ as Jesus lamenting the harm such offences would do in the world. Quarles thinks ‘the world’ here points especially to persecution.

vv.h: If your hand or your foot causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away
b: Wesley applied it widely: ‘If the most dear enjoyment, the most beloved and useful person, turn thee out of, or hinder thee in the way’. He added, ‘Is not this a hard saying? Yes; if thou take counsel with flesh and blood.’ Calvin: ‘we would rather choose to pluck out our eyes, or cut off our hands, than give encouragement to offenses’.

‘The fire of hell’ is literally ‘the Gehenna of fire’ (BSB footnote). Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), which became a picture of final judgement.

18.diff: What is Jesus warning against? Many interpreters, including Calvin and Wesley, read these verses as a warning to believers not to lead others into sin by example or teaching, and to cut away anything in their own lives (habits, pleasures, even relationships) that draws them from God. Quarles notes that some have also applied the cut-off limbs to church discipline, removing a member who leads others astray. Quarles argues instead that ‘the world’ (18:7) is the source of the stumbling, and that Jesus is chiefly warning persecutors who try to make believers deny him; the hand and eye may then stand for what a believer must be willing to lose rather than renounce Christ (compare 10:28). Chrysostom took the hand and eye to mean close friends and relatives who lead us into sin, ‘For nothing is so hurtful as bad company’ (Homily 59 on Matthew). These readings overlap: all agree that Jesus protects his little ones and that nothing is worth losing eternal life for.

b: Jesus warned his disciples: ‘Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell’ (10:28). Hebrews urges believers to ‘throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles’ (Hebrews 12:1).

Paul warned believers ‘not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in your brother’s way’ (Romans 14:13), and told the Corinthians that sinning against a weaker brother is sinning against Christ (1 Corinthians 8:12).

l.t: Mark: their worm never dies.
Luke: offences will come, but woe to the one through whom they come.
The same warning about eye and hand and sexual sin.
Fear the One who can destroy soul and body.
The Valley of Hinnom, a place of judgement.
Do not put a stumbling block in a brother’s way.
Sinning against a weak brother is sinning against Christ.

qs: Who are ‘these little ones’, and why does Jesus defend them so strongly?
What kinds of things cause believers to stumble today?
Is there anything in your life that you need to ‘cut off’ because it is leading you away from God?

18.h: The Parable of the Lost Sheep
18.ctx: Some later manuscripts add verse 11, ‘For the Son of Man came to save the lost’ (BSB footnote; compare Luke 19:10). Luke tells this parable in a different setting, answering Pharisees who grumbled that Jesus ate with sinners (Luke 15:1–7). In Matthew it is about how God and his people care for straying believers.
18.mean: ‘See that you do not look down on any of these little ones,’ Jesus says. The humble, weak and easily overlooked members of God’s family must never be treated as unimportant. Why? ‘For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven.’ The least of Jesus’ followers are so precious to God that angels who stand in his very presence are concerned with them. Then Jesus tells a story. A man has a hundred sheep, and one goes astray. Won’t he leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go to search for the lost one? And if he finds it, he rejoices more over that one than over the ninety-nine that did not wander. ‘In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.’ A practical person might say that one sheep out of a hundred is an acceptable loss. But a good shepherd does not think like that. Every sheep matters to him, and Jesus says every one of his little ones matters to the Father. Notice the contrast with the previous verses. There Jesus warned against causing a little one to stumble. Here he describes what God does when one strays: he goes after it. And he expects his people to share that heart. The verses that follow (18:15–20) show how: by going to a brother who has sinned, to win him back. Wesley noted the order in these verses: ‘The angels, the Son, the Father.’ All heaven is concerned with the least believer. This should change how we see the people in our church who are easy to overlook, and how we respond when someone drifts away. It is not enough to notice that someone has stopped coming. The Good Shepherd goes looking, and so should we. And for anyone who has wandered, here is good news: the Father is not willing that you should perish. He is looking for you.
18.big: God so values each humble believer that he seeks the one who strays like a shepherd seeking a lost sheep; his people must never look down on the little ones but share his searching love.

vv.h: See that you do not look down on any of these little ones
b: Calvin: ‘pride is the mother of disdain’; it would be ‘strange indeed that a mortal man should despise, or treat as of no account, those whom God holds in such high esteem.’ Quarles notes that the humble, who demand no honour, are often given none; Jesus insists that they be honoured.

vv.h: their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father in heaven
b: Even Moses was not allowed to see God’s face (Exodus 33:20). Wesley compared these angels to ‘chief ministers in earthly courts, who daily converse with their princes.’ Scripture teaches that angels are ‘ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation’ (Hebrews 1:14), and that ‘The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him’ (Psalm 34:7). Whether each believer has a particular guardian angel is discussed under Where readings differ.

vv.h: will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go out to search for the one that is lost?
b: Quarles notes that a shepherd would probably leave the flock with a helper or a dog; the point is not recklessness but how much each sheep matters. God promised in Ezekiel, ‘I will seek the lost, bring back the strays’ (Ezekiel 34:16), and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep by name (John 10:3, 11).

vv.h: And if he finds it, truly I tell you, he rejoices more over that one sheep
b: Calvin draws the lesson from Matthew’s setting: ‘we ought to bear with their imperfections, and endeavor, when they wander, to bring them back to the road.’ In Luke the same parable ends, ‘there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents’ (Luke 15:7).

vv.h: your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish
b: Calvin: ‘the object of the discourse is to lead us to beware of losing what God wishes to be saved.’ Quarles, who holds that true believers will persevere, adds that though God’s little ones ‘may get lost, they will not be lost’, linking this with John 10:28: ‘they will never perish.’ Christians differ on whether a true believer can finally fall away (see the glossary on perseverance), but all agree that God’s heart goes out to every straying believer.

18.diff: Does each believer have a guardian angel? Catholic teaching draws from this verse that ‘Beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd leading him to life’ (Catechism 336, quoting Basil), and the Orthodox Longer Catechism answers ‘Without doubt’ when asked whether each of us has guardian angels, citing this verse (Q. 106). Calvin agreed that angels guard believers, but thought the idea ‘that God assigned to each believer his own angel, does not rest on solid grounds’, since, as he read Psalm 34:7 and other passages, ‘not one angel only, but many’ guard the godly. Quarles notes that the angels here are described as worshippers in heaven, not as earthly protectors. All agree that God cares for his people through his angels (Psalm 91:11; Hebrews 1:14) and that the point of the verse is how precious the little ones are to God.

b: The shepherd theme runs through Scripture: ‘The LORD is my shepherd’ (Psalm 23:1); ‘We all like sheep have gone astray’ (Isaiah 53:6). Peter says Christians were ‘like sheep going astray’, but ‘now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls’ (1 Peter 2:25).

James ends his letter with the same concern: ‘if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back … Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death’ (James 5:19–20).

l.t: Luke: joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
God himself will seek his lost sheep.
The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him.
The good shepherd; no one can snatch them from my hand.
Angels sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.
Bringing back one who wanders from the truth.
Returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

qs: Why does Jesus mention the angels of the little ones?
How does the parable change the way we should think about people who drift away from church?
Is there someone you could ‘go after’ this week?

18.ctx: Jesus now gives practical steps for dealing with a fellow believer who sins. ‘The church’ (ekklēsia) appears here for only the second time in the Gospels (compare 16:18). The rule of ‘two or three witnesses’ comes from Deuteronomy 19:15 (BSB footnote). Some manuscripts lack ‘against you’ in verse 15 (BSB footnote). Compare Luke 17:3.
18.mean: Having said that the Father seeks the straying sheep, Jesus shows how his people should do the same. ‘If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over.’ The first step is private. The aim is not to embarrass, punish or win an argument, but to win a brother. Many quarrels would end here if this step were taken honestly and gently. If he will not listen, take one or two others with you. Under the law, no one could be condemned on the word of a single witness (Deuteronomy 19:15). The witnesses protect both sides: they help establish what really happened, and they add weight to the appeal. If he still refuses to listen, tell it to the church. The whole community now calls him to repent. And if he refuses even the church, ‘regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector.’ That does not mean hating him. Jesus ate with tax collectors and welcomed Gentiles. It means he is no longer treated as a brother in fellowship (compare 1 Corinthians 5:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:14), but as someone outside who still needs to be won to Christ. Then Jesus gives the church solemn authority: ‘whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.’ He gave the same words to Peter in 16:19; here they apply to the church’s decisions in discipline. When a church acts faithfully under Christ, its judgement reflects heaven’s. Calvin noted that most people go wrong in one of two ways: ‘either to deceive themselves mutually by deadly flatteries, or to pursue with excessive bitterness those whom they ought to cure.’ Jesus’ way is neither. It takes sin seriously, because sin harms people and relationships. And it takes people seriously, because the goal at every step is restoration. Wesley lamented how rarely churches actually follow these steps. Christians practise discipline in different ways (see Where readings differ), but this pattern still challenges every church.
18.big: When a brother sins, go to him privately, then with witnesses, then to the church, always aiming to win him back; the church’s faithful decisions carry heaven’s authority.

vv.h: If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately
b: The law already said, ‘You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor’ (Leviticus 19:17). Wesley insisted that ‘our Lord gives no liberty to omit this; or to exchange it for either of the following steps.’ Going to others first, or simply nursing a grudge, is not Jesus’ way.

Calvin: Christ ‘prescribes a middle course’, enjoining his disciples ‘to forgive one another, but to do so in such a manner as to endeavor to correct their faults.’ Paul adds: restore him ‘with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted’ (Galatians 6:1).

vv.h: every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses
b: Quarles notes that in Deuteronomy 19:15 the witnesses’ role is to tell true charges from false ones. They are not there to gang up on the offender but to make sure the matter is judged fairly. Wesley suggests choosing people ‘whom he esteems or loves’.

vv.h: tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, regard him as you would a pagan or a tax collector
b: Wesley took ‘the church’ to mean its leaders: ‘Tell it to the elders of the Church’. On the last step he added: ‘Let him be to thee as the heathen — To whom thou still owest earnest good will, and all the offices of humanity.’ Paul gives similar instructions: ‘Do not associate with him … Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother’ (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

vv.h: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven
b: Here ‘you’ is plural: the authority is given to the church together. Calvin distinguished this from 16:19: there Christ spoke of ‘authority in doctrine’, here ‘he appoints discipline, which is an appendage to doctrine.’ He added that heaven ratifies not ‘every kind of decision’, but ‘only that in which he presides’. Wesley: binding ‘By excommunication, pronounced in the spirit and power of Christ’, and loosing ‘By absolution from that sentence’.

18.diff: How should churches practise discipline? Presbyterian churches commit the keys to church officers, who ‘retain, and remit sins’ and ‘shut that kingdom against the impenitent, both by the Word, and censures; and to open it unto penitent sinners’ (Westminster Confession 30.2). Baptist and other congregational churches give this power to the gathered congregation: Christ has given each local church ‘all that power and authority, which is in any way needful for their carrying on that order in worship and discipline’ (1689 Baptist Confession 26.7). Catholic teaching links binding and loosing to ‘the college of the apostles united to its head’ (Catechism 1444) and to the sacrament of Penance: ‘whomever you exclude from your communion, will be excluded from communion with God’ (Catechism 1445). Wesley read ‘the church’ as its elders, and noted that in the early church ‘absolution meant no more than a discharge from Church censure.’ All agree that the aim of discipline is repentance and restoration, and that it must be carried out humbly, under Christ’s word.

b: Paul applies these principles in Corinth. He tells the church to act ‘When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus’ (1 Corinthians 5:4), and later urges them to forgive and comfort an offender who had repented (traditionally taken to be the same man), ‘so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow’ (2 Corinthians 2:6–8).

Jesus’ pattern begins with private, humble confrontation. Paul warns against taking disputes between believers to pagan courts (1 Corinthians 6:1–8), and urges believers to grow up into Christ by ‘speaking the truth in love’ (Ephesians 4:15).

l.t: If your brother sins, rebuke him; if he repents, forgive him.
Rebuke your neighbour; do not hate him; love him as yourself.
Two or three witnesses.
The keys given to Peter.
Restore him gently; bear one another’s burdens.
Church discipline in Corinth.
Forgive and comfort the one who repents.
Do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

qs: Why does Jesus insist that the first step be taken privately?
What does it mean to treat someone as a pagan or a tax collector, given how Jesus treated such people?
Is there someone you need to go to, gently and privately, to try to win back?

18.ctx: These two verses follow straight on from the teaching on church discipline. ‘Two or three’ echoes the ‘two or three witnesses’ of 18:16. Jesus promises his presence again at the very end of the Gospel: ‘I am with you always’ (28:20).
18.mean: Jesus continues: ‘Again, I tell you truly that if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven. For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them.’ These verses are often quoted as a general promise about prayer, or as comfort for a small prayer meeting. That is not wrong, but their first setting matters. Jesus has just described the hardest moments in church life: confronting a brother, involving witnesses, bringing a matter to the church, binding and loosing. The ‘two or three’ are the same as the two or three witnesses in verse 16. Quarles and others think Jesus is first promising help in exactly those situations. When believers agree together and ask the Father for wisdom in dealing with sin and restoring a brother, he will answer. And when they gather in Jesus’ name, he is present with them. Church discipline is not merely a human committee deciding about someone; it is done in the presence of Christ. Paul seems to have had this in mind when he told the Corinthians to act ‘When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus … along with the power of the Lord Jesus’ (1 Corinthians 5:4). Calvin, however, thought the promise was ‘more extensive’ than discipline alone, and Wesley applied it to all united prayer and worship. Either way, two great truths shine out. First, Jesus promises his own presence: ‘there am I with them’. A later Jewish saying says that when two people study God’s law together, God’s presence is with them. Jesus speaks of his own presence in the same way. He is Immanuel, ‘God with us’ (1:23). Second, there is power in believers agreeing together in prayer. Wesley wrote, ‘How great then is the power of joint prayer!’ The smallest gathering of believers, two or three in his name, is never alone.
18.big: When believers gather in Jesus’ name, especially to seek wisdom in hard matters, the Father hears their united prayer and Jesus himself is present with them.

vv.h: if two of you on the earth agree about anything you ask for, it will be done for you by My Father in heaven
b: Quarles notes that the word translated ‘anything’ (pragma) often means a matter or case, as in disputes between believers (1 Corinthians 6:1), which supports reading this as prayer about the matter just discussed. Wesley read it more widely: ‘all your united prayers, shall be heard’, and added, ‘If two of you — Suppose a man and his wife.’ The promise is not a blank cheque; it is made to those who ask in agreement with each other and in Jesus’ name.

vv.h: For where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them
b: Quarles notes a saying in the Mishnah: when two sit together and words of the law pass between them, God’s presence rests with them (Avot 3:2). Jesus speaks of his own presence in the same way, an implicit claim to be God with us (1:23; 28:20). Calvin: Christ will be present ‘to guide them by his counsel’. Wesley: ‘By my Spirit, to quicken their prayers, guide their counsels, and answer their petitions.’

The early church prayed together in this way: ‘With one accord they all continued in prayer’ (Acts 1:14), and when they prayed together after persecution, ‘their meeting place was shaken’ (Acts 4:31).
Jesus’ presence with his gathered people is a foretaste of the day when ‘the dwelling place of God is with man’ (Revelation 21:3).

l.t: Immanuel, God with us.
I am with you always, to the very end of the age.
Ask, and it will be given to you.
Assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus, with his power.
The believers pray together and the place is shaken.
Whatever you ask in my name, I will do.

qs: How does reading these verses in the context of 18:15–18 change or deepen their meaning?
What does it mean to gather ‘in Jesus’ name’?
Who could you agree with in prayer about a matter that concerns you both?

18.ctx: Peter’s question follows directly from Jesus’ teaching on dealing with a brother who sins. Luke records a related saying: forgive even ‘seven times in a day’ (Luke 17:4). A talent was worth about twenty years’ wages for a labourer, and a denarius about a day’s wage (BSB footnotes). This parable is found only in Matthew.
18.mean: Peter asks, ‘Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?’ He probably thought he was being generous. Jesus answers, ‘not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!’ (or ‘seventy times seven’). The point is not to keep count until the seventy-eighth offence. It is to stop counting. Then Jesus tells a story. A king settles accounts with his servants. One owes ten thousand talents. A talent was about twenty years’ wages, so this is an impossible sum, like owing billions. The king orders that the man, his wife, his children and everything he has be sold. The servant falls on his knees: ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay back everything.’ He never could. But the master has compassion, cancels the whole debt and lets him go. That same servant goes out and finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii, about a hundred days’ wages. Not nothing, but tiny compared with what he has just been forgiven. He grabs him by the throat: ‘Pay back what you owe me!’ The fellow servant falls down and begs with almost the same words: ‘Have patience with me, and I will pay you back.’ But he refuses, and has him thrown into prison. The other servants are distressed and tell the master. The master calls him in: ‘You wicked servant! I forgave all your debt because you begged me. Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?’ In anger he hands him over to the jailers until he pays everything. Then Jesus says: ‘That is how My heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother from your heart.’ The story makes the point unforgettable. Our debt to God is beyond anything we could ever repay, and he has forgiven it freely. What others owe us is small by comparison. Someone who has received such mercy must not refuse mercy to others. Christians differ on what verse 35 implies about forgiveness being withdrawn (see Where readings differ). But Jesus’ warning is plain. Forgiveness is not a feeling we wait for. It is a debt we cancel, from the heart, because ours has been cancelled.
18.big: God has forgiven us a debt we could never pay; those who have received such mercy must forgive others from the heart, without keeping count.

vv.h: Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?
b: Quarles notes that a later rabbinic teaching said God himself forgives a repeated sin three times (b. Yoma 86b). By that standard, seven times looked generous. Calvin thought Peter spoke ‘according to the natural feelings and disposition of the flesh’, fearing that too much leniency would invite more offences.

vv.h: not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!
b: The Greek can mean ‘seventy-seven times’ or ‘seventy times seven’ (BSB footnote). Either way it recalls Lamech, who boasted of vengeance: ‘If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold’ (Genesis 4:24). Jesus reverses unlimited revenge into unlimited forgiveness. Wesley: ‘as often as there is occasion. A certain number is put for an uncertain.’ Love ‘keeps no account of wrongs’ (1 Corinthians 13:5).

vv.h: a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought to him
b: Ten thousand was the largest number with a single word in Greek, and the talent the largest unit of money. Quarles calculates that a labourer would need about two hundred thousand years to earn it. Wesley: ‘Hereby our Lord intimates the vast number and weight of our offenses against God, and our utter incapacity of making him any satisfaction.’ Selling a debtor and his family into slavery was allowed in many ancient societies (compare 2 Kings 4:1).

vv.h: Have patience with me, and I will pay back everything … His master had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him
b: He begged, but what he asked for was more time, and he promised what he could never deliver: ‘I will pay back everything.’ Yet the master did far more than he asked. He did not give him more time; he cancelled the debt. Calvin: if God chose ‘to demand from us what we owe, how necessary it is for us to betake ourselves to prayer, because this is the only refuge that remains for transgressors.’ The psalmist says, ‘If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness’ (Psalm 130:3–4).

vv.h: one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii. He grabbed him and began to choke him
b: A hundred denarii was a real debt, about a hundred days’ wages. But Quarles calculates that the first debt was about six hundred thousand times larger. The fellow servant’s plea repeats the first servant’s own words. Calvin pointed to the three contrasts: master and servant, huge and small sums, ‘extraordinary kindness with extreme cruelty.’ ‘How inconsiderable are the offenses, with which brethren are chargeable towards us, if we take into account our obligation to God?’

vv.h: You wicked servant! … Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had on you?
b: The other servants were ‘greatly distressed’. Calvin noted that ‘the men who live among us will be so many witnesses against us before God’. Quarles points out that Jesus calls unforgiveness ‘wicked’, a word Matthew also uses of the evil one (13:19, 38). Jesus had said, ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy’ (5:7).

vv.h: his master turned him over to the jailers to be tortured, until he should repay all that he owed
b: Since the debt could never be repaid, the punishment would never end. Jesus applies it directly: this is how the Father will treat anyone who will not forgive ‘from your heart’. It repeats his teaching on the Lord’s Prayer: ‘if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours’ (6:15).

Quarles stresses that forgiving others does not earn God’s forgiveness, since the debt is unpayable; but it is necessary evidence that we have truly received mercy. ‘From your heart’ means real forgiveness, not just words. Calvin distinguished letting go of revenge and continuing to love even an unrepentant enemy, from fully restoring a brother who repents (Luke 17:3).

18.diff: Does God take back forgiveness? In the parable the master revokes his pardon. Wesley drew the Arminian conclusion: the debtor ‘was freely and fully forgiven’, then ‘wilfully and grievously offended’, and ‘His pardon was retracted’. He asked, ‘shall we still say, but when we are once freely and fully forgiven, our pardon can never be retracted?’ Calvin, from the Reformed side, warned against pressing the detail: ‘it is foolish to inquire how God punishes those sins which he has already forgiven; for the simple meaning is this: though he offers mercy to all, yet severe creditors, from whom no forgiveness can be obtained, are unworthy of enjoying it.’ Quarles and many Reformed readers add that a persistently unforgiving heart shows that God’s forgiveness was never truly received. Catholic teaching holds that those who fall into grave sin after baptism ‘have thus lost their baptismal grace’, and that the sacrament of Penance offers them ‘a new possibility to convert and to recover the grace of justification’ (Catechism 1446). All agree that this is one of Jesus’ most serious warnings, and that the forgiven must forgive.

b: The New Testament grounds Christian forgiveness in God’s: ‘forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you’ (Ephesians 4:32); ‘Forgive as the Lord forgave you’ (Colossians 3:13). God revealed himself as ‘compassionate and gracious … forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin’ (Exodus 34:6–7).

Jesus forgave even those who crucified him: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34). Stephen followed his example (Acts 7:60). Paul writes that ‘God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us’ (Romans 5:8).

l.t: Forgive seven times in a day.
Lamech’s boast of seventy-sevenfold vengeance.
If you kept track of iniquities, who could stand?
Forgive us our debts, as we have forgiven our debtors.
Blessed are the merciful.
Forgive as God in Christ forgave you.
Bear with one another and forgive.
Father, forgive them.

qs: Why does Jesus make the first debt so enormous and the second so small?
What is the difference between forgiving someone and pretending nothing happened?
Is there someone you need to forgive ‘from your heart’? What would help you do it?

19.ctx: ‘When Jesus had finished saying these things’ marks the end of Matthew’s fourth teaching block. Jesus now leaves Galilee for the last time and heads towards Jerusalem through the region east of the Jordan. Jewish teachers were divided over divorce: the school of Shammai allowed it only for serious sexual wrong, the school of Hillel for almost any reason (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). Compare Mark 10:1–12 and Matthew 5:31–32.
19.mean: Some Pharisees come to test Jesus: ‘Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?’ They want to drag him into a fierce debate. Most expected the argument to turn on Deuteronomy 24:1–4, which allowed a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce. Jesus goes back much further, to the beginning. ‘Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator “made them male and female,” and said, “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh”?’ Then he draws the conclusion: ‘So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.’ Marriage is not just a human contract that people can end when they choose. God himself joins husband and wife. The Pharisees push back: then why did Moses command divorce? Jesus corrects them. Moses did not command it; he permitted it, ‘because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning.’ The law of divorce was a limit placed on sinful people, not God’s ideal. Then Jesus states his own teaching: ‘whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery.’ The disciples are shocked. ‘If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.’ Jesus replies that not everyone can accept this, but only those to whom it has been given. Some people cannot marry, some have been made unable, and some choose to remain single ‘for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.’ Singleness is not second best. Jesus himself was unmarried. This passage calls us to see marriage as God sees it: a lifelong, exclusive union that he creates. Christians differ on exactly when divorce and remarriage are allowed (see Where readings differ). But Jesus’ heart is clear. He calls husbands and wives to faithfulness, he names hardness of heart as the root of broken marriages, and he honours those who stay single to serve God.
19.big: God made marriage as a lifelong one-flesh union that no one should break; divorce was a concession to hard hearts, and singleness for the kingdom is also a gift.

vv.h: He left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan
b: Wesley: ‘from that time walked no more in Galilee.’ Quarles notes that the crowds who follow and are healed here will later welcome Jesus into Jerusalem (21:8–9). The journey to Jerusalem has begun, and it leads to the cross.

vv.h: Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?
b: Quarles notes that Josephus, who says he followed the Pharisees’ rules, restated Moses’ law as allowing divorce ‘for any cause whatsoever’ (Antiquities 4.253), and that the Mishnah records the school of Hillel allowing divorce even if a wife spoiled a meal (Gittin 9:10). Wesley: ‘for any thing which he dislikes in her. This the scribes allowed.’ The test was a trap: any answer would anger someone, and Herod Antipas had killed John for speaking on marriage (14:3–4).

vv.h: the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife’
b: Jesus quotes Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 (BSB footnotes). Wesley: ‘By making them one man and one woman, he condemned polygamy: by making them one flesh, he condemned divorce.’ Calvin: ‘he who divorces his wife tears from him, as it were, the half of himself.’

vv.h: So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate
b: Quarles notes that Jesus treats ‘be united’ as something God does: God is the one who joins husband and wife. The word for ‘man’ here means a human being, so the contrast is between what God joins and what humans try to undo. Calvin: ‘Who, art thou that allowest thyself to burst asunder what God hath joined?’

vv.h: Why then … did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce?
b: The Pharisees refer to Deuteronomy 24:1 (BSB footnote). That law did not command divorce; it regulated it, requiring a written certificate and forbidding the first husband to take her back after she had remarried (Deuteronomy 24:1–4).

vv.h: Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning
b: Wesley: ‘Moses permitted (not commanded) it, because of the hardness of your hearts - Because neither your fathers nor you could bear the more excellent way.’ Calvin: Moses permitted it ‘on account of their obstinacy, and not because he approved of it as lawful.’ Quarles notes that ‘the beginning’ means God’s design before sin entered the world.

vv.h: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery
b: Only Matthew records the exception, here and in 5:32. ‘Sexual immorality’ (porneia) is a broad word for sexual sin. Quarles thinks Jesus allowed the innocent spouse to divorce for it and probably to remarry. Calvin: by such sin the guilty spouse ‘cuts herself off, as a rotten member, from her husband, and sets him at liberty.’ Wesley: ‘I revoke that indulgence from this day’. Some manuscripts add, ‘And he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery’ (BSB footnote; compare 5:32). See Where readings differ.

vv.h: If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry
b: The disciples’ reaction shows how strict Jesus’ teaching sounded in a world where divorce was easy for men. Quarles notes that they had missed the point: they wanted to avoid a hard marriage law by avoiding God’s good gift of marriage altogether.

vv.h: Not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given
b: Calvin: ‘the gift of continence is a special gift’, and anyone who binds himself to celibacy without it ‘is widely mistaken.’ Wesley: the gift comes to some ‘by natural constitution’, to others ‘by violence’, and to others ‘by grace with their choice: who steadily withstand their natural inclinations, that they may wait upon God without distraction.’

vv.h: still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven
b: A eunuch was a man unable to father children, either from birth or because he had been castrated, often to serve in a royal court. Jesus does not mean literal castration but a choice to stay unmarried in order to serve God. Wesley: ‘Happy they! who have abstained from marriage (though without condemning or despising it) that they might walk more closely with God!’ Paul says the same: singleness is a gift for some, marriage for others (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35).

19.diff: Divorce, remarriage and celibacy. The exception clause (here and 5:32) appears only in Matthew. Reformed and most Protestant churches read it as permitting divorce, and remarriage of the innocent party, for adultery; the Westminster Confession also allows divorce for wilful desertion that cannot be remedied (24.5–6; compare 1 Corinthians 7:15). Between the baptized, Catholic teaching holds that ‘a ratified and consummated marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power or for any reason other than death’ (Catechism 2382), and it does not read the exception as permitting remarriage; some Catholic scholars take porneia to mean a marriage that was unlawful from the start. Some Protestant scholars (for example Heth and Wenham in Jesus and Divorce) hold that Jesus allows no remarriage while the first spouse lives. The Orthodox Church opposes divorce but, as a pastoral concession, ‘does permit divorced individuals to marry a second and even a third time’ (Orthodox Church in America). On celibacy, Catholic teaching normally chooses Latin-rite priests from men who ‘intend to remain celibate “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven”’ (Catechism 1579), while in the Eastern Churches ‘married men can be ordained as deacons and priests’ (1580). Protestants honour singleness as a gift but do not require it of ministers; Calvin warned against vowing celibacy without the gift. See also the note on 5:31.

b: Malachi records God’s words: ‘I hate divorce’ … ‘So guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith’ (Malachi 2:16). Paul applies Jesus’ teaching in 1 Corinthians 7:10–16 and describes marriage as a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–33).

Quarles notes that the answer to hard hearts is the new covenant, in which God promised, ‘I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh’ (Ezekiel 36:26). Christ makes possible a faithfulness and forgiveness in marriage that the law could only command.

l.t: Mark’s account: whoever divorces and remarries commits adultery.
The Sermon on the Mount on divorce.
Male and female; the two become one flesh.
The certificate of divorce.
Do not break faith with the wife of your youth.
Paul on marriage, divorce and singleness.
Marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.

qs: Why does Jesus go back to Genesis rather than arguing about Deuteronomy?
What does ‘hardness of heart’ have to do with broken marriages, then and now?
How can our church honour both marriage and those who are single?

19.ctx: Parents seem to have brought children to respected teachers for blessing. Laying hands on someone’s head while praying for them goes back to Jacob blessing his grandsons (Genesis 48:14–20). Compare Mark 10:13–16 and Luke 18:15–17.
19.mean: People bring little children to Jesus so that he will place his hands on them and pray for them. The disciples rebuke them. They seem to think that the Master is too busy and too important for children. Perhaps they think they are protecting him. Jesus will have none of it. ‘Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.’ He lays his hands on them, and then moves on. This short scene teaches a great deal. First, it shows Jesus’ heart. In a world where children had little status, he made time for them, touched them and prayed for them. Mark adds that he took them in his arms (Mark 10:16). No one is too small or unimportant for Jesus. Second, it shows the disciples’ blind spot. They had just been told that whoever humbles himself like a child is the greatest in the kingdom (18:4), and that welcoming a child in Jesus’ name is welcoming him (18:5). Yet here they are, turning children away. It is easy to agree with Jesus’ teaching and still miss it in practice. Third, it shows who the kingdom belongs to: ‘such as these’. Children cannot earn anything or bring anything. They simply come, and receive. That is how everyone enters the kingdom. Wesley put it this way: ‘Little children, either in a natural or spiritual sense, have a right to enter into my kingdom.’ This passage has been important in debates about baptising infants (see Where readings differ). Whatever our view on that, every church can take Jesus’ words to heart: do not hinder the little children. Make room for them. Pray for them. Bring them to Jesus.
19.big: Jesus welcomes and blesses the children his disciples tried to turn away; the kingdom belongs to those who come to him like children.

vv.h: little children were brought to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them and pray for them
b: Quarles notes that the parents were asking for a blessing rather than healing. Wesley: ‘This was a rite which was very early used, in praying for a blessing on young persons. See Gen. xlviii, 14, 20.’

vv.h: And the disciples rebuked those who brought them
b: Wesley: ‘probably thinking such an employ beneath the dignity of their Master.’ Quarles cites a saying in the Mishnah that, as he reads it, spending time chatting with children is a waste that leads to ruin (Avot 3:10). The disciples had forgotten what Jesus taught in 18:1–5.

vv.h: Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these
b: Calvin inferred that Christ’s ‘grace is extended even to those who are of that age.’ Mark says Jesus was ‘indignant’ with the disciples (Mark 10:14). God is praised in the psalms because He ‘blesses the children within you’ (Psalm 147:13).

vv.h: after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there
b: Jesus did what the parents asked before continuing his journey to Jerusalem. Quarles suggests some of these children may have been among those who later shouted ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ in the temple (21:15–16).

19.diff: Children and baptism. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptise infants, and have often appealed to this passage. Calvin called it ‘a shield against the Anabaptists’: since baptism is ‘the pledge and figure of the forgiveness of sins, and likewise of adoption by God, it ought not to be denied to infants’. The Catholic Catechism says that ‘The sheer gratuitousness of the grace of salvation is particularly manifest in infant Baptism’ (1250). Baptists and many other evangelicals reply that Jesus blessed the children but did not baptise them, and that baptism is for those who ‘do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ’ (1689 Baptist Confession 29.2). All agree that children are welcome to Jesus. See also the note on Mark 10:13.

b: God’s promises have always included children: ‘This promise belongs to you and your children’ (Acts 2:39). Parents are called to teach their children God’s ways (Deuteronomy 6:6–7; Ephesians 6:4).

Jesus’ welcome of children fits his praise of the Father for revealing the truth ‘to little children’ (11:25), and his reply when children praised him in the temple: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’ (21:16).

l.t: Mark: Jesus was indignant and took the children in his arms.
Luke: even infants were brought.
Become like little children; whoever welcomes a child welcomes me.
Jacob lays his hands on his grandsons and blesses them.
Children shout ‘Hosanna’ in the temple.
The promise is for you and your children.

qs: Why do you think the disciples tried to send the children away?
What does it mean that the kingdom belongs to ‘such as these’?
How can our church make sure we never hinder children from coming to Jesus?
