19.ctx: Matthew calls him a young man (19:20); Luke calls him a ruler (Luke 18:18). Some manuscripts have ‘Good Teacher’ and ‘Why do you call Me good?’, as in Mark and Luke (BSB footnote). Jesus’ list in verses 18–19 comes from Exodus 20:12–16 and Leviticus 19:18 (BSB footnote). Compare Mark 10:17–22 and Luke 18:18–23.
19.mean: A young man comes to Jesus with the most important question anyone can ask: ‘Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?’ He assumes that eternal life is something he can earn by doing the right good deed. Jesus answers, ‘Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is only One who is good.’ Only God is truly good. Then: ‘If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.’ ‘Which ones?’ the young man asks. Jesus lists commandments from the second half of the Ten Commandments, about how we treat others, and adds, ‘love your neighbor as yourself.’ The young man is confident: ‘All these I have kept. What do I still lack?’ He senses that something is still missing. Jesus puts his finger on it: ‘If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.’ When the young man hears this, he goes away sad, ‘because he had great wealth.’ Notice which commandment Jesus did not mention: ‘You shall not covet’. That seems to have been the very one this man was breaking. His wealth had become his god. He thought he loved his neighbour, but he would not part with his money for the poor. He thought he loved God, but when he had to choose between God and money, he chose money. Calvin said the command to sell everything was ‘the scrutiny of a concealed vice.’ Jesus was not giving a rule that every Christian must sell everything (see Where readings differ). He was showing this man what stood between him and God. And notice the real answer to his question: ‘Then come, follow Me.’ Eternal life is not earned by a good deed. It is found in following Jesus, who is himself the Good One. The tragedy is that the young man came so close. He asked the right question, of the right person, and heard the right answer. And he went away sad. Every one of us must ask: what would I be unwilling to give up for Jesus?
19.big: Eternal life cannot be earned by good deeds; Jesus exposes the rich young man’s love of wealth and calls him to give it up and follow him, but he goes away sad.

vv.h: Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?
b: Quarles notes that in Matthew ‘Teacher’ is the title used by people who do not follow Jesus (8:19; 12:38; 22:16). Some Jewish writings of the time taught that a good deed such as almsgiving could atone for sin (Tobit 12:9; Sirach 3:30). Wesley: ‘Many of the poor had followed him from the beginning. One rich man came at last.’

vv.h: Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is only One who is good
b: Quarles hears an echo of Israel’s creed, ‘The LORD is One’ (Deuteronomy 6:4): only God is perfectly good, so no one can earn eternal life by being good enough. Calvin did not think Jesus was here hinting at his own divinity, as many interpreters have; rather he was calling the young man to accept his teaching as coming from God. Wesley: none is good ‘Supremely, originally, essentially, but God.’

vv.h: If you want to enter life, keep the commandments
b: Interpreters read this differently. Quarles thinks Jesus was showing the man his inability: who can keep all the commandments? Wesley insisted Jesus gave ‘a plain, direct, serious answer to a serious question’: keep them ‘From a principle of loving faith. Believe, and thence love and obey.’ Calvin: ‘let every man who endeavors to regulate his life by obedience to Christ direct his whole attention to keep the commandments of the law.’

vv.h: Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself
b: Calvin explained why Jesus chose the second table: ‘as the observation of the first table is often feigned by hypocrites, the second table is better adapted for making a scrutiny.’ Quarles notes that Jesus left out the tenth commandment, ‘You shall not covet’ (Exodus 20:17), which was exactly this man’s weakness.

vv.h: All these I have kept … What do I still lack?
b: Wesley: ‘So he imagined; and perhaps he had, as to the letter; but not as to the spirit’. Jesus had taught that the commandments reach the heart: anger is murder, lust is adultery (5:21–30). Yet the man’s question shows an honest sense that something was missing.

vv.h: If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me
b: ‘Perfect’ recalls 5:48: ‘Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.’ Wesley explains: ‘That is, to be a real Christian’, and Jesus ‘saw his bosom sin was love of the world’. He adds: ‘To him therefore he gave this particular direction, which he never designed for a general rule.’ Calvin: it ‘was not an addition to the law, but the scrutiny of a concealed vice.’ The heart of Jesus’ answer is the last phrase: ‘follow Me.’

vv.h: When the young man heard this, he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth
b: Jesus had warned, ‘You cannot serve both God and money’ (6:24), and ‘where your treasure is, there your heart will be also’ (6:21). The man is like the seed among thorns, choked by ‘the deceitfulness of wealth’ (13:22). Calvin: ‘if we are not prepared to endure poverty, it is manifest that covetousness reigns in us.’ He added that whether the young man later repented ‘we know not’.

19.diff: ‘If you want to be perfect’. Catholic teaching says Jesus’ second reply ‘does not do away with the first: following Jesus Christ involves keeping the Commandments’, and that here the call to follow him ‘is joined to the call to poverty and chastity. The evangelical counsels are inseparable from the Commandments’ (Catechism 2053); some are called to embrace voluntary poverty, as in religious orders. Calvin saw the command as ‘the scrutiny of a concealed vice’, not a higher way for a few. Wesley read ‘perfect’ as ‘to be a real Christian’ and said the command to sell all was ‘never designed for a general rule’: ‘To sell all was an absolute duty to him; to many of us it would be an absolute sin.’ All agree that nothing may come before Christ, and that greed is a form of idolatry (Colossians 3:5). See also the note on Mark 10:17.

b: Paul warns that ‘the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil’ (1 Timothy 6:10), and instructs the rich ‘not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God’, and ‘to be generous and ready to share’ (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

The young man’s story contrasts with Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector who gave half his possessions to the poor when Jesus came to his house (Luke 19:1–10), and with the disciples who left everything to follow Jesus (19:27).

l.t: Mark: Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Luke: a ruler, very rich.
The Ten Commandments, including ‘You shall not covet’.
Love your neighbour as yourself.
Treasure in heaven; you cannot serve God and money.
Zacchaeus gives to the poor.
The love of money; instructions for the rich.

qs: What did the young man think eternal life depended on? How did Jesus answer him?
Why do you think Jesus left out the commandment against coveting?
What would you find hardest to give up if Jesus asked you to follow him?

19.ctx: These verses continue straight on from the rich young man. The camel was the largest animal in the region and the eye of a needle the smallest opening anyone knew. Compare Mark 10:23–27 and Luke 18:24–27.
19.mean: As the young man walks away, Jesus turns to his disciples. ‘Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.’ Then he says it again, more strongly: ‘it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.’ The picture is deliberately absurd. A camel cannot go through the eye of a needle. Jesus is saying that, humanly speaking, it is impossible for a rich person to be saved. The disciples are greatly astonished. ‘Who then can be saved?’ Many people in their day assumed that wealth was a sign of God’s blessing; if even the rich, so obviously favoured by God, cannot be saved, what hope is there for anyone else? Jesus looks at them and says, ‘With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.’ This is the key. Salvation is never a human achievement, for rich or poor. No one can squeeze through the needle’s eye by their own effort. But God can do the impossible. He can free a rich person from the grip of money, as he did with Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1–10). He can save anyone. Wesley noticed that Jesus did not soften his warning at all; he made the salvation of a rich man ‘the utmost effort of Omnipotence.’ Jesus’ words are uncomfortable for many of us. By the standards of history and of most of the world, many people in Britain today are rich. Wealth brings comfort, security and choices. It also brings danger. It tempts us to trust in what we have, to feel we do not need God, and to hold on tightly to our possessions. Jesus does not say that wealth itself is sin. But he says it is a great danger, one only God can rescue us from. The right response is not despair but humble dependence: to admit that we cannot save ourselves, and to trust the God for whom nothing is impossible.
19.big: It is impossible for the rich, or anyone, to save themselves; but with God all things are possible, even freeing someone from the grip of wealth.

vv.h: it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven
b: Calvin: Christ warns ‘how great an obstacle is presented by riches.’ He noted that in Mark Jesus speaks of ‘those who trust in riches’ (Mark 10:24, in some manuscripts), but thought this confirms rather than softens the warning.

vv.h: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle
b: Wesley calls it ‘a proverbial expression’: ‘humanly speaking, it is an absolute impossibility.’ Quarles notes the deliberate contrast between the largest common animal and one of the smallest openings.

vv.h: Who then can be saved?
b: Quarles notes the common belief that riches were a reward for righteousness; a later saying in the Mishnah, from Rabbi Meir, holds that wealth and poverty come not from a trade but ‘all is in accordance with a person’s merit’ (Kiddushin 4:14). Wesley answered: ‘A poor man; a peasant; a beggar: ten thousand of them, sooner than one that is rich.’

vv.h: With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible
b: Wesley: ‘O what a speaking look was there!’ Jesus ‘does not retract what he had said: no, nor soften it in the least degree, but rather strengthens it’. Calvin: Christ does not take away the disciples’ anxiety, so that, ‘distrusting themselves, they may implore strength from heaven.’ The angel said to Mary, ‘no word from God will ever fail’ (Luke 1:37).

The Bible warns repeatedly about trusting wealth: ‘He who trusts in his riches will fall’ (Proverbs 11:28). James rebukes rich oppressors (James 5:1–6), and Revelation describes a church that said, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing’, not realising it was ‘wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked’ (Revelation 3:17).
Yet Scripture also shows rich believers serving God: Abraham, Joseph of Arimathea (27:57), and the women who supported Jesus ‘out of their own means’ (Luke 8:3). God can save and use the rich.

l.t: Mark: how hard it is for those who trust in riches.
Luke: what is impossible with man is possible with God.
No word from God will ever fail.
Is anything too difficult for the LORD?
Rich, and needing nothing, yet poor.
Saved by grace through faith, not by works.

qs: Why were the disciples so astonished by what Jesus said?
In what ways might wealth make it harder to depend on God?
What hope does verse 26 give to people who feel far from God?

Mishnah, Kiddushin 4:14 (Sefaria)

19.h: The Reward of Those Who Follow
19.ctx: Peter speaks for the Twelve after the rich young man has gone away. ‘The renewal of all things’ can also be translated ‘the regeneration’ (BSB footnote). Compare Mark 10:28–31 and Luke 18:28–30; 22:28–30.
19.mean: Peter has watched the rich young man refuse to leave his wealth. Now he says, ‘Look, we have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?’ It is an honest question. They have left boats, nets, homes and families. Jesus does not rebuke him. He makes a remarkable promise. ‘Truly I tell you, in the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.’ ‘The renewal of all things’ means the new creation, when God makes everything new and removes every effect of sin (Isaiah 65:17). The Son of Man will reign in glory, and his apostles will share in his rule. Then the promise widens to every disciple: ‘everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of My name will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.’ Following Jesus costs something real. For some, it means leaving home or work. For others, it means losing the approval or even the company of their family (10:35–37). But nothing given up for Jesus is lost. What we receive is ‘a hundredfold’: far more than we gave. Mark adds that this begins even now, ‘along with persecutions’ (Mark 10:30), in the new family of God’s people. And it ends in eternal life. Then comes a warning: ‘But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.’ God’s rewards will turn the world’s rankings upside down. The rich young man was ‘first’ in this world, but he walked away. The disciples were nobodies, but they followed. The next parable (20:1–16) shows that even the rewards are a gift of grace, not wages earned. No one should follow Jesus to get ahead. But no one who follows Jesus will ever regret it.
19.big: Jesus promises that his apostles will share his rule in the renewed creation, and that everyone who gives up anything for him will receive far more and inherit eternal life.

vv.h: Look, we have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?
b: Quarles argues that Peter is not boasting but anxious: after ‘Who then can be saved?’ (19:25), he wants to know whether the disciples will share the treasure in heaven the young man refused. Luke has, ‘we have left all we had’ (Luke 18:28).

vv.h: in the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne
b: The Greek word (palingenesia) means a new birth or new beginning. Quarles links it to Matthew’s opening words, literally ‘the book of the genesis of Jesus Christ’ (1:1; BSB ‘the record of the genealogy’): Jesus brings a new genesis. Here the word means the renewal of creation, not the personal new birth of Titus 3:5. Wesley: ‘In the final renovation of all things’. The Son of Man on his glorious throne appears again in 25:31, at the final judgement.

vv.h: you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel
b: Calvin: the apostles will be like ‘assessors, or first councilors and judges’; the number twelve testified that God ‘purposed to collect the remnant of his people which was scattered.’ Quarles takes the twelve tribes to mean Israel itself, and ‘judging’ to mean real judgement; he notes that some commentators take it to mean ruling over the people of God. Wesley noted that a condition is implied: ‘the throne of Judas another took’ (Acts 1:20–26).

vv.h: everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of My name will receive a hundredfold
b: Some editions lack ‘or wife’ (BSB footnote). Wesley: they receive a hundredfold ‘In value, though not in kind, even in the present world.’ Quarles notes that houses, fields and families in the promise show that the life to come is not a ghostly existence but life on a renewed earth.

vv.h: But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first
b: Calvin: the saying was ‘added in order to shake off the indolence of the flesh’; it is no use beginning well if we lose heart halfway. Wesley thought that both first and last may be saved, ‘though with different degrees of glory.’ The saying is repeated at the end of the next parable (20:16).

The hope of a renewed creation runs through Scripture: ‘I will create new heavens and a new earth’ (Isaiah 65:17); ‘Behold, I make all things new’ (Revelation 21:5). Paul says creation itself ‘will be set free from its bondage to decay’ (Romans 8:21).

Jesus promised his disciples at the Last Supper that they would ‘eat and drink at My table in My kingdom’ and ‘sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel’ (Luke 22:30). Paul says believers will judge the world and even angels (1 Corinthians 6:2–3).

l.t: Mark: a hundredfold now, with persecutions, and eternal life.
Thrones for those who stood by Jesus in his trials.
New heavens and a new earth.
Thrones set in place; the saints receive the kingdom.
The Son of Man on his glorious throne.
Creation set free from its bondage to decay.
I make all things new.

qs: What did the disciples give up to follow Jesus? What did Jesus promise them?
What does ‘the renewal of all things’ tell us about the life to come?
Has following Jesus cost you anything? How does this promise encourage you?

20.ctx: This parable follows straight on from 19:30 and ends with the same saying (20:16); the chapter break was added much later. A denarius was a normal day’s wage for a labourer (BSB footnote). The working day ran from about six in the morning to six in the evening; ‘the eleventh hour’ was about five in the afternoon (BSB footnotes). Only Matthew records this parable.
20.mean: Jesus tells a story about a landowner who goes out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. He agrees to pay them a denarius, a fair day’s wage. He goes back at about nine, at noon and at three, and sends more workers in, promising to pay ‘whatever is right’. Then, at about five in the afternoon, with only an hour of daylight left, he finds others still standing around. ‘Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing?’ ‘Because no one has hired us.’ So he sends them in too. At evening the foreman pays the workers, starting with those hired last. They receive a full denarius. Those hired first expect more, but they also receive a denarius, and they grumble that the owner has made the latecomers ‘equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day.’ The owner answers: ‘Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius?’ And then: ‘Or are you envious because I am generous?’ ‘So the last will be first, and the first will be last.’ The parable answers Peter’s question, ‘What then will there be for us?’ (19:27). Yes, there is reward. But God’s rewards are not wages calculated by the hour. They are gifts of his generosity. The landowner cheats no one: the first workers get exactly what they agreed. But he gives the last far more than they earned, because he is good. Quarles compares the workers hired last, passed over all day, to the tax collectors and sinners Jesus welcomed. The grumbling of the first workers is a warning to the disciples, and to every long-serving Christian. It is possible to work hard for God and then resent his kindness to others. Grace is never fair by our standards. Thank God that it is not.
20.big: God rewards his servants not by strict wages but by his generosity; those who come late receive the same grace, and no one should resent his goodness to others.

vv.h: a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. He agreed to pay them a denarius
b: Quarles notes that the landowner stands for God; in verse 8 he is called ‘lord’ of the vineyard. The vineyard is a familiar Old Testament picture of God’s people (Isaiah 5:1–7), though Quarles thinks it carries no special meaning in this parable. A denarius was enough to feed a family for a day. Wesley: ‘All who profess to be Christians are in this sense labourers’.

vv.h: I will pay you whatever is right
b: The hours are given in the BSB footnotes: about nine, noon and three. Quarles notes that the owner promises only ‘whatever is right’; God never gives less than is just, though he often gives more.

vv.h: Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing? … Because no one has hired us
b: Quarles points out that these men were not lazy. They had waited all day hoping for work, and had perhaps been passed over because they looked weak, sick or old. Even an hour’s pay would buy their families a little food. Wesley: the eleventh hour means ‘very late; long after the rest were called.’

vv.h: starting with the last ones hired and moving on to the first … each of them also received a denarius
b: The law required that a labourer be paid the same day (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:15). Quarles notes that the order of payment lets the first workers see the owner’s generosity. Wesley read the evening as ‘Of life; or of the world.’

vv.h: you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day
b: Their complaint sounds reasonable: equal pay for unequal work seems unfair. Calvin answered that God ‘owes no man any thing’, and ‘gives the name of a hire to the crown which he bestows freely.’ Wesley: ‘those who were equally holy here, whenever they were called, will be equally happy hereafter.’

vv.h: Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius?
b: ‘Friend’ is a polite but distant address, used again in 22:12 and 26:50. The owner has kept his promise exactly. Nothing has been taken from the first workers; something has been given to the others.

vv.h: Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?
b: Literally, ‘Is your eye evil because I am good?’ Quarles notes that ‘good’ is the same word as in 19:17, ‘There is only One who is good’, and that the ‘evil eye’ recalls 6:23 (BSB ‘bad’ eyes), where it stands for a selfish heart. Wesley: ‘Art thou envious, because I am gracious?’

vv.h: So the last will be first, and the first will be last
b: Some later manuscripts add, ‘For many are called, but few are chosen’ (BSB footnote; compare 22:14). Calvin: those called first ‘ought to run with so much the greater alacrity’, and all should be willing ‘to share with them a common prize’, ‘because God is not limited to any person, but calls freely whomsoever He pleases’.

20.diff: What is the parable about? Interpreters have found different emphases. Wesley thought its ‘primary scope’ was ‘That many of the Jews would be rejected, and many of the Gentiles accepted’, and its secondary point that some late converts will be ‘first, and highest’ in glory, so that there are degrees of reward. Calvin rejected the Jews-and-Gentiles reading as one of the ‘subtleties’ that are ‘unseasonable’: the Lord ‘makes no distinction in the bargain, but only in the time’. He also declined to read it as teaching equal glory for all; its point, he said, is that those called first have no claim to be preferred, because God ‘calls freely whomsoever He pleases’. Quarles reads it as illustrating the great reversal of 19:30 and correcting any idea that rewards are earned: God gives far more than anyone deserves. Wesley also applied it to ‘those in every age who did not hear, or at least understand the Gospel call, till their day of life was drawing to a period.’ All agree that the parable magnifies God’s generosity and warns against envy.

b: The parable echoes Jesus’ welcome of tax collectors and sinners, which the religious leaders resented (9:10–13; 11:19). Luke’s parable of the prodigal son ends with an elder brother who, like the first workers, cannot rejoice at his father’s generosity (Luke 15:25–32).

Paul teaches that salvation is a gift, not wages: ‘the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation. However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness’ (Romans 4:4–5). The thief on the cross entered paradise at the very end (Luke 23:42–43).

l.t: Peter’s question and the saying the parable explains.
Israel as the LORD’s vineyard.
Pay the hired worker the same day.
The elder brother resents his father’s generosity.
The thief on the cross: today you will be with me in paradise.
Wages versus gift; faith credited as righteousness.
Saved by grace, not by works.

qs: Why did the first workers feel they had been treated unfairly? Had they been?
What does the parable teach about how God rewards his people?
Do you ever resent God’s kindness to someone you think deserves it less than you?

20.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion
20.ctx: This is the third and most detailed of Jesus’ predictions of his death (16:21; 17:22–23). He is now on the road up to Jerusalem with crowds of pilgrims going to the Passover. John records that the Jewish council could not carry out a death sentence itself (John 18:31), so they would hand him to the Romans. Compare Mark 10:32–34 and Luke 18:31–34.
20.mean: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them, for the third time, what is going to happen. ‘Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified. And on the third day He will be raised to life.’ This prediction is the most detailed so far. Jesus names who will condemn him: the chief priests and scribes. He names who will execute him: the Gentiles, meaning the Romans. He names what will be done to him: mockery, flogging and crucifixion. Every detail came true (27:26–31). And again he says that on the third day he will be raised. Notice that Jesus is walking towards this, not away from it. He is not trapped or taken by surprise. He knows exactly what is waiting in Jerusalem, and he goes anyway. Calvin wrote that he ‘knowingly and willingly hastens to undergo it.’ This was not because suffering meant nothing to him; Gethsemane will show how much he dreaded it (26:38–39). It was because he came to give his life (20:28). Notice too how the disciples respond: this time Matthew records no reaction at all. Peter protested the first time (16:22); they grieved the second (17:23). Luke says that this time ‘the disciples did not understand any of these things’ (Luke 18:34). In the very next scene two of them ask for the best seats in the kingdom. They were still thinking of glory without the cross. In an honour-and-shame culture, being publicly mocked was one of the worst things that could happen to anyone. The Son of Man, to whom all nations will one day bow (Daniel 7:14), would first be spat on and laughed at. Psalm 22 had spoken of this: ‘All who see me mock me’ (Psalm 22:7). He bore the shame so that we could be welcomed into honour.
20.big: For the third time Jesus foretells in detail that he will be condemned, mocked, flogged and crucified, and rise on the third day; he walks towards it willingly.

vv.h: As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside
b: Jerusalem stands high in the hills, so travellers always went ‘up’ to it. Mark says Jesus walked ahead of them, and they were astonished and afraid (Mark 10:32). He told the Twelve privately, away from the excited crowds.

vv.h: the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death
b: Quarles notes that the title ‘Son of Man’ (Daniel 7) spoke of glory, and he reads Daniel as also foretelling that ‘the Messiah will be cut off and will have nothing’ (Daniel 9:26). The council would later condemn Jesus for blasphemy (26:65–66). Calvin: ‘he knowingly and willingly hastens to undergo it.’

vv.h: will deliver Him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified. And on the third day He will be raised to life
b: Only Matthew’s account names crucifixion here. Roman flogging, with a whip of leather straps weighted with bone or metal, was so brutal that some victims died from it. Quarles notes that Psalm 22 and Isaiah 53 foretold the Messiah’s mockery and wounds, but neither named the third day. Jesus had linked his three days to Jonah (12:40), and many compare Hosea 6:2; Quarles holds that Jesus’ precise knowledge came from God.

Psalm 22 describes the righteous sufferer: ‘All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads’ (Psalm 22:7), and ‘they have pierced my hands and feet’ (22:16). Isaiah’s Servant says, ‘I offered My back to those who struck Me’ and ‘I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle’ (Isaiah 50:6).
Hebrews says Jesus ‘for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame’ (Hebrews 12:2). Peter writes that ‘When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate’ (1 Peter 2:23).

l.t: Mark: Jesus walked ahead of them; they were afraid.
Luke: they understood none of these things.
The flogging and mockery fulfilled.
Mocked, pierced; they divide my garments.
I gave my back to those who strike me.
He endured the cross, scorning its shame.

qs: What new details does Jesus give in this third prediction?
Why does it matter that Jesus went to Jerusalem knowing what would happen?
Why do you think the disciples still did not understand?

20.ctx: The mother of Zebedee’s sons was the mother of James and John, two of Jesus’ first disciples (4:21). She was among the women at the cross (27:56). In Mark, James and John make the request themselves (Mark 10:35–40). The right and left hands of a king were places of highest honour (1 Kings 2:19).
20.mean: Jesus has just told the Twelve, for the third time, that he is going to Jerusalem to be mocked, flogged and crucified. Immediately the mother of James and John comes with her sons, kneels before him and asks a favour: ‘Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left.’ The timing is painful. Jesus is heading for a cross; they are thinking about thrones. Jesus answers the sons directly: ‘You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?’ In the Old Testament the ‘cup’ is a picture of suffering, and especially of God’s judgement on sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus will pray in Gethsemane, ‘let this cup pass from Me’ (26:39). They answer at once, ‘We can.’ They have no idea what they are saying. Within days they will run away when Jesus is arrested (26:56). Yet Jesus tells them, ‘You will indeed drink My cup.’ They will share in his sufferings. James became the first apostle whose death for Christ is recorded (Acts 12:1–2), and early tradition says John was banished to the island of Patmos (compare Revelation 1:9). But the places at his right and left are not Jesus’ to grant; they belong to those for whom the Father has prepared them. This passage exposes a temptation that never goes away: to want to be important in God’s work, to use Christian things to get ahead, even to use family connections to win favour. Calvin said their ignorance was blameworthy because ‘their ambition led them to desire more than was proper’, and because they imagined ‘a phantom in the air’ instead of Christ’s heavenly kingdom. Yet Jesus is patient with them. He does not reject them; he redirects them. The way to share in his kingdom is to share in his cup, to follow him in suffering and service. The next verses spell this out.
20.big: Two disciples seek the highest places in Jesus’ kingdom; he asks whether they can drink his cup of suffering, and teaches that the Father assigns honour in his kingdom.

vv.h: the mother of Zebedee’s sons came to Jesus with her sons and knelt down to make a request
b: Quarles thinks the sons were the real authors of the request, since Jesus answers them and the other disciples are angry with them, not their mother (20:24). Wesley: ‘Considering what he had been just speaking, was ever any thing more unreasonable?’

vv.h: Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left
b: Wesley: ‘Still they expected a temporal kingdom.’ Jesus had promised the Twelve thrones (19:28); they wanted the two best. Quarles notes that in Daniel the Son of Man reigns beside the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9, 13–14), and that Psalm 110:1 places the Messiah at God’s right hand; the brothers did not understand how far above them Jesus’ throne would be.

vv.h: You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?
b: The cup is the cup of suffering and of God’s wrath against sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Some manuscripts add, ‘or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized’ (BSB footnote; compare Mark 10:38). Wesley: ‘All who share in my kingdom must first share in my sufferings.’ Calvin imagined Jesus saying, ‘Does your present warfare allow you so much leisure, that you are now making arrangements for a triumphal procession?’

vv.h: We can, the brothers answered
b: Their confidence was sincere but untested. Quarles notes that only days later ‘all the disciples deserted Him and fled’ (26:56). Peter would make the same kind of boast (26:33–35).

vv.h: You will indeed drink My cup … But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant
b: James was put to death by Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:1–2), and early tradition says John was banished to Patmos (compare Revelation 1:9). Calvin: ‘in the persons of two men, he addresses all his followers’: all are to be ‘conformed to the image of Christ’. Wesley insisted that Jesus ‘does not deny that this is his to give’; he gives it only to those for whom it is prepared. Calvin: ‘As to the degree in which some men rise above others, it is not our business to inquire’.

Jesus is the one who will sit at the Father’s right hand: ‘The LORD said to my Lord: “Sit at My right hand”’ (Psalm 110:1; Matthew 22:44; 26:64). The writer of Hebrews says he ‘sat down at the right hand of the throne of God’ after enduring the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

Many commentators see an irony here: on the day of his ‘enthronement’ at Golgotha, the places at Jesus’ right and left were taken by two robbers (27:38), though Quarles doubts the link. The way to glory runs through the cross, for him and for his followers (Romans 8:17).

l.t: Mark: James and John ask for themselves.
The cup of the LORD’s wrath.
Sit at my right hand.
Gethsemane: ‘let this cup pass from Me’.
Two robbers crucified, one on his right and one on his left.
James put to death with the sword.
Heirs with Christ if we share in his sufferings.

qs: Why is the timing of this request so striking?
What is the ‘cup’ that Jesus was going to drink?
In what ways are we tempted to seek importance or recognition in Christian life?

20.ctx: The other ten disciples are angry with James and John, probably because they wanted the top places themselves (compare Luke 22:24). This saying is one of the clearest statements in the Gospels of why Jesus came. Compare Mark 10:41–45 and Luke 22:24–27.
20.mean: When the other ten hear what James and John asked for, they are indignant. Their anger is not because they are humbler. They want the same thing. So Jesus calls them all together and teaches them about greatness. ‘You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them. It shall not be this way among you.’ The world’s idea of greatness is power over others: to give orders, to be served, to be on top. Jesus says his followers must turn that upside down. ‘Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave.’ The servant and the slave had no status at all. Yet Jesus says that is where real greatness lies: in serving others, putting their good before our own. Then he points to himself as the example and the reason. ‘Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.’ The Son of Man in Daniel’s vision was to be served by all peoples (Daniel 7:14). He has every right to be served. Yet he came to serve. And his service goes all the way to death. A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner. Jesus says his life is that price, paid ‘for many’, in their place. This echoes Isaiah’s Servant, who ‘bore the sin of many’ and would ‘justify many’ (Isaiah 53:11–12). Calvin wrote, ‘his life is the price of our redemption; whence it follows, that we obtain an undeserved reconciliation with God’. This is the heart of the gospel. We were captives to sin and death, unable to free ourselves. Jesus paid the price with his own life. Christians have discussed exactly what ‘for many’ means (see Where readings differ). But the call that flows from it is the same for all: if the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life, his followers cannot live to be served.
20.big: In Jesus’ kingdom greatness means serving others, because the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.

vv.h: When the ten heard about this, they were indignant with the two brothers
b: Quarles notes that the ten were driven by the same ambition; Luke records that a dispute about who was greatest broke out even at the Last Supper (Luke 22:24).

vv.h: the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them
b: Quarles notes that Jesus calls this pagan behaviour, like loving only those who love you (5:46–47). Wesley: ‘you imagine, the chief in my kingdom will do as they: but it will be quite otherwise.’

vv.h: whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave
b: ‘Servant’ (diakonos) is the word from which ‘deacon’ comes; ‘slave’ (doulos) is stronger still. Jesus does not forbid leadership in the church, but he redefines it as service. Peter later told elders to shepherd the flock ‘not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock’ (1 Peter 5:3).

vv.h: just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve
b: Calvin: Christ ‘voluntarily took upon himself the form of a servant’ (Philippians 2:7). At the Last Supper Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and said, ‘I have set you an example’ (John 13:15).

vv.h: and to give His life as a ransom for many
b: Quarles notes the echoes of Isaiah 53: the Servant gives his life (psychē) as a guilt offering and bears the sin of ‘many’ (Isaiah 53:10–12). A ransom (lytron) was the price of release. Calvin: ‘his life is the price of our redemption’, and the price ‘is to be found nowhere else than in the death of Christ.’ On ‘many’, see Where readings differ.

20.diff: A ransom ‘for many’. The traditions below all read this verse as a statement of Christ’s redeeming death in the place of others. They differ over ‘many’. Reformed theology (‘definite’ or ‘particular’ redemption) holds that Christ’s death is ‘abundantly sufficient to expiate the sins of the whole world’, but that God intended its saving power to ‘extend to all the elect’ (Canons of Dort II.3, 8). Calvin himself, commenting here, said ‘many’ is ‘not put definitely for a fixed number, but for a large number; for he contrasts himself with all others.’ (Calvin’s own view of the extent of the atonement is debated by his interpreters.) Arminian theology holds that ‘Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the world, died for all men and for every man’, though only believers receive forgiveness (Remonstrance, art. 2). Catholic teaching says ‘this last term is not restrictive’, and that ‘There is not, never has been, and never will be a single human being for whom Christ did not suffer’ (Catechism 605). See also the note on Mark 10:35.

b: The New Testament returns again and again to the ransom: Christ ‘gave Himself as a ransom for all’ (1 Timothy 2:6); ‘you were redeemed … with the precious blood of Christ’ (1 Peter 1:18–19). Paul says Christ, though in the form of God, ‘emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant’ (Philippians 2:7).

Isaiah’s fourth Servant Song (Isaiah 52:13–53:12) is the background: the Servant is ‘raised and lifted up and highly exalted’ (52:13) precisely because he ‘poured out His life unto death’ and ‘bore the sin of many’ (53:12).

l.t: Mark’s account of the saying.
Luke: I am among you as one who serves.
The Servant bears the sin of many.
Jesus washes the disciples’ feet.
Christ took the form of a servant.
Christ gave himself as a ransom for all.
Redeemed with the precious blood of Christ.

qs: How is Jesus’ idea of greatness different from the world’s?
What does it mean that Jesus gave his life ‘as a ransom’?
Where could you serve someone this week in a way that costs you something?

20.h: The Blind Men by the Road
20.ctx: Jericho lay about 15 miles east-north-east of Jerusalem (some 20 miles by road), near the Jordan, on the pilgrim road. Mark and Luke tell of one blind man, and Mark names him Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46–52; Luke 18:35–43). Luke places the healing as Jesus approached Jericho; Matthew and Mark as he left it.
20.mean: As Jesus leaves Jericho on the last stage of the road to Jerusalem, a large crowd follows him. Two blind men are sitting by the road. When they hear that Jesus is passing by, they cry out, ‘Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!’ The crowd tells them to be quiet. Perhaps they think Jesus has more important business in Jerusalem than two blind beggars. But the men shout all the louder: ‘Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!’ Jesus stops. He calls them and asks, ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ ‘Lord,’ they answer, ‘let our eyes be opened.’ Moved with compassion, Jesus touches their eyes, and at once they receive their sight and follow him. This healing comes straight after Jesus has said that he came not to be served but to serve (20:28). Here we see what that means. The crowd treats the blind men as an interruption; Jesus treats them as the reason he came. He stops the whole procession for them. Notice the question he asks: ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ It is almost the same question he asked the mother of James and John (20:21; in Mark 10:36 and 10:51 the words are identical). She asked for power and position; the blind men ask for mercy and sight. The contrast is deliberate. The blind men also see more clearly than many with eyes. They call Jesus ‘Lord’ and ‘Son of David’, the Messiah from David’s line. Their cry for mercy is the prayer of the Psalms, addressed there to God. Their request, ‘let our eyes be opened’, recalls Isaiah’s promise of what God would do when he came to save: ‘the eyes of the blind will be opened’ (Isaiah 35:5). The story ends with the best possible outcome: they ‘followed Him.’ They did not just receive a gift and go home. They became disciples, following Jesus on the road to Jerusalem and the cross. This is a picture of every true conversion: we cry out for mercy, Jesus opens our eyes, and we follow him.
20.big: Two blind men cry to Jesus, the Son of David, for mercy; he stops for them, opens their eyes in compassion, and they follow him.

vv.h: two blind men sitting beside the road. When they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, ‘Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!’
b: Wesley explained the difference from Mark and Luke: they ‘mention only one of them, blind Bartimeus. He was far the more eminent of the two, and, as it seems, spoke for both.’ Calvin: by calling him Son of David they ‘apply to Christ, not only as some Prophet, but as that person whom God had promised to be the only Author of salvation.’ See Where readings differ.

vv.h: The crowd admonished them to be silent, but they cried out all the louder
b: Quarles notes that in the Greek Old Testament ‘have mercy’ is almost always addressed to God, and that the men’s persistence is like the Canaanite woman’s (15:22–27). Wesley applied it: ‘so they will all who begin to cry after the Son of David. But let those who feel their need of him cry the more’.

vv.h: Jesus stopped and called them. ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’
b: The great procession halts for two beggars. Jesus asked James and John’s mother almost the same question in 20:21. The servant King puts himself at the disposal of the needy.

vv.h: Lord, … let our eyes be opened
b: Quarles hears an echo of Isaiah 35:5: ‘Then the eyes of the blind will be opened’, a promise of what God himself would do. Jesus had pointed to this sign when John the Baptist asked who he was (11:5).

vv.h: Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they received their sight and followed Him
b: Only Matthew says Jesus touched their eyes. ‘Followed Him’ is the language of discipleship (4:20; 9:9). Quarles notes they were physically blind but saw more clearly than the crowds who did not grasp who Jesus was.

20.diff: One blind man or two, leaving or entering? Matthew mentions two blind men; Mark and Luke mention one, and Luke says it happened as Jesus approached Jericho (Luke 18:35). Wesley suggested that Bartimaeus ‘spoke for both’, so the other Gospels mention only him. Calvin rejected the idea of separate healings, called the difference ‘a puzzling contradiction’, and offered a ‘conjecture’: the man called out as Jesus approached but was not heard ‘on account of the noise’, so he waited by the road as Jesus left. Another suggestion is that there were two Jerichos, the old site and Herod’s new town nearby, so Jesus could be leaving one and approaching the other. Ancient writers often varied such details in retelling the same event. See also the note on Mark 10:46.

b: The prophets promised that God would open blind eyes when he came to save (Isaiah 29:18; 35:5; 42:7). Jesus read Isaiah 61 in Nazareth, including ‘recovery of sight to the blind’ (Luke 4:18).

Physical blindness in the Gospels often pictures spiritual blindness. Jesus called the Pharisees ‘blind guides’ (15:14; 23:16), while John records a healed man saying, ‘I was blind, but now I see!’ (John 9:25). Paul says God has shone in our hearts ‘to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ’ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

l.t: Mark: blind Bartimaeus.
Luke: as Jesus approached Jericho.
Two blind men healed earlier: ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David!’
The eyes of the blind will be opened.
Almost the same question: ‘What do you want?’
I was blind, but now I see.
God shines in our hearts the light of Christ’s glory.

qs: Why did the crowd try to silence the blind men, and why did Jesus stop?
Compare the blind men’s request with that of James and John’s mother. What do you notice?
What would you say if Jesus asked you, ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’

21.ctx: Jesus arrives at Jerusalem for the Passover, the last week of his life. Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just east of the city; its exact site is uncertain. Thousands of pilgrims, many from Galilee, would be on the road. Compare Mark 11:1–11, Luke 19:28–40 and John 12:12–19.
21.mean: After months on the road, Jesus reaches the edge of Jerusalem. He sends two disciples into a village to bring a donkey and her colt, telling them exactly what they will find and what to say: ‘the Lord needs them.’ Matthew explains why. The prophet had said, ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’ Jesus is acting out Zechariah’s prophecy on purpose. Until now he has often told people to keep quiet about who he is. Now, days before his death, he openly claims to be Israel’s King. But look at the kind of king he is. Conquerors rode war-horses. Jesus comes on a borrowed donkey, with his friends’ cloaks for a saddle. The crowd catches the meaning. They spread their cloaks on the road, as Israel once did for a new king (2 Kings 9:13), cut branches, and shout words from Psalm 118: ‘Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!’ ‘Hosanna’ meant ‘Save, we pray’ and had become a shout of praise (BSB footnote). As Jesus enters the city, ‘the whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?”’ The crowds answer, ‘This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.’ That is true, but it is not the whole truth. Within a week, a crowd in the same city will shout, ‘Crucify Him!’ (27:22). Wesley drew the lesson: the King’s humble entry is ‘for the honour of his humility, and for the utter confusion of all worldly pomp and grandeur.’ Jesus is a real King, with a real claim on our lives. But his kingdom does not come by force. It comes through a gentle King who rides to Jerusalem to die. The question the city asked is the question everyone must answer: ‘Who is this?’
21.big: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the gentle King of Zechariah’s prophecy, openly claiming his throne, though the city does not yet know who he is.

vv.h: Go into the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied there, with her colt beside her
b: Bethphage was on the Mount of Olives (BSB), within a short walk of Jerusalem. Quarles thinks Jesus’ exact knowledge of the animals and their owner’s reply is more likely supernatural than a prior arrangement, though either is possible. Calvin: Jesus did not send for the animals because he was tired, but ‘to show, by a solemn performance, what was the nature of his kingdom.’

vv.h: See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey
b: Matthew joins Isaiah 62:11 (‘Say to Daughter Zion’) to Zechariah 9:9 (BSB footnote), as Wesley and Quarles note. He leaves out Zechariah’s words ‘righteous and victorious’ and keeps ‘gentle’: Calvin noted that Matthew took the part that showed Christ would be ‘unlike earthly kings’. Wesley: ‘The Prince of Peace did not take a horse, a warlike animal. But he will ride on that by and by’ (Revelation 19:11). Quarles notes that the King of Zion in the prophets is often the LORD himself (Zechariah 14:9).

vv.h: They brought the donkey and the colt and laid their cloaks on them, and Jesus sat on them
b: Quarles takes ‘on them’ to mean on the cloaks. Mark, Luke and John mention only the colt Jesus rode. Calvin held that ‘the colt only was used by Christ’. Quarles notes R. T. France’s suggestion that the mother came too, which would calm a colt that had never been ridden (Mark 11:2). See Where readings differ.

vv.h: A massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees
b: Wesley: ‘A custom which was usual at the creation of a king, 2 Kings ix, 13.’ John says the branches were from palm trees (John 12:13), which is why Christians call the day Palm Sunday.

vv.h: Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!
b: The words come from Psalm 118:25–26 (BSB footnotes), part of the psalms sung at the great feasts. Calvin: the crowd followed ‘the form of prayer, which the Holy Spirit had prescribed to the whole Church by the mouth of the Prophet.’ Wesley noted the contrast with the cry of ‘Crucify him’ a few days later.

vv.h: the whole city was stirred and asked, ‘Who is this?’
b: The word for ‘stirred’ is the one Matthew uses for the earth shaking at Jesus’ death (27:51). The pilgrims call him ‘the prophet’, perhaps thinking of the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). Wesley: some would stumble at ‘Nazareth’, but anyone who inquired ‘would find, he was not of Nazareth, but Bethlehem’ (2:1–6).

21.diff: One animal or two? Only Matthew mentions both a donkey and her colt. Some modern scholars (Quarles notes this view) think Matthew misread the Hebrew poetry of Zechariah 9:9, which says the same thing twice (‘on a donkey, on a colt’), as describing two animals. Others reply that Matthew, a Jew, knew Hebrew poetry well and was simply reporting that the colt’s mother came too; Quarles takes this view. Calvin thought Matthew spoke loosely, mentioning ‘two instead of one’, and that ‘the colt only was used by Christ’, as the other Gospels say. Most readers agree that Jesus rode the young colt, as Zechariah foretold, though Calvin admitted that ‘Matthew appears to say that he rode on both of them’.

b: Quarles notes that Zechariah’s prophecy echoes Jacob’s blessing on Judah, from whose line the ruler would come: ‘He ties his donkey to the vine, his colt to the choicest branch’ (Genesis 49:11). The King who comes on a donkey is the promised ruler from Judah.

Zechariah goes on: God will ‘cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem’, and the King will ‘proclaim peace to the nations’ (Zechariah 9:10). Jesus’ gentle entry is a sign of the peace his kingdom brings. John adds that the disciples understood all this only ‘after Jesus was glorified’ (John 12:16).

l.t: Mark’s account of the entry.
Palm branches; the disciples understood later.
Your King comes, humble and riding on a donkey.
Say to Daughter Zion: See, your Savior comes!
Save us, we pray; blessed is he who comes.
Judah’s ruler ties his donkey to the vine.
Garments spread for a new king.

qs: Why do you think Jesus, who had often avoided publicity, now made such a public entry?
What does the donkey tell us about the kind of King Jesus is?
The city asked, ‘Who is this?’ How would you answer that question for someone today?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 21:1–9 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 21

21.ctx: The temple courts were packed before Passover. Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice and had to pay the temple tax in an approved coin, so traders and money changers set up in the outer court, the only part Gentiles could enter. Compare Mark 11:15–19, Luke 19:45–48 and John 2:13–22.
21.mean: Jesus goes straight to the temple. He drives out all who are buying and selling, and overturns the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. Doves were the sacrifice of the poor (Leviticus 5:7). Then he explains himself from Scripture: ‘It is written: “My house will be called a house of prayer.” But you are making it “a den of robbers.”’ The first words come from Isaiah 56:7. The second come from Jeremiah 7:11, where God warned people who did wrong all week and then ran to the temple as if it made them safe. A den is where robbers hide after a crime. The temple had become a hiding place for people who used religion for gain. This is an act of authority. Malachi had promised, ‘the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple’ (Malachi 3:1). Now he has come, and he is cleaning his house. But the scene does not end with anger. ‘The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them.’ The same hands that overturned tables now heal. Then children start shouting, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ The chief priests and scribes are indignant. ‘Do You hear what these children are saying?’ ‘Yes,’ Jesus answers, and quotes Psalm 8: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise.’ In the psalm, that praise is given to God. Jesus accepts it for himself. The religious leaders see wonders and hear praise, and are only angry. The children see the same things and worship. This passage asks hard questions of any church. Is our worship a place of prayer, or a place where we hide? Do we make room for the poor, the blind, the lame and the children? Jesus still comes to his house. He clears out what offends him, and he heals those who come to him in need.
21.big: Jesus comes to the temple as its Lord, clearing out those who used it for gain and healing the needy, while children praise him and the leaders seethe.

vv.h: He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves
b: Wesley placed the trading in ‘the outer court of it, where the Gentiles used to worship.’ Quarles notes that the temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian silver coins because of their high silver content, so the money changers took a fee, and that some rabbis complained about the price of doves. Calvin: by this act Jesus showed himself ‘both King and High Priest’.

vv.h: My house will be called a house of prayer. But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’
b: Mark’s version includes Isaiah’s words ‘for all the nations’ (Mark 11:17); Matthew’s does not. Quarles takes this to mean that Matthew’s focus is on greed rather than the shutting out of Gentiles, though many commentators stress both. Calvin on Jeremiah 7:11: the prophet ‘exclaims that God is not bound to the temple, or tied to ceremonies’.

vv.h: The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them
b: Only Matthew records these healings in the temple. Quarles sees Isaiah’s promise being fulfilled: ‘Then the eyes of the blind will be opened … Then the lame will leap like a deer’ (Isaiah 35:5–6).

vv.h: From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise
b: Jesus quotes Psalm 8:2 in its Greek form (BSB footnote ‘see also LXX’); the Hebrew has ‘strength’ (the BSB’s Psalm 8:2 also follows the Greek, with ‘strength’ in its footnote). Quarles notes that the psalm praises the LORD, so Jesus is accepting praise due to God. Calvin: ‘God needs no other orators to proclaim his power than mere infants’.

vv.h: He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night
b: Bethany, the home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus (John 11:1), was on the far side of the Mount of Olives. Jesus seems to have spent each night of this week outside the city (compare Luke 21:37).

21.diff: Once or twice? Matthew, Mark and Luke place a temple cleansing in Jesus’ last week; John places one at the start of his ministry (John 2:13–22). Calvin and Wesley held that there were two: Wesley wrote that Jesus ‘had cast them out three years before’ and, ‘Upon the repetition of the offense, he used sharper words.’ Most modern scholars think there was one cleansing, and that John placed it early for theological reasons; many evangelical scholars, with Calvin and Wesley, hold that there were two. Both views are held by scholars who accept the accuracy of the Gospels. See also the notes on Mark 11:15 and John 2:12.

b: Quarles connects the scene with Zechariah’s picture of the coming day of the LORD: ‘there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Hosts’ (Zechariah 14:21; ‘Canaanite’ can also mean ‘trader’). Malachi asked, ‘who can endure the day of His coming?’ (Malachi 3:2).

The cleansing points beyond itself. Jesus will soon speak of the temple’s destruction (24:1–2), and in John he says his own body is the true temple (John 2:19–21). Paul calls the church, and each believer, God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19).

l.t: ‘A house of prayer for all the nations.’
John’s account of a cleansing; ‘Zeal for Your house will consume Me.’
A house of prayer for all the nations.
Has this house become a den of robbers?
From the mouths of children and infants.
The Lord will suddenly come to His temple.
No longer a Canaanite in the house of the LORD.

qs: What made Jesus so angry in the temple? What might make him angry in churches today?
Why do you think Matthew puts the overturned tables and the healing of the blind and lame side by side?
The children praised Jesus while the experts complained. What can we learn from the children here?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 21:10–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 21

21.ctx: Fig trees in Israel put out leaves in spring, and small early figs often appear with the leaves. Mark says it was ‘not the season for figs’ (Mark 11:13). The prophets sometimes pictured Israel as a fig tree or vine that God searched for fruit (Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1). Compare Mark 11:12–14, 20–25.
21.mean: Early in the morning, on his way back into the city, Jesus is hungry. He sees a fig tree by the road, in full leaf, and goes to look for fruit. There is nothing but leaves. ‘May you never bear fruit again!’ he says, and the tree withers at once. This can seem strange, even unfair. Why curse a tree? The answer is that this is an acted parable, like the signs the prophets performed. Jesus has just come from the temple, which looked full of life but bore no fruit for God. The fig tree, with its fine leaves and empty branches, is a picture of that. Jeremiah had used the same picture: ‘There will be no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the tree, and even the leaf will wither’ (Jeremiah 8:13). Calvin insisted that ‘it was not the fury of passion that led him to curse the tree’; it was ‘an outward sign of the end which awaits hypocrites’. It is a rare miracle of judgement, and it falls on a tree, not on a person. It is a warning given while there is still time. The disciples are amazed: ‘How did the fig tree wither so quickly?’ Jesus turns their amazement into a lesson on faith. ‘If you have faith and do not doubt’, he says, they could even tell ‘this mountain’ to be thrown into the sea, and it would happen. ‘If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer.’ This is not a blank cheque for anything we want. Jesus is speaking of faith in God, and of prayer that seeks God’s kingdom. The fig tree warns us against religion that is all leaves and no fruit. The promise invites us to trust God completely. A life rooted in faith and prayer is the opposite of a withered tree.
21.big: The withered fig tree is a living parable of judgement on showy but fruitless religion, and Jesus turns it into a call to faith-filled prayer.

vv.h: Seeing a fig tree by the road, He went up to it but found nothing on it except leaves
b: Calvin took the hunger as real: ‘Christ did not pretend hunger, but was actually hungry.’ Leaves on a fig tree normally promised early fruit, so the tree ‘advertised’ what it did not have. Quarles notes the link with Jesus’ earlier warnings that a tree is known by its fruit (7:16–20; 3:10).

vv.h: ‘May you never bear fruit again!’ He said. And immediately the tree withered
b: Mark tells the story in two parts, with the withering noticed the next morning (Mark 11:14, 20). Calvin: ‘It appears more clearly from Mark, that the fig-tree did not instantly wither, or, at least, that it was not observed by his disciples, until they saw it next day’. Wesley: the miracle was meant ‘to confirm and increase their faith’ and ‘to warn them against unfruitfulness.’

vv.h: How did the fig tree wither so quickly?
b: Quarles reads this as an exclamation of amazement rather than a request for a scientific explanation. Mark has Peter speak for the group (Mark 11:21).

vv.h: even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen
b: Moving mountains was a figure of speech for doing the impossible (compare 17:20). Quarles notes that ‘this mountain’ could also point to the Mount of Olives (compare Zechariah 14:4) or to the temple mount, whose system Jesus had just judged.

vv.h: If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer
b: Calvin: ‘Christ does not give a loose rein to the wishes of men’; prayer is placed ‘after the rule of faith’, held by ‘the bridle of the word of God’. John writes: ‘If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us’ (1 John 5:14).

21.diff: ‘Whatever you ask’. Some teachers (the ‘word of faith’ or prosperity movement) take promises like this as a guarantee that anything asked with enough faith will be given. Most Christians of every tradition read it within the rest of Scripture: faith rests on God, not on the strength of our believing, and prayer is shaped by ‘not as I will, but as You will’ (26:39) and by asking ‘according to His will’ (1 John 5:14). Calvin said prayer must be ruled by faith and by God’s word. See also the note on Mark 11:20.

b: The prophets pictured God searching his people for fruit and finding none: ‘no early fig that I crave’ (Micah 7:1); ‘I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. I saw your fathers as the firstfruits of the fig tree’ (Hosea 9:10). Luke records a parable of a fig tree given one more year to bear fruit (Luke 13:6–9).

Jesus later uses the fig tree in a hopeful way: when its branches become tender and its leaves come out, ‘you know that summer is near’ (24:32). James urges anyone who asks God for wisdom to ‘ask in faith, without doubting’ (James 1:6).

l.t: Mark’s account, with the lesson on forgiveness in prayer.
No figs on the tree; even the leaf will wither.
No early fig that I crave.
The parable of the barren fig tree.
Faith like a mustard seed moves mountains.
Asking according to God’s will.

qs: Why might Jesus have chosen a fig tree to make his point about the temple?
What would ‘all leaves and no fruit’ look like in a Christian’s life today?
How do we hold together the bold promise of verse 22 and praying ‘Your will be done’?
