Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 21:10–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 21

21.ctx: The chief priests and elders were leaders of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council in Jerusalem, and had charge of the temple. ‘These things’ means the cleansing of the temple and Jesus’ teaching there. Compare Mark 11:27–33 and Luke 20:1–8.
21.mean: The day after the cleansing, Jesus is back in the temple courts, teaching. The chief priests and elders come to him with a sharp question: ‘By what authority are You doing these things? And who gave You this authority?’ They have a point, from their side. The temple was under their control. Jesus held no office, had trained under no famous rabbi, and had just overturned their trade. Who did he think he was? Jesus answers with a question of his own. ‘What was the source of John’s baptism? Was it from heaven or from men?’ This is not a dodge. John had pointed to Jesus as the one coming after him (3:11). If John was sent by God, then his witness to Jesus was true, and Jesus’ authority comes from the same place. The leaders huddle together. If they say ‘from heaven’, Jesus will ask why they did not believe John. If they say ‘from men’, they fear the crowd, who all regard John as a prophet. So they say, ‘We do not know.’ It is a revealing answer. These men were meant to be the spiritual guides of Israel, able to tell a true prophet from a false one. Yet on the most important question of their day they claim to have no opinion. They were not really asking for the truth; they were protecting their position. Jesus replies, ‘Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.’ He will not argue with people who have already decided not to listen. But the parables that follow make his answer plain enough. This passage warns us how easy it is to dodge the truth when it is costly. Wesley noted that Jesus had ‘often told them before, and they would not believe him.’ The question for us is not whether we have enough information, but whether we are willing to follow where it leads.
21.big: When the leaders question Jesus’ authority, his question about John exposes that they are not seeking truth but protecting their position.

vv.h: By what authority are You doing these things? And who gave You this authority?
b: Wesley: the leaders came in ‘a considerable company, to give the more weight to what they said’, and thought Jesus had no right to teach, ‘being neither priest, nor Levite, nor scribe.’ Matthew has already noted that Jesus taught ‘as one who had authority, and not as their scribes’ (7:29).

vv.h: What was the source of John’s baptism? Was it from heaven or from men?
b: Wesley: ‘By what authority did he act and teach? Did man or God give him that authority? Was it not God? But if so, the consequence was clear. For John testified that Jesus was the Christ.’ Calvin: ‘Christ employed no cunning stratagem in order to escape, but fully and perfectly answered the question … for it was impossible to acknowledge that John was a servant of God, without acknowledging that he was Himself the Lord.’

vv.h: we are afraid of the people, for they all regard John as a prophet
b: Luke says they feared being stoned (Luke 20:6). Josephus records that some Jews saw a later defeat of Herod’s army as God’s punishment for killing John (Antiquities 18.116–119).

vv.h: We do not know … Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things
b: Wesley: ‘Not again, in express terms: he had often told them before, and they would not believe him.’ Calvin: ‘all wicked men, though they pretend to be desirous of learning, shut the gate of truth, if they feel it to be opposed to their wicked desires.’

Quarles notes that Malachi had promised a messenger to prepare the way before the Lord came to his temple (Malachi 3:1), and Elijah before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5–6). Jesus has already said John is that messenger (11:10, 14). If the leaders had accepted John, they would have known who had just come to the temple.

The question of Jesus’ authority runs through Matthew, from the Sermon on the Mount (7:29) to the healing of the paralysed man (9:6–8) to the last scene: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me’ (28:18).

l.t: Mark’s account.
‘All the people will stone us.’
John points to the one coming after him.
He taught as one who had authority.
My messenger will prepare the way before Me.
All authority in heaven and on earth.

qs: Why did the leaders answer ‘We do not know’? What were they really afraid of?
In what ways do people today avoid questions about Jesus because the answer would be costly?
What would it look like to accept Jesus’ authority in an area of your life this week?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 21:23–27 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 21
Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119 (Whiston): John the Baptist

21.h: The Parable of the Two Sons
21.ctx: Jesus is still answering the chief priests and elders who questioned his authority (21:23). This parable is found only in Matthew. A vineyard was a familiar picture of Israel and its life before God (Isaiah 5:1–7).
21.mean: ‘But what do you think?’ Jesus asks the leaders, and tells a short story. A man has two sons. He tells the first, ‘Son, go and work today in the vineyard.’ The son says, ‘I will not.’ But later he changes his mind and goes. The father says the same to the second son, who answers politely, ‘I will, sir.’ But he does not go. ‘Which of the two did the will of his father?’ The answer is obvious: ‘The first.’ Then Jesus springs the trap. ‘Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you.’ These were the people the leaders despised most. Tax collectors worked for Rome and were known for cheating. Prostitutes were outcasts. Like the first son, they had said ‘no’ to God with their lives. But when John the Baptist came preaching repentance, they believed him and changed. The religious leaders were like the second son. They said all the right things. They spoke of God, kept the rules, and looked obedient. But when God sent John ‘in the way of righteousness’, they did not believe him. And even when they saw sinners transformed, ‘you did not repent and believe him.’ Wesley put it sharply: theirs ‘was bare profession, contradicted by all their actions.’ Calvin added that Jesus ‘does not excuse their vices’ of the tax collectors and prostitutes, but shows that they did not stay in them. Neither son was ideal. The best son would say ‘yes’ and go. But the parable makes one thing very clear: God is not impressed by words alone. What matters is what we do. A late repentance is better than a polite refusal. The door into the kingdom is open to the worst of sinners who turn back to God, and it can be closed by our own pride. The parable asks each of us: which son am I?
21.big: Doing the Father’s will matters more than saying the right words; repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of religious people who never repent.

vv.h: There was a man who had two sons. He went to the first one and said, ‘Son, go and work today in the vineyard.’
b: Quarles notes that the Greek word here is ‘child’ (teknon). The father is God; the work is obedience to his will.

vv.h: ‘I will not,’ he replied. But later he changed his mind and went
b: The word for ‘changed his mind’ is used again in verse 32 for what the leaders failed to do. Some editions read simply ‘But he went’ (BSB footnote).

vv.h: ‘I will, sir,’ he said. But he did not go
b: Calvin: ‘Christ does not here give the commendation to slowness’; both delay and empty promises are wrong, but ‘this hypocrisy is less to be endured than the fierceness which, in process of time, is subdued.’ Compare 7:21: ‘Not everyone who says to Me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom’.

vv.h: the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you
b: Some manuscripts, followed by the NE and WH editions (BSB footnote), tell the story with the sons in the opposite order, so that the answer becomes ‘The latter’; the meaning is the same. Quarles thinks ‘before you’ suggests that most of these leaders will never enter, though Acts records that ‘a great number of priests became obedient to the faith’ (Acts 6:7).

vv.h: For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes did
b: Wesley: John came ‘Walking in it, as well as teaching it.’ Luke records that ‘Even tax collectors came to be baptized’ (Luke 3:12). Calvin: ‘As John was a faithful servant of God, whatever he taught Christ ascribes to God himself.’

Luke records the same contrast: the people and tax collectors who had been baptized by John ‘acknowledged God’s justice’, while the Pharisees and experts in the law ‘rejected God’s purpose for themselves’ (Luke 7:29–30). The parable of the prodigal son tells of a son who said no and came home, and an elder brother who stayed and grumbled (Luke 15:11–32).

Quarles notes that the Law described the stubborn, rebellious son (Deuteronomy 21:18–21), and Isaiah began with God’s complaint: ‘I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me’ (Isaiah 1:2).

l.t: Tax collectors accepted John; the Pharisees rejected God’s purpose.
Not everyone who says ‘Lord, Lord’.
The lost son and the elder brother.
Tax collectors come to John asking what to do.
I raised children, but they rebelled.
Faith shown by what we do.

qs: Which son do you find it easier to be like, and why?
Why do you think the ‘worst’ people believed John while the religious leaders did not?
Is there an area where you have said ‘I will, sir’ to God but not gone?

src.l: Charles L. Quarles, Matthew, Evangelical Biblical Theology Commentary (Lexham Academic), via Logos
Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 21:28–32 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Matthew 21

21.h: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
21.ctx: Jesus is still speaking to the chief priests and elders (21:23, 45). His opening words echo Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where ‘the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel’ (Isaiah 5:7). Compare Mark 12:1–12 and Luke 20:9–19.
21.mean: ‘Listen to another parable.’ A landowner plants a vineyard, builds a wall, a winepress and a tower, rents it to tenants and goes away. At harvest he sends servants to collect his share. The tenants beat one, kill another and stone a third. He sends more servants, and they are treated the same way. ‘Finally, he sent his son to them. “They will respect my son,” he said.’ But the tenants say, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance.’ So they throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. Jesus’ hearers knew Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, so the meaning was clear. The landowner is God. The servants are the prophets, rejected again and again. The son is Jesus himself, and he is telling them what they are about to do to him. ‘What will he do to those tenants?’ Jesus asks. They answer, ‘He will bring those wretches to a wretched end’. They have passed sentence on themselves, as David once did when Nathan told him a story (2 Samuel 12). Jesus then quotes Psalm 118: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.’ The leaders will reject him, but God will raise him up as the cornerstone of a new temple. ‘Therefore I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit.’ The leaders realise he is talking about them, and want to arrest him, but fear the crowds. This parable shows God’s astonishing patience: servant after servant, and finally his own Son. It shows the depth of human rebellion. And it shows God’s victory: the rejected Son becomes the cornerstone. Calvin warned that this was ‘written for the sake of all of us’: no people or church owns the kingdom by right. God looks for fruit.
21.big: Jesus tells the leaders, in a parable, that they are about to kill God’s Son as their fathers killed the prophets, but the rejected stone will become the cornerstone.

vv.h: There was a landowner who planted a vineyard. He put a wall around it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower
b: Quarles notes that each of these details comes from Isaiah 5:1–2. Wesley: ‘God planted the Church in Canaan; and hedged it round about - First with the law, then with his peculiar providence’; the tower is ‘The temple’.

vv.h: They beat one, killed another, and stoned a third
b: Wesley: the servants are ‘His extraordinary messengers, the prophets’ and the tenants ‘The ordinary preachers or ministers of the Jews.’ Jeremiah was beaten (Jeremiah 20:2) and Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned (2 Chronicles 24:21). Jesus will return to this theme in 23:34–37.

vv.h: This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance
b: Jesus speaks of himself as the Son, distinct from all the servants before him. ‘Threw him out of the vineyard and killed him’ may hint that Jesus would die outside the city (compare Hebrews 13:12). Calvin: ‘now they are ready to slay his Son; but they will not go unpunished’.

vv.h: He will bring those wretches to a wretched end
b: The Greek has a play on words, ‘bad men badly’. Wesley thought the reply may have come from bystanders, since he took the leaders to be the ones who said ‘God forbid’ (Luke 20:16; BSB ‘May such a thing never happen!’).

vv.h: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone
b: Psalm 118:22–23 (BSB footnote), from the same psalm the crowds sang in 21:9. Quarles notes a possible wordplay in Hebrew between ‘stone’ (eben) and ‘son’ (ben). Peter later preached this verse to the same council (Acts 4:11). Wesley: Christ is the cornerstone ‘for uniting the Gentiles’ to the church.

vv.h: the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit
b: Calvin: ‘God was not bound to them’, but this ‘was written for the sake of all of us, that, if God choose us to be His people, we may not grow wanton through a vain and wicked confidence in the flesh’ (compare Romans 11:21). Quarles reads ‘a people’ as the community of those who repent and follow Jesus, Jew and Gentile together, rather than simply ‘the Gentiles’. See Where readings differ.

vv.h: He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed
b: Some early manuscripts do not include this verse (BSB footnote; compare Luke 20:18). It joins Isaiah’s stone of stumbling (Isaiah 8:14–15) to Daniel’s stone that crushes the kingdoms (Daniel 2:34–35, 44). Wesley: ‘He is said to fall on this stone, who hears the Gospel and does not believe.’

vv.h: they knew that Jesus was speaking about them
b: Calvin: God’s word is ‘a hot iron to wound bad consciences’. The leaders’ fear of the crowd, who ‘regarded Him as a prophet’, holds them back for now (compare 26:3–5).

21.diff: ‘Taken away from you’. Readers differ on whom Jesus means. Many modern commentators stress that he is speaking to the leaders, who ‘knew that Jesus was speaking about them’ (21:45). Calvin took ‘you’ to include the Jewish nation of that day (‘God was not bound to them’), and then applied the warning to Christians: ‘if he spared not the natural branches … what will he do with those which were engrafted?’ Wesley took ‘the kingdom of God’ to mean ‘the Gospel’. Quarles reads ‘a people who will produce its fruit’ not as Jews replaced by Gentiles, but as the community of all who repent and follow Jesus, Jew and Gentile together. Christians have sometimes misused texts like this to condemn the Jewish people as a whole, with terrible consequences. The Catholic Catechism, quoting the Second Vatican Council, teaches that ‘the Jews should not be spoken of as rejected or accursed as if this followed from holy Scripture’ (597), and that to the Jews belong the covenants and promises, ‘for the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable’ (839, quoting Romans 11:29). Christians also read Romans 11:26 (‘all Israel will be saved’) differently. Many look for a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ, while Calvin wrote, ‘I extend the word Israel to all the people of God.’

b: Isaiah’s song ends: ‘He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress’ (Isaiah 5:7). Jesus’ parable takes up the story: God looked for fruit, sent his servants, and finally his Son.

The rejected stone became the foundation of a new temple made of people: ‘you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house’ (1 Peter 2:5). Paul warns Gentile believers, ‘Do not be arrogant, but be afraid. For if God did not spare the natural branches, He will certainly not spare you either’ (Romans 11:20–21).

l.t: Mark’s account: a beloved son.
‘May such a thing never happen!’
The song of the vineyard.
The stone the builders rejected.
A stone of stumbling.
The stone that crushes the kingdoms.
Peter: ‘the stone you builders rejected’.
Natural and grafted branches; the gifts of God irrevocable.

qs: What does this parable show about God’s patience?
How does Jesus see his own death in this story? What does that tell us about him?
Calvin said this warning was written for all of us. What fruit is God looking for in our church?

22.ctx: This is the third parable Jesus tells the chief priests and Pharisees in the temple (21:28, 33, 45). The prophets pictured the age to come as a great feast prepared by God (Isaiah 25:6–8), and Jesus has spoken of many coming ‘to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’ (8:11). Luke records a similar parable (Luke 14:15–24).
22.mean: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding banquet for his son.’ In that world, guests were invited in advance and then called when the feast was ready. The king sends his servants to call the guests, ‘but they refused to come.’ He sends more servants with a warm appeal: the meat is ready, ‘everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.’ But the guests pay no attention. One goes to his field, another to his business. The rest seize the servants, mistreat them and kill them. The king is enraged. He sends his troops to destroy the murderers and burn their city. Then he tells his servants to go to the crossroads and invite everyone they find. They gather ‘both evil and good’, and the hall is filled. The meaning follows on from the last parable. The king is God, the son is Jesus, and the feast is the joy of his kingdom. The first guests are those in Israel who had long been invited through the prophets but refused when the moment came. The new guests are everyone else, the people no one expected to see at a royal wedding. Then comes a twist. The king comes in to see his guests and finds a man without wedding clothes. ‘Friend,’ he asks, ‘how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ The man is speechless. He is thrown out into the darkness. ‘For many are called, but few are chosen.’ The invitation is free and wide; no one earned a place at the table. But coming in does not mean we can stay as we are. The guest who would not put on wedding clothes despised the king as much as those who stayed away. Calvin drew the lesson: ‘Let us not flatter ourselves with the empty title of faith’. God’s grace welcomes us as we are, and then clothes us for the feast. We are invited to come, and to come ready to be changed.
22.big: God’s invitation to his Son’s wedding feast goes out to all, good and bad, but those who come must be clothed for it; many are called, but few are chosen.

vv.h: a king who prepared a wedding banquet for his son. He sent his servants to call those he had invited
b: Quarles notes that Jesus has already called himself the bridegroom (9:15) and will do so again (25:1–10). The guests had been invited earlier and were now being called; Calvin saw in this the ‘double favor’ Israel had received, chosen first and then called by the prophets.

vv.h: ‘everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.’ But they paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business
b: Wesley: ‘One must mind what he has; another, gain what he wants. How many perish by misusing lawful things!’ Farms and business are not wrong in themselves; they become wrong when they keep us from God’s call.

vv.h: he sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city
b: Many readers, Wesley among them, see a pointer to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70: ‘The Roman armies employed of God for that purpose.’ Quarles notes that in Isaiah God also used a foreign army as the rod of his anger (Isaiah 10:5–6).

vv.h: the servants went out into the streets and gathered everyone they could find, both evil and good
b: Wesley: they gathered ‘By preaching everwhere’ [sic]. ‘Both evil and good’ recalls God’s kindness to ‘the evil and the good’ (5:45). Quarles notes that Wisdom also calls out ‘at the city gates’ (Proverbs 1:21).

vv.h: ‘Friend,’ he asked, ‘how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ But the man was speechless
b: ‘Friend’ is the cool address Matthew also uses in 20:13 and 26:50. The man has no excuse. Calvin answered the objection that a poor man could not afford fine clothes: ‘whomsoever the Lord invites he at the same time supplies with clothing’. See Where readings differ.

vv.h: throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth
b: The same picture of final judgement as in 8:12 and 25:30. Calvin: ‘not all who have once entered the Church will become partakers of everlasting life’.

vv.h: For many are called, but few are chosen
b: Wesley: ‘Many hear; few believe. Yea, many are members of the visible, but few of the invisible Church.’ Calvin warned against trying ‘an ingenious explanation of every minute clause’, and said that here he would ‘enter no farther … into the question about the eternal election of God’.

22.diff: The wedding clothes. Wesley: ‘The righteousness of Christ, first imputed, then implanted.’ Quarles reads them as the clean life that comes from repentance, pointing to the bride’s ‘fine linen’, ‘the righteous acts of the saints’ (Revelation 19:8), and to ‘clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). Calvin called the choice between faith and a holy life ‘a useless controversy; for faith cannot be separated from good works, nor do good works proceed from any other source than from faith.’ ‘Few are chosen’. Reformed theology distinguishes the outward call of the gospel, which many hear, from God’s effectual calling of the elect: the Canons of Dort say that ‘As many as are called by the gospel are unfeignedly called’, but that those who obey owe it ‘wholly’ to God (Third and Fourth Heads, arts. 8, 10). Wesleyan readers take ‘chosen’ to mean those who accept the call: ‘Many hear; few believe.’ One parable or two? Calvin treated this and Luke 14:15–24 as the same parable; Quarles thinks the differences show they are two.

b: Isaiah promised that ‘the LORD of Hosts will prepare a lavish banquet for all the peoples’ and ‘swallow up death forever’ (Isaiah 25:6, 8). Revelation sees it fulfilled: ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb’ (Revelation 19:9).

Paul uses the picture of clothing for what Christ gives: ‘all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ’ (Galatians 3:27). Calvin pointed to Ezekiel 16, where God finds his people naked and clothes them in fine garments (Ezekiel 16:8–14).

l.t: The parable of the great banquet.
The LORD’s banquet for all peoples.
Many will come from east and west to the banquet.
The bridegroom comes; the door is shut.
The marriage supper of the Lamb; fine linen.
God clothes his people in fine garments.
Clothed with Christ.

qs: What reasons do people give today for turning down God’s invitation?
Why do you think Jesus added the story of the man without wedding clothes?
How does this parable hold together the free welcome of grace and the call to be changed?

22.ctx: Judea had been under direct Roman rule since AD 6, when a census for taxation provoked a revolt (compare Acts 5:37). The poll tax was a hated sign of foreign rule. The Herodians supported the family of Herod, who ruled under Rome, so they and the Pharisees made strange allies. Compare Mark 12:13–17 and Luke 20:20–26.
22.mean: The Pharisees plot to trap Jesus. They send their students along with some Herodians, and start with flattery: ‘Teacher, we know that You are honest and that You teach the way of God in accordance with the truth.’ Then they spring the question: ‘Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?’ It is a perfect trap. Wesley explained: if Jesus says yes, the Pharisees can accuse him to the people as a traitor to his nation; if he says no, the Herodians can report him to the Roman governor as a rebel. Jesus sees through it at once. ‘You hypocrites, why are you testing Me? Show Me the coin used for the tax.’ They bring a denarius. Notice that Jesus does not seem to carry one, but they do. ‘Whose image is this, and whose inscription?’ ‘Caesar’s,’ they answer. ‘Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.’ They are amazed, and go away. The answer has two halves. The first is simple. The coin bears Caesar’s image. It is his; give it back. Governments have a real, God-given authority, and paying taxes is part of our duty (Romans 13:7). But the second half is greater. What bears God’s image? We do. Every human being is made ‘in the image of God’ (Genesis 1:27). Caesar may have our coins; God has a claim on our whole selves. The coin was probably a denarius of Tiberius, which called him the son of a god (see the history note). Jesus quietly cuts Caesar down to size. Caesar is owed taxes, not worship. Calvin saw here ‘a clear distinction between spiritual and civil government’. Christians are to be good citizens, pay what we owe and pray for those in authority. But no ruler owns our conscience. When the two clash, ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29). Above all, this passage asks: have you given to God what is God’s, which is yourself?
22.big: Jesus escapes the trap by giving Caesar his due coin and claiming for God the far greater thing that bears his image: ourselves.

vv.h: They sent their disciples to Him along with the Herodians
b: The Herodians were ‘A Jewish political party that sympathized with the rulers of the Herodian dynasty, and therefore Rome’ (Lexham Bible Dictionary). Wesley: they were ‘zealous for the interest of the Roman government’. Quarles notes that Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, received 200 talents a year in tribute from Galilee and Perea (Josephus, Antiquities 17.318), and that he had already killed John (14:1–12).

vv.h: we know that You are honest and that You teach the way of God in accordance with the truth
b: Their words are true, though they do not mean them. Quarles notes that the flattery was meant to push Jesus into a blunt yes or no. Wesley: ‘Thou favourest no man for his riches or greatness.’

vv.h: Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not? … You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?
b: Wesley: ‘If he had said, Yes, the Pharisees would have accused him to the people, as a betrayer of the liberties of his country. If he had said, No, the Herodians would have accused him to the Roman governor.’ He calls them hypocrites for ‘Pretending a scruple of conscience.’

vv.h: Whose image is this, and whose inscription? … Caesar’s
b: A denarius was a day’s wage (BSB footnote). Quarles notes that Matthew alone calls it ‘the coin used for the tax’, fitting for a former tax collector. Wesley: ‘The current coin of every nation shows who is the supreme governor of it.’ See the history note.

vv.h: Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s
b: Quarles connects ‘image’ with Genesis 1:26–27 and ‘inscription’ with Isaiah’s picture of God’s people writing on their hands, ‘The LORD’s’ (Isaiah 44:5). Calvin: ‘outward subjection does not prevent us from having within us a conscience free in the sight of God.’ Wesley turned it on both groups: ‘ye Herodians, while ye are zealous for Caesar, see that ye render to God the things that are God’s.’

vv.h: And when they heard this, they were amazed. So they left Him and went away
b: Calvin: God ‘not only disappoints their expectation, but even drives them back with disgrace.’ Their plan has failed, but they are not changed. Two more groups will try their questions before the day is out.

22.diff: Church and state. Christians agree that we owe governments taxes and lawful obedience (Romans 13:1–7), and that when rulers command what God forbids, ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29). Calvin: ‘if princes claim any part of the authority of God, we ought not to obey them any farther than can be done without offending God.’ The Westminster Confession calls it ‘the duty of people to pray for magistrates … to pay them tribute or other dues, to obey their lawful commands’ (23.4). The Catholic Catechism says it is ‘morally obligatory to pay taxes, to exercise the right to vote, and to defend one’s country’ (2240), but that ‘The citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the demands of the moral order’ (2242, citing this verse). The Anabaptist tradition has historically kept apart from state power: the Schleitheim Confession (1527) held ‘that it is not appropriate for a Christian to serve as a magistrate’. Most other traditions see public office as a legitimate Christian calling. See also the note on Mark 12:13.

b: The coin used for the Roman poll tax was the silver denarius, a day’s wage (BSB footnote; compare 20:2). Quarles thinks it was most likely the common denarius of the emperor Tiberius (AD 14–37). Examples survive in many museums. One side shows the emperor’s head with the words TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, ‘Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus’. The other shows a seated woman, often identified as Livia or the goddess Pax, with PONTIF MAXIM, ‘high priest’.

So the coin itself made religious claims. It called the emperor the son of a god, and his priestly title appeared on the other side. When Jesus asked ‘Whose image is this, and whose inscription?’ his hearers knew exactly what was stamped on it. It is widely accepted that this was the coin, though other denarii also circulated.

b: The Old Testament teaches that God rules over rulers: ‘By me kings reign’ (Proverbs 8:15), and Jesus told Pilate, ‘You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above’ (John 19:11). The apostles urged Christians to pray ‘for kings and all those in authority’ (1 Timothy 2:2) and to ‘fear God, honor the king’ (1 Peter 2:17).
‘The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof’ (Psalm 24:1). Quarles notes that this psalm was sung in the temple each week; everything, Caesar included, belongs to God.

l.t: Mark’s account.
Luke: they hoped to hand him over to the governor.
Made in the image of God.
Writing on the hand, ‘The LORD’s’.
Submit to the governing authorities; pay taxes.
We must obey God rather than men.
Fear God, honor the king.

qs: Why was the question about taxes such a clever trap?
What things in our lives are ‘Caesar’s’, and what belongs to God?
Where might obeying God and obeying the authorities come into conflict for Christians today?

22.ctx: The Sadducees were a Jewish school of thought, linked with the priestly leadership, who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8). The law of Moses said that if a man died childless, his brother should marry the widow so that the dead man’s name would carry on (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). Compare Mark 12:18–27 and Luke 20:27–40.
22.mean: On the same day, a new group comes with a question: ‘the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection.’ They tell a story designed to make the resurrection look ridiculous. Moses said a man should marry his brother’s childless widow. Suppose seven brothers each marry the same woman and each dies childless. ‘In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven?’ Wesley thought this was a stock objection, used ‘upon all occasions’. Jesus answers bluntly: ‘You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.’ Those are the two roots of their error. First, they underestimate God’s power. The life to come is not just this life restarted. ‘In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.’ Luke adds that ‘they can no longer die’ (Luke 20:36). Marriage belongs to this age, where people die and children are born. Jesus does not say that we become angels, or that love is lost, but that the new creation is greater than anything the Sadducees could imagine. Second, they do not know the Scriptures. The Sadducees appealed to Moses, so Jesus answers from Moses. At the burning bush, God said, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ Not ‘I was’, but ‘I am’, centuries after they had died. ‘He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.’ If God has bound himself to Abraham in covenant, death cannot end that relationship. The God who calls himself their God will raise them up. The crowds are astonished. This passage gives Christians great hope. Our future does not depend on how much we can imagine, but on the power of God and the promises of his word. The God of Abraham is the God of the living, and all who belong to him will live.
22.big: Jesus answers the Sadducees from God’s power and from Moses himself: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is the God of the living, so the resurrection is certain.

vv.h: the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection … Moses declared that if a man dies without having children, his brother is to marry the widow
b: Josephus says the Sadducees taught ‘that souls die with the bodies’ (Antiquities 18.16). They quote Deuteronomy 25:5 (BSB footnote). Quarles notes that this time there is no flattery, and that for people with no hope of resurrection, a son to carry on a man’s name was the only way he would be remembered.

vv.h: In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven?
b: Wesley: ‘this story seems to have been a kind of common-place objection, which no doubt they brought upon all occasions.’ Quarles notes that the case was designed to set Jesus’ teaching on marriage (19:4–6) against the resurrection: in the resurrection, it seemed, she would have seven husbands at once.

vv.h: You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God
b: Calvin: ‘since God makes known His will clearly in the Scriptures, the want of acquaintance with them is the source and cause of all errors’; the resurrection ‘will be incredible to us, till our minds rise to the contemplation of the boundless power of God’. Wesley: ‘How many errors flow from the same source?’

vv.h: In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven
b: Wesley: like angels in being ‘Incorruptible and immortal’. Calvin: not ‘in all respects, like the angels, but only so far as they shall be free from every infirmity of the present life’. Quarles thinks Jesus is not saying resurrection bodies are sexless, but that the redeemed, like the angels, are immortal and taken up with seeing the Father’s face (18:10).

vv.h: have you not read what God said to you: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?
b: Jesus quotes Exodus 3:6 (BSB footnote). Quarles notes that he calls it what God said ‘to you’, treating the written word as God speaking to his readers. Daniel 12:2 teaches the resurrection more plainly, but the Sadducees insisted on proof from the books of Moses; the Mishnah later denied a share in the world to come to anyone who says ‘There is no resurrection of the dead derived from the Torah’ (Sanhedrin 10:1). Wesley: ‘The Sadducees had a peculiar value for the books of Moses.’

vv.h: He is not the God of the dead, but of the living
b: Wesley set out the argument: the words ‘Thy God’ imply ‘both benefit from God to man, and duty from man to God’; so ‘Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are not dead, but living.’ Calvin: God had made his covenant with the fathers, and ‘in what respect would they have the preference, if they had been extinguished by death?’ Luke adds, ‘for to Him all are alive’ (Luke 20:38).

vv.h: When the crowds heard this, they were astonished at His teaching
b: Wesley: ‘At the clearness and solidity of his answers.’ Luke records that some of the scribes said, ‘Teacher, You have spoken well’ (Luke 20:39).

22.diff: Do the dead live now? Most traditions see in verse 32 that the faithful departed are alive to God now, awaiting the resurrection of the body. Wesley drew the conclusion: ‘Therefore, the soul does not die with the body.’ The Westminster Confession teaches that the souls of the righteous ‘behold the face of God, in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies’ (32.1). Seventh-day Adventists hold that ‘death is an unconscious state for all people’ until Christ appears (Fundamental Belief 26), so they do not read the verse as teaching conscious life before the resurrection. All agree that Jesus is affirming the bodily resurrection. See also the note on Mark 12:18.

b: The Sadducees were one of the three main Jewish schools of thought in Jesus’ day, alongside the Pharisees and the Essenes. None of their own writings survive, so we know them only from others: the New Testament, Josephus and later rabbinic writings (Lexham Bible Dictionary).

All these sources agree that they denied the resurrection. Josephus says they taught ‘that souls die with the bodies’ (Antiquities 18.16) and rejected the idea of reward and punishment after death (Jewish War 2.165). Acts adds that they denied angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). Most scholars think they gave the written Scriptures supreme authority and rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions, though some argue they had interpretive traditions of their own. Older books often describe them as the wealthy priestly aristocracy, but recent scholarship has questioned how far that was true. After the temple fell in AD 70 they disappear from history.

b: Quarles notes that ‘the God of’ Abraham is covenant language: God promised to be God to Abraham and his offspring in ‘an everlasting covenant’ (Genesis 17:7). Paul describes the resurrection body: ‘What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable’ (1 Corinthians 15:42).

Moses asked to see God’s glory and was told, ‘no one can see Me and live’ (Exodus 33:20). Quarles notes that in the resurrection the redeemed will see God’s face; John writes, ‘we will see Him as He is’ (1 John 3:2).

l.t: Mark’s account: ‘You are badly mistaken.’
Sons of the resurrection; to Him all are alive.
I am the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
The brother-in-law’s duty.
Many who sleep in the dust will awake.
The resurrection body.
We will see Him as He is.

qs: Jesus said the Sadducees knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Which of these do we most often forget?
What comfort does ‘He is not the God of the dead, but of the living’ give when someone we love has died?
Why do you think Jesus answered from Moses rather than from a clearer text like Daniel 12?

22.ctx: Jewish teachers often debated which commandments were greater and which lesser. Every day, faithful Jews recited the Shema, which begins ‘Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One’ (Deuteronomy 6:4–9). Compare Mark 12:28–34 and Luke 10:25–28.
22.mean: Hearing that Jesus has silenced the Sadducees, the Pharisees gather again. One of them, an expert in the law, tests him: ‘Teacher, which commandment is the greatest in the Law?’ It was a question the rabbis debated often. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6, words every Jew knew by heart: ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment.’ The heart, soul and mind together mean the whole person. God does not want a corner of our lives, or our outward obedience only. He wants our love, with everything we are. Jesus was not asked for a second commandment, but he gives one anyway: ‘And the second is like it: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”’ This comes from Leviticus 19:18. It is ‘like’ the first because love for God always overflows into love for the people he has made. Calvin put it this way: true love for others will never exist ‘unless where the love of God reigns’, and yet ‘it is impossible for the love of God to reign without producing brotherly kindness among men.’ Then Jesus adds: ‘All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.’ Picture a door hanging on two hinges. Every other command in Scripture hangs on these two. The rules about worship show us how to love God. The rules about property, honesty and justice show us how to love our neighbour. Quarles notes that the experts tried to boil the law down to one great principle; Jesus insists on two that cannot be separated. This simple answer searches us deeply. We can keep many rules and still fail to love. We can say we love God and still ignore the person next to us (1 John 4:20). And no one has ever kept these two commandments perfectly except Jesus himself. They show us what we owe, and they drive us to the One who loved God and neighbour completely, for us.
22.big: The whole law hangs on two inseparable commands: love God with everything you are, and love your neighbour as yourself.

vv.h: One of them, an expert in the law, tested Him with a question: ‘Teacher, which commandment is the greatest in the Law?’
b: Quarles notes that this is the only time Matthew uses the word ‘expert in the law’, and thinks the Pharisees chose their best scholar. Wesley thought the man asked ‘Not, as it seems, with any ill design’. Mark records that Jesus told him, ‘You are not far from the kingdom of God’ (Mark 12:34).

vv.h: Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind
b: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:5 (BSB footnote), where the Hebrew has ‘heart … soul … strength’; Mark and Luke include all four words (Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27). Quarles explains that the Hebrew ‘heart’ covered both feelings and thinking, so the Greek adds ‘mind’. The Mishnah explained ‘with all your soul’ as ‘even if God takes your soul’, and ‘with all your might’ as ‘with all your money’ (Berakhot 9:5).

vv.h: This is the first and greatest commandment
b: Calvin: Mark’s fuller quotation begins ‘Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One’ (Mark 12:29), a reminder that we worship the true Creator, and that ‘it is a pleasing inducement to love him, when he freely adopts us as his people.’ God’s love comes first (Deuteronomy 7:7–8; 1 John 4:19).

vv.h: And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’
b: Leviticus 19:18 (BSB footnote). Quarles notes that Jesus quotes it three times in Matthew (5:43; 19:19; 22:39). In Leviticus it comes in a list of commands against cheating, slander and revenge. Calvin denied that it commands self-love first: Moses ‘did not intend to put the love of ourselves in the first place’. Hillel, a little before Jesus, summed up the law as ‘That which is hateful to you do not do to another’ (Shabbat 31a).

vv.h: All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments
b: Quarles pictures two pegs holding a heavy weight: remove one and the other gives way. Calvin: Jesus does not ‘limit to them all the doctrine of Scripture’, for the free forgiveness of sins is not found in these commands; ‘it is one thing to demand what we owe, and another thing to offer what we do not possess.’ The Catholic Catechism: ‘The Decalogue must be interpreted in light of this twofold yet single commandment of love’ (2055).

Moses promised a day when God would change hearts: ‘The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts … and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul’ (Deuteronomy 30:6). Quarles sees this fulfilled in the new covenant.

The apostles echo Jesus’ teaching. Paul: ‘The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: “Love your neighbor as yourself”’ (Galatians 5:14; compare Romans 13:9–10). James calls it ‘the royal law’ (James 2:8). John: ‘Whoever loves God must love his brother as well’ (1 John 4:21).

l.t: ‘You are not far from the kingdom of God.’
The good Samaritan: who is my neighbour?
Hear, O Israel; love the LORD with all your heart.
Love your neighbour as yourself.
God will circumcise your hearts to love Him.
Love is the fulfilment of the law.
We love because He first loved us.

qs: Why do you think Jesus gave a second commandment when he was only asked for one?
What does loving God with your mind look like in practice?
Who is the hardest ‘neighbour’ for you to love right now, and what would loving them look like this week?

22.ctx: Most Jews expected the Messiah to be a descendant of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Psalm 110, which begins ‘The LORD said to my Lord’, is quoted several times in the New Testament. Compare Mark 12:35–37 and Luke 20:41–44.
22.mean: Jesus has answered every question put to him. Now he asks one of his own. While the Pharisees are gathered together, he says, ‘What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?’ The answer is easy: ‘David’s.’ Most people expected the Messiah to come from David’s family. But Jesus presses further. ‘How then does David in the Spirit call Him “Lord”?’ He quotes Psalm 110: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ In the psalm, God (the LORD) speaks to someone David calls ‘my Lord’, and invites him to sit at his right hand, sharing his throne. ‘So if David calls Him “Lord,” how can He be David’s son?’ In that culture a father did not call his son ‘lord’; it was the other way round. If the great King David calls the Messiah his Lord, the Messiah must be far greater than David. He is David’s son, but he is also David’s Lord. ‘No one was able to answer a word, and from that day on no one dared to question Him any further.’ Matthew’s readers know the answer. At Jesus’ baptism and transfiguration, the voice from heaven said, ‘This is My beloved Son’ (3:17; 17:5). Jesus is the son of David by human birth (1:1), and he is the Son of God. Paul puts both together: Jesus was ‘a descendant of David according to the flesh’ and ‘declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection’ (Romans 1:3–4). Within days, Jesus will tell the high priest that he will be seen ‘sitting at the right hand of Power’ (26:64), and the high priest will call it blasphemy. After the resurrection, Peter will preach this very psalm (Acts 2:34–36). Calvin noted that David, as king, calls him Lord, so ‘there is something in him greater than man.’ The question Jesus asked is the question that matters most: ‘What do you think about the Christ?’
22.big: With one question from Psalm 110, Jesus shows that the Messiah is not only David’s son but David’s Lord, enthroned at God’s right hand.

vv.h: What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?
b: Quarles notes that Matthew puts the question directly to the Pharisees (‘What do you think’), where Mark has ‘How can the scribes say’ and Luke ‘How can it be said’ (Mark 12:35; Luke 20:41), and that only Matthew records their answer. Their answer is right, but not complete.

vv.h: How then does David in the Spirit call Him ‘Lord’?
b: ‘In the Spirit’ means by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Calvin: the phrase is emphatic, showing ‘that the psalm was not composed in reference to the person of David, but was dictated by the prophetic Spirit to describe the future reign of Christ’. Wesley: ‘If he be, as you suppose, a mere man, the son of a man?’

vv.h: The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.’
b: Psalm 110:1 (BSB footnote). In the Hebrew the first ‘Lord’ is the divine name, the LORD. Wesley: this dominion ‘shows both the heavenly majesty of the king, and the nature of his kingdom.’ Calvin noted that the same psalm speaks of a priest ‘forever, in the order of Melchizedek’ (Psalm 110:4), which ‘does not apply either to David, or to any other earthly king’.

vv.h: So if David calls Him ‘Lord,’ how can He be David’s son?
b: Calvin: because David, ‘king and head of the people, calls him Lord … it follows, that there is something in him greater than man.’ Quarles links the question to the high priest’s words at the trial: ‘Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God’ (26:63).

vv.h: No one was able to answer a word, and from that day on no one dared to question Him any further
b: This ends the series of tests that began in 21:23. Quarles: the whole section shows Jesus to be the supreme Teacher; compare ‘I have more insight than all my teachers’ (Psalm 119:99). Their next move will not be a question but a plot (26:3–4).

22.diff: Who is ‘my Lord’? Christians have read Psalm 110 as speaking of Christ from the start, following Jesus and the apostles (Acts 2:34–36; Hebrews 1:13). Calvin noted that Jewish interpreters of his day applied it to David’s own reign, and argued that its eternal priesthood (110:4) fits no earthly king. Many modern scholars think the psalm was written for a king of David’s line rather than by David. Jesus’ argument assumes David wrote it, as its heading says (‘A Psalm of David’) and as his hearers all agreed. See also the note on Mark 12:35.

b: Psalm 110:1 runs right through the New Testament: Jesus quotes it at his trial (26:64), Peter preaches it at Pentecost (Acts 2:34–35), and Hebrews builds on it (Hebrews 1:13; 10:12–13). The risen Jesus calls himself ‘the Root and the Offspring of David’ (Revelation 22:16): both before David and after him.

God promised David a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Matthew opens by calling Jesus ‘the son of David’ (1:1), and Paul joins the two titles: descended from David, declared Son of God (Romans 1:3–4).

l.t: The large crowd listened with delight.
Luke’s account.
The LORD said to my Lord; a priest forever.
Peter preaches Psalm 110: both Lord and Christ.
At the right hand of Power.
Son of David, Son of God.
Sit at My right hand.

qs: Why do you think Jesus asked this question at the end of a day of debates?
What does it mean for us that Jesus is both David’s son and David’s Lord?
If someone asked you, ‘What do you think about the Christ?’, what would you say?

23.ctx: Jesus is still in the temple courts (21:23; 24:1), speaking now to the crowds and his disciples after the leaders’ questions have failed. The scribes were the trained teachers of the law; most Pharisees were not scribes, but many scribes were Pharisees. Chapter 23 is the last public teaching in Matthew. Compare Mark 12:38–40, Luke 11:37–54 and 20:45–47.
23.mean: Jesus turns to the crowds and his own disciples and warns them about their religious leaders. ‘The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach.’ Their first fault is that they load heavy burdens on others and will not ‘lift a finger’ to help. Jesus charges them with making God’s law a heavy load for ordinary people. Jesus, by contrast, says, ‘My yoke is easy and My burden is light’ (11:30). Their second fault is that ‘All their deeds are done for men to see.’ They make their phylacteries broad and their tassels long. These were meant as reminders to obey God (Deuteronomy 6:8; Numbers 15:38–39), but they had become advertisements. They love the best seats, the respectful greetings and the title ‘Rabbi’. Then Jesus turns to his disciples. ‘But you are not to be called “Rabbi,” for you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers.’ Do not call anyone on earth your father in this way, ‘for you have one Father, who is in heaven.’ And do not be called instructors, ‘for you have one Instructor, the Christ.’ Jesus is not banning ordinary words; Paul calls himself a father to his converts (1 Corinthians 4:15). He is forbidding the hunger for status, and any honour that belongs to God alone. In his community there is one Father, one Teacher, and everyone else is a brother or sister. ‘The greatest among you shall be your servant. For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.’ These words are not only about first-century Pharisees. Every church and every Christian leader faces the same temptations: to say one thing and do another, to load burdens on others, to perform for an audience, and to love titles. Jesus’ answer is to remember who we are: children of one Father, students of one Teacher, servants of one another.
23.big: Jesus warns against leaders who teach but do not practise, load burdens on others and crave honour; his followers are brothers under one Father and one Teacher, and the greatest is the servant.

vv.h: The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat
b: Wesley: they ‘read and expound the law of Moses, and are their appointed teachers.’ Stone seats have been found in later synagogues, but whether ‘Moses’ seat’ was a real chair in Jesus’ day is debated (see the history note). Quarles notes that Jesus himself sat on the mountain to teach (5:1), as Moses was thought to have sat on Sinai.

vv.h: So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach
b: Jesus has elsewhere rejected parts of their teaching (15:3–14; 16:12), so ‘everything’ needs explaining. Wesley: ‘Which they read out of the law, and enforce therefrom.’ Calvin: Jesus tells believers ‘to attend to their words, and not to their actions’, because bad pastors should not hinder God’s children ‘from holiness of life.’ Quarles suggests the words are ironic, or quote the leaders’ own claim. See Where readings differ.

vv.h: They tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them
b: The Mishnah itself notes that the rules for the Sabbath, festival offerings and misuse of holy things ‘are like mountains suspended by a hair, as they have little written about them in the Torah’: many rules hang on a few verses (Chagigah 1:8). Peter later refused to put on Gentile believers ‘a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear’ (Acts 15:10).

vv.h: All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels
b: Phylacteries were small boxes containing Scripture, tied on the forehead and arm (Deuteronomy 6:8); tassels were worn on the corners of garments (Numbers 15:38–39). Jesus himself wore them: the ‘fringe of His cloak’ (9:20; 14:36) is the same word. Wesley thought some wore phylacteries ‘as a kind of charm’. Compare 6:1: ‘Be careful not to perform your righteous acts before men to be seen by them.’

vv.h: They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, the greetings in the marketplaces
b: James warns churches against giving the best seats to the rich (James 2:2–4). Quarles notes that ‘Rabbi’ was increasingly used as a title of honour for the scribes in Jesus’ day.

vv.h: And do not call anyone on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven
b: Quarles notes that a later rabbi taught students to give their teacher ‘the reverence of heaven’ (Avot 4:12). Wesley: the rabbis required disciples ‘To believe implicitly what they affirmed’ and ‘To obey implicitly what they enjoined’, so Jesus ‘forbids us either to receive any such reverence, or to pay any such to any but God.’ Calvin: ‘the honor of a father is falsely ascribed to men, when it obscures the glory of God.’

vv.h: The greatest among you shall be your servant. For whoever exalts himself will be humbled
b: Jesus has said this before (18:4; 20:26–27). Wesley: ‘no one sentence of our Lord’s is so often repeated as this’ (compare Luke 14:11; 18:14). Calvin: ‘the highest honor in the Church is not government, but service.’

23.diff: ‘Do not call anyone on earth your father’. Some Protestants object to calling clergy ‘Father’. Catholics, Orthodox and many Anglicans use the title for priests; Catholic Answers explains that ‘Jesus is not forbidding us to call men “fathers” who actually are such—either literally or spiritually’, as Paul called himself a father (1 Corinthians 4:15). Calvin also said ‘it is not only lawful to call men on earth fathers, but it would be wicked to deprive them of that honor’; the fault is when the title ‘obscures the glory of God’. Quarles thinks Jesus was ‘probably prohibiting the abuse and not all use’ of such titles. All agree that Jesus forbids status-seeking in his church. ‘Observe everything they tell you’. Readers differ on how to square this with Jesus’ criticism of the Pharisees’ teaching. Wesley and Calvin limit it to what the scribes taught from the law of Moses. Quarles thinks it is ironic, a permission, or a quotation of the leaders’ claim, which Jesus then corrects.

b: Moses’ seat. Stone seats have been found in several ancient synagogues. The best known, carved from a single block of basalt, comes from Chorazin; the original is in the Israel Museum. But that synagogue was rebuilt in the 3rd or 4th century AD, long after Jesus. Scholars are divided over whether ‘Moses’ seat’ in Jesus’ day was a real chair for the teacher or a figure of speech for the authority to teach the law. Quarles thinks it was probably a real seat.

Phylacteries (Hebrew tefillin) are small boxes holding the passages Exodus 13:1–16 and Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and 11:13–21, worn on the forehead and left arm. Josephus mentions the practice (Antiquities 4.213), and finds at Qumran show phylacteries in use as far back as the 2nd century BC. Matthew 23:5 is the only place the word appears in the Bible. Scholars debate whether some people also treated them as charms against evil (Lexham Bible Dictionary); Wesley thought so.

b: Jesus’ invitation stands in contrast: ‘Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest … For My yoke is easy and My burden is light’ (11:28–30). The yoke of the Pharisees crushed; the yoke of Christ gives rest.

Quarles notes that the Old Testament condemns pride again and again (Proverbs 16:18; Isaiah 2:11), and that Paul rebuked Christians who made celebrities of their leaders: ‘I follow Paul … I follow Apollos’ (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4). Peter: ‘God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble’ (1 Peter 5:5).

l.t: Beware of the scribes.
Luke’s woes at a Pharisee’s table.
Bind them on your hands and foreheads.
Tassels to remember the commandments.
My yoke is easy and my burden is light.
Not so among you: the greatest must serve.
Leaders are only servants; God gives the growth.

qs: Which of the faults in verses 3–7 is the greatest temptation for Christians today?
What does it mean in practice that ‘you are all brothers’?
How can your church or small group honour those who serve without turning them into celebrities?

23.ctx: Jesus now speaks directly to the scribes and Pharisees in seven ‘woes’. The prophets often began announcements of judgement with ‘Woe’ (Isaiah 5:8–22; Habakkuk 2:6–19). Verse 14 is found in the Byzantine and Textus Receptus texts but not in most modern editions (BSB footnote). Compare Luke 11:42–52.
23.mean: ‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites!’ Seven times Jesus says ‘Woe to you’. A woe is the opposite of a blessing. Wesley noticed that Jesus began his public teaching with blessings on the mountain and ends it with woes in the temple (his text, including verse 14, counted eight). The first woe: ‘You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter.’ By opposing Jesus, the leaders were not only refusing God’s kingdom themselves; they were standing in the doorway, keeping others out. The second woe: ‘You traverse land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are.’ Their zeal was real, but it brought people into their own blindness rather than to God. The third woe calls them ‘blind guides’. They had a system of oaths: swearing ‘by the temple’ meant nothing, but swearing ‘by the gold of the temple’ was binding. Jesus tears the system apart. ‘You blind fools! Which is greater: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred?’ The temple is God’s house; to swear by it is to swear ‘by the One who dwells in it.’ Heaven is ‘God’s throne’. Every oath is made in God’s presence, so every promise matters. Jesus had already said, ‘Let your “Yes” be “Yes,” and your “No,” “No”’ (5:37). These are hard words, and they were spoken with authority by the one who will judge the world. But Wesley called them ‘not … imprecations, but solemn, compassionate declarations of the misery, which these stubborn sinners were bringing upon themselves.’ On Luke 13:32 he also warned that Jesus’ office allowed ‘that severity of language … to which we have no call’. The woes are not a licence for us to denounce others. They are a mirror. Do we help people into the kingdom, or stand in their way? Do we make disciples of Christ, or of ourselves? Do we play games with truth?
23.big: Jesus pronounces woes on leaders who block the way into the kingdom, make converts to their own blindness, and play games with oaths, as if God were not present.

vv.h: You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter
b: Luke has, ‘you have taken away the key to knowledge’ (Luke 11:52). Quarles lists how the leaders had opposed Jesus from the start (9:34; 12:14, 24). Wesley: ‘Ye go not in - For ye are not poor in spirit; and ye hinder those that would be so.’

vv.h: You defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers
b: The Byzantine and Textus Receptus texts include this verse (BSB footnote); its words match Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. Most modern translations leave it out of the text of Matthew.

vv.h: You traverse land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are
b: A proselyte was a Gentile convert to Judaism (Lexham Bible Dictionary; compare Acts 2:11). ‘Hell’ is ‘Gehenna’ (BSB footnote). Quarles quotes Davies and Allison: ‘The problem is not conversion to Judaism, but conversion to Judaism without the Messiah.’ Calvin: it was ‘nothing else than to hurry them from Scylla to Charybdis.’

vv.h: Which is greater: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred?
b: Wesley: hypocrites names their character, but ‘blind guides’ names ‘their influence upon others.’ The Mishnah agreed that ‘The altar sanctifies only items that are suited to it’ (Zevachim 9:1); Jesus uses their own reasoning, from the lesser to the greater. Compare 15:14: ‘If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.’

vv.h: he who swears by the temple swears by it and by the One who dwells in it
b: Wesley: ‘every oath by a creature is an implicit appeal to God.’ Quarles notes that the rabbis taught that buying a house did not include its movable contents unless the seller said ‘and everything in it’ (Bava Batra 4); Jesus says the altar, the temple and heaven always include God. Compare 5:33–37.

23.diff: Woe as curse or lament? Wesley read the woes ‘not as imprecations, but solemn, compassionate declarations’. Quarles notes that prophets’ woes mixed grief with judgement, and that Jesus, as the coming Judge (25:31–46), not only announces judgement but will carry it out. Both see real warning and real sorrow (23:37). Was Jesus unfair to the Pharisees? Some modern scholars, Jewish and Christian, think so. Quarles replies that Jesus generalised but did not say every Pharisee was guilty; that the Pharisees’ own later writings make some of the same criticisms; that such sharp language was common in ancient debate; and that the stakes, people kept out of the kingdom, demanded it. Should we speak like this? Wesley, on Luke 13:32, warned that Jesus’ ‘extraordinary office justified him in using that severity of language’, ‘to which we have no call’. Christians have also misused this chapter against Jewish people; these words were addressed to particular leaders, and Jesus wept over the city as he spoke (23:37; Luke 19:41).

b: Isaiah described Israel’s leaders in the same way: ‘Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious’ (Isaiah 56:10). Quarles hears this behind ‘blind guides’. Jesus opened his teaching with ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (5:3); the leaders had shut the door on themselves.

On oaths, Jesus had already said, ‘not to swear at all: either by heaven, for it is God’s throne; or by the earth, for it is His footstool’ (5:34–35). James repeats it (James 5:12). Truthfulness is part of being honest before God.

l.t: Luke’s woes: you have taken away the key to knowledge.
They defraud widows of their houses.
Israel’s watchmen are blind.
Let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’.
Blind guides; both will fall into a pit.
The prophet’s woes.
Do not swear; let your yes be yes.

qs: What might it look like today to ‘shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces’?
Why does Jesus care so much about the tricks people played with oaths?
How do we take these warnings to heart without becoming judgemental of others?

23.ctx: The law required a tenth of crops to be given to God (Leviticus 27:30; Deuteronomy 14:22). Touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), and tombs were often whitewashed with lime. Compare Luke 11:39–44.
23.mean: The next three woes all expose the same problem: religion that gets the small, outward things right and the great, inward things wrong. ‘You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.’ Mint and dill were kitchen herbs. The Pharisees were so careful that they gave God a tenth of every little leaf. Jesus does not mock their care; they should have tithed, ‘without neglecting’ the greater things. But they had lost all sense of proportion. ‘You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.’ Both gnats and camels were unclean food (BSB footnote). Picture a man carefully filtering a tiny insect out of his cup and then gulping down a camel, hump and all. That is what it looks like to fuss over herbs while ignoring justice and mercy. The fifth woe turns to washing. The Pharisees had detailed rules for cleaning cups and dishes, yet the cups were filled by greed and self-indulgence. Jesus says the vessel that matters is the human heart: clean the inside first, and the outside will follow. The sixth woe is the most vivid. They are ‘like whitewashed tombs’, neat and white on the outside, but full of dead men’s bones within. In the same way, they look righteous to others, while inside they are full of hypocrisy and wickedness. These words search every religious person. It is possible to be correct in every detail and dead at the centre. God ‘sees the heart’ (1 Samuel 16:7). He does not want our tithes instead of our justice, or our clean image instead of a clean heart. Only God can clean us from the inside out, as he promised: ‘I will give you a new heart’ (Ezekiel 36:26).
23.big: Jesus condemns religion that fusses over small outward things while neglecting justice, mercy, faithfulness and a clean heart.

vv.h: You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness
b: Quarles notes that the rabbis agreed even dill must be tithed, and hears Micah 6:8 (‘to act justly, to love mercy’) and Hosea 6:6 (‘I desire mercy’) behind Jesus’ words. Wesley: ‘Judgment — That is, justice’; and faith: ‘The word here means fidelity.’ Calvin: Jesus ‘acknowledges that whatever God has enjoined ought to be performed’, but insists ‘chiefly on the principal points’.

vv.h: You blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel
b: Gnats and camels were both forbidden food (Leviticus 11:4, 23; BSB footnote). Wesley complained of the old misprint ‘strain at a gnat’, ‘which quite alters the sense’: the point is straining the drink to remove a gnat.

vv.h: You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence
b: Quarles notes that the Pharisees themselves taught that an unclean inside made the whole cup unclean; Jesus applies their logic to the heart. Wesley: ‘These miserable men procured unjustly what they used intemperately.’ Compare 15:18–20: evil comes from the heart.

vv.h: You are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful on the outside but on the inside are full of dead men’s bones
b: Anyone who touched ‘a human bone or a grave’ was unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). Quarles notes that the rabbis treated a corpse as the most serious source of uncleanness of all.

vv.h: on the outside you appear to be righteous, but on the inside you are full of hypocrisy and wickedness
b: Jesus had said that the righteousness of his followers must exceed ‘that of the scribes and Pharisees’ (5:20). Quarles notes that the pure heart (5:8) is a gift of the new covenant, when God puts his law ‘in their minds’ and inscribes it ‘on their hearts’ (Jeremiah 31:33).

The prophets made the same point. Micah: ‘what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?’ (Micah 6:8). Jesus has twice quoted Hosea, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’ (9:13; 12:7).

Wesley summed up the chapter as exposing ‘every thing that commonly passes in the world for religion’, including ‘A scrupulous exactness in little observances, though with the neglect of justice, mercy, and faith’ and ‘A nice cautiousness to cleanse the outward behaviour, but without any regard to inward purity’.

l.t: Luke: you neglect justice and the love of God.
Act justly, love mercy, walk humbly.
I desire mercy, not sacrifice.
What comes out of the heart defiles.
Uncleanness from a corpse or grave.
The LORD sees the heart.
A new heart and a new spirit.

qs: What are some ‘gnats’ and ‘camels’ in church life today?
Why is it easier to clean the outside of the cup than the inside?
Which of ‘justice, mercy, and faithfulness’ do you most need God’s help with?

23.ctx: Tombs and monuments to the prophets stood around Jerusalem in Jesus’ day. The Hebrew Bible, as Jews arranged it, began with Genesis and probably ended with 2 Chronicles, as it does today. Compare Luke 11:47–51.
23.mean: The seventh woe is the climax. The leaders build tombs for the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous. They say that if they had lived in their fathers’ days, they would never have joined in killing the prophets. But Jesus turns their words against them. By calling those killers their ‘fathers’, they admit whose sons they are, and their actions are about to prove it. Wesley put it sharply: they showed ‘A professed veneration for all good men, except those among whom they live.’ It is always easier to honour prophets who are safely dead than to listen to the one standing in front of you. ‘Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers.’ Scripture speaks of sin building up until God’s patience ends (Genesis 15:16). Jesus is not commanding them to sin; Wesley called it ‘A word of permission, not of command’. They are about to complete their fathers’ work by killing God’s Son. Then come the fiercest words in the Gospels: ‘You snakes! You brood of vipers!’ John the Baptist had used the same words (3:7). Jesus goes on: ‘I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers.’ In the Old Testament it is the LORD who sends the prophets; Jesus speaks as God. They will kill, flog and hunt down his messengers, and Acts records some of this (Acts 5:40; 7:58; 12:2). So the guilt of all the righteous blood shed on earth will come on them, from Abel, the first murder in Scripture (Genesis 4), to Zechariah, most likely the priest stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24), probably the last in the Hebrew order of books (see Where readings differ). ‘Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.’ Within forty years Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed. These words show how seriously God takes the rejection of his messengers. They also show his patience: century after century, he kept sending.
23.big: Those who honoured the dead prophets were about to kill God’s Son and his messengers, filling up their fathers’ sins; judgement would fall on that generation.

vv.h: So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets
b: Wesley: ‘Ye build the tombs of the prophets — And that is all, for ye neither observe their sayings, nor imitate their actions.’ Quarles notes that none of these tombs appear to survive, though a tomb complex on the Mount of Olives later called the tombs of the prophets dates from about the first century BC.

vv.h: Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers
b: The BSB footnote gives ‘Or Go ahead, then, and complete’. Quarles notes that some early copyists, troubled by the command, changed it to a statement. Calvin: Jesus ‘does not bid them do what they are doing’, but says they ‘finish the web which they had begun.’ Compare Genesis 15:16: ‘the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.’

vv.h: You snakes! You brood of vipers! How will you escape the sentence of hell?
b: John used the same words (3:7), and so had Jesus (12:34). Wesley: ‘Our Lord having now lost all hope of reclaiming these, speaks so as to affright others from the like sins.’ ‘Hell’ is ‘Gehenna’ (BSB footnote).

vv.h: I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers. Some of them you will kill and crucify
b: Wesley: ‘Is not this speaking as one having authority?’ Quarles notes that in the Old Testament it is the LORD who sends the prophets (2 Chronicles 24:19; Jeremiah 7:25); here Jesus takes that role. Luke has ‘the wisdom of God said’ (Luke 11:49). Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58), James killed with the sword (Acts 12:2), and Paul received the synagogue lashes five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).

vv.h: from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar
b: Abel’s blood ‘cries out’ from the ground (Genesis 4:10); the dying Zechariah son of Jehoiada said, ‘May the LORD see this and call you to account’ (2 Chronicles 24:22). Wesley: Jesus chose him because ‘he was the last of the prophets on record that were slain by the Jews for reproving their wickedness’. On ‘son of Berechiah’, see Where readings differ.

vv.h: Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation
b: Quarles notes that a generation was about forty years, so this points to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. These words were spoken to that generation. The Catholic Catechism warns that blame for Jesus’ death cannot be extended ‘to other Jews of different times and places’ (597).

23.diff: Zechariah son of Berechiah. Most readers identify this Zechariah with Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned ‘in the courtyard of the house of the LORD’ (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), the last murder in the Hebrew Bible’s order of books, as Abel’s is the first. But Zechariah 1:1 names the later prophet as ‘Zechariah son of Berechiah’. Calvin held firmly to the son of Jehoiada, saying of the later prophet ‘we nowhere read that he was slain’. Wesley took Berechiah to be another name for Jehoiada (‘Termed Jehoiada, 2 Chron. xxiv, 20’). Some scholars think Matthew confused the two; Quarles rejects this and lists other suggestions: ‘son of Jehoiada’ may mean descendant, with Berechiah as his father; an old Jewish tradition (the Targum on Lamentations 2:20) says the prophet Zechariah son of Iddo was also killed in the sanctuary; or ‘son of Berechiah’ was added by a copyist, since Luke 11:51 has only ‘Zechariah’ and the early Codex Sinaiticus omits it in Matthew. A Zechariah killed in the temple by Zealots during the Jewish revolt (Josephus, Jewish War 4.334–344) is sometimes suggested, but Jesus speaks of a past murder.

b: Stephen made the same charge before the council: ‘Which of the prophets did your fathers fail to persecute? They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One’ (Acts 7:52). Abel’s blood cried for justice, but Christ’s blood ‘speaks a better word than the blood of Abel’ (Hebrews 12:24).
Quarles sees a very high view of Christ here: the God who ‘sent prophets to bring the people back to Him’ (2 Chronicles 24:19) is now speaking in Jesus, who says, ‘I am sending you prophets’.

l.t: From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah.
Abel’s blood cries out from the ground.
Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned in the temple court.
John: ‘You brood of vipers’.
Stephen’s charge and death.
Blood that speaks a better word than Abel’s.

qs: Why is it easier to honour prophets of the past than to listen to God’s word today?
What does it tell us about Jesus that he says, ‘I am sending you prophets’?
How should we read words of judgement like these without turning them against other people?
