23.ctx: Jesus ends his public teaching with grief over the city. Luke records similar words earlier, on the way to Jerusalem (Luke 13:34–35), and tells how Jesus wept over the city as he approached it (Luke 19:41–44). Immediately afterwards, Jesus leaves the temple and foretells its destruction (24:1–2).
23.mean: After the woes comes weeping. ‘O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!’ The repeated name is the cry of a broken heart, like David’s cry, ‘O my son Absalom!’ (2 Samuel 18:33). Jesus is not glad that judgement is coming. He longs to save. The picture he chooses is tender and humble: a hen spreading her wings over her chicks to shelter them from danger. In the Psalms, it is God who shelters his people under his wings (Psalm 91:4). Jesus speaks of doing what only God does, and of having wanted to do it ‘how often’. But ‘you were unwilling’. Love can be refused. ‘Look, your house is left to you desolate.’ The temple, God’s house, has become ‘your house’. Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD leave the temple before Babylon destroyed it, moving out through the east gate to the mountain east of the city (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). In the next verses, Jesus walks out of the temple and sits on the Mount of Olives, east of the city (24:1–3). God’s presence is leaving his house. ‘For I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.”’ These were the words the pilgrims shouted when he entered the city (21:9). Christians have read this last sentence in different ways: as a warning of judgement day, or as a hope that Jerusalem will one day welcome him (see Where readings differ). Either way, Jesus will be acknowledged in the end. This passage shows the heart of God. The same Jesus who spoke the woes now weeps. His judgements are real, but they are never cold. He still longs to gather people under his wings, and the only thing that keeps us out is our unwillingness to come.
23.big: Jesus grieves over Jerusalem like a mother hen whose chicks will not come; the temple is left desolate, and the city will not see him again until it says, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’

vv.h: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her
b: Quarles hears the book of Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah’s: ‘Streams of tears flow from my eyes over the destruction of the daughter of my people’ (Lamentations 3:48). Calvin: Jesus warns his followers not to be shaken when the holy city kills its Redeemer, for it ‘had been accustomed to strangle or stone the prophets’. Stoning recalls Zechariah (2 Chronicles 24:21) and 21:35.

vv.h: how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
b: God shelters his people under his wings (Ruth 2:12; Psalm 91:4; Deuteronomy 32:11). Calvin: ‘Christ, speaking in the person of God, compares himself to a hen’, ‘an amazing and unparalleled instance of love’. Wesley on Luke 13:34: ‘Three solemn visits he had made to Jerusalem since his baptism for this very purpose.’ Quarles notes that ‘longed’ and ‘unwilling’ are the same Greek verb: I willed, you did not will. See Where readings differ.

vv.h: Look, your house is left to you desolate
b: Some manuscripts and editions omit ‘desolate’ (BSB footnote). Wesley: ‘The temple, which is now your house, not God’s’; ‘Our Lord spake this as he was going out of it for the last time.’ Quarles: the temple, made holy by God’s presence (23:21), is now abandoned by him.

vv.h: you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’
b: Psalm 118:26 (BSB footnote), the words of 21:9. Quarles notes that Jesus speaks of his own departure where the prophets spoke of the LORD’s, and that the verse ends with hope: compare Peter’s call, ‘Repent, then, and turn back … that He may send Jesus’ (Acts 3:19–20). See Where readings differ.

23.diff: ‘You were unwilling’. Arminian and Wesleyan readers see here God’s sincere desire to save, which people can resist: the Remonstrance (1610) said of grace that ‘it is not irresistible, inasmuch as it is written concerning many, that they have resisted the Holy Ghost.’ Reformed readers agree that the offer is sincere and the refusal culpable: the Canons of Dort say ‘As many as are called by the gospel are unfeignedly called’, and when they refuse, ‘The fault lies in themselves’ (Third and Fourth Heads, arts. 8–9). Calvin explained the verse as God’s will ‘manifested by the nature of the word’, which calls everyone, as distinct from his ‘secret purpose’; ‘whomsoever he efficaciously wills to gather, he inwardly draws by his Spirit’. All see real love in the picture of the hen, though Calvin heard ‘indignation rather than of compassion’ in ‘how often’, aimed chiefly at the scribes. ‘Until you say’. Calvin read verse 39 as a threat to all who despise the gospel: the Redeemer they reject they will find to be their Judge, and they will confess him ‘when it is too late’. He declined to limit it to the last day. Wesley saw a promise: ‘after a long interval of desolation and misery, ye say, Blessed is he … This also shall be accomplished in its season.’ Quarles says the passage ‘ends with a hopeful promise’: the Messiah will return when his people repent (Acts 3:19–21). Paul’s hope for Israel in Romans 11:26 is read in different ways (see the note on 21:33). Wesley’s note on Luke 13:35 is more guarded.

b: Quarles traces Ezekiel’s vision: the glory of the LORD left the temple threshold, paused at the east gate, and ‘stood over the mountain east of the city’ (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Jesus now leaves the temple and sits on the Mount of Olives (24:1–3).

Zechariah foresaw a day when God would pour out ‘a spirit of grace and prayer’ on Jerusalem, and ‘they will look on Me, the One they have pierced’ (Zechariah 12:10). Readers take this, like verse 39, in different ways. Calvin cited it to show that those who reject the Redeemer will one day see him as their Judge. Others hear hope in it, as in Paul’s words, ‘And so all Israel will be saved’ (Romans 11:26).

l.t: Luke: how often I have longed to gather your children.
Jesus weeps over the city.
Under His wings you will find refuge.
The glory of the LORD leaves the temple.
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.
Jesus leaves the temple for the Mount of Olives.
All Israel will be saved.

qs: What does it tell us about Jesus that he weeps over the city he has just warned?
Why do you think he chose the picture of a hen and her chicks?
What keeps people today ‘unwilling’ to come under his wings?

24.ctx: Jesus has just left the temple for the last time (23:38–39). Herod the Great had rebuilt and enlarged it on a vast scale, and it was one of the wonders of the Roman world. Chapters 24–25 are the fifth and last of Jesus’ long teaching blocks in Matthew, often called the Olivet Discourse because it was given on the Mount of Olives. Compare Mark 13:1–8 and Luke 21:5–11.
24.mean: As Jesus walks away from the temple, his disciples point out its buildings. Josephus, who saw it, called it the most marvellous building he had ever seen or heard of, covered in gold that flashed in the sun. Its stones were enormous. Surely this would stand forever. Jesus answers: ‘Do you see all these things?’ … ‘Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.’ Within forty years, in AD 70, the Romans burned the temple and levelled the city (see the history note). Later, sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, the disciples ask privately: ‘when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?’ They seem to assume that the fall of the temple and the end of the world must be the same event. Wesley thought they were mixing together two events that Jesus would answer ‘distinctly’; Calvin thought they were confusing the beginning of Christ’s reign with its completion. Jesus begins, not with a date, but with a warning: ‘See to it that no one deceives you.’ Many will come claiming, ‘I am the Christ.’ There will be wars and rumours of wars, famines and earthquakes. ‘See to it that you are not alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come.’ They are only ‘the beginning of birth pains’. This opening sets the tone for the whole discourse. Jesus does not feed our curiosity with a timetable. He prepares his followers to stay faithful in a troubled world. Disasters and wars are real, and they are painful, but they are not a sign that God has lost control. They ‘must happen’. Like birth pains, they point towards something new being born. Christians read the details of this chapter in different ways (see Where readings differ). But every reading agrees on the first command: do not be deceived, and do not be afraid.
24.big: Jesus foretells the temple’s destruction and warns his disciples not to be deceived or alarmed by false messiahs, wars and disasters, which are only the beginning of birth pains.

vv.h: Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down
b: Mark records a disciple saying, ‘Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!’ (Mark 13:1). Quarles notes that some Jews of the time thought the temple could never fall. Wesley: ‘This was most punctually fulfilled; for after the temple was burnt, Titus, the Roman general, ordered the very foundations of it to be dug up’. Compare Jesus’ lament in Luke 19:44: ‘They will not leave one stone on another’.

vv.h: when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?
b: Calvin: having believed ‘from their infancy that the temple would stand till the end of time’, the disciples ‘associate the coming of Christ and the end of the world as things inseparable from each other’. Wesley: ‘The disciples inquire confusedly … Our Lord answers distinctly’. ‘Coming’ (parousia) was used for the visit of a king. Calvin noted that Mark and Luke record only the question about the temple; Matthew adds ‘Your coming and … the end of the age’.

vv.h: See to it that no one deceives you. For many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will deceive many
b: Wesley: ‘never did so many impostors appear in the world as a few years before the destruction of Jerusalem’. See the history note. Calvin noted that the Church, ‘so long as its pilgrimage in the world shall last, will be exposed to these evils.’

vv.h: These things must happen, but the end is still to come
b: Quarles notes that ‘must’ points to God’s control of history (Daniel 2:21, 28), and that the years before AD 70 saw a famine in Claudius’s reign (Acts 11:28), earthquakes across the Roman world, and in AD 69 four emperors in one year. Calvin: ‘the preaching of the Gospel is like sowing the seed, and therefore we ought to wait patiently for the time of reaping’.

vv.h: All these are the beginning of birth pains
b: The prophets used birth pains for intense suffering (Isaiah 13:8; Jeremiah 6:24). Quarles notes that early labour pains are mild compared with what follows, and that they come closer together as birth approaches. Paul uses the same picture of creation waiting for its renewal (Romans 8:22).

24.diff: How should we read this chapter? Christians read Matthew 24 in several ways. Futurist readers, such as the Scofield Reference Notes and Dallas Theological Seminary, apply most of it to a future ‘great tribulation’ before Christ’s return. Others, such as R. T. France, read everything up to verse 35 as fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, with Christ’s final coming the subject from verse 36. Many hold that Jesus answers both questions, describing AD 70 and his final coming. Quarles takes this view, and notes that scholars disagree on where Jesus moves from one to the other: some at 24:21 (Blomberg, Carson), some at 24:32, and some at 24:36 (France). Some see AD 70 as a preview of the end, ‘a single prophecy with two fulfillments’; the Lexham Bible Dictionary thinks Matthew’s ‘abomination’ refers to both. Wesley divided the chapter into four parts: the signs before the temple’s fall, the signs of Christ’s coming (29–31), the time of the temple’s fall (32–35), and the time of the end (36). Calvin read much of it as describing the whole life of the church between Christ’s first and second comings. The Catholic Catechism teaches that before Christ returns ‘the Church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers’ (675). All agree that Christ will come again, and that his followers must be watchful.

b: In AD 70 the Roman general Titus captured Jerusalem after a long siege. Josephus, who was with the Roman army, records that the temple was burned on the tenth of the month Ab, the same day, he notes, that Babylon had burned the first temple (Jewish War 6.250). Afterwards Titus ordered the city and temple to be demolished, leaving only three towers (Phasaelus, Hippicus and Mariamne) and part of the city wall on the west side, as a camp for the garrison; the rest was ‘laid even with the ground’ (Jewish War 7.1–3).

Josephus gives the number taken captive in the war as 97,000 and the dead in the siege as 1,100,000 (Jewish War 6.420). Massive stones from the platform Herod built around the temple can still be seen, most famously at the Western Wall, but the temple itself has never been rebuilt.

b: Josephus describes several men who drew crowds with promises of miracles in the years before the revolt. Theudas told his followers that he would divide the Jordan by his command; the Roman governor’s cavalry killed many and beheaded him (Antiquities 20.97–98). An Egyptian ‘false prophet’ led a large crowd from the wilderness to the Mount of Olives, promising that the walls of Jerusalem would fall at his command; he escaped when the Romans attacked (Jewish War 2.261–263; Antiquities 20.169–172).

The Egyptian also appears in Acts (21:38), which gives a smaller number for his followers (four thousand, against Josephus’s thirty thousand). Acts 5:36 also mentions a Theudas, though whether he is the same man is debated (see the note on Acts 5:33). Josephus says such men ‘deceived and deluded the people’ (Jewish War 2.259), the very danger Jesus warned of (24:4–5, 24).

Quarles sees the temple’s fall as the outcome of chapter 23: the fruitless tree, the leaders’ hypocrisy, the murder of God’s messengers and the city’s refusal to come.
Paul faced Christians who were shaken by claims that the Day of the Lord had already come: ‘Let no one deceive you in any way’ (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Calvin: Christ ‘exhorts them to long patience’.

Jesus begins with ‘do not be deceived’ and ‘do not be alarmed’. Which of these do you need more today?

24.ctx: Jesus had already warned the Twelve that they would be handed over and flogged (10:16–23). Within a generation James son of Zebedee had been killed (Acts 12:2), and under the emperor Nero, after the fire of Rome in AD 64, Christians were put to death in Rome (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Compare Mark 13:9–13 and Luke 21:12–19.
24.mean: Jesus now speaks of what his followers themselves will face. ‘Then they will deliver you over to be persecuted and killed, and you will be hated by all nations because of My name.’ This is not the result of doing wrong, but of belonging to Jesus. The hatred will come from outside, and the danger will come from inside too. ‘Many will fall away and will betray and hate one another, and many false prophets will arise and deceive many.’ When following Jesus becomes costly, some who seemed to be disciples will give up, and some will even hand over their brothers and sisters to save themselves. False teachers will offer an easier message. ‘Because of the multiplication of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold.’ In a world full of evil, it is easy for love, for God and for others, to cool. Wesley compared it to the church at Ephesus, which had left its ‘first love’ (Revelation 2:4). But there is a promise: ‘the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.’ Endurance does not earn salvation, but Jesus says it matters (see Where readings differ). And there is a mission: ‘this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.’ Persecution will not stop the gospel. Wesley and Quarles both note that the apostles carried it across the Roman world before Jerusalem fell; Paul could write of the gospel ‘proclaimed to every creature under heaven’ (Colossians 1:23). Christians today also hear in this verse a call to finish the task among every people. This passage is a sober word for comfortable Christians. Following Jesus has always cost something, and still costs many believers their lives. It asks us whether our love is growing warm or cold, and whether we are ready to hold on to the end. And it reminds us that God’s purpose cannot fail: the good news of his kingdom will reach the nations.
24.big: Jesus warns of persecution, betrayal, false prophets and cooling love, but promises that those who endure will be saved and the gospel will reach all nations.

vv.h: you will be hated by all nations because of My name
b: Wesley: ‘in no nation will the children of the devil tolerate the children of God.’ Quarles notes that the hatred now comes from ‘all nations’, not just Galilee and Judea as in chapter 10, showing that the church will have spread among the Gentiles.

vv.h: At that time many will fall away and will betray and hate one another
b: To ‘fall away’ is to deny Christ under pressure (10:33; 13:21). Quarles notes Tacitus’s report that in Nero’s persecution those arrested were made to name others (Annals 15.44).

vv.h: Because of the multiplication of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold
b: Quarles thinks these false prophets arise within the church, like those of 7:15–23, and that the love that cools is mainly love for Jesus (10:37–39). Wesley: ‘The generality of those who love God will (like the Church at Ephesus, Rev. ii, 4, ) leave their first love.’

vv.h: But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved
b: Jesus said the same in 10:22. Wesley (on verse 10) urged holding fast faith, love and hope ‘unto the end’. Quarles thinks ‘the end’ here may mean the end of the crisis around Jerusalem, as in 24:6 and 14.

vv.h: this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come
b: The ‘world’ (oikoumenē) often meant the Roman world (Luke 2:1). Wesley: ‘Not universally: this is not done yet: but in general through the several parts of the world … And this was done by St. Paul and the other apostles, before Jerusalem was destroyed.’ He added that Josephus’s history of the war ‘is the best commentary on this chapter’.

24.diff: ‘Then the end will come’. Readers differ on what ‘the end’ means here. Wesley and Quarles take it as the end of the city and temple in AD 70, since by then the gospel had spread across the Roman world (Romans 10:18; Colossians 1:23). The Scofield notes apply it to the end of the age, with the gospel preached again by a believing Jewish remnant. Calvin, and many others, take it as the end of history (‘the end and renovation of the world’), so that the church’s mission to every nation must be completed before Christ returns. On every reading, the church is sent to all nations (28:19), and those who endure are saved. ‘Perseveres to the end’. Reformed readers see perseverance as the mark of those God keeps; Wesleyan and Arminian readers stress that falling away is a real danger. Both take the warning seriously.

b: The early church saw these words come true. Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58–60) and James killed with the sword (Acts 12:2); Peter and Paul died under Nero, as early tradition records. Yet ‘the word of God continued to spread’ (Acts 6:7; 12:24).

Quarles connects the worldwide mission with the Old Testament hope that the nations would come to worship the true God (Isaiah 2:2–4; 49:6) and with the kingdom given to ‘a people who will produce its fruit’ (21:43).

l.t: Brought before governors and kings.
By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.
Sheep among wolves; endure to the end.
False prophets known by their fruit.
Ephesus: you have left your first love.
Make disciples of all nations.
The gospel bearing fruit in the whole world.

qs: Why might love ‘grow cold’ when wickedness increases? Where do you see that danger today?
What helps a Christian to persevere to the end?
How should the promise that the gospel will reach all nations shape our prayers and giving?

24.ctx: Daniel spoke of ‘the abomination of desolation’ set up in the temple (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11; BSB footnote). In 167 BC the Greek king Antiochus IV had stopped the sacrifices and set up a pagan altar in the temple (1 Maccabees 1:54). Luke’s version says, ‘when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies’ (Luke 21:20). Compare Mark 13:14–23.
24.mean: Jesus now gives his disciples a sign to watch for: ‘the abomination of desolation’ that Daniel spoke of, standing in the holy place. Jews remembered how the Greek king Antiochus had defiled the temple with a pagan altar. Jesus says something like it will happen again. When it does, his followers in Judea must flee to the mountains at once. There will be no time to go back for belongings. A man in the field must not even go home for his cloak. Jesus feels for those who will suffer most, such as pregnant women and nursing mothers. He tells his disciples to pray that they will not have to escape in winter or on the Sabbath. The distress of those days will be worse than anything the world has seen. Only God’s mercy will limit it: ‘for the sake of the elect, those days will be cut short.’ In the middle of the crisis, false messiahs and false prophets will appear. They will do signs and wonders to deceive even God’s chosen people. Jesus says simply, ‘See, I have told you in advance.’ Christians have long disagreed about what the abomination was or will be (see Where readings differ). Many see its fulfilment in the events of AD 66–70, when Jerusalem fell; Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church escaped to Pella before the war. Others expect a future fulfilment before Christ returns. Whatever view we take, these words show Jesus’ care for his people in the worst of times. He warns them ahead. He tells them to act without delay. He grieves for the weak, limits the suffering, and keeps his own from being deceived. His words still teach us to listen to him above every frightening voice.
24.big: Jesus warns his followers to flee without delay when they see the abomination Daniel foretold, promises that God will shorten the days of great distress, and guards them against false messiahs.

vv.h: So when you see standing in the holy place ‘the abomination of desolation,’ spoken of by the prophet Daniel (let the reader understand)
b: Mark has ‘standing where it should not be’ (Mark 13:14); Matthew specifies ‘the holy place’, the temple. Wesley: Daniel’s ‘abomination that maketh desolate’ means ‘the standards of the desolating legions, on which they bear the abominable images of their idols’. Calvin thought Jesus drew on Daniel 12:11, which foretold that after Antiochus the temple would face a new profanation ‘when all its sacredness and majesty will be for ever lost.’ Quarles thinks ‘let the reader understand’ calls the reader of Daniel to think carefully. See Where readings differ.

vv.h: then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains
b: Flat roofs were reached by outside stairs, so there would be no time to go back in (Wesley). The cloak was a labourer’s blanket at night (Deuteronomy 24:12–13). Wesley: ‘So the Christians did, and were preserved’. See the history note.

vv.h: Pray that your flight will not occur in the winter or on the Sabbath
b: Quarles notes that winter brought cold and flooded the dry valleys, and that on the Sabbath shops would be shut and travel limited. Wesley believed the Christians’ flight in fact came in spring.

vv.h: there will be great tribulation, unseen from the beginning of the world until now, and never to be seen again
b: The words echo Daniel 12:1. Josephus wrote of the war that ‘the misfortunes of all men, from the beginning of the world, if they be compared to these of the Jews, are not so considerable’ (Jewish War 1.12). Wesley on verse 21: ‘Have not many things spoken in the chapter … a farther and much more extensive meaning than has been yet fulfilled?’

vv.h: false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders to deceive even the elect, if that were possible
b: Quarles notes that ‘signs and wonders’ recalls Moses (Deuteronomy 6:22), and that the would-be deliverers of the time promised a new exodus. Wesley: ‘it is not possible that God should suffer the body of Christians to be thus deceived.’ ‘See, I have told you in advance’: forewarned is forearmed.

24.diff: What is the abomination? Christians have given several answers. Many see it fulfilled before AD 70. Wesley took it to be ‘the standards of the desolating legions’, the Roman army’s idolatrous banners; Quarles thinks it more likely refers to the Zealot rebels’ takeover and defilement of the temple from AD 66, which came early enough for Christians to escape, and he sets aside the view that it is Israel’s rejection of Jesus. Calvin saw it as the final profanation of the temple that ended the sacrifices for good. Futurist readers expect a future fulfilment. The Scofield notes identify it with ‘the “man of sin,” or “Beast”’ (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8), and say that Luke’s account refers to AD 70 but Matthew’s to ‘a future crisis in Jerusalem’; Dallas Theological Seminary links Jesus’ ‘great tribulation’ to the last half of Daniel’s seventieth week. Others see a double fulfilment, in AD 70 and at the end (Lexham Bible Dictionary). ‘If that were possible’. Reformed readers see a promise that the elect will not finally be deceived. Wesley also held that God would not let ‘the body of Christians’ be deceived, but Arminian (Wesleyan) readers apply this to the church as a whole and stress that individual believers face a real danger. See also the note on Mark 13:14.

b: The church historian Eusebius (about AD 325) wrote that ‘the people of the church in Jerusalem had been commanded by a revelation, vouchsafed to approved men there before the war, to leave the city and to dwell in a certain town of Perea called Pella’ (Church History 3.5.3). Pella lay in the hills east of the Jordan. Quarles notes that later writers repeat the story, and that Epiphanius links it to Christ’s instructions.

Many take this as the fulfilment of 24:15–16 (Lexham Bible Dictionary), and Wesley saw the Roman general Cestius’s sudden withdrawal from Jerusalem in AD 66 as the signal the Christians took. Josephus records that after Cestius’s retreat ‘many of the most eminent of the Jews swam away from the city, as from a ship when it was going to sink’ (Jewish War 2.556).

Jesus’ warning shows his care. Peter wrote later that the Lord ‘knows how to rescue the godly from trials’ (2 Peter 2:9).

l.t: Standing where it should not be.
Jerusalem surrounded by armies.
The abomination that causes desolation.
A time of distress unlike any before.
False prophets with signs and wonders.
The man of lawlessness and deceiving wonders.

qs: What does Jesus’ concern for pregnant women and nursing mothers tell us about him?
Why does Jesus say ‘I have told you in advance’? How do his warnings protect us?
How should Christians respond when people claim special signs and wonders today?

24.h: The Return of the Son of Man
24.ctx: Jesus continues the warning about false messiahs (24:23–25) and then speaks of ‘the coming of the Son of Man’. His words draw on the prophets, who used darkened sun and falling stars for God’s judgement on nations (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; BSB footnote), and on Daniel’s vision of one like a son of man coming with the clouds (Daniel 7:13–14). Compare Mark 13:24–27 and Luke 21:25–28.
24.mean: Rumours will fly. People will say the Messiah is out in the wilderness, or hidden in some inner room. Jesus says: do not go, and do not believe it. His true coming will not be a secret known only to a few. It will be like lightning that flashes from east to west. No one needs a rumour to know that lightning has struck. Then Jesus uses the language of the prophets. After the distress of those days, the sun and moon will go dark, the stars will fall, and the powers of heaven will be shaken. The sign of the Son of Man will appear, the tribes will mourn, and they will see ‘the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.’ He will send his angels with a loud trumpet call to gather his chosen people from the four corners of the earth. Christians understand these verses in two main ways (see Where readings differ). Most, with Calvin and Wesley, read them as Christ’s personal return at the end of history. Others, Quarles among them, point out that the prophets used darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of nations, and that in Daniel the Son of Man comes to God to receive his kingdom; they read the verses as Christ’s vindication in the judgement on Jerusalem. Both readings agree on what matters most. Jesus, rejected and soon to be crucified, is the Son of Man of Daniel’s vision. He has power and great glory, he commands the angels, and he gathers his people from every corner of the earth. And his coming at the end will be public and unmistakable. No one needs to chase rumours or fear missing it. Our part is to trust him and be ready.
24.big: The Son of Man’s coming will be as unmistakable as lightning, not a rumour to chase; he comes with power and great glory and gathers his elect from the four winds.

vv.h: For just as the lightning comes from the east and flashes as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man
b: Wesley: ‘the next coming of Christ will be as quick as lightning; so that there will not be time for any such previous warning.’ Calvin read the lightning as the sudden spread of the gospel ‘through every part of the world’, set against false Christs who gathered men in the desert ‘to throw off the yoke of the Roman government by force’. Quarles notes that Josephus describes would-be deliverers leading crowds into the wilderness.

vv.h: Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather
b: The Greek word can mean eagles or vultures. Wesley took the eagles to be the Roman armies, whose standards bore eagles, gathering for the judgement on Jerusalem in AD 70. Quarles hears the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:26, 49 (a nation swooping ‘like an eagle’). Calvin took Christ as the one around whom ‘all the children of God must be gathered’. Many others read it as a proverb: you cannot miss it.

vv.h: The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from the sky
b: The BSB footnote points to Isaiah 13:10 (Babylon), Isaiah 34:4 (Edom) and Joel 2:10. Quarles notes that the prophets used such language for the fall of nations. Calvin rejected the view that ‘the tribulation of those days’ means the destruction of Jerusalem: it is ‘a general recapitulation (ἀνακεφαλαίωσις) of all the evils of which Christ had previously spoken.’ Wesley: ‘Here our Lord begins to speak of his last coming’.

vv.h: They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory
b: See Daniel 7:13–14 (BSB footnote), where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. ‘All the tribes of the earth will mourn’ echoes Zechariah 12:10–12; Revelation 1:7 joins the same two passages. Quarles notes that the words can also mean ‘all the tribes of the land’. Wesley thought the sign might be the cross.

vv.h: He will send out His angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather His elect from the four winds
b: Jesus calls them ‘His angels’. The trumpet recalls Isaiah 27:13, and Quarles notes that ‘the four winds’ recalls Zechariah 2:6. Wesley: the elect are ‘all that have endured to the end in the faith which worketh by love.’ Paul also speaks of the trumpet at the Lord’s coming (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

24.diff: Second coming or AD 70? Most Christians, with Calvin and Wesley, read verses 29–31 as Christ’s personal return at the end of history. Wesley: ‘Here our Lord begins to speak of his last coming. But he speaks not so much in the language of man as of God, with whom a thousand years are as one day’. Dallas Theological Seminary teaches that the great tribulation ‘will climax in the return of the Lord Jesus Christ’, ‘in person on the clouds of heaven’. Quarles, with some other scholars (he names France), argues instead that ‘immediately after’ ties these verses to AD 70; that the prophets used darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of nations; and that in Daniel the Son of Man comes to God to receive his kingdom. On that view, these verses describe Christ’s vindication in the judgement on Jerusalem, and his final coming is the subject from verse 36. Quarles still holds that verse 27 speaks of Christ’s visible return. All Christian traditions confess that Christ ‘shall come again with glory to judge the quick and the dead’ (Nicene Creed). See also the note on Mark 13:24.

b: Daniel saw the Son of Man ‘coming with the clouds of heaven’; ‘He was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him’ (Daniel 7:13–14). At his trial Jesus told the high priest, ‘you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven’ (26:64).

The New Testament consistently teaches a public, glorious return: ‘This same Jesus … will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven’ (Acts 1:11); ‘every eye will see Him’ (Revelation 1:7).

l.t: Mark’s account.
Lift up your heads, your redemption is near.
Sun, moon and stars darkened (Babylon).
One like a son of man with the clouds of heaven.
They will look on Me, the One they have pierced, and mourn.
The trumpet of God; caught up to meet the Lord.
He will come back in the same way.

qs: Why does Jesus warn so strongly against chasing rumours about his coming?
What does Daniel 7 add to our understanding of who Jesus is?
How does the certainty of Christ’s glorious return give hope to his people now?

24.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree
24.ctx: Quarles notes that in the middle of spring the fig tree’s branches become supple and its buds turn to leaves, a sign that summer is near. Compare Mark 13:28–31 and Luke 21:29–33.
24.mean: Jesus uses something every farmer knew. ‘Now learn this lesson from the fig tree: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near.’ In the same way, ‘when you see all these things, you will know that He is near, right at the door.’ The Greek can also mean ‘it is near’ (BSB footnote). Then Jesus says something very specific: ‘Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.’ And he guarantees his words in the strongest possible way: ‘Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.’ The fig tree answers the disciples’ first question, ‘when will these things happen?’ Just as new leaves tell you summer is close, the signs Jesus has described would tell his followers that what he foretold was close. Calvin and Wesley both took ‘this generation’ to mean the people living then; Wesley noted that the city and temple fell ‘thirty-nine or forty years after.’ Others think Jesus is speaking of the final generation before his return, or of the Jewish people (see Where readings differ). Verse 35 is one of the most remarkable claims Jesus ever made. The prophets said, ‘the word of our God stands forever’ (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus says the same of his own words. Everything we can see, the earth beneath us and the sky above, will one day pass away. His words will not. This is why we can trust everything else he says in this chapter, including his promise to come again. If his words about the temple came true, his words about the end can be trusted too. It is also why his teaching should shape our lives. Fashions, ideas and empires come and go. The words of Jesus remain, and those who build on them build on rock (7:24).
24.big: As fig leaves signal summer, the signs Jesus gave would show that what he foretold was near; heaven and earth will pass away, but his words never will.

vv.h: As soon as its branches become tender and sprout leaves, you know that summer is near
b: The BSB footnote gives ‘parable’ as an alternative for ‘lesson’. Quarles notes that the fig tree answers the ‘when’ question of 24:3. Earlier the barren fig tree was a sign of judgement (21:18–22).

vv.h: when you see all these things, you will know that He is near, right at the door
b: ‘Or it is near’ (BSB footnote). Quarles hears the prophets’ warning, ‘the Day of the LORD is near’ (Isaiah 13:6; Joel 1:15), used of God’s judgements in history. ‘At the door’ suggests a near threat (compare Genesis 4:7).

vv.h: this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened
b: Calvin: ‘within fifty years the city was destroyed and the temple was razed’; Jesus ‘expressly foretold that those things related to their own age.’ Wesley: ‘great part of that generation would be passed away, but not the whole. Just so it was.’ Quarles notes that Jesus regularly uses ‘this generation’ for his contemporaries (11:16; 12:41–45; 23:36). See Where readings differ.

vv.h: Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away
b: Jesus said the same of the Law in 5:18. Quarles notes that God promised his covenant would last as long as the fixed order of day and night (Jeremiah 31:35–37; 33:19–22); Jesus says his words will outlast heaven and earth themselves.

24.diff: ‘This generation’. Calvin, Wesley and Quarles take it to mean the people alive when Jesus spoke, who saw the temple fall in AD 70; this view usually holds that ‘all these things’ means the events leading to that fall. The Scofield notes take ‘generation’ to mean the Jewish ‘race, kind, family’, preserved until the end: ‘none of “these things” … occurred at the destruction of Jerusalem by Titus’. Others, especially many modern futurists, take it as the generation alive when the final signs begin. Some critical scholars (Quarles discusses the view) think Jesus, or the Gospel writers, expected the end within that lifetime and were mistaken; Quarles replies that this rests on reading verses 29–31 as the second coming. See also the note on Mark 13:28.

b: ‘The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever’ (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus places his own words alongside God’s word. Peter quotes Isaiah’s words and adds, ‘this is the word that was proclaimed to you’ (1 Peter 1:25).

Quarles notes that Daniel 9:24–27 is a rare prophecy with a timeline, and that even the prophets ‘searched and investigated carefully’ to know the time (1 Peter 1:10–11). On Quarles’s reading, Jesus gives the time of the temple’s fall: within one generation.

l.t: Mark’s account.
Look at the fig tree and all the trees.
The barren fig tree.
The word of our God stands forever.
As sure as the fixed order of creation.
Until heaven and earth pass away.

qs: What signs do you notice in nature that tell you a season is changing? How does Jesus use this?
What do you think Jesus means by ‘this generation’, and why does it matter how we read it?
If Jesus’ words will never pass away, how much time do we give to them each week?

24.ctx: Quarles notes that the Greek opens with peri de, ‘now concerning’, which often marks a new topic (compare 22:31, ‘But concerning’). Here Jesus turns to the day of his coming. In Genesis, the flood came on a world that went on with ordinary life until the day Noah entered the ark (Genesis 6–7). Compare Mark 13:32–37 and Luke 17:26–36; 12:39–40.
24.mean: Jesus gave signs for the fall of the temple, but for the day of his return he gives none. ‘No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.’ Jesus says that not even the Son knows (Christians explain this in different ways; see Where readings differ). If Jesus would not give a date, anyone who claims to have worked it out claims more than he did. Then Jesus describes what that day will be like. It will be like the days of Noah. People were eating and drinking, marrying and planning their futures. These are not wicked things in themselves. The problem was that life went on as if God would never act, until the flood came and swept them away. In the same way, two men will be working in a field, or two women grinding grain together, and one will be taken and the other left. People side by side, doing the same work, will face very different futures. Their outward lives looked alike; their readiness did not. So Jesus says, ‘keep watch, because you do not know the day on which your Lord will come.’ He gives a simple picture. If a homeowner knew when a thief was coming, he would stay awake. But thieves do not send warnings. ‘For this reason, you also must be ready’. The Westminster Confession says Christ keeps the day unknown so that people ‘may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful’. Watching does not mean staring at the sky or trying to decode the news. It means living each day as someone who belongs to Jesus and expects to meet him: faithful, awake and unashamed. The question is not ‘When will he come?’ but ‘If he came today, would he find me ready?’
24.big: No one knows the day of Christ’s return, not even the Son on earth, so his followers must live ready at every hour, unlike Noah’s generation.

vv.h: No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father
b: The BYZ and TR editions, following many later manuscripts, omit ‘nor the Son’ (BSB footnote); it stands in Mark 13:32. Calvin: ‘that man must be singularly mad, who would hesitate to submit to the ignorance which even the Son of God himself did not hesitate to endure on our account.’ Wesley: ‘Not while our Lord was on earth.’ See Where readings differ.

vv.h: they were oblivious until the flood came and swept them all away
b: Quarles notes that eating, drinking and marrying are ordinary things; the people lived as if they had all the time in the world. Calvin wished believers to ‘walk in the light of faith, that while they are uncertain as to the time, they may patiently wait’. Peter uses the flood as a warning of the coming judgement (2 Peter 3:5–7).

vv.h: Two men will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left
b: Luke adds ‘two people will be in one bed’ (Luke 17:34). Wesley: one is taken ‘Into God’s immediate protection: and one is left - To share the common calamities.’ Quarles thinks ‘taken’ means taken away in judgement, matching ‘swept them all away’ in verse 39. See Where readings differ.

vv.h: Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day on which your Lord will come
b: Quarles notes that ‘your Lord will come’ echoes Old Testament promises of the LORD’s coming. Wesley: ‘Either to require your soul of you, or to avenge himself of this nation.’

vv.h: If the homeowner had known in which watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have kept watch
b: ‘Broken into’ is literally ‘dug through’; Quarles notes that thieves often dug through mud-brick walls. The picture of the Lord coming ‘like a thief’ runs through the New Testament (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 16:15). Quarles quotes Blomberg on the parables that follow: Christ’s return is ‘completely unexpected’, then ‘sooner than expected’, then ‘later than expected’.

24.diff: ‘One will be taken’. Quarles notes that some interpreters see here the ‘rapture’ of believers before a time of tribulation; Dallas Theological Seminary teaches that the next great event will be ‘the coming of the Lord in the air to receive to Himself into heaven’ his people (art. 18), though it cites other passages for this. Quarles argues that ‘taken’ here means taken away in judgement, like those the flood ‘swept away’. Wesley read it the other way: taken ‘Into God’s immediate protection’. Calvin drew a practical lesson: no one should wait for a companion before getting ready; Christ meant ‘to enjoin every one to make haste’. All agree on the point: be ready. ‘Nor the Son’. In the 4th century Arians used this verse to deny Christ’s full deity. The church answered that Christ is one person with two natures, ‘the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union’ (Chalcedon, 451), and that he speaks as man, who ‘grew in wisdom’ (Luke 2:52). The Catholic Catechism says that what Christ ‘admitted to not knowing in this area, he elsewhere declared himself not sent to reveal’ (474). See also the note on Mark 13:32.

b: The Westminster Confession: Christ ‘will have that day unknown to men, that they may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful, because they know not at what hour the Lord will come; and may be ever prepared to say, Come Lord Jesus, come quickly, Amen’ (33.3). The Catholic Catechism: Christ’s coming ‘could be accomplished at any moment’ (673).

Jesus told his disciples after the resurrection, ‘It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority’ (Acts 1:7). Paul: ‘The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber’ (Romans 13:11).

l.t: Keep watch; you do not know when the master will return.
As in the days of Noah and of Lot.
The flood; the LORD shut him in.
If the homeowner had known.
The Day of the Lord like a thief in the night.
Scoffers, the flood, and the Lord’s patience.
Not for you to know times or seasons.

qs: Why do you think God has kept the day of Christ’s return hidden?
Noah’s neighbours were doing ordinary things. How can ordinary life make us forget God?
What would ‘keeping watch’ look like in your week, practically?

24.ctx: In wealthy households a trusted slave could be put in charge of the other servants, as Joseph was over Potiphar’s house (Genesis 39:4). This is the second of four parables about readiness for Christ’s return. Compare Luke 12:42–46.
24.mean: Jesus tells a story about a master who goes away and leaves one servant in charge of his household. The servant’s job is simple: give the others their food at the proper time. If the master comes back and finds him doing just that, he will be blessed and put in charge of everything the master owns. But suppose the servant is wicked. He tells himself, ‘My master will be away a long time.’ So he starts beating his fellow servants and partying with drunkards. He treats the master’s household as his own, and the master’s food as his own feast. Then the master returns on a day he does not expect. The punishment is terrible: the servant is cut to pieces and given a place with the hypocrites, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. The meaning is clear. The master is Jesus, who has gone away and will return. The servants are those who belong to him, especially those he has given responsibility for others. Wesley thought ministers might be ‘primarily intended’, and wrote that ‘no hypocrisy can be baser, than to call ourselves ministers of Christ, while we are the slaves of avarice, ambition, or sensuality.’ But the parable speaks to every disciple. Everything we have is entrusted to us, and the test is how we treat others while the Master seems far away. The faithful servant is not doing anything spectacular. He is simply doing his job, day after day, caring for others, whether or not anyone is watching. The wicked servant’s problem began with a thought: my master will be away a long time. When we stop expecting Christ, we start living for ourselves. Quarles sums it up: Christian thinking ‘acknowledges delay’, but Christian living ‘should assume imminence.’
24.big: The faithful servant keeps caring for the household until the master returns; the one who thinks ‘My master will be away a long time’ abuses others and is judged as a hypocrite.

vv.h: Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom the master has put in charge of his household
b: Wesley: wise means ‘Every moment retaining the clearest conviction, that all he now has is only intrusted to him as a steward’; faithful means ‘Thinking, speaking, and acting continually, in a manner suitable to that conviction.’ The Scofield notes: ‘It is faithfulness, not ability, in the Lord’s service that is first approved by Him.’

vv.h: Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns
b: Quarles notes that ‘household’ means the other servants, and that the duty was to give them their rations (Luke 12:42), a picture of caring for fellow disciples. Paul: ‘it is required of stewards that they be found faithful’ (1 Corinthians 4:2).

vv.h: suppose that servant is wicked and says in his heart, ‘My master will be away a long time.’
b: Quarles notes that the servant acts like a master but the opposite of his own master, perhaps feasting on the very food he should have shared. Wesley: ‘Now evil, having put away faith and a good conscience.’

vv.h: he will cut him to pieces and assign him a place with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth
b: Luke has ‘with the unbelievers’ (Luke 12:46). Quarles notes that ‘hypocrites’ recalls chapter 23: those who think themselves Jesus’ servants can share the hypocrites’ fate. ‘Weeping and gnashing of teeth’ describes final judgement (8:12; 13:42; 22:13; 25:30).

Peter applies the same idea to every believer: ‘As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another’ (1 Peter 4:10). He also warns leaders not to lord it over those entrusted to them (1 Peter 5:2–3).

Quarles notes that critics sometimes say the church invented Jesus’ sayings about delay when his return did not come quickly, and replies that such sayings belong to the earliest material shared by Matthew and Luke. Peter answers the scoffers: ‘The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise … but is patient with you’ (2 Peter 3:9).

l.t: To whom much is given, much will be required.
Joseph put in charge of Potiphar’s household.
Woe to you, hypocrites.
Stewards must be found faithful.
Shepherd the flock, not lording it over them.
The Lord is not slow; he is patient.

qs: What has God entrusted to you, and who depends on you to be faithful?
Why does thinking ‘My master will be away a long time’ lead to such bad behaviour?
Wesley thought this might apply especially to ministers. How should it shape the way leaders treat others?

25.h: The Parable of the Ten Virgins
25.ctx: Weddings usually took place at night. Young women from the bride’s circle would wait with lamps, go out to meet the bridegroom and escort him to the celebration. Small clay lamps burned olive oil and needed refilling. This parable is found only in Matthew; compare Luke 12:35–36 and 13:25–27.
25.mean: ‘At that time the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom.’ Five are foolish and five are wise. The difference seems small: the wise take extra oil in flasks; the foolish do not. Then comes the long wait. ‘When the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep.’ All ten sleep, wise and foolish alike. Then, at midnight, the cry rings out: ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’ They all wake and trim their lamps, and now the difference shows. ‘Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out.’ The wise cannot help: there may not be enough for both. While the foolish go to buy oil, the bridegroom arrives. ‘Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding banquet, and the door was shut.’ Later the others come back: ‘Lord, lord, open the door for us!’ But he replies, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ Jesus draws the lesson: ‘Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.’ The bridegroom is Jesus himself (9:15). The ten virgins all look like followers: they all have lamps, all go out, all wait. But some are not ready. This parable makes three things clear. First, Christ may come later than people expect, and readiness must last through the long wait. Second, readiness cannot be borrowed. No one can be ready for someone else; each person must come to Christ for themselves. Third, there comes a moment when the door is shut, as the LORD shut the door of Noah’s ark (Genesis 7:16). ‘Lord, lord’ is not enough; Jesus had warned that some who call him Lord will hear, ‘I never knew you’ (7:21–23). Christians differ over what the oil stands for (see Where readings differ), but the call is plain. Do not settle for looking like a disciple. Be ready, and stay ready, for the Bridegroom is coming.
25.big: The bridegroom came later than expected; those who were ready went in, and the door was shut on those who were not, so keep watch.

vv.h: the wise ones took oil in flasks along with their lamps
b: Wesley: the bridesmaids would wait at the bride’s house ‘with burning lamps or torches in their hands’, then go to meet the bridegroom and ‘conduct him to the bride.’ Calvin: ‘it was a childish speculation of Jerome and others, to adduce this passage in praise of virginity’; the parable answers the uneasiness caused by the delay of Christ’s coming.

vv.h: When the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep
b: ‘Delayed’ is the same word as in 24:48. Calvin did not read the sleep as sin: it means ‘earthly occupations, in which believers must be engaged’. Wesley: ‘the wise enjoying a true, the foolish a false peace.’

vv.h: Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out
b: Wesley: ‘Our faith is dead. What a time to discover this!’ Calvin: this is a reproof of ‘the late repentance of those who never think of what they are in want of, till the door is shut against every remedy.’

vv.h: there may not be enough for both us and you. Instead, go to those who sell oil and buy some for yourselves
b: Quarles: the point is not that the wise were selfish, but that no one can be ready on another’s behalf. Wesley: ‘no man has more than holiness enough for himself’. Calvin and Wesley both noted that God’s ‘buying’ needs no price (Isaiah 55:1): ‘Without money and without price: that is, to God, to Christ’ (Wesley).

vv.h: the door was shut … ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’
b: Quarles hears an echo of the flood: ‘Then the LORD shut him in’ (Genesis 7:16). ‘Lord, lord’ is the same cry as in 7:21–23. Luke records a similar warning about a shut door (Luke 13:25).

vv.h: Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour
b: The BYZ and TR editions add ‘when the Son of Man comes’ (BSB footnote). Wesley: the one who watches ‘is quiet; but not secure.’

25.diff: What is the oil? Interpreters have long debated it. Wesley: ‘The lamp is faith. A lamp and oil with it, is faith working by love.’ Calvin took it as the grace and ‘supplies necessary for completing the course of their life’, ‘a stock of provisions for a journey’. Others have seen the Holy Spirit or good works. Quarles thinks such identifications over-read the story: the oil simply stands for being ready, since the wise are called ‘those who were ready’. All agree that the parable warns against a faith that looks right but does not last. Who are the virgins? Calvin read the ‘kingdom of heaven’ here as ‘the condition of the future Church’, and Quarles takes the ten as professing disciples, both genuine and false.

b: Jesus told his disciples, ‘Be dressed for service and keep your lamps burning’, ‘like servants waiting for their master to return from the wedding banquet’ (Luke 12:35–36). Revelation pictures the end as a wedding: ‘the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready’ (Revelation 19:7).
Quarles: ‘Jesus will come later than people expect, but sooner than many are ready for.’

l.t: Keep your lamps burning.
The door shut; ‘I do not know where you are from.’
‘Lord, Lord’; the wise and foolish builders.
Jesus the bridegroom.
Then the LORD shut him in.
Come, buy without money and without cost.
The marriage supper of the Lamb.

qs: All ten virgins fell asleep. What, then, was the real difference between the wise and the foolish?
Why can readiness not be borrowed from someone else?
What helps us keep our ‘lamps burning’ through a long wait?

25.ctx: A talent was a very large sum of money, ‘about twenty years’ wages for a laborer’ (BSB footnote). Luke records a similar parable about ten servants and ten minas (Luke 19:11–27).
25.mean: Jesus tells of a man who goes on a journey and entrusts his wealth to his servants: five talents to one, two to another, one to a third, ‘each according to his own ability.’ The first two put the money to work and double it. The third digs a hole and buries it. After a long time the master returns to settle accounts. The first two come gladly with their profit, and each hears the same words: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! … Enter into the joy of your master!’ The one with two talents receives exactly the same praise as the one with five. The master looks for faithfulness, not size. Then the third servant comes. He says he knew his master was a hard man, so he was afraid and hid the money, and now he hands it back. The master calls him wicked and lazy. Even if he feared to take risks, he could at least have put the money in the bank to earn interest. His talent is taken and given to the one with ten, and he is thrown into the outer darkness. The master is Jesus, who has gone away and will return after a long time. Everything we have, money, abilities, time and opportunities, is his, entrusted to us to use for him and for others. Calvin said Christ ‘does not distinguish between natural gifts and the gifts of the Spirit’; all come from God. The third servant’s real problem was what he believed about his master. He saw him as harsh and grasping, so he did nothing. Wesley: ‘He never knew God, who thinks him a hard master.’ And he was not condemned for doing harm, but for doing nothing. Wesley drew the lesson sharply: ‘there is no such thing as negative goodness.’
25.big: Christ has entrusted his servants with his possessions; the faithful use them and share their master’s joy, while the servant who buried his talent out of a false view of his master is cast out.

vv.h: To one he gave five talents, to another two talents, and to another one talent—each according to his own ability
b: Calvin: ‘no man is found by God to be suitable till He has made him so.’ Wesley rendered ‘according to his own mighty power’ and noted that the master’s journey was ‘To heaven.’ The Lexham Bible Dictionary gives the talent as about twenty years’ wages, so even one talent was a fortune.

vv.h: But the servant who had received the one talent went off, dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master’s money
b: The BSB footnote notes that ‘at once’ may belong with the master’s departure or with the servant’s work. Wesley: the third servant ‘Made his having fewer talents than others a pretense for not improving any.’

vv.h: Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!
b: Quarles notes that ‘after a long time’ fits the theme of delay, and that ‘enter into’ is Matthew’s language for entering the kingdom (7:21; 18:3). Calvin compared the life of the godly to trading, whose gain is ‘general usefulness, which illustrates the glory of God’.

vv.h: Master, I knew that you are a hard man, reaping where you have not sown
b: Wesley: ‘He never knew God, who thinks him a hard master’; ‘So does every obstinate sinner, in one kind or other, lay the blame of his own sins on God.’ Quarles quotes Nolland: the excuse is ‘only a cover-up for wicked sloth.’

vv.h: You wicked, lazy servant! … Then you should have deposited my money with the bankers
b: Wesley: ‘This is not an allowing, but a strong denial of the charge.’ The master takes the servant at his word: even on his own view, he should have done the least he could. Compare Luke 19:22–23.

vv.h: For everyone who has will be given more … And throw that worthless servant into the outer darkness
b: The saying also appears in 13:12. Wesley: ‘for barely doing no harm, he is consigned to outer darkness. He is pronounced a wicked, because he was a slothful, an unprofitable servant.’ ‘Outer darkness’ and ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’ describe final judgement (8:12; 22:13).

25.diff: What are the talents? Calvin took them as every gift from God, natural or spiritual, together with the calling and opportunities to use them for others. Quarles thinks they stand especially for the money and resources Christ entrusts to his people, to be used for the good of others, as the servant in 24:45 fed the household; the words ‘lazy’ and ‘worthless’ show that time and energy are included too. Many readers apply the parable to every kind of gift. Reward and grace. Calvin stressed that God first makes his servants able; the rewards are his gift. Wesley warned against trusting in ‘mere harmlessness’. Christians agree that faithful service is rewarded (compare 1 Corinthians 3:12–15) and that idle profession will not stand.

b: Peter: ‘As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another’ (1 Peter 4:10). Paul: ‘We have different gifts according to the grace given us’ (Romans 12:6).

Quarles: watching for Christ does not mean gazing idly at the sky, which would be like burying the talent, but serving actively until he comes. Hebrews: ‘let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching’ (Hebrews 10:25).

l.t: The parable of the ten minas.
The faithful and wise servant.
Whoever has will be given more.
Good stewards of God’s grace.
Different gifts according to grace.
Each one’s work will be tested.

qs: Why do you think the two-talent servant received exactly the same praise as the five-talent servant?
How did the third servant’s view of his master shape what he did?
What ‘talents’ has God entrusted to you, and are any of them buried?

25.ctx: This is the last teaching in Jesus’ final discourse, given privately to his disciples, before the passion story begins (26:1–2). Ezekiel pictured God judging ‘between one sheep and another, between the rams and the goats’ (Ezekiel 34:17).
25.mean: Jesus ends his teaching with a scene of the last judgement. The Son of Man comes in glory with all his angels and sits on his throne. All the nations are gathered before him, and he separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, the sheep on his right, the place of honour, and the goats on his left. The King welcomes those on his right: ‘Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’ The reason he gives is surprising. When he was hungry and thirsty, they fed him. When he was a stranger, they took him in. When he was naked, sick or in prison, they clothed him, cared for him and visited him. The righteous are astonished; they never saw him in need. ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.’ Then he turns to those on his left and sends them away into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. They too are astonished. They never saw him in need either. But in neglecting the least, they neglected him. The scene ends with two destinies: eternal punishment and eternal life. This shows who Jesus is. The humble teacher about to be crucified is the King and Judge of all nations, doing what the prophets said God himself would do. It also shows how seriously he takes love in action. The righteous did not earn the kingdom by their own goodness; the Father prepared it for them long before. Their simple, unnoticed acts of mercy came from belonging to him (see Where readings differ). Christians debate who ‘the least of these brothers’ are (see Where readings differ). Calvin and Quarles read them as Jesus’ disciples in need; many others apply the words to all who suffer. Either way, Christ is honoured or neglected in the people in front of us.
25.big: The Son of Man will judge the nations as King, welcoming those whose love for the least of his brothers showed they were his, and sending away those who neglected him in them.

vv.h: When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne
b: Quarles hears Zechariah 14:5: ‘Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him’, now said of the Son of Man, and Daniel 7:9–14, where thrones are set and books opened. Wesley called the passage ‘one of the noblest instances of the true sublime.’ Compare 16:27 and 19:28.

vv.h: He will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats
b: Quarles notes that ‘them’ is masculine in Greek, while ‘nations’ is neuter: the judgement is of individuals, not whole nations. In Ezekiel 34 it is the LORD who judges between sheep and goats, so the Son of Man takes a task that belongs to God.

vv.h: Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world
b: Calvin: by calling them ‘blessed of the Father, he reminds them, that their salvation proceeded from the undeserved favor of God.’ Quarles calls this one of the clearest statements of God’s gracious election in the first three Gospels; the deeds that follow are evidence, not merit. Wesley: the kingdom was ‘Purchased by my blood, for all who have believed in me with the faith which wrought by love.’

vv.h: I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat … I was in prison and you visited Me
b: Wesley: ‘Prisoners need to be visited above all others, as they are commonly solitary and forsaken by the rest of the world.’ The righteous are surprised; Wesley: ‘neither of them have the same estimation of their own works as the Judge hath.’ The Catholic Catechism’s ‘corporal works of mercy’, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked and visiting the sick and imprisoned, echo this passage (2447).

vv.h: whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me
b: Jesus calls those who do his Father’s will his brothers (12:50), and his disciples ‘little ones’ (10:42). Calvin: ‘Believers only are expressly recommended to our notice; not that he bids us altogether despise others’; but ‘Christ is either neglected or honored in the person of those who need our assistance.’ Wesley: ‘What encouragement is here to assist the household of faith? But let us likewise remember to do good to all men.’

vv.h: Depart from Me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels
b: Quarles notes the differences: the righteous are ‘blessed by My Father’, the wicked simply ‘cursed’; the kingdom was prepared for people, but the fire ‘for the devil and his angels’. Wesley: ‘Not originally for you: you are intruders into everlasting fire.’ Calvin: ‘the term fire represents metaphorically that dreadful punishment which our senses are unable to comprehend.’

vv.h: And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life
b: The same word ‘eternal’ is used of both. Wesley: ‘Either therefore the punishment is strictly eternal, or the reward is not: the very same expression being applied to the former as to the latter.’ See Where readings differ.

25.diff: Who are ‘the least of these’? Calvin, Quarles and many others take them as Jesus’ disciples in need (compare 10:40–42; 12:50); Calvin added that this does not mean we ‘altogether despise others’. Many others, including much Catholic teaching, apply the words to all the poor and needy; the Catechism says ‘we shall be separated from him if we fail to meet the serious needs of the poor and the little ones who are his brethren’ (1033). Wesley held both: help ‘the household of faith’, but ‘do good to all men’ (compare Galatians 6:10). Saved by works? Protestants read the deeds as the evidence of real faith, not its cause, since the kingdom was ‘prepared for you from the foundation of the world’; Catholics read them as the fruit of grace that God rewards: ‘The charity of Christ is the source in us of all our merits before God’ (Catechism 2011). Both agree that faith that never shows love is not saving faith (James 2:14–17). ‘Eternal punishment’. Most traditions hold that it is unending: Wesley (above), the Westminster Confession (‘eternal torments’, 33.2), the Catholic Catechism (‘the existence of hell and its eternity’, 1035) and Dallas Theological Seminary (‘not to be annihilated’). Quarles describes it as ‘eternal, conscious torment’. Those who hold conditional immortality, including Seventh-day Adventists (‘fire from God will consume them’, Fundamental Belief 27) and, tentatively, John Stott, read it as a final, irreversible destruction. See also the note on Mark 9:42.

b: The prophets called for this kind of love: ‘to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him’ (Isaiah 58:7). ‘Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD’ (Proverbs 19:17). John: ‘If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?’ (1 John 3:17).

The Catholic Catechism says the Last Judgment ‘calls men to conversion while God is still giving them “the acceptable time”’ (1041). The Westminster Confession says the day of judgement is appointed ‘both to deter all men from sin; and for the greater consolation of the godly in their adversity’ (33.3).

l.t: I will judge between sheep and goats; my servant David will shepherd them.
The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him.
Thrones set, books opened, the Son of Man given dominion.
A cup of cold water to one of these little ones.
Share your bread with the hungry.
Faith without works is dead.
We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

qs: Why were both groups surprised by what the King said?
Who are the ‘least of these’ in our town, and in our church?
How does the truth that Christ is honoured or neglected in people change the way we treat them this week?

26.ctx: Jesus has finished his last long block of teaching (chapters 24–25). Matthew ends each of the other four blocks with a similar phrase (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1), but only here does he say ‘all these things’: the teaching is over and the suffering begins. Passover was the great spring festival, and Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims, many of them from Galilee. The high priest Caiaphas held office from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long time.
26.mean:
Jesus has said all he came to say. Now he tells his disciples what will happen next: ‘You know that the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.’ He has spoken of his death three times before (16:21; 17:22–23; 20:18–19). This time he gives the day.

At the same moment, the leaders are meeting in the courtyard of Caiaphas the high priest. They agree to arrest Jesus quietly and kill him. But they are nervous. The city is full of pilgrims, and many of them admire Jesus. So they say: ‘not during the feast … or there may be a riot.’

Matthew lets us see two plans side by side. The leaders plan to wait until after the feast. Jesus says it will happen at the feast. As the story goes on, their plan changes, because Judas comes to them with an offer (26:14–16). Jesus will die at Passover after all, just as he said.

This matters because Passover was about rescue. Each year Israel remembered how God brought them out of slavery in Egypt, and how the blood of a lamb protected them on the night of judgment (Exodus 12). Jesus’ death at Passover is no accident. Paul would later write, ‘Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed’ (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The words ‘handed over’ run through the whole story. Judas hands Jesus over to the leaders. They hand him over to Pilate. Pilate hands him over to be crucified. Yet behind them all, God the Father is giving up his Son for the world. The men who plot in the courtyard think they are in control. They are not.
26.big: Jesus foretells that he will be handed over to be crucified at Passover, while the leaders secretly plot to kill him after the feast.

vv.h: the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified
b: Wesley: ‘When he had spoken all he had to speak. Till then he would not enter upon his passion: then he would delay it no longer.’ Quarles notes that ‘handed over’ can point to Judas, to the leaders, or to God himself giving up his Son (compare 26:24; John 3:16; Romans 8:32). Crucifixion was the most shameful Roman death; Josephus called it the most wretched way of dying.

vv.h: the chief priests and elders of the people assembled in the courtyard of the high priest
b: Quarles notes that a meeting in the high priest’s courtyard was probably an informal gathering, not a full session of the council. Josephus counts twenty-eight high priests in the 107 years from Herod the Great to the fall of the temple; Quarles takes Caiaphas’s long tenure to mean he knew how to stay on good terms with Rome.

vv.h: they conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him
b: Quarles notes that the Greek word for ‘covertly’ (dolos, cunning or deceit) is used in the Greek Old Testament for planned murder (Exodus 21:14). Psalm 31:13 describes enemies who ‘conspire against me and plot to take my life’.

vv.h: “But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”
b: Wesley: ‘This was the result of human wisdom. But when Judas came they changed their purpose. So the counsel of God took place, and the true paschal Lamb was offered up on the great day of the paschal solemnity.’ Quarles quotes John Chrysostom, who observed that they feared the people but not God.

John records the meeting that set the plot in motion, where Caiaphas said, ‘it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish’, and John comments that he spoke more truly than he knew (John 11:49–53).

Peter later preached that Jesus ‘was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death’ (Acts 2:23). Both are true at once: God’s purpose stands, and those who did evil were responsible for it.

l.t: Mark’s account.
Luke’s account.
Caiaphas: one man must die for the people.
The first Passover.
Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
Delivered up by God’s set plan.
He did not spare His own Son.

qs: Matthew sets the leaders’ plan beside Jesus’ words. Whose plan actually happens, and what does that tell us?
Why do you think Jesus chose to die at Passover rather than at some other time?
The leaders feared the crowd but not God. Where are you tempted to fear people more than God?
