26.ctx: Bethany was a village on the far side of the Mount of Olives, under two miles from Jerusalem; Jesus was staying there during the festival (21:17). Mark tells the same story, and John says the woman was Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, and that the meal took place six days before Passover (John 12:1–8). Matthew and Mark seem to place it here to set her love beside Judas’s betrayal. Luke records an anointing by a ‘sinful woman’ earlier in Jesus’ ministry (Luke 7:36–50), usually taken to be a different event.
26.mean:
Jesus is at a meal in Bethany, in the home of a man known as Simon the Leper. Perhaps Jesus had healed him. A woman comes in with an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume and pours it over Jesus’ head.

The disciples are annoyed. ‘Why this waste?’ they ask. The perfume could have been sold and the money given to the poor. That sounds sensible, even godly. John tells us that Judas led the complaint, and that he was really a thief (John 12:4–6).

Jesus defends her. ‘She has done a beautiful deed to Me.’ He reminds them that there will always be poor people to help, and they should help them. But he will not be with them much longer. Then he explains what she has done: ‘she has prepared My body for burial.’ She may not have understood it fully, but her gift fits what is about to happen. Executed criminals were often not given an honourable burial. Jesus has been anointed in advance.

Then comes a remarkable promise: ‘wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.’ Jesus expects his message to go to the whole world (24:14; 28:19). And it has. We are reading about her now.

The contrast with the next scene is sharp. She gives something precious to Jesus and asks nothing back. Judas goes to sell Jesus for money (26:14–16). Love that seems wasteful to others is precious to Jesus. It is not a choice between loving Jesus and caring for the poor. Those who love him most will care for those he cares about.
26.big: A woman pours costly perfume on Jesus, and he defends her ‘waste’ as a beautiful act that prepares his body for burial and will be remembered wherever the gospel is preached.

vv.h: a woman came to Him with an alabaster jar of expensive perfume, which she poured on His head
b: Anointing the head could mark a king (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6). Quarles notes that Matthew may intend a hint of this, but that Jesus himself explains it as preparation for burial. The BSB footnote notes that ‘Simon the Leper’ may reflect an Aramaic phrase meaning ‘Simon the Potter’ or ‘Jar Maker’.

vv.h: Why this waste?
b: Wesley: ‘It seems several of them were angry, and spoke, though none so warmly as Judas Iscariot.’ John says Judas ‘did not say this because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief’ (John 12:6).

vv.h: She has done a beautiful deed to Me. The poor you will always have with you
b: Jesus echoes Deuteronomy 15:11: ‘There will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother.’ Far from excusing neglect of the poor, the verse commands generosity. Wesley: ‘Such is the wise and gracious providence of God, that we may have always opportunities of relieving their wants’. Calvin distinguished ‘the ordinary service, which ought to be maintained among believers, and that extraordinary service, which ceased after his ascension’.

vv.h: she has prepared My body for burial
b: Wesley: ‘Indeed this was not her design: but our Lord puts this construction upon it’. Calvin said Jesus valued the ointment ‘solely in reference to his burial’, and that ‘his grave would yield a sweet odor, as it breathed life and salvation through the whole world.’ The women who came to anoint his body after his death would find the tomb empty (Mark 16:1).

vv.h: wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her
b: Quarles connects this with the commission to make disciples of all nations (28:19). Jesus, about to be betrayed and killed, speaks calmly of a worldwide gospel.

26.diff: Was this the same anointing as in John and Luke? John tells the same story with more detail: the woman is Mary of Bethany, she anoints Jesus’ feet, and the date is six days before Passover (John 12:1–8). Most interpreters take Matthew, Mark and John to describe one event. Calvin is firm about this, and Quarles suggests that, if so, Matthew and Mark place it here for its meaning rather than its date. Luke’s account of a ‘sinful woman’ in the home of a Pharisee named Simon (Luke 7:36–50) is usually taken to be a different occasion, earlier in Jesus’ ministry. Calvin noted that differences between John’s account and Matthew’s had led some ‘erroneously to imagine that it is a different narrative’.

b: Mary of Bethany is the one who earlier ‘sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message’ while Martha served (Luke 10:38–42). If John is right that she was the woman here, her extravagant gift came from time spent listening to Jesus.
Jesus’ concern for the poor runs through Matthew (5:3; 6:2–4; 19:21; 25:35–40). James and John later warned against faith that ignores a brother or sister in need (James 2:15–17; 1 John 3:17).

l.t: Mark’s account: ‘She has done what she could.’
Mary of Bethany anoints Jesus’ feet.
A different anointing in a Pharisee’s home.
Open wide your hand to the poor.
Mary sits at Jesus’ feet.
Though He was rich, He became poor for your sake.

qs: Why did the disciples see the woman’s gift as waste? What did Jesus see?
Jesus says, ‘The poor you will always have with you.’ How can this verse be misused, and what does it really mean in its Old Testament setting?
What would ‘wasteful’ love for Jesus look like in your life this week?

26.ctx: Judas Iscariot is always named last in the lists of the Twelve, with a note that he betrayed Jesus (10:4). He looked after the group’s money (John 12:6; 13:29). Matthew alone gives the price: thirty pieces of silver, probably silver shekels. In the Law of Moses this was the compensation paid if an ox gored a slave to death (Exodus 21:32). The prophet Zechariah was paid the same sum, sarcastically called ‘this magnificent price’ (Zechariah 11:12–13).
26.mean:
Straight after the woman’s gift, Matthew shows us Judas. He was ‘one of the Twelve’, chosen by Jesus, sent out to preach, a witness of his miracles. Now he goes to the chief priests with a question: ‘What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?’

The question shows what is in his heart. He does not ask what is right. He asks what he can get. The priests count out thirty pieces of silver. This was not a fortune. In the Law it was the sum an ox’s owner paid if his ox killed another man’s slave (Exodus 21:32). The Son of God is sold for the price of a slave.

Many people have wondered why Judas did it. The Gospels give hints rather than a full answer. John says he was a thief who stole from the money bag (John 12:6). Luke and John say Satan entered him (Luke 22:3; John 13:27). Matthew points to money. Calvin wrote that ‘the cause and source of so great blindness in Judas was avarice’, that is, greed.

From then on, Judas ‘looked for an opportunity’. He needed a time when Jesus was away from the crowds. He would find it at night, in a garden.

The story of Judas is a warning. He spent his days close to Jesus, yet his heart was never truly given to him. Being near Jesus is not the same as belonging to him. And love of money can grow quietly until a person will sell what is most precious for very little (1 Timothy 6:10).
26.big: Judas, one of the Twelve, offers to hand Jesus over to the chief priests and agrees to do it for thirty pieces of silver.

vv.h: one of the Twelve, the one called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests
b: The Lexham Bible Dictionary calls the name ‘Iscariot’ obscure; it probably refers to his home town (some manuscripts of John read ‘from Kerioth’). Jesus had said, ‘Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!’ (John 6:70).

vv.h: What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?
b: Quarles takes the question as showing a mercenary motive. Calvin: ‘the cause and source of so great blindness in Judas was avarice’. Wesley: thirty pieces of silver, ‘the price of a slave, Exod. xxi, 32.’ Matthew will later show this fulfilling Zechariah 11:12–13 (27:9–10).

vv.h: from then on Judas looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus
b: Luke adds that he looked for an opportunity ‘in the absence of a crowd’ (Luke 22:6). The leaders’ fear of the crowd (26:5) made Judas useful to them.

26.diff: Why did Judas betray Jesus? The Gospels give several hints: greed (26:15; John 12:6), the work of Satan (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27), and perhaps disappointment that Jesus was not the kind of king he expected, though this last is a guess, not something the Gospels say. The Lexham Bible Dictionary lists these and other suggestions. The Lexham Bible Dictionary notes that Marvin Meyer and Bart Ehrman have read the so-called Gospel of Judas, a 2nd-century writing, as presenting him as the disciple who understood Jesus best and helped him to his death in obedience; April DeConick disputes this reading. The New Testament gives no support to such a picture: Jesus calls his act a betrayal and pronounces a ‘woe’ on him (26:24). Calvin warned that whether Satan entered Judas bodily ‘is an idle speculation’; the point is the warning to us.

b: Psalm 41:9 was taken up by Jesus himself: ‘Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me’ (quoted in John 13:18).
Paul warns that ‘the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil’ and that by craving it some ‘have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows’ (1 Timothy 6:10).

l.t: Mark’s account: they promised to give him money.
Satan entered Judas.
Thirty shekels: the price of a slave.
Thirty pieces of silver: ‘this magnificent price’.
My close friend has lifted up his heel against me.
The love of money is a root of evil.

qs: Judas asked, ‘What are you willing to give me?’ How does that question show what was in his heart?
How could someone spend three years close to Jesus and still betray him? What warning is there for us?
Where might love of money, comfort or approval be quietly shaping your choices?

26.ctx: The Feast of Unleavened Bread lasted seven days and began with the Passover meal (Exodus 12:14–20). Mark explains that ‘the first day’ here was the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed (Mark 14:12), that is, the 14th of Nisan. Luke says Jesus sent Peter and John (Luke 22:8). Each lamb had to be shared by a group, and Jesus and the Twelve formed one such household. See the history note on how Passover was kept.
26.mean:
Matthew presents this as the day the Passover lambs were killed. The disciples ask Jesus where he wants them to prepare the meal. The city is crammed with pilgrims, and every room is in demand.

Jesus already has a plan. ‘Go into the city to a certain man and tell him that the Teacher says, “My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house.”’ Matthew does not name the man. Perhaps he was a follower of Jesus. Mark and Luke add that he would show them a large upstairs room, already furnished (Mark 14:15; Luke 22:12).

Notice the words ‘My time is near’. Jesus is not being swept along by events. He knows exactly what is coming and when. The leaders are plotting and Judas is watching for his chance, but Jesus is the one setting the time.

The disciples do as Jesus told them and get the Passover ready. A Passover meal normally included the lamb, the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs that recalled the bitterness of slavery, the wine, and the sauce for dipping. Everything about the meal pointed back to the night God rescued his people from Egypt.

This ordinary preparation is part of something much bigger. Jesus is about to give the old meal a new meaning. The lamb that was killed so that Israel could go free pointed forward to him. John the Baptist had called him ‘the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world’ (John 1:29). Peter and John, who prepared this meal, would later write of him as the Lamb whose blood redeems his people (1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9).
26.big: Jesus, knowing that his time has come, sends his disciples to prepare the Passover meal at a house he has chosen.

vv.h: Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?
b: The BSB footnote gives the literal Greek, ‘On the first of the Unleavened’. Wesley: ‘Being Thursday, the fourteenth day of the first month, Exod. xii, 6, 15.’ Quarles notes that by custom all leaven was searched out the night before and burned by midday.

vv.h: My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house.
b: Wesley: ‘That is, the time of my suffering.’ Quarles notes that only Matthew includes ‘My time is near’, which suggests the host already knew Jesus well. Jesus calls himself ‘the Teacher’, the title he claimed for himself alone in 23:8.

vv.h: So the disciples did as Jesus had directed them and prepared the Passover
b: Matthew’s wording may echo the obedience of Israel at the first Passover: ‘they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron’ (Exodus 12:28).

26.diff: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal? Matthew, Mark and Luke clearly present it as one (26:17–19). John’s Gospel seems to place Jesus’ death on the day the lambs were killed, before the Passover meal (John 18:28; 19:14). Christians have explained this in different ways. Wesley simply took the Synoptic dating (‘Thursday, the fourteenth day’). Calvin accepted John’s timing and argued that Jesus kept the day appointed by the Law while the people, by an old custom, put their meal off by a day that year: ‘I have no doubt, therefore, that Christ observed the day appointed by the Law, and that the Jews followed a custom which had been long in use.’ Quarles thinks the meal was held the evening before the lambs were sacrificed, noting that no lamb is mentioned, so that Jesus died at the very time the Passover lambs were killed. Others, such as Routledge (cited in the Lexham Bible Dictionary), stress that the Gospels say plainly they were preparing to ‘eat the Passover’. Several other harmonisations have been proposed. All four Gospels connect Jesus’ death with Passover.

hist.t: How Passover was kept in Jesus’ day
b: Passover remembered the night God brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 12). Pilgrims crowded into Jerusalem. On the afternoon of the 14th of the month Nisan the lambs were killed in the temple courts, and the meal was eaten that evening, which by Jewish reckoning was the start of the 15th. Josephus says the sacrifices were offered ‘from the ninth hour till the eleventh’ (about 3 to 5 pm), with ‘a company not less than ten’ for each lamb. He reports that when the high priests once counted, the number of sacrifices was 256,500 (Jewish War 6.423–424). Whatever the exact figure, the city was packed.

Most of what we know about the meal itself comes from the Mishnah (tractate Pesahim), written down about AD 200. Quarles thinks its pattern probably applied in Jesus’ day: several cups of wine, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, a dish to dip them in, a child asking why this night is different, the story of the exodus retold, and the singing of the ‘Hallel’ Psalms (113–118). Since the Mishnah is later, how much of this detail goes back to the time of Jesus is uncertain.

b: At the first Passover the blood of the lamb on the doorposts meant that judgment ‘passed over’ the house (Exodus 12:13). Quarles notes that Jesus’ death at Passover presents him as the one whose blood protects his people from judgment.

Paul tells the church to keep the festival ‘not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth’ (1 Corinthians 5:8). The Christian life is a lasting Passover.

l.t: A large upper room, furnished and ready.
Jesus sends Peter and John.
Jesus knew His hour had come.
The first Passover.
The Lamb of God.
Redeemed with the precious blood of Christ.

qs: What does ‘My time is near’ tell us about how Jesus faced his death?
The disciples prepared the meal exactly as Jesus said. What simple acts of obedience is he asking of you?
How does knowing the story of the first Passover help you understand what Jesus did?

26.ctx: At a Passover meal people reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow. Bread and bitter herbs were dipped in a shared bowl of sauce. John records that Jesus washed the disciples’ feet at this meal and that the beloved disciple asked who the betrayer was (John 13:1–30). Psalms 41 and 55 speak of betrayal by a close friend.
26.mean:
Evening comes, and Jesus reclines at the table with the Twelve. In the middle of the meal he says something that stops everyone: ‘Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me.’

The disciples are deeply upset. One by one they ask, ‘Surely not I, Lord?’ In Greek the question expects the answer ‘No’. None of them points at Judas. They do not suspect him, and each one wonders whether he himself could do such a thing. That honest fear is healthier than easy confidence.

Jesus answers: ‘The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me.’ To share a meal was a sign of friendship. Betrayal by someone you have eaten with was especially painful (Psalm 41:9).

Then Jesus says two things that belong together. ‘The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him.’ His death is part of God’s plan, foretold in Scripture. ‘But woe to that man by whom He is betrayed.’ God’s plan does not excuse Judas. He is fully responsible for what he chooses. ‘It would be better for him if he had not been born.’

Judas speaks last: ‘Surely not I, Rabbi?’ The others call Jesus ‘Lord’. Judas calls him only ‘Rabbi’, teacher. Jesus replies, ‘You have said it yourself.’ It is a quiet ‘yes’. Jesus knows. Even now, he does not shame Judas before the others. The door is still open, but Judas will walk out of it.

This scene teaches us two things at once. God is in control, even of the worst evil. And each of us is responsible for what we do with Jesus.
26.big: At the meal at Passover time Jesus announces that one of the Twelve will betray him, declaring that his death fulfils Scripture yet pronouncing woe on the betrayer.

vv.h: Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me
b: The BSB footnote notes that the BYZ and TR editions read ‘the Twelve’ for ‘the twelve disciples’. Jewish days ran from sunset, so ‘evening’ began a new day.

vv.h: Surely not I, Lord?
b: Quarles notes that the form of the question expects a ‘no’, and that since none of them suspected Judas, Jesus’ knowledge here is more than human insight.

vv.h: The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me
b: Wesley: ‘Which it seems Judas was doing at that very time.’ Quarles describes the bowl as holding a paste of fruit and nuts in which the bitter herbs were dipped (compare Exodus 12:8).

vv.h: The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed
b: Calvin: ‘By this expression we are taught what a dreadful vengeance awaits the wicked, for whom it would have been better that they had never been born.’ Wesley asked: ‘May not the same be said of every man that finally perishes? But who can reconcile this, if it were true of Judas alone, with the doctrine of universal salvation?’ His point is that the saying would make no sense if all were finally saved.

vv.h: Surely not I, Rabbi?”Jesus answered, “You have said it yourself.
b: Wesley: ‘That is, it is as thou hast said.’ Quarles notes that Judas calls Jesus ‘Rabbi’ here and at the arrest (26:49), never ‘Lord’. Jesus gives the same answer to the high priest (26:64).

26.diff: God’s plan and Judas’s guilt. Jesus says both that the Son of Man goes ‘as it is written’ and that Judas is under woe. Christians affirm both truths but explain them differently. The Reformed Westminster Confession says God ‘ordain whatsoever comes to pass: yet so, as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures’ (3.1). The Catholic Catechism says God’s eternal plan ‘includes in it each person’s free response to his grace’, and that ‘God permitted the acts that flowed from their blindness’ (600), speaking of those who condemned Jesus. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians commonly stress that God’s foreknowledge of a choice does not cause it. Peter’s sermon holds the two together without explaining how: Jesus was handed over ‘by God’s set plan and foreknowledge’, yet those who killed him did wrong (Acts 2:23).

b: John records that Jesus, ‘troubled in spirit’, gave Judas the piece of bread he had dipped, and that ‘as soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out into the night’ (John 13:21–30).
Quarles connects ‘as it is written’ with Psalm 109, which Peter quotes about Judas in Acts 1:20, and with the righteous sufferer of the Psalms who is betrayed by a friend.

l.t: Mark’s account.
The hand of My betrayer is with Me on the table.
Judas takes the morsel and goes out into the night.
The one who shared my bread.
It is not an enemy who taunts me.
Peter on Judas and the Psalms.

qs: Each disciple asked, ‘Surely not I?’ Why is that a better response than ‘I would never do that’?
Jesus says his death is written in Scripture, yet Judas is responsible. How do you hold those two truths together?
Jesus knew what Judas would do and still shared the meal with him. What does that show you about Jesus?

26.ctx: This is the first account of what Christians call the Lord’s Supper, Holy Communion or the Eucharist (from the Greek for ‘thanksgiving’). Paul’s account (1 Corinthians 11:23–26), written in the early 50s, is the earliest record of it. At Passover the head of the household gave thanks over the bread and over cups of wine and explained what the meal meant. The ‘blood of the covenant’ recalls the covenant at Sinai, sealed with sacrificial blood (Exodus 24:8), and the ‘new covenant’ promised by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31–34).
26.mean:
During the meal Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and hands it to his disciples. ‘Take and eat; this is My body.’ Then he takes a cup, gives thanks again, and passes it round. ‘Drink from it, all of you. This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.’

At Passover, the head of the family explained what each part of the meal meant. The bread recalled the haste of leaving Egypt. Now Jesus gives the bread and the cup a new meaning. He ties them to his own body, soon to be broken, and his own blood, soon to be poured out on the cross. (Christians describe how Christ is present in the Supper in different ways; see Different readings.)

The ‘blood of the covenant’ takes us back to Mount Sinai. There Moses sprinkled the blood of sacrifices on the people and said, ‘This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you’ (Exodus 24:8). Centuries later Jeremiah promised a new covenant, when God would write his law on people’s hearts and remember their sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus says his death will seal that new covenant.

Only Matthew records the words ‘for the forgiveness of sins’. This was the reason for Jesus’ name: ‘He will save His people from their sins’ (1:21). His blood is poured out ‘for many’, echoing the Servant in Isaiah who ‘bore the sin of many’ (Isaiah 53:12).

Then Jesus looks ahead. He will not drink wine again until he drinks it new with them in his Father’s kingdom. The meal points back to the cross and forward to a great feast when Jesus returns (8:11; Revelation 19:9).

They sing a hymn and go out into the night. Every time Christians share this meal, they remember his death and look for his coming (1 Corinthians 11:26).
26.big: At the meal at Passover time Jesus gives bread and wine as his body and his blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, and looks forward to drinking it new in his Father’s kingdom.

vv.h: Take and eat; this is My body
b: Wesley: ‘This bread is, that is, signifies or represents my body, according to the style of the sacred writers.’ Calvin: ‘The true eating of the flesh of Christ, therefore, is not only pointed out by the sign, but is likewise exhibited in reality.’ Other traditions read ‘is’ more literally; see Different readings.

vv.h: This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins
b: The BSB footnote notes that the BYZ and TR editions read ‘the new covenant’; Luke and Paul both have ‘new covenant’ (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). Calvin took ‘many’ to mean ‘not a part of the world only, but the whole human race; for he contrasts many with one’. Wesley: ‘As many as spring from Adam.’ Many Reformed Christians, following the Canons of Dort (Second Head, art. 8), hold that Christ’s death was intended to save the elect and read ‘many’ in that light, so Calvin’s comment is debated among his heirs. Quarles notes the echo of Isaiah 53:11–12.

vv.h: I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father’s kingdom
b: The prophets pictured God’s coming kingdom as a feast with fine wine (Isaiah 25:6). Quarles links this with the messianic banquet (8:11; 22:1–14). Wesley: ‘I shall taste no more wine, till I drink wine of quite another kind in the glorious kingdom of my Father. And of this you shall also partake with me.’

vv.h: And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives
b: Wesley: the hymn ‘consisteth of six psalms, from the 113th to the 118th’. These psalms are known as the Hallel. Psalm 118 includes the words, ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’ (Psalm 118:22; compare 21:42).

26.diff: What does ‘This is My body’ mean? Almost all Christians keep the Lord’s Supper (Quakers and the Salvation Army do not), and agree that Jesus gave it and that it proclaims his death (1 Corinthians 11:26). Most also see it as a sharing in Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16). They differ on how he is present. The Catholic Church teaches that at the consecration the whole substance of the bread and wine becomes the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), and that the Eucharist is ‘the memorial of his sacrifice’ (Catechism 1376; 611). The Orthodox Church also speaks of a real change, while calling the manner a mystery. Lutherans confess ‘the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the bread and wine’ (Small Catechism). The Reformed, with Calvin, deny any ‘change of the substance’ but hold that believers ‘spiritually, receive, and feed upon, Christ crucified’ (Westminster Confession 29.7); the 1689 Baptist Confession uses the same words (30.7). Many other Baptists and evangelicals stress remembrance and proclamation. Wesley’s note reads ‘is’ as ‘signifies or represents’, though Wesley also counted the Supper among the ‘means of grace’ through which God works. Quarles also reads ‘is’ as ‘represents’, comparing Jesus’ explanations of the parables (13:37–39). See the glossary entry on the Lord’s Supper.

b: Paul, who received this tradition within a few years of the resurrection, adds Jesus’ words ‘do this in remembrance of Me’ and comments, ‘as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes’ (1 Corinthians 11:24–26).

Hebrews explains the new covenant through Jeremiah 31: Christ ‘entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption’, and is ‘the mediator of a new covenant’ (Hebrews 9:12, 15).

l.t: Mark’s account.
Do this in remembrance of Me.
Paul’s account: proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.
The blood of the covenant at Sinai.
The new covenant: I will remember their sins no more.
He bore the sin of many.
A participation in the body and blood of Christ.

qs: What did the bread and cup mean at Passover, and what new meaning did Jesus give them?
Jesus says his blood is poured out ‘for the forgiveness of sins’. What difference does that make when you come to Communion?
The Supper looks back to the cross and forward to Jesus’ return. Which of these do you tend to forget?

26.ctx: Jesus and the disciples walk from the city across the Kidron Valley to the Mount of Olives. Zechariah 13:7, which Jesus quotes, speaks of the LORD’s own shepherd being struck and the flock scattered, and goes on to describe a refined people who call on God’s name (Zechariah 13:8–9). Luke and John place Jesus’ warning to Peter at the supper itself (Luke 22:31–34; John 13:36–38).
26.mean:
On the way out to the Mount of Olives Jesus says something hard: ‘This very night you will all fall away on account of Me.’ Not just Judas. All of them.

He quotes the prophet Zechariah: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ In Zechariah the LORD himself calls for the shepherd to be struck. The death of Jesus is not simply something men do to him. It is part of God’s plan. When the shepherd falls, the sheep will run.

But Jesus immediately adds a promise: ‘after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.’ He knows they will fail, and he has already planned to gather them again. Like a shepherd walking ahead of his flock, he will lead them on.

Peter cannot accept it. ‘Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will.’ He means it. He loves Jesus. But he trusts his own strength, and he compares himself with the others.

Jesus answers with painful precision: ‘this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.’ Peter insists: ‘Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.’ All the others say the same.

Within hours they will all run away, and Peter will do exactly what Jesus said. But Jesus has already promised to meet them after he rises. His faithfulness does not depend on theirs. Wesley put it like this: ‘Though you forsake me, I will not for this forsake you.’

This is good news for anyone who has failed Jesus. Our confidence is not in how strong our love is, but in how strong his is.
26.big: Jesus warns that all the disciples will fall away as Scripture foretold, and that Peter will deny him three times, but promises to go ahead of them to Galilee after he rises.

vv.h: I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered
b: Quarles notes that ‘fall away’ here means to abandon Jesus, and that in Zechariah 13:7 the shepherd is ‘the man who is My companion’, standing close to the LORD himself. Calvin applied the prophecy more widely than most commentators: ‘though almost all commentators confine the passage in Zechariah 13:7 to the person of Christ alone, yet I extend it farther’. He added: ‘there is no unity that brings salvation but that which keeps the sheep united under Christ’s crook.’

vv.h: But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee
b: Wesley: ‘as a shepherd before his sheep … Though you forsake me, I will not for this forsake you.’ The promise is repeated at the empty tomb (28:7) and kept on a mountain in Galilee (28:16).

vv.h: this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times
b: Wesley explained ‘before cock crowing’ as ‘before three in the morning, the usual time of cock crowing’. Mark records that the rooster would crow twice (Mark 14:30).

vv.h: Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You
b: Wesley: ‘such was the tenderness of our Lord, that he would not aggravate their sin by making any reply.’ Quarles quotes Origen: no one is able to keep from falling away except by the Holy Spirit.

26.diff: Who is the shepherd in Zechariah 13:7? Most Christian interpreters, following Jesus’ own use of the verse here, read Zechariah’s shepherd as pointing to the Messiah. Quarles notes that the shepherd is called the LORD’s ‘companion’ and is linked with the pierced one of Zechariah 12:10, and he cites Craig Blomberg’s view that this is direct prophecy fulfilled straightforwardly. Calvin took a broader view. He thought the prophecy also described the loss of good leaders in Israel in the troubled period after the tyrant Antiochus (2nd century BC), so that ‘a government, on which the salvation of the people depends, will no longer exist’; Jesus’ arrest and the scattering of the disciples then fit the same pattern.

b: Jesus told Peter, ‘Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers’ (Luke 22:31–32). Peter’s failure was already covered by Jesus’ prayer.
Paul warns that ‘the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall’, and promises that God ‘will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear’ (1 Corinthians 10:12–13).

l.t: Before the rooster crows twice.
I have prayed for you, that your faith will not fail.
Will you really lay down your life for Me?
Strike the shepherd; the sheep will be scattered.
God will gather his scattered sheep.
Whoever thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.

qs: Peter compared himself with the others: ‘Even if all fall away … I never will.’ Why is that kind of comparison dangerous?
Jesus promised to meet them in Galilee before they had even failed. What does that tell you about how he treats those who let him down?
Where are you relying on your own strength to stay faithful rather than on Jesus?

26.ctx: Gethsemane means ‘oil press’. It was an olive grove on the lower western slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from the temple; John calls it a garden and says Jesus often met there with his disciples (John 18:1–2). In the Old Testament the ‘cup’ is often a picture of God’s judgment poured out on sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Luke adds that Jesus’ sweat became ‘like drops of blood’ (Luke 22:44; some manuscripts do not include verses 43–44).
26.mean:
Jesus comes to an olive grove called Gethsemane. He tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, and takes Peter, James and John with him. Then Jesus becomes ‘sorrowful and deeply distressed’. He tells them, ‘My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death.’

He goes a little further, falls on his face and prays: ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.’

What is this cup? The prophets spoke of a cup of God’s anger against sin (Isaiah 51:17). Quarles and many Protestants hear in this that Jesus is about to bear the judgment that sin deserves. Other Christians put more weight on the horror of death itself and on Jesus’ willing obedience (see Different readings). Either way, his soul shrinks back. Calvin warned that we must not be embarrassed by Jesus’ fear and sorrow, because our rescue depends on his being truly human. He feels what we feel.

Yet he does not turn back. ‘Not as I will, but as You will.’ These are the words he taught his disciples to pray: ‘Your will be done’ (6:10). The second time he prays, ‘if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done.’ He now accepts that there is no other way.

Three times he comes back and finds his friends asleep. ‘Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.’ They want to stay awake, but they cannot.

At last Jesus stands up. ‘Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!’ He does not wait to be dragged away. He walks out to meet them. Because he said yes to the Father in the garden, he can go to the cross in peace.
26.big: In anguish Jesus prays for the cup to pass from him, yet submits to his Father’s will, while his disciples sleep instead of keeping watch.

vv.h: He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee and began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed
b: These three had seen his glory on the mountain (17:1–8). Now they see his anguish. Wesley: ‘Probably from feeling the arrows of the Almighty stick fast in his soul, while God laid on him the iniquities of us all.’

vv.h: My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death
b: Quarles hears an echo of the lament in Psalms 42–43: ‘Why are you downcast, O my soul?’ (Psalm 42:5). Calvin quoted Ambrose: ‘He grieved for me, who had no cause of grief for himself’.

vv.h: My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.
b: Quarles notes that the cup is the cup of God’s wrath (Isaiah 51:17–22; Jeremiah 25:15–29), and that the Greek for ‘pass’ is the word used in the Greek Old Testament for the LORD ‘passing over’ Israel’s houses (Exodus 12:23). The Catholic Catechism says that here Jesus ‘expresses the horror that death represented for his human nature’, and that ‘by accepting in his human will that the Father’s will be done, he accepts his death as redemptive’ (612).

vv.h: Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.
b: Wesley: ‘How gentle a rebuke was this, and how kind an apology!’ Calvin: Jesus ‘gives them the praise of willingness, in order that their weakness may not throw them into despair, and yet urges them to prayer’. Compare ‘lead us not into temptation’ (6:13).

vv.h: My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done
b: Quarles notes that the second prayer repeats the Lord’s Prayer word for word, ‘Your will be done’ (6:10). Hebrews says Jesus ‘offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears’ and ‘was heard because of His reverence’ (Hebrews 5:7).

vv.h: Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!
b: Quarles notes that Jesus walks towards those coming to arrest him. John records that he went out to meet them and asked, ‘Whom are you seeking?’ (John 18:4).

26.diff: What does the prayer tell us about God’s plan? Some, such as the ‘open theist’ Gregory Boyd, argue that Jesus’ prayer shows that divine plans are, in principle, open to change. Quarles answers that this is a desperate plea, not a statement of doctrine, and that Jesus’ words in 26:53–54 show that God had the power to rescue him but that his plan required the cross. Most Christian traditions, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, read the prayer as showing that Jesus had a true human will which freely and fully submitted to the Father’s will (Catechism 612). Calvin stressed the reality of Christ’s fear: without it, ‘our redemption will perish and be lost.’ What was the cup? Quarles reads it as the cup of God’s wrath against sin (Isaiah 51:17), and Wesley spoke of ‘the arrows of the Almighty’. The Catholic Catechism stresses ‘the horror that death represented for his human nature’ and Jesus’ obedient acceptance of a redemptive death (612).

b: Hebrews draws comfort from this scene: ‘we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin’ (Hebrews 4:15).
Isaiah describes ‘the cup of His fury’ which God would take from his people’s hands (Isaiah 51:17, 22). Jesus drinks it so that they do not have to.

l.t: Abba, Father, all things are possible for You.
His sweat was like drops of blood.
Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?
The cup of God’s wrath taken away.
Why are you downcast, O my soul?
Loud cries and tears; he learned obedience.
A high priest who sympathizes with our weakness.

qs: What do you think the ‘cup’ was that Jesus shrank from?
Jesus was honest about his anguish and still said, ‘Not as I will, but as You will.’ How can you pray like that in a hard situation?
‘The spirit is willing, but the body is weak.’ Where do you see this in your own life, and what does Jesus tell us to do about it?

26.ctx: The crowd was sent by the chief priests and elders; it probably included temple police. John mentions a band of soldiers and names the disciple with the sword as Peter and the servant as Malchus (John 18:3, 10). A Roman legion had about 6,000 soldiers. A kiss was a normal greeting between a disciple and his teacher. Luke records that Jesus healed the servant’s ear (Luke 22:51).
26.mean:
While Jesus is still speaking, Judas arrives with a large crowd carrying swords and clubs. He has arranged a signal: ‘The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.’ In the dark, among the olive trees, they need to be sure which man is Jesus.

Judas goes straight up to him. ‘Greetings, Rabbi!’ he says, and kisses him. A sign of love becomes the tool of betrayal. Jesus replies, ‘Friend, do what you came for.’ Jesus replies calmly. He is not caught off guard.

The men seize Jesus. One of his companions draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant. John tells us it was Peter. Peter is still trying to keep his promise to die with Jesus.

Jesus stops him. ‘Put your sword back in its place. For all who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ Then he explains. If he wanted rescue, he could ask his Father, and more than twelve legions of angels would come at once. That is tens of thousands. Jesus is not helpless. He is choosing this. ‘But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?’

Jesus turns to the crowd. Why come at night with weapons, as if he were a dangerous outlaw? He taught openly in the temple every day. Yet even this, he says, has happened so that the prophets’ words would be fulfilled.

Then comes one of the saddest sentences in the Gospel: ‘all the disciples deserted Him and fled.’ The shepherd has been struck, and the sheep are scattered, just as Jesus said.

Jesus goes alone, not because he is weak, but because he has chosen the way of the cross.
26.big: Judas betrays Jesus with a kiss; Jesus forbids his disciples to defend him with the sword, freely gives himself up to fulfil the Scriptures, and all the disciples flee.

vv.h: Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him
b: Calvin noted that ‘it was a very common practice among the Jews to welcome friends with a kiss’, which made Judas’s kiss ‘a pretense’. Quarles recalls Joab, who greeted Amasa with a kiss and stabbed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10). Proverbs 27:6: ‘the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.’

vv.h: Friend,” Jesus replied, “do what you came for
b: The BSB footnote gives another possible translation: ‘Friend, for what have you come?’ Quarles notes that the word for ‘friend’ here is the one Jesus uses in the parables for someone in the wrong (20:13; 22:12). Wesley: ‘With what composure does he go forth to meet the traitor! With what calmness receive that malignant kiss!’

vv.h: Put your sword back in its place,” Jesus said to him. “For all who draw the sword will die by the sword.
b: Calvin: ‘By these words, Christ confirms the precept of the Law, which forbids private individuals to use the sword.’ Wesley explained ‘all they that take the sword’ as ‘Without God’s giving it them: without sufficient authority.’ See Different readings.

vv.h: more than twelve legions of angels
b: Quarles notes that twelve legions would be over 70,000. Jesus could have been rescued, but ‘it must happen this way’ (compare 16:21). Wesley: the least of the angels, ‘it is probable, could overturn the earth’.

vv.h: Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled
b: The word for ‘outlaw’ (lēstēs) was also used of armed rebels. Quarles lists Scriptures Jesus may have in mind, including Isaiah 53:12, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors’ (quoted in Luke 22:37), and Zechariah 13:7 (26:31). Mark adds a young man who fled naked (Mark 14:51–52).

26.diff: ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword’: may Christians ever use force? The Anabaptist tradition reads Jesus’ command, with the Sermon on the Mount, as forbidding Christians to use the sword: the sword is ‘ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ’ (Schleitheim Confession, 1527). Mennonites and Quakers have historically held to nonviolence. Most other traditions read the verse as addressed to Peter’s act: a private person using violence to stop God’s plan. Calvin said Jesus here forbids ‘private individuals’ to use the sword, but distinguished ‘a civil court and the court of conscience’, holding that defence against a robber is not punishable, provided it is without ‘excessive wrath’. The Westminster Confession says that Christian rulers ‘may lawfully, now under the new testament, wage war, upon just and necessary occasion’ (23.2). Quarles calls the verse a ‘favorite prooftext’ for pacifism but thinks it is not a universal rule. Compare the note on 5:38–42.

b: Peter himself later wrote that Christ ‘did not retaliate’ when insulted and ‘entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly’, leaving us ‘an example, that you should follow in His footsteps’ (1 Peter 2:21–23).
Jesus told Pilate, ‘My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest by the Jews’ (John 18:36). His kingdom does not spread by force of arms.

l.t: A young man flees naked.
Jesus heals the servant’s ear.
Peter, Malchus, and ‘I am He’.
Joab’s treacherous kiss.
Numbered with the transgressors.
When He suffered, He made no threats.
My kingdom is not of this world.

qs: What does Jesus’ calm response to Judas show you about him?
Why did Jesus refuse both Peter’s sword and the angels’ help?
When you feel threatened or wronged, what is your first instinct? How does Jesus’ example challenge it?

26.ctx: The Sanhedrin was the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem, led by the high priest. According to John, the leaders could not carry out the death penalty themselves under Roman rule (John 18:31). John records that Jesus was first questioned by Annas, Caiaphas’s father-in-law and a former high priest (John 18:13, 19–24). Matthew and Mark describe a hearing at night, and all three Synoptic Gospels a meeting in the morning (27:1). Daniel 7:13–14 describes ‘One like the Son of Man, coming with the clouds of heaven’, and Psalm 110:1 the Lord’s king seated at God’s right hand.
26.mean:
Jesus is taken to the house of Caiaphas, where the council has gathered in the middle of the night. Peter follows at a distance and slips into the courtyard to see what will happen.

The leaders have already decided the outcome. They look for false testimony so that they can put Jesus to death. Many witnesses come, but their stories do not agree. The Law required at least two witnesses to agree (Deuteronomy 19:15). At last two come forward with a twisted version of something Jesus once said: ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days.’ John tells us that Jesus had been speaking about his own body (John 2:19–21).

Jesus says nothing. Isaiah had written of the Servant, ‘He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth’ (Isaiah 53:7).

Then the high priest puts him under oath: ‘Tell us if You are the Christ, the Son of God.’ Now Jesus speaks. ‘You have said it yourself.’ It means yes. Then he goes further: ‘from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.’ He joins two great Old Testament pictures: the king at God’s right hand (Psalm 110:1) and the heavenly Son of Man who receives everlasting rule (Daniel 7:13–14). The prisoner says that they will see him enthroned.

The high priest tears his clothes. ‘He has blasphemed!’ That is, Jesus has insulted God. The council agrees: ‘He deserves to die.’ Then they spit in his face, hit him, and mock him: ‘Prophesy to us, Christ! Who hit You?’

It is a terrible irony. Meanwhile, outside in the courtyard, Jesus’ prophecy about Peter is coming true.
26.big: Before the council Jesus stays silent against false witnesses, then declares under oath that he is the Christ and the Son of Man who will sit at God’s right hand, and is condemned for blasphemy and mocked.

vv.h: Peter followed Him at a distance, right up to the courtyard of the high priest
b: Wesley: ‘love constrained him to follow his Master; fear made him follow afar off.’ Quarles notes that the ‘guards’ Peter sat with were court officers, making it a dangerous place for him.

vv.h: I am able to destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days
b: Wesley called these ‘false witnesses’, ‘although part of what they said was true; because our Lord did not speak some of those words at all; nor any of them in this sense.’ Quarles notes that to claim power to rebuild the temple in three days was to claim divine power.

vv.h: But Jesus remained silent
b: Compare Isaiah 53:7. The high priest’s oath, ‘by the living God’, put Jesus under a solemn obligation to answer. Calvin said the high priest ‘contrived an unfounded charge of blasphemy’ while refusing to inquire honestly.

vv.h: from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven
b: The BSB footnote gives ‘the right hand of the Mighty One’ as an alternative and points to Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. Quarles notes that ‘Power’ is a reverent way of saying ‘God’. Wesley: ‘Our Lord looked very unlike that person now!’

vv.h: He has blasphemed! Why do we need any more witnesses?
b: Quarles notes the rule in the Mishnah (a later rabbinic text, about AD 200) that judges who heard blasphemy tore their clothes and did not mend them (Sanhedrin 7:5). Leviticus 24:16 commanded death for blasphemy. Wesley: Caiaphas ‘expressed, in the most artful manner, his horror’.

vv.h: Then they spit in His face and struck Him
b: Compare the Servant: ‘I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle’ (Isaiah 50:6). Quarles notes that only Matthew says ‘in His face’. The mockery, ‘Prophesy to us’, happens while Jesus’ prophecy about Peter is being fulfilled (26:69–75).

26.diff: When will they ‘see the Son of Man … coming on the clouds’? Calvin read this as the second coming: ‘by this word hereafter he distinguishes between his first and second coming’, and the wicked ‘will be compelled to behold him on high coming from heaven’. Quarles notes that ‘from now on’ points to something beginning at once, and takes it as Jesus’ vindication and enthronement: the signs at his death, his resurrection, Pentecost and the judgment on the temple in AD 70. On this reading the ‘coming’ of Daniel 7:13 is a coming to God to receive the kingdom, as in Daniel, rather than to earth. Some readers combine the two: Jesus’ rule begins with his resurrection and will be seen by all when he returns (compare 24:30; 28:18).

b: Mark does not name the high priest, but Matthew and John do: Caiaphas. Josephus calls him ‘Joseph Caiaphas’ and records his appointment under the governor Valerius Gratus. He held office from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long time, covering nearly all of Pilate’s governorship.

The Caiaphas ossuary (Widely accepted). In 1990 builders accidentally uncovered a family tomb in modern Jerusalem. One finely decorated bone box (ossuary) is inscribed ‘Joseph, son of Caiaphas’. Many scholars think it is the high priest’s. It cannot be certain, because Joseph was a common name and the inscription does not mention the high priesthood.

src.l: Josephus, Antiquities 18.33–35 (Whiston): Joseph Caiaphas made high priest
‘Caiaphas’ (Archaeological Evidence), Lexham Bible Dictionary

b: The Mishnah (about AD 200) lays down rules for capital trials: they were to be held by day, not on the eve of a Sabbath or festival, with a second day before a guilty verdict, and with arguments for acquittal heard first (Sanhedrin 4–5). By those rules the hearing in Matthew 26 broke several laws. Quarles thinks the Mishnah’s rules are probably an accurate picture of procedure in Jesus’ day.

Many scholars are less sure. The Lexham Bible Dictionary notes that ‘the key question regards the extent to which procedures found in the Mishnah (compiled in the early third century) were practiced in the first century’, and that the later rabbinic picture of the council ‘has often been retrojected’ onto the first century. If the rules did apply, the leaders may simply have bent them in an emergency, before the festival and before Pilate’s court opened at dawn. Matthew, Mark and John describe questioning at the high priest’s house at night, while Luke has Jesus held there overnight and brought before the council at daybreak. All four agree that he was handed to Pilate in the morning.

b: Stephen, on trial before the same council, saw ‘the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’ (Acts 7:56), and was killed for saying so.

Jesus’ answer is the clearest claim to divine authority in Matthew. Daniel’s Son of Man receives ‘dominion, glory, and kingship’, that ‘the people of every nation and language’ should serve him (Daniel 7:14). The risen Jesus will claim exactly this: ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me’ (28:18).

l.t: ‘I am,’ said Jesus.
If I tell you, you will not believe.
Before Annas, then Caiaphas.
One like a son of man, coming with the clouds.
Sit at My right hand.
He did not open His mouth.
I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle.
Stephen sees the Son of Man at God’s right hand.

qs: Why do you think Jesus stayed silent before the false witnesses but spoke when asked if he was the Christ?
Jesus, on trial, tells his judges that they will see him enthroned. How does that change the way you see this scene?
Jesus was mocked and struck and did not retaliate. How does his example help you when you are treated unfairly?

26.ctx: Peter was from Bethsaida and lived in Capernaum, in Galilee; Galileans had a distinctive accent. All four Gospels record his three denials (Mark 14:66–72; Luke 22:54–62; John 18:15–27). Luke adds that ‘the Lord turned and looked at Peter’ (Luke 22:61). John later records Jesus’ threefold question to Peter, ‘Do you love Me?’ (John 21:15–17).
26.mean:
Out in the courtyard, a servant girl comes up to Peter. ‘You also were with Jesus the Galilean.’ In front of everyone Peter says, ‘I do not know what you are talking about.’

He moves away to the gateway. Another servant girl sees him and tells the people there, ‘This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.’ This time Peter denies it with an oath: ‘I do not know the man!’ He will not even say Jesus’ name.

A little later a group of bystanders come up to him. ‘Surely you are one of them, for your accent gives you away.’ Peter’s Galilean voice betrays him. Now he begins ‘to curse and swear’, calling down curses if he is lying. ‘I do not know the man!’

At that moment a rooster crows.

Peter remembers. A few hours earlier he had said, ‘Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.’ And Jesus had said, ‘Before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.’ Peter goes outside and weeps bitterly.

Each denial is stronger than the last, and each time Peter moves further away. Fear has taken hold of the man who drew his sword in the garden. Brave in a fight, he is broken by a servant girl’s question.

Yet this is not the end of Peter’s story. His tears are the start of real repentance. After the resurrection Jesus sends a special message to ‘His disciples and Peter’ (Mark 16:7), and later restores him by asking three times, ‘Do you love Me?’ (John 21:15–17). Calvin called Peter’s fall ‘a bright mirror of our weakness’, and his repentance ‘a striking instance of the goodness and mercy of God’. If Peter could be forgiven, so can we.
26.big: Peter, warming himself in the high priest’s courtyard, denies three times that he knows Jesus, then hears the rooster crow, remembers Jesus’ words and weeps bitterly.

vv.h: But he denied it before them all
b: Jesus had warned, ‘whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven’ (10:33). Quarles notes that each denial is more public and more forceful than the one before.

vv.h: And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man!”
b: Jesus had taught that his followers should not need oaths, but let their ‘Yes’ be yes (5:33–37). Wesley: ‘To which possibly he was not unaccustomed, before our Lord called him.’

vv.h: Surely you are one of them,” they said, “for your accent gives you away
b: Wesley: ‘such is the overruling providence of God, that the world, in the height of their zeal, commonly catch hold of the very weakest of all arguments against the children of God.’ Quarles notes that the witnesses now include men, whose word carried more weight in court.

vv.h: At that he began to curse and swear to them
b: Quarles notes that to ‘curse’ means to call down God’s judgment, whether on himself, on his accusers or even on Jesus; the text does not say which. Wesley: ‘Having now quite lost the reins, the government of himself.’

vv.h: And he went outside and wept bitterly
b: Calvin: ‘Peter’s fall, which is here related, is a bright mirror of our weakness. In his repentance, also, a striking instance of the goodness and mercy of God is held out to us.’ He added that the story is useful ‘to comfort those who have fallen, by holding out to them the hope of pardon’.

26.diff: How serious was Peter’s denial? Quarles notes that some early writers tried to soften it. Ambrose and Hilary suggested that Peter only denied knowing ‘the man’, not denying that Jesus was God. Jerome called this ‘frivolous’. Origen thought Peter could not stand firm until the Spirit came. Most interpreters since, following Calvin, see it as a real and serious sin that shows how weak any believer can be, and Peter’s restoration as a picture of God’s mercy to the fallen. The difference between Peter and Judas is not the size of their sins but what they did next: Peter wept and came back to Jesus; Judas went back to the priests (27:3–5).

b: Peter, restored, became the rock Jesus had promised (16:18). Weeks later he stood up in Jerusalem and boldly preached the risen Christ (Acts 2:14–36). Years later he wrote: ‘Be sober-minded and alert. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion … the God of all grace … will Himself restore you’ (1 Peter 5:8–10).

Paul describes ‘godly sorrow’ that ‘brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret’, unlike ‘worldly sorrow’ that ‘brings death’ (2 Corinthians 7:10). Peter and Judas illustrate the difference.

l.t: The rooster crows a second time.
The Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Peter warms himself at the fire.
Whoever denies Me before men.
Do you love Me? Feed My sheep.
Godly sorrow and worldly sorrow.
God will restore you.

qs: Peter was brave with a sword but afraid of a servant girl. Why do you think small pressures can be harder to resist than big ones?
What made Peter’s tears different from Judas’s remorse?
Is there a failure you need to bring back to Jesus? What does Peter’s story tell you about how he will receive you?

27.ctx: At dawn the council met again and sent Jesus to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, whose sentence was needed for a crucifixion. Matthew then tells what happened to Judas; Acts gives a shorter, different account of his death (Acts 1:18–19). The quotation in 27:9–10 draws mainly on Zechariah 11:12–13, where the prophet’s wages of thirty pieces of silver are thrown to ‘the potter’ in the house of the LORD, together with themes from Jeremiah, who bought a field (Jeremiah 32:6–9) and preached at the potter’s house and the Valley of Hinnom (Jeremiah 18–19).
27.mean:
At first light the leaders confirm their decision. Jesus must die. They tie him up and hand him over to Pilate the governor, because, as John records, the council could not carry out an execution itself (John 18:31).

Judas sees that Jesus has been condemned, and he is filled with remorse. He takes the thirty pieces of silver back to the priests. ‘I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.’ What he says is true. Jesus is innocent, and Judas knows it.

The priests do not care. ‘What is that to us? You bear the responsibility.’ They have what they wanted. These religious leaders, who were meant to be shepherds, push away a man in despair.

Judas throws the money into the temple, goes away and takes his own life. Matthew does not tell us whether he ever asked for mercy. He went to the priests, not to Jesus. Calvin saw in him regret, but not a real change of heart.

Now the priests have a problem. They pick up the coins and say, ‘It is unlawful to put this into the treasury, since it is blood money’, money paid for a death. They are careful about the rules on money, but not about condemning an innocent man. So they buy a potter’s field to bury foreigners. Ever since, Matthew says, it has been called the Field of Blood.

Matthew sees prophecy fulfilled even here. In Zechariah’s story, the shepherd God sent was paid off with thirty pieces of silver, a slave’s price, as if he were worth little, and the money was thrown to the potter (Zechariah 11:12–13). Matthew sees the same pattern here: Jesus has been valued at that price.

The contrast with Peter is striking. Both failed Jesus on the same night. Peter wept and came back to him. No sin is too great for Jesus to forgive. If you are carrying guilt or despair, Peter’s story, not Judas’s, is the invitation: come back to Jesus, and talk to someone you trust.
27.big: Judas, seized with remorse, returns the silver and hangs himself, and the priests buy a potter’s field with the blood money, fulfilling what the prophets foretold.

vv.h: They bound Him, led Him away, and handed Him over to Pilate the governor
b: Wesley explains that the council met in a temple court ‘which was never opened in the night’, so they waited till morning. Quarles notes that Jewish law prescribed stoning for blasphemy, but that the leaders needed Rome to carry out an execution (John 18:31).

vv.h: I have sinned by betraying innocent blood
b: Quarles notes the curse in Deuteronomy 27:25 on anyone ‘who accepts a bribe to kill an innocent person’. Calvin: Judas ‘repented; not that he reformed, but that the crime which he had committed gave him uneasiness’. Wesley on the priests: ‘How easily could they digest innocent blood!’

vv.h: Then he went away and hanged himself
b: Acts 1:18 gives a different account of his death (he ‘fell headlong’); see Different readings. Jesus had said it would have been better for him not to have been born (26:24).

vv.h: It is unlawful to put this into the treasury, since it is blood money
b: Wesley: ‘It is not lawful (say they) to put it into the treasury - But very lawful to slay the innocent!’ He suggested the field was cheap because it had been dug for potters’ clay. Compare Jesus’ charge that they strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (23:24).

vv.h: They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel
b: The BSB footnote points to Jeremiah 19:1–15, Jeremiah 32:6–9 and Zechariah 11:12–13. Quarles thinks Matthew combines Zechariah’s words with Jeremiah’s field and potter, and names Jeremiah because the field purchase comes from him. See Different readings.

27.diff: Why ‘Jeremiah’? The words quoted are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13. Calvin admitted, ‘How the name of Jeremiah crept in, I confess that I do not know’, and thought it had been ‘put down by mistake’. Wesley said the name ‘was added to the text in latter copies’ and ‘is evidently a mistake’, although modern Greek editions print ‘Jeremiah’ and the BSB notes no other reading. Quarles and many modern interpreters think Matthew is deliberately combining Zechariah with Jeremiah, whose prophecies about a potter, a field bought with silver and innocent blood in the Valley of Hinnom (Jeremiah 19; 32) shape the passage; Matthew names Jeremiah because the field purchase comes from him. Mark does something similar, introducing words from Malachi and Isaiah as ‘written in Isaiah the prophet’ (Mark 1:2–3, in the best manuscripts). How did Judas die? Matthew says he hanged himself; Acts says he fell headlong, and that the field was called Akeldama (Acts 1:18–19). The Lexham Bible Dictionary notes that some harmonise these by suggesting the rope or branch broke and he fell; and that I. Howard Marshall suggested the priests’ purchase could be counted as Judas’s, since it was his money. Marshall also allowed that the writers may simply be reporting what was said in Jerusalem, without intending their accounts to be harmonised.

b: Matthew says the field bought with Judas’s money ‘has been called the Field of Blood to this day’ (27:8). Acts gives its Aramaic name, Akeldama, ‘Field of Blood’ (Acts 1:19). In the 4th century Eusebius and Jerome placed it south of the Valley of Hinnom, near where it meets the Kidron Valley, south of the old city.

A Greek Orthodox convent of St Onuphrius stands near the traditional site today. The area has red clay, fitting the name ‘potter’s field’, and it was used for burials for centuries. Whether this is the very field cannot be proved, but the tradition is old.

src.l: ‘Akeldama’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Nolland; Marshall)

b: In Zechariah 11 the prophet acts out the part of a shepherd rejected by the flock. When he asks for his wages they weigh out thirty pieces of silver, and the LORD says, ‘Throw it to the potter’, and the prophet adds, ‘this magnificent price at which they valued me’ (Zechariah 11:13). The rejection of the shepherd is the rejection of God himself.

Paul distinguishes ‘godly sorrow’, which ‘brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret’, from ‘worldly sorrow’, which ‘brings death’ (2 Corinthians 7:10). Calvin’s French version of his commentary contrasts Judas’s forced regret with ‘a true conversion of the man to God’. Quarles notes, however, that Matthew uses the same word for ‘remorse’ of the son who changed his mind and obeyed (21:29), so the word alone does not decide.

The priests were careful about the rules for money but not about justice. Where can religious people fall into the same trap today?
What would you say to someone who thinks they have gone too far to be forgiven?

27.ctx: Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36/37. He normally lived at Caesarea on the coast but came to Jerusalem at festivals to keep order. A claim to be ‘King of the Jews’ was a political charge: it suggested rebellion against Caesar. Luke records that the leaders accused Jesus of forbidding taxes to Caesar (Luke 23:2), and John records a longer conversation about his kingdom (John 18:33–38).
27.mean:
Jesus now stands before the Roman governor. Pilate begins with one question: ‘Are You the King of the Jews?’

To a Roman, that question was about politics. A man who called himself a king might be planning a revolt. The chief priests and elders had judged Jesus guilty of blasphemy, which would mean little to a Roman governor. Luke tells us that they accused him before Pilate of opposing Roman rule (Luke 23:2).

Jesus answers, ‘You have said so.’ It is a careful yes. He is the King of the Jews, the promised son of David. But he is not the kind of king Pilate fears. As John records, he told Pilate, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ (John 18:36).

Then the chief priests and elders pile up accusations. Jesus says nothing. Pilate is puzzled. ‘Do You not hear how many charges they are bringing against You?’ Still Jesus gives no answer, not even to one charge. Pilate is amazed.

Prisoners would often beg for their lives or argue their case. Jesus does neither. Wesley points out that he had openly said he was the Christ before Caiaphas, and the King before Pilate, ‘clearly showing thereby, that his answering no more, was not owing to any fear.’ He is silent because he has chosen to go to the cross.

Isaiah had foretold this: ‘as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth’ (Isaiah 53:7). He had also said that kings would be silenced by the Servant (Isaiah 52:15). The governor marvels at a prisoner who will not defend himself.

The silence of Jesus speaks. He is not a victim trapped by events. He is the willing Lamb.
27.big: Before Pilate Jesus acknowledges that he is the King of the Jews but makes no reply to the leaders’ accusations, leaving the governor amazed.

vv.h: Are You the King of the Jews?”“You have said so,” Jesus replied
b: Quarles notes that ‘You have said so’ is a qualified yes, like Jesus’ answer to Caiaphas (26:64). Wesley: ‘Jesus before Caiaphas avows himself to be the Christ, before Pilate to be a king’. The same title will be fixed above the cross (27:37).

vv.h: And when He was accused by the chief priests and elders, He gave no answer
b: Compare Isaiah 53:7. Peter later wrote that ‘when they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate’ (1 Peter 2:23).

vv.h: But Jesus gave no answer, not even to a single charge, much to the governor’s amazement
b: Quarles hears an echo of Isaiah 52:15, where kings ‘shut their mouths’ because of the Servant. Paul reminded Timothy of ‘Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate’ (1 Timothy 6:13).

Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36/37 and is one of the best-attested figures of the period. Josephus describes him bringing Roman standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem by night, backing down when crowds offered to die rather than see their law broken, and later using temple funds for an aqueduct and having protesters clubbed. The Roman historian Tacitus writes that ‘Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus’.

The Pilate Stone. In 1961 Italian archaeologists excavating the theatre at Caesarea Maritima found a reused limestone block with a Latin inscription recording that Pilate dedicated a building in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It gives his title as ‘prefect of Judea’ and is now in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

b: The early creeds name Pilate: Jesus ‘was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate’ (Nicene Creed). The name ties the gospel to a real date and a real place in history.

Jesus’ kingship is a theme from Matthew’s first chapter: the son of David (1:1), the one born ‘King of the Jews’ whom the Magi came to worship (2:2). Now a Roman governor asks the same question, and soon soldiers will mock him with the same title (27:29).

27.ctx: Barabbas was a well-known prisoner; Mark and Luke say he had taken part in an uprising and committed murder (Mark 15:7; Luke 23:19), and John calls him an ‘insurrectionist’ (John 18:40). Pilate sat on the ‘judgment seat’ (Greek bēma), a raised platform from which a governor gave verdicts. Washing hands to show innocence of blood appears in the Law (Deuteronomy 21:6–9). Roman flogging, which usually came before crucifixion, was brutal and could itself kill.
27.mean:
Pilate has a custom at Passover of releasing one prisoner chosen by the crowd. He sees a way out. He offers them a choice: ‘Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?’ Barabbas was a notorious prisoner, a rebel and a murderer. Pilate knows that the leaders have handed Jesus over ‘out of envy’, and he expects the crowd to choose Jesus.

While he sits in judgment, his wife sends him a message: ‘Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him.’ Pilate’s wife, outside the quarrel, is troubled enough to warn him.

But the chief priests and elders work on the crowd. When Pilate asks again, they shout, ‘Barabbas!’ And Jesus? ‘Crucify Him!’ Pilate asks, ‘Why? What evil has He done?’ No one gives a reason. They just shout louder.

Pilate sees that a riot is starting. He takes water and washes his hands in front of them. ‘I am innocent of this man’s blood. You bear the responsibility.’ But washing his hands cannot wash away his guilt. He is the judge, and he knows Jesus is innocent. Calvin asked, ‘how could a few drops of water wash away the stain of a crime’?

The crowd, stirred up by the chief priests and elders, answers, ‘His blood be on us and on our children!’ Sadly, this verse was later misused to blame all Jewish people for Jesus’ death, with terrible results. Matthew is not saying that. The crowd that day did not speak for all Jews, then or since. And Jesus had said that his blood would be ‘poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’ (26:28).

So Barabbas, the guilty man, goes free, and Jesus, the innocent one, is flogged and handed over to die. Many Christians have seen in this exchange a picture of the gospel: the innocent dies in the place of the guilty.
27.big: Offered a choice, the crowd demands the release of Barabbas and the crucifixion of Jesus; Pilate, though he knows Jesus is innocent, washes his hands and hands him over to be crucified.

vv.h: Which one do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?
b: The BSB footnote notes that some editions read ‘Jesus Barabbas’ in verses 16 and 17; see the history note. Calvin thought Pilate deliberately chose ‘a very wicked man, by contrast with whom Christ might be set free’. Wesley on ‘envy’: ‘they envied him, because the people magnified him.’

vv.h: Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him
b: Only Matthew records this. God had spoken through dreams earlier in Matthew to protect Jesus (1:20; 2:12–13, 22). Calvin rejected the common view that the devil sent the dream, as ‘in the highest degree improbable’, and thought it came ‘by an extraordinary inspiration of God’. Quarles notes the irony: the judge is warned that he will answer for his judgment.

vv.h: But they shouted all the louder, “Crucify Him!”
b: Peter later told the people of Jerusalem: ‘You rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you’ (Acts 3:14). He added, ‘I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders’ (Acts 3:17).

vv.h: he took water and washed his hands before the crowd. “I am innocent of this man’s blood,” he said
b: The BSB footnote notes that the BYZ and TR editions read ‘this righteous blood’. Calvin: ‘how could a few drops of water wash away the stain of a crime which no satisfaction of any kind could obliterate?’ Wesley: hand-washing ‘was a custom frequently used among the heathens as well as among the Jews, in token of innocency.’ Quarles quotes Chrysostom, who called Pilate ‘extremely cowardly and weak’.

vv.h: His blood be on us and on our children!
b: The Catholic Catechism notes that this was ‘a formula for ratifying a judicial sentence’ and that responsibility cannot be extended ‘to other Jews of different times and places, based merely on the crowd’s cry’ (597). Quarles: ‘This, in no way, justifies the hateful labeling of all Jewish people as “Christ-killers”’. See Different readings.

vv.h: So Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified
b: Isaiah wrote of the Servant: ‘He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed’ (Isaiah 53:5).

27.diff: ‘His blood be on us and on our children’. For centuries this verse was used to blame the Jewish people as a whole for Jesus’ death, and to justify contempt and violence against them. Christian churches today widely reject that reading. The Catholic Church, quoting the Second Vatican Council, teaches that ‘neither all Jews indiscriminately at that time, nor Jews today, can be charged with the crimes committed during his Passion’, and that ‘all sinners were the authors of Christ’s Passion’ (Catechism 597–598). Quarles, writing as an evangelical, says the verse ‘in no way’ justifies calling Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’; the crowd did not speak for all Jews, and Jesus’ first followers were almost all Jews themselves. Interpreters differ on what Matthew meant by ‘our children’. Many, including Quarles, link it with Jesus’ warnings of judgment on ‘this generation’ and the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 (23:35–36). That does not mean God rejected the Jewish people: Paul insists that ‘God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew’ (Romans 11:2), and the Catechism, quoting Vatican II, says ‘the Jews should not be spoken of as rejected or accursed as if this followed from holy Scripture’ (597). Some read ‘our children’ more simply as the crowd’s emphatic acceptance of responsibility. Quarles also notes the irony that Jesus’ blood, poured out ‘for the forgiveness of sins’ (26:28), is the very thing that can cleanse those who shed it. Older Protestant commentators, including Calvin and Wesley, read the cry as a curse that fell on the whole nation; churches in their own traditions now reject that reading. Calvin’s general lesson still stands: ‘how carefully we ought to guard against headlong rashness in all our judgments’.

b: Matthew, Mark and John all mention a custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast (27:15; Mark 15:6; John 18:39). No other ancient source mentions it, as the Lexham Bible Dictionary notes, so it cannot be checked from outside the Bible, and some scholars doubt it on that ground. Quarles points to a possible hint in the Mishnah, which allows a Passover lamb to be killed for someone who has been promised release from prison (Pesahim 8:6).

In some ancient copies of Matthew the prisoner is called ‘Jesus Barabbas’ (27:16–17), and two modern Greek editions (SBL and NA) print it that way, as the BSB footnote says. ‘Barabbas’ means ‘son of the father’. If that reading is original, Pilate’s question is sharper still: which Jesus do you want?

b: The exchange of Barabbas for Jesus pictures what Peter wrote: ‘Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God’ (1 Peter 3:18). Paul: ‘God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God’ (2 Corinthians 5:21).
On the cross Jesus prayed, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34). At Pentecost thousands in the same city repented and were baptised (Acts 2:36–41).

How has 27:25 been misused in history, and why is that reading wrong?
Barabbas went free while Jesus was condemned. How does that picture help you understand what Jesus did for you?

27.ctx: See the note on Mark 15:16. A soldier’s scarlet cloak served as the mock royal robe.
27.mean: The soldiers strip Jesus, put a scarlet robe on him, a crown of thorns on his head and a staff in his hand, kneel and mock: ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ They spit on him and beat him, then lead him away to crucify him.
27.big: The true King is crowned with thorns.

b: Christian tradition since the Middle Ages placed the trial at the Antonia Fortress beside the temple, and visitors are still shown a paved area under the Sisters of Zion convent there. Archaeologists now date that pavement to the 2nd century AD, after Jesus’ time.

Most scholars now think Pilate stayed at Herod’s former palace on the western hill when he came to Jerusalem, and that this is the ‘Praetorium’ (Mark 15:16). Josephus says a later governor, Florus, set up his judgment seat there. The exact spot is not certain.
